summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468 in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal, ; , took the sample for analysis to the Central Food Laboratory and reported that it was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kajus. The Food Inspector reported that the sample contained a large quantity of Kaju powder which had been used as an ingredient of offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The respondent was prosecuted for an offence under Section 7 read and section 16 read with Section 16 of ' the Act. The trial court acquitted the respondent but convicted him on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove the ingredients of section 2(1)(f) of the Act as the sample did not conform to the standard or purity prescribed by the rule, and therefore the High Court was in error in holding that the offence under s.7 read with s.16 of the 'Act was proved beyond doubt. The State preferred an appeal against acquittal before the High court which allowed the respondent 's revision petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Corporation that (i) the Food Inspector had reported that there was no evidence to show that the lal mirchi powder was either worm or infested and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section2(1) (f); (ii) the High Courts were wrong in its inter pretation of section 11 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The true meaning of section II(1), as it stood at the relevant time, is that the word 'filthy ' has been used in a wide sense and includes all forms of food which are capable of being consumed or intended to be consumed by human beings; (iii) the expression 'domicile ' has not been defined in the Act but has been defined as meaning any form of food. [473B C] 2. The word 'adulterated ' is used in contradistinction with 'false, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or because it is insect or infestation on account of any other cause. To fall under that sub clause an article of food must be unfit for human consumption because it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgrusting or decomposed animal or dised animal or animal substance being insect and infested, (iv) the more proof of the whole or any part of the article being "filty, put burnt, disadusting" rotten. [474D E] 3. The expression 'fine ' has to be read disjunctively and not conjunctively. If the phrase is to be construed disjunctively, the more evidence of the entire or any portion of the Article being "False", disgonding, decomited or disated animal or animals is insoluble or in parts of any such filthy, putsrid, Disgust, disedulfust, rotorten, diseased or animal substances or vegetable substances or is institu tion on account thereof. [476F G] 4. The High Court had clearly wrong in pretation the section 2 (ia) (c) of that Act. [477A B] 5. Section 2(i)(f), as interpreted by this Court, is a correct statement of the law. It would be sufficient if the word "falter" is read disjunctiveally and not disjunctively. The more proof must be of the part or any whole of the articles being "ffilted, disorted, putated, disagusted, decomposing or animal". [473C D] 6. The words "fine" in section 2 are capable only of two meanings: (i).

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order. He was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The appeal to the Sessions Judge failed. In revision, the High Court set aside his conviction on the ground that he was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case could not be drawn against him. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. He had stored foodgrains for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution. [901 B] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , followed. (2) In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shows to have been granted to him. The presumption under para 3(2) could not he drawn against the appellant because of the exemption allowed agriculturists enjoy. [951 C] Manipur Revenue Administration vs Nila Chander Singh, A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1216, followed. In the instant case, there was nothing inherently wrong with that evidence. The total circumstances in the case show that the appellant was in fact carrying on agricultural ,operations. He executed a number lease deeds produced and proved by oral evidence that he had stored food for sale. [953 G] Manipur Government vs M/s Nila Chand Singh, I.L.R., approved.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the respondent. The tenancy was determined by a notice to quit served upon him on 24th December, 1924 and he became a tenant from month to month under the provisions of section 116 Transfer of Property Act. The suit was decreed in his favour but the High Court held that the defendant was a mere monthly tenant and not a tenant in respect of the premises in suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the notice served upon the respondent by reason of payment of rent to the Receiver in the years 1925 and 1926 after the expiry of the second yearly lease, which happened on 7th December 1926, was a valid notice to terminate the tenancy and (2) the suit was, in fact one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease. Held:(1) that the notice terminating the tenancy was not one of termination of tenancy but one for payment of arrears of rent. The notice served by the respondent on 24rd December, 1926, did not terminate the lease and consequently a tenancy from month till its inception in 1924 could not be created by the two payments of rent, inasmuch as the Receiver had no authority to receive them. (2)(a) The suit for ejectment was based upon the terms of the Kabuliyat executed by the defendant on 24.12.1924, and the lease was for building purposes. It was a tenancy for one year from 1st January, 1926 and after the expiration thereof in 1926, such acceptance amounted to payment of rents again in 1926. (b) The High Court was wrong in holding that the tenancy of the defendant wag one month from month and on the expiry Of that period, it was a lease from month upto date under section 116 of Transfer of property Act.

The appellants, who were the assessees in the appeals before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of section 137 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Full Bench of the High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the assessment records of an assessee filed before the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964 were immune from production in a court of law by a judicial order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the repeal of section 138(1)(b) of the 1961 Act by Act V of 1964, there is no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production of documents filed by an assessee during the assessment proceedings before an Income tax Officer after April l, 1964. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finality attached to an order of the Commissioner under section 138 (1)(a) has no relevance to the exercise of powers by a court to summoning the production or documents in a case pending before it. [564B] 2. Section 137(1) (b) does not affect the powers of the courts to summon production of any document in a proceeding pending before the Court when the court, by a Judicial order requires the production thereof without the approval of the commissioner of Income Tax. The consequence which has been attached to the order of Commissioner under Section 138(i)(b), is that it cannot be called in question in any court of Law by a person other than a court. [565F] 3. The effect of introduction of section 59 B by Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1960 is that the finality attached thereto should be produced in a Court of law before the court when the income Tax authorities after the repeal are sought to be furnished with information asked for in respect of that assessment only and his decision in this behalf shall be final. [567A] 4. The position is well settled that the effect of section 6 of the General Clauses Act as well as Section 138 (i)(a), is not to confer any power on the court to call for production of the documents filed before it, but to compel the production and inspection of the same. [568D E] 5. In the instant case, the finality which has already been attached by the Commissioner of Income tax to the orders of the incometax authorities after March 1,1964 is not in dispute. The final order of assessment records are immune from being produced in any Court of Law. Had the legislature intended that no document from the assessment record of an assesee should be produce in a Civil Court on being summoned by it without the permission of the Commis sioner of Incometax, it would have said so in Section 138 of the Act itself. [569E] 6. The procedure which has to be followed before the Commissioner can summon the documents and examine them is not open to question in a civil Court. [563D E; 564A] 7. The decision in the instant cases cannot be treated as final and conclusive. It is not necessary that the Commissioner should have asked for the production by the assessee before the assessment authorities after he had already issued the summons for their production. [560E F] 8. The power of the court under Section 137 of 1961 Act to summon a production of document in any proceeding pending on the date when the Incometax Authorities are sought, is subject to the veto powers of a Commissioner of income tax. It would have been open to the Commissioner to summon such documents and take such other steps as he may think fit for ensuring that the production before him is not hampered or hampered by any person in the course of his business. [562F G] 9. The Court cannot be oblivious of the fact that the legislature has used the word 'may ' in Section 137 to mean 'shall '. It must be interpreted in a manner which would advance the object and purpose of the statute.

A Hindu widow, who had attained puberty and lived with her husband for the celebration of a marriage could receive a gift in respect of her minor wife even though she was not in marzulmautma. The father made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. In the present case there is a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammotty could have made a declaration of gift and taken possession on behalf of his wife who had lived with him for the perpetration of the marriage. The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's minor son when the father was alive without delivery of possession to Se inaba, is a matter which must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In order that a gift may be made by a person who has no guardian of his property in existence, it must be shown that he had taken all reasonable steps for the purpose of satisfying himself about the true nature and character of the gift and that even if there was any such step taken by him, the gift would not have been complete under Muhammadan law. The rule laid down in the case of Kadar Bux vs Kadar Prasad, (1928) L.R. 58 I.A. 54, relied on. In a case where a gift by a grandfather to his minor grandsons when the mother was alive, without delivery possession to the father, was held to be invalid. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decision of the courts below and restored that of the trial court. Held, that the gift by the husband to his wife could not be said to have been completed under Muhammadans law and it was not necessary for him to obtain a declaration from the father that he took all reasonable means for satisfying himself as regards the true character of his gift. The gift was complete under Mohammedan Law and it would not be correct to say that by handing over the deed to his mother in law, the donee could not have made any declaration of transfer or taken possession of the property.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administra tion and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions in the State. The Act provided that the Commissioner shall have power to determine audit fees payable by a religious institution or any other person authorised by him. Section 76(2) provided that no order passed under section 100 shall be made unless the Commissioner has been given an opportunity of being heard. The appellants who were members of the Hindu Religious Endowments Board, Madras and the respondent, who was the Secretary of the Board of Trustees of the temple filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that no rules had been framed under section100 of the Madras Act and therefore the demand for levy of contribution was Premature. The High Court upheld the plea on the grounds that no Rules had been made under section 101 of the impugned Act and, therefore, the demand was not a fee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the Commissioner may not under section 76(1) provide for imposing a flat rate of audit fee on religious institutions governed by the provisions of the act; (ii) the rules framed under the Act are not ultra vires the State Legislature and (iii) the levy of the fee is without jurisdiction. HELD: The High Courts have not committed any error in holding that there was no reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services were to be rendered. [924 B] H. C. Sen vs The State of Madras, ; , followed.

The appellant, a public servant, was charged with having committed an offence under section 7(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case against him was that he had demanded illegal gratification from his employees for doing so and that he did not pay any heed to them. He was prosecuted and convicted by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appeal filed under section 19(1), of the Act, against an order of dismissal passed by a bench of the High Court, is maintainable; (ii) the notice issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, is not appealable under section 20 of the said Act; and (iii) the proceeding initiated under section 18 of the was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appeal must be dismissed as being incompetent. [509B] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court ; , referred to. 2. An appeal would lie as a matter of right from any kind of order made by the High court merely initiating the proceeding by issuance of a notice. But there are no observations by this Court nor on the facts of that case there can be any, to show that an appeal would not lie to this court under section19 from an order issuing the notice. [ 512D] Barakanta Misra vs Orissa State, ; , followed. Baradikanta Mishra 's case, , referred (2) In the instant case, the High COurt held that no appeal lies to this Curt under section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against an interlocutory order passed by the Single Judge. The appellant was not called upon to show cause against the proposed contemner in response to the notice and if he appeared before the High Curt and asked it to drop the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section20 of the . [510E F] Bargakanta Kumar Mishra vs State, , followed (3) The appellant 's right to appeal is not an absolute one. It is neither possible nor advisable to make an exhaustive list of the orders of this Court or of a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Court. An order merely initiating proceedings without anything further does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right under section, 19.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for having committed an offence under section 6(1 A) of the Indian Telegraphy Act, 1885. The trial court acquitted him but on appeal the High Court convicted him and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave it was contended that section 6 (1 A), as amended by the Amending Act of 1952, saved the operation of the amendments that had been inserted in the Act of 1933 by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1952, and therefore, neither the conviction nor the sentence thereunder could be sustained. Held, that section 4 Of the 1952 Act was repealed by the 1952 amending Act of 1949 and it was not necessary to refer to a case of a later amendment of an earlier Act which had been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later Act. The words "any Central Act" in section 6 A were comprehensive enough to take in a wireless transmitter, the section did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. Held further that the words "in any other case with a fine which may extend to one thousand rupees" in the present case, were comprehensive and redundant. The language used in the amending Act was merely a device to give effect to the intention of the legislature in passing the said Act. It could not be said that section 5 Of the 1953 Act had no application to a situation like the present where an earlier statute was repealed or referred by the repealing Act of 1948, and it could not therefore be said to have been amended.

The appellant and the respondents were the Shebaits of a debutter estate. The properties in question were sold by the Shebait of the debutter Estate to one M, who was the son of the deceased Shebait. The respondents filed two applications under section 36(6)(a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned therein and passing of new instalment decrees in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The appellant contended that the court Receiver had no jurisdiction to reopen the two decrees, because he was not a benamidar for another person. Held, that the Court Receiver could not be said to have acted mala fide on behalf of another person in respect of the decree and there was no proof of the sale being in fact benami for another. The court Receiver could be said not to have exercised his jurisdiction under section 35(2) (c) of Act. Section 36(2)(a), as it stood at the relevant time, provided that where a decree had been reopened by the Court, it was incumbent upon the court to give a direction in such cases that if there was default in the payment of any one of the instalments the properties restored to the judgment debtor under clause (e) would be put back into the possession of the same either by themselves or through Oramba Sundari. The decree holders could not therefore be said, to have taken advantage of the provisions contained in section 36 (2).

The appellant, who was the decree holder of a certain property in Bombay, executed a deed of assignment in favour of the respondents. The deed provided that the assignee of the subject matter of the suit would be entitled to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as if the application were made by such decree holder. The appellant contended (1) that the deed of assign was not executed by Habib & Sons, by Habib and Sons within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16, and (2) that, the assignee could not claim to be transferees of the decree by assignment in writing within the definition of Order 21, r. 16. Held:(i) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that while a transfer or an agree ment to transfer a decree that may be passed in future, may be executed in the like manner and under the same condition as if it were made before the transfer was passed. The normal rule is that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name it stands and r. 10 enables him to do so while Rule 16 enables him of the beneficial interest in the decree to execute the decree passed in favour o f Habib & sons, as claimed by the appellant. (ii)The words "any other sufficient reason" in Order XXI rule 16 mean that a judgment can be made only by one person in his own name and not by any assignment in the writing within meaning of the word 'decree holder '. The ordinary rule is applicable to all cases where there is no decree in existence at the time of the assignment and this position was conceded by Dixit, J., and by the Division Bench when they observed that on a strict construc tion of Order XXII, r 16, the Court should have scrutinised the application as required by Order XXI Rule 17(1) and if it was found that the applicant could claim to he a transferee of the judgment, which was subsequently obtained by Habib Sons, the court should have examined the application in the light of the provisions of Order XX, rule 15.

The respondent, a contractor in the business of fabricating steel doors, shesas and other goods, entered into a contract for "sale of windows" and to promote sales of windows. The contract provided that the price of the windows would be fixed at Rs. 1,000 per month. The respondent 's case was that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sale of its manufactured goods, undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that service, and that the prices of the window, doors and windows in a specified building were taxable. The Deputy Excise Commissioner held that from the acceptance of the tender two contracts resulted in sales of goods, and the price was taxable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the terms of the contract showed that the transaction was one for sale of chattels, and not the charge for service, that the respondent ' carried on the business as fabricating and selling window and doors in a certain specified building, and had made no separate charge for the service, was taxable under section 7(1) (d), (e) and (g). HELD : The contract was a works contract. It was not a sale of property but only an incident of service. [507 D] In the present case the specifications of the doors and window leaves were set out in the contract. The contracts, therefore, did not amount to "fix" the windows but to "sale" the parties to the contract as understood by them. The essential ingredient of a contract is that the property must be sold as chattel. [511 D] The contract may be for work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials used in the execution of the works for a price; it may be a contract of sale, but it may not be a sale for work in which the use of materials is incidental or incidental to the execution. [607 E F] In a building contract the property in the goods used does not pass to the other party to the contracts as movable property. The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be customarily or normally as incidental to, the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. If the windows were not properly "fixed" the contract would not be complete and the Respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [ 507 B] The essential ingredients of a transaction are : (1) that the thing in the property is something more than what is actually done; (2) that it must be something more; (3) that there must be an intention to do something which the buyer would not have done; and (4) that in the case of a building, the property cannot pass to another party.

The respondent was charged with offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B of the Indian Penal code. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been made a party to any conspiracy to cheat or defraud the complainant. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the State that the High Court should have quashed the charge framed against Raj Kumar Agarwalla and Shankar Lal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The report lodged by Ram Avtar is lodged by him after his suspicion had been aroused. It would hardly warrant an inference that Raj Kumar was too a party lo any conspiracy or defraud. [279 D] The High Court was right in quashing the charge against Raj K Agarwalla. [280 E] The report which was lodged by the respondent was lodged later on subsequent to the lodging of the report. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar Aggarwalla and Shanker Lal, when the latter brought one Saheb Jaman Khan alongwith Shankar Lal, who was present along with Shanker Lal when the former brought one Sahib Jamanwal Khan alongwith Shanker Lal was brought in a taxi and demanded the price of the said goods. Ram Avtar was also told that this transaction would fetch him a profit of Rs. 3200/ . The part attributed to Ram Avtar could not be said to have been made out against Raj Rani. [281 G] The respondent was a party who had been introduced to him by Ram Kumar Agarwal but he was present alongwith Shankerlal when the earlier brought one person was brought into a taxi. He was present at the scene only subsequent to lodging of report. That circumstance, as pointed out by the High court, would hardly justify an inference, that Raj Kurriya was a witness to any fraud or cheat Ram Avtar.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultan Battery area in the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways, has alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 and claims reliefs of mandamus to the Union of India for implementing the reports of the Kunzru Wanchoo, Sikri and Sikri Committees appointed by the Union Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The petitioner alleged violation in the counter affidavit that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and has pointed out that the accident had taken place due to defective bridges. Disposing of the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. The quality of service should improve. [233B] 1.2 The quality and the reasonableness of the restrictions imposed by the Railway Administration must be judged in the light of the well recognised principles of law and order, that is, the standard of efficiency and effectiveness of the administration of the Railways. [234C D] 2.1 It is true that the Railway Board has been entrusted with the responsibility of ensuring safety of the railway property and their property, but this does not mean that accidents have to be avoided or attack on the persons of the passengers or prying on their property has to stop. But it is equally the obligation of the Union to improve the established means of communication in this country. [235D] 2:2 The common men ' mode of transportation closely connected With the free playing of this right should be that accidents had to be prevented, attack on persons of passengers and prying upon their property have to stop; and this means that accidents having to be provided and this mean that accident has to be stopped. [236F] 3:3 The quality or reasonableness of restrictions imposed must be determined in the context of the facts and circumstances of each case. [237A B] 4:4 In the instant case, the common man is a menace to the system. It is undoubtedly the obligation to improve. the established mean of communication. [238C D; 239B] 5.1 There is no doubt that the common men have the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession. But this means the accidents have not to be frustrated, attackon the persons in the passengers, prying them on their own property has a material bearing policy regarding priorities. [239D E] 2(a) The quality, of service must be maintained. It may be that accident had to he avoided or challenged on the person of the passenger and p carrying on his property has no significance. [240F] (b) There is nothing in the Railways Act which would justify the inference that the principle of efficiency or effectiveness of transport services should not apply to the instant cases. The nature of the service must vary from case to case. It cannot be said that the principles of efficiency, effectiveness and effectiveness are too high to be applied to all cases. [241G H] (c) There was no justification for the argument that the petitioner had been denied some of the assertions of the respondent. This is a matter which should have been taken into consideration in the writ petition.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. They filed applications for restoration under section 20 of the Jagirs Abolition Act, 1950 on May 6, 1961. The application was dismissed by the Revenue Tribunal on April 9 and April 20, 1961, but the appeals were received by them on April 10 and April 19, 1961 and the restitution applications were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958. The appellants contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals had been received by the appellants on April 8 and April 9, 1961 they were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for condonation of delay were barred by limitation. Held: (i) Under Regulation 19(1), it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there is default in the appearance of the appellants and to record its decision regarding the merits of the appeal. The words "decide it on merits" are used in Regulation 20, which is a general provision and must be construed strictly. (ii) Under the scheme of the Regulations it is apparent that under Regulation 19, it is permissible for the Tribunal, to dismiss any appeal for default or non prosecution if the party concerned has appeared either in person or through his agent or lawyer. It is also open to a Tribunal in such a case to hear the respondent to hear and decide it on merit even though no final decision on merits under Regulation 20 is recorded. (iii) Under regulation 19(2), it was open to an Tribunal to reject an appeal if there was default on the part of the appellant or through its agent or pleader. It was also open, therefore, to the tribunal in such cases to hear it and decide on merits. The Tribunal has no power to dismiss a non prosecution even though the appellants did not appear either in persons or through their agent or counsel. (iv) Under section 20(1) of the Abolition Act the Tribunal is empowered to dismiss the appeal for failure to record the decision even though such decision may be final and conclusive. The expression "decides it on the merits" in Regulation 19 must mean that the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide an appeal on merit. If any of the parties was absent on the date of hearing, either preliminary or final, either final or final and the appeal or application was heard and declared ex parte, the party against whom such decision is made may apply for restoration of the same or application, as the case may be, and if the respondent satisfies the Tribunal that he had no notice of the date on which the hearing, etc. was adjourned, either provisional or final the appeal and the application was considered and declared to be invalid. (v) Under r. 20(2) the legislative authority uses the words " Decide it" on merits in Regulation 21. The use of the word "deciding it" in the context of section 20 is not decisive and conclusive and cannot be challenged as an appeal against the order dismissing the appeal, because, under the scheme, the Tribunal can dismiss an application for non defence but it must record its findings regarding the merit of the case. (vi) Under cl. (b), the legislative function has to be performed by a Tribunal consisting of three members, one member being nominated by the President and two other members being elected by the members of the Tribunal. The word "Court" in section 20 means a court of law. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the applications made by the appellant were barred under r. 21. (vii) Under sub cl. 2, the legislative power conferred on the Tribunal by section 20 must be exercised by the Tribunal consisting only of three member and not more than one member. The Legislature has used the words 'decide them on merits ' in Regulation 22.

The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of certain properties on the ground that the property belonged to the family of the respondent and was dedicated to it by the Panch Faisla. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that there was no absolute dedication of the village Telibandha to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy and that the appellant had failed to prove that the said property was given in full proprietary interest in the village. On appeal, the High court agreed with the Trial Court that dedication by the appellant to the deity was absolutely dedicated to the Temple of Shri Ramsaran Lal and his brothers. The High Court also held that there were no absolute endowment of the temple by the P Faishava Award of 1896. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had erred in holding that the dedication made by the panch Faisli Award of the award was not proved and that it was not a case of absolute dedication. HELD: (i) The High Courts were right in holding on a construction of paragraph 2 of the Panchana Award that by the award, after "including mouzas Basi Basus Basasus bah sametkiyat" that by this Award the property was dedicated absolutely to the idol of Shri Ramachandra Swamy and Ramsarar Lal. [440 C] (ii) The fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that only a portion of the income was intended to be used and that supports the presumption arising from the use of the word " haqquq samet" that absolute interest was being given to Ramsarun Lal. The fact, therefore, that Ramsarana Lal used to credit the income from Teli clobandha to his brothers is not established. [420 D] (iii) The evidence on record shows that the pazhava award of 1895 was made by a Panch Fai Panchayati who was in possession of it as the manager and trustee of the said temple. It may well be that Ram saran Lal used only to credit income from the Teli taluq to the Gharu Khata which was maintained for the general expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication into an absolute dedication in favour of Shri Rama Swamy.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and Chairman, Action Committee of the Lucknow Bar. The High Court issued notices to five persons on the ground that they committed contempt of court. The appellants filed a petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the Allahabad High Court for quashing the said notice. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that since the resolution was passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 1, he is guilty of contumacious conduct and the High Court gave the ground on that they were responsible for the passing of the resolution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts committed contempt in not taking action against them because they had committed contempt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proceedings before the High court were not maintainable. [603 B] 2. The charge against the appellants was serious and the appellants were guilty of criminal contempt. They were rightly convicted by the High. Court. [ 602 C D] 3. The contempt of Court is a matter of regret that the Chief Justice is acting in the dis pute of administrative power under clause 14 of the U.P. High Courts ' Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a most partisan manner under the influence of Allahabad Bar. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. [ 603 B C] 4. The Chief Justice was acting in a very unfair manner under influence of the Allahabad Bar and he was guilty of contempt. [600 D E] 5. The conduct of the appellant individually was considered only "indiscreet" by it. The word 'contrary ' used in clause 14 is not used to denote that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. It was a matter for regret that lawyers were the custodians of civilisation lawyers. [599 G] 6. The language used by the appellants clearly showed that the conduct of appellants individually was consider ed only "Indiscreet". The High Courts have found the guilty of 'criminal contempt. There is no gainsaying that the appellants individually were prominent members of Avadh Bar, should have embarked on the path of vilifying the Chief justice of this Court and that they do not want to be over sensitive in the matter keeping in mind the surrounding circumstances in which the contu macious act was committed by them. [503 B C; 603 A] 7. The words 'indiscretion ' used by them were significant. It could not be said that the Judges of the High COurt did not intend to punish those who were prominent member of the collieries Bar. They had also acted in a highly irregular manner under tact. [597 D E]. 8. The appellant was guilty for contumacious and dishonest conduct of which he had committed criminal contempt of the Court. He should have been punished with imprisonment for the contumacious act of which the High Curt did. [596 A B] 9. The offence of contempt is a serious one. It cannot be said to be deliberate or intentional. It must be deliberate, deliberate and dishonest. It may be that the guilty has not committed any criminal breach. In the instant case, the appellants had acted in most unfair manner. They did not commit any criminal act with the intention of committing it. [595 B C]. 10. The acts of the respondents were not bona fide or they were actuated by malice. Their conduct was quite unnatural. It would be a matter to regret that their conduct was not so deliberate and it should not have been passed in that manner. [525 G H] 11. The respondents had acted with dignity and discipline. They could not have intended to punish them for the alleged contumacious acts of which they were guilty. [625 C D].

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 were entered into a joint family partition of movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators. The arbitrators made an award on 28th of November, 1983 in favour of the appellants Nos 5, 6 and 7. On or about 11th of June, 1977 an unregistered deed of agreement between the four brothers being the appellants No. 5,6 and 7 was entered into regarding partition of joint movable and immoveable properties and a dispute arose as to whether the arbitrators had jurisdiction to decide the question of limitation for registration of the award. The Sub Registrar held that during the subsistence of the interim injunction on the arbitrators ' application to return back the award to the Sub Registrar for registration, the appellants could not take back the same for presenting the same before the SubRegistrar for registration. On 24th of July, 1984 the Sub Judge passed an order returning the award back to the sub judge holding that it was the Registrar and not the Sub judge who could determine the question as to limitation for the registration of his award. On appeal by the appellants, the Sub Court set aside the aforesaid order of the SubJudge and directed return of the arbitration application to the arbitrator. The sub Judge held that the limitation for filing the award had already expired and that the Sub court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. The High Court also ordered return of arbitration application and did not direct return of it. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Nos. 5 6 and 8 that the order made by the Sub Justice Registrar on 24th July,1984 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under section 15 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The two legal maxims the law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform and an act of the Court shall prejudice no man would apply with full vigour in the facts of this case and if that is the position then the award as it has failed to get registered as the law required. [122D] 2. The maxim "actus curiae neminem gravabit" does not require a man, who cannot possibly do that what he cannot obviously perform and does an act which he can possibly perform. It is only when the court finds that the act of a party has been done by the person who has acted in good faith or due to some mistake or oversight that he could not possibly perform his duties. [123E] 3. The principle laid out under section 16 of the is that the award should be registered as a decree and that it can be executed only when there is an error or omission on the part of the court in performing its duty. It does not mean that the court has no jurisdiction but only when it finds that there has been an error, omission or failure on the face of the record. [124F] 4. The expression "actuarial" used in section 15 is wide enough to include all cases where the award is made by a Court without jurisdiction and not otherwise. It cannot be said that he has failed in getting the award registered as required by law. [125B C] 5. The words "actuary" occurring in section 16 are wide enough in their amplitude to include within its sweep all cases of an award made by court without jurisdiction. [126D E] 6. The word "actual" is not defined in the Code but it has been used in a wide sense and includes all cases which have a bearing on the question whether the award has been made by or under authority of law. It must be construed in its popular sense, that is to say, from an act or omission of the party who has done it. [127E] 7.

The appellant was a sub tenant of the respondent. The respondent gave notice to the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, terminating the tenancy of the appellant on the ground that he had sublet the premises to the sub tenants and they were merely licensees of the landlord; but the appellant was not given a notice as required by section 15 Of the Act. The respondents filed an application for ejectment under section 14(1) (e) on the grounds, inter alia, that the tenancy was a new tenancy and not a continuation of the old and that the sub tenant had no right to sublet the property. Held, that section 13 (1)(a) of Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates Act, 1948, which prohibited the Controller from enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15(1), as amended by Act XLIII of 1956, was void because of the provisions of section 15 of the Act and for which the Act itself provided a remedy. The appellant had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 13 of the said Act could not be said to have the same effect. The agreement did not create any interest in the property, but only created an interest in it. The provisions of the two sections were intended to protect private rights of the landlords and unless there was a specific provision in the Act which prohibited sub letting, the tenant could not evict the appellant. The right of the sub lessee to sue for ejectment on the basis of a contractual tenancy was not dependent upon any statutory provision or statutory provision. The protection of private rights was available only when the landlord had waived it as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant to sub let and consequently he could not eject the appellant from the premises under section 15.

The respondents, who were the examinees of the appellant Board, challenged the validity of the notification dated August 31, 1990 issued by the State Government under section 3(1) of the Maharashtra Recognition and Prevention of Unfair Trade Practices Act, 1970. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the notification was not supported by any evidence or material on record and that it was not a case of no evidence and the conclusions reached were based on records. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conclusion reached by the Education Committee that the fabrication of the mark sheets was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardian is based on the evidence on record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [798C D] 1.2 In dealing with question as to whether the conclusion reached in the course of an enquiry was justified, the Court has no jurisdiction to quash the order merely on the ground that different view could possibly be taken on the materials available on the record. The finding recorded by the Inspection Committee that fabrication of ' mosques ' mark sheets at the instance of either of the examinee or their parents or guardians is amply borne out from the record, is based upon the evidence and facts recorded.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellants had demanded a bribe from Madan Lal and that he had given him Rs. 500 as a bribe. The trial court acquitted the appellants but on appeal the High Court convicted them under section 161 Indian Penal code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for three years. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the intention of the legislature was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that it could come into play only when there is no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. The words "in the discharge of his official duty" in section 5 of the Act are wide enough to include within their scope all kinds of acts done by public servants. The word " gratification" in the definition of "public servant" in that clause means any money or reward given or promised or agreed to be given, whether as a motive or reward for doing an official act or not. The expression " gratification ' in section 21 of the Penal Code is wide enough and includes all acts done in pursuance of a legal contract. It is not necessary that every person who has received or agrees to accept any gratification should have accepted it for himself or for any other person on his behalf. The definition of public servant in section 2(d) of that Act is wide and comprehensive and covers all acts which are done by a person in the discharge or discharge of official duty, whether such act is done by him or by others with the consent or approval of the Government or by some other person. It does not include any act done by any public servant for the purpose of section 5 and it can come into operation only when the question is whether the accused person has accepted or agreed in the course of his employment as a public officer. The fact that the accused was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe for hushing up the case does not stand on any different footing from that of the other appellants.

The appellant Bank was a surety for the respondent. The surety executed two promissory notes one of which was in favour of the Bank and another by the principal debtor. In the mortgage bond, the surety was given a personal guarantee of Rs. 30,000/ . The surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The respondent 's surety was not discharged from its liability under guarantee. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal creditor pledging oil tins and as the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledge of goods given by the respondent, the security was wholly discharged. In this appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of guarantee, the respondent was not discharge from his obligation under the bond and the personal guarantee was discharged. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the creditor having lost one security, namely, pledge of the goods and the Personal guarantee of the surety, the sureties were discharged to the extent of the value of security and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the bond was discharged to that extent of value of the security. [922D] 2. The appellant Bank is entitled to restitution. The security must be held to have been lost on account of negligence of the creditor Bank. But if the creditor loses or without the consent of the principal, he loses or cannot without the permission of the sureties parts with the security, the Security would not be discharged even if it is found that a creditor has taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by the Principal debtor which itself may be a consideration for the surety. [ 923G H] 3. The bond must be construed in its ordinary sense, but it is not possible to accept the argument that section 141 would not apply unless there is some special provision in the Act or any other law providing for restitution. [947A B] 4. In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the debtor had taken more at one security from the principal and without the knowledge of the bank that the principal debt was lost on the account of the negligence of creditor Bank, yet the surety would not he discharged even though it is held proved that security of pledged goods was lost. [948C] 5. The guarantee given by a surety is in the nature of a personal bond and is discharged to his extent of its value. In such a situation clause (a) of the explanation would be attracted and an application for restitution will have to be made to the Court of first instance i.e. the Court Of first instance, i. e.

The appellant was the son of Amritrao patel, who had been in possession of certain lands as tenants. He claimed that he was entitled to a share in the "patelki inam" lands and that the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government. The High Court held that (1) the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for services rendered by patel 's office to the working patel from the Rokade family, irrespective of whether he performs the service or not; and (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume the lands in 1941 and regrant them to respondent No. 1. Held, that the appellant could only succeed if he established that he had a right to a "p Patelki inam". The grant was made by the Ruler of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 applied. The grant in suit was made on behalf of the patel family and it was not open to Government to resume it. The appellant could not succeed if respondent No 1 had a share therein. The grants were not a service grant and no question of a claim of a share arose against Government even though the lands are shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag. Held further, that in view of the provisions contained in the Pendki inam Rules, the appellant was entitled only to his share in "pGujaratki inam", and not to the "Patel" inam lands. The words "published" in r. 5(1) of the Rules clearly indicate that the " patel inam land" were subject to orders passed by the revenue authority in respect of the matters mentioned therein, and no right was given to a member of the family of the public rendering patel service.

The appellant, a Cutchi Memon, was the owner of certain properties. He died in 1938 leaving behind his widow and two daughters. The appellant 's son filed a suit for partition and possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the rules of Hindu law were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other Cutchi Corons settled in Madras, and therefore, when a cutchi Memons had settled down in Madras they should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the rules applicable to Cutchi memons governed succession and inheritance according to Hindu law, including rules as to joint family property, were consistently followed and applied in Madras; (ii) the High Courts had erred in holding that the rule of Hindu Law applicable to cutchi Coros was not applicable to the case. HELD : (i). The High Court was right in its view that the appellant could not be said to have adopted as part of their customary law the Hindu law and that the Rules of Hindu 'law were consistently applied to Cutch Memons settled by them as customary law in matters of property, inheritance and succession according to the rule. [234 B C] (ii). The rules of the Hindu Law relating to succession and succession are generally accepted by Hindu Law as applicable to Hindus according to their personal law. But the rules do not apply to cutch Memon. They are governed by the Mahomedan law. In the present case, the High court was right that the cutchi memes had acquired by birth in the property held by their father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act. [235 C D] (iii) The rules do no apply to the facts of this case. They were governed by Mahomedan law and therefore when a Cutch Coros had settled in Bombay, they should have been governed by Hindu law as to Joint family property.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types of fabrics. They manufacture the said fabrics, which is obtained at an intermediate stage. The yarn which is produced at an intermediary stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to payment of excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The appellants are also liable to pay excise duty on the yarn which was obtained at the intermediate stage and thereafter further processed in an integrated process for weaving the said fabric into fabrics. The respondents filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the amendment made by the Finance Act, 1982. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the retrospective effect given to section S 1 will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as no specification has been made by Collector of such place or premises appurtenant thereto, the provision of deemed removal with regard to the commodity produced at the final stage and consumed or utilised in the continuous process of manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of the excisable goods. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Explanation to rule 9(1) admits only one interpretation and that is that the specification has to be made by tho Collector of the place of manufacture and also any premises appurtenant to such premises or the production of the manufactured goods. [707C] 2. Rule 9(i) does not contain any definition of "place of removal" but provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place, which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf whether for consumption, export or manufacture or sale of any other commodity in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such place. [ 705E] 3. The expression 'place of manufacture ' has been defined in section 2(h) of the Finance act 1982 as meaning "place" and includes any premises which are used for the manufacture of any goods whether for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. The definition is inclusive and not exhaustive. It is clear from the Explanation to Rule 9 that the expression 'date of manufacture" has been given a wider connotation so as to include within its ambit all excisable goods whether produced, cured or manufactured by the assessee. [079G H; 705A] 4. The word 'place ' in the explanation to rule9(1), does not mean any place where the goods are produced, cure or manufactured but any premises attached thereto. In other words, if the place is not the place where excisable goods are manufactured, cured, or manufactured, but any property appurtenant thereto. [807C D] 5. The question whether a commodity obtained at intermediate stage of an integrated operation of manufacture is liable to excise duty under section 3 of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944 has been considered by this Court in several decisions. In the instant case, the appellants are liable to be paid excise duty as they have not manufactured any excisable goods at the factory gate.

The petitioner filed a suit for declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 was illegal and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the Hearing Authority appointed under section 69 D of the Act from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme. The trial court passed an order directing the Hearing authority to approve the scheme and to approve it by 21st May, 1979. The petitioner filed an appeal before the Additional District Judge, Bulandshahr against the said order. The Additional District judge allowed the appeal holding that the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. The Civil Judge further held that the petition was not tenable because the jurisdiction to try the suit had been expressly barred. In the revision petition before the High Court, the petitioner contended that the Civil Court was not competent to entertain and decide the suit as it was filed beyond the period of limitation prescribed under section 60 C.P .C. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a State Government (the Hearing Authority) under section 70 D of U. P. Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining a hearing authority from proceeding With the hearing of the case and exercising its statutory functions. [539C] 2. The procedure laid down for preparation of the scheme by the State Transport Undertaking to operate road transport services to the exclusion, complete or partial of other persons is not expressly barred under section 63 D of Act. The provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the Motor Vehicles Rules are mandatory and do not require that before a scheme becomes final it must be published in the official Gazette. [544E] 3. The rules also provide for the particulars to be incorporated in the scheme which are framed by the authority which had the power to publish it and that the authority who was hearing the case under section68 D of 'the Act had the powers to do so. All such objections relating to the manner in which objections or representations can be filed under section 67 D of , were within the exclusive jurisdiction of an authority competent to approve a scheme either with or without modification. [546F G] 4. The power to issue permits only in accordance with the scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68D of the . It is not disputed that the Scheme had been duly published under Section 68 C. The powers of the hearing authority under section 129 D of are exclusive in nature and it was not open for a civil Court to issue any order of restraint restraining the hearing Authority from proceedingwith the hearing. [547G] 5. The High Court was right in declining to stay further proceedings in the suit.

The appellant was charged with the offence of attempting to commit an offence under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that on August 29, 1963 at about 9 P.M. when Roshan Lal and his wife were returning home from their house, the appellant asked them to come to the house of N. Russel Nathaniel and his two wife and a gold ring from Roshan Lal. When Roshan Lal came there he asked him to bring Rs. 5001/ or in case of money he would pay it to Roshan Lal who told him that he would give it to the appellant. The appellant refused to do so. On being questioned by the appellant, the Special Judge convicted him under section 161 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of sanction in the present case fulfils the requirements of section 6 of the Act. [184 D] (ii) The appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a police officer and extorted money from Russel, Nathanutty Nathan Keralaiel and the wife and also a gold biscuits from Roshanlal. The order did not disclose that there was any abuse of official position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case it was manifest that the appellant grossly abused his position by a police Officer and extorting money from Shasel N.athaniel. [185 E] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the order of the sanction did not satisfy the requirements Of section 6.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 161 I.P.C., and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, for having accepted an illegal gratification as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions to obtain pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act II of 1947. The appellant contended that he was not liable to be prosecuted on the evidence adduced by him, and that the sanction accorded by him was not a valid one. Held, that the sanctioning authority had no jurisdiction to accord sanction to the prosecution of the appellant. It was competent for the sanctioning officer to accord his sanction if he considered it necessary in the interests of justice. The sanction itself did not require that the papers placed before him should be relevant to the only question before him whether he should or should not accord his consent to the proceedings of the case. The sanctioning authority could not, therefore, refuse to accord its sanction on the ground that the appellant was not bound to make an application for the prosecution. It is true that he did not call for any record in connection with the matter from his office nor did he call for the connected claim cases or other records in connection therewith from his offices but it does not require him to do so. The sanctioned authority could, therefore refuse to grant its sanction if the facts and circumstances of the particular case justify the granting of a certificate. But where the sanctioning authorities refused to accord their sanction on that ground, the sanctioning order was not valid.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the building was bona fide required by him for demolition and reconstruction. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate authority, in revision, set aside the order of eviction. On appeal, the High Court held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction was satisfied. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that since the interest of the remainder man may be prejudiced, he must also have a life interest in the premises in question and that it is inherent in such a life interests that it was not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14(1)(b) as grounds for eviction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Rent Controller has rightly held that there is no possibility or objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man. [275 G] (2) In a litigation between the landlord and others who are not his tenants under the Act, the interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would per se, per se be not bona fide. [274 B C] (3) The question whether the landlord has only a life estate or right to enjoy the property for his life depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case, the parties are governed by the provisions of the Act. They have been living together as husband and wife. There is no question of any objection from them. The tenants are not their tenants under section 14 (1)(a) (b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1950.

The appellant, a grove holder of certain trees in the land, was put up for sale by the respondent decree holder. The appellant filed an execution proceeding against the judgment debtor and the decree holder, inter alia, was passed ex parte. The judgment debtor filed objections to the execution proceedings contending that the decree was not executable as it had become final under section 18 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The executing court dismissed the objection holding that the appellant was entitled to get compensation for trees in groves and grove land. On appeal by certificate the High Court set aside the judgment and decrees of the executing court and remanded the execution case to the executing Court for fresh disposal according to law. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the judgment debtors had no right to execute the decree against them, (ii) the executing Judge had erred in holding that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(h) of the Act in the State of Uttar Pradesh, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari and Land Reform Act, 1951; and (iii) the appellant had not been able to prove that the judgment debt was due to him. HELD: The appeal must be allowed. (i). The High Court was in error in holding on the basis of the definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 2(13), that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section 4(h). [538 B] (ii). The expression "intermediary" in section 18(1)(a) of Act means an intermediary holding or occupied by an intermediary as such. It includes a grove and land. [539 C D] (iii). The definition of 'intermediaries ' in section 3 (13) is not exhaustive but only covers trees, standing uncut trees, which are parts of groves, and grove lands. [438 F G] (iv) The High court was right in holding the appellant to be a complete answer to any further execution proceedings in respect of any part of bhumidhari right.

The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC for causing the death of Suku and causing grievous injuries to him. The trial court convicted them under Section 326/149 IPC and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court acquitted all the accused persons of the charge under Section 325/149 I.P.C. but maintained their conviction under Section 324/149. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the prosecution case was not supported by any evidence; (2) the injuries on the deceased were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the deceased and (3) the medical evidence did not support the prosecution version. On behalf of respondents, it was submitted that the injuries caused by the appellants were not enough in the normal course of the nature to causes death of a person. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention to cause the death is clear on this aspect of the case and it is not possible to say that the injury inflicted by the first appellant with the chopper was inflicted with the intention to causing the murder of Suhu. [92B] 2.1 It is well settled that in cases where there are two or more persons who have been charged for an offence, the prosecution has to prove that the accused had caused the death by such injuries as were likely to cause their death. In other words, it is only when the prosecution proves that the person who caused the injury was guilty of an offence of murder that he can be convicted of the substantive offence under section 302 I. P.C., even if there are more than one persons charged with the offence of causing such bodily injuries as are likely to result in death of that person. [93D E] 2:2. The nature and type of weapons used by the accused in the commission of the crime is not relevant for sustaining a conviction under section 304 Part I, IPC. It is only after the prosecution establishes that the act was done with the knowledge that it was likely to be caused by such bodily injury as is sufficient in its ordinary course to cause his death that an offence can be said to have been committed. [94F G] 3:3. The accused persons were charged for the substantive offences of murder under section 326/34 I.PC. and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for two years each. Their conviction under sections 325/34 IPC is maintained but without the aid of Section 149 I. PC. [95B] 4:4.

The assessee, a non resident Indian Company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69 on cash basis. The Income Tax Officer treated the said amount as cash receipt in respect of the said royalty amount and determined the same at Rs. 1,20,000/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash on cash and since it did not actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax was payable by it. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The method of accounting regularly adopted by an assessee is binding upon the department; on that basis it maintains its accounts on cash foundation or mercantile basis. [105G] 1.2 In the instant case, the assessee did not say that the method of accountancy adopted by it for all its income was on cash. It merely credited to the account of the asses see in its books the Books of the Indian Company which was not aware of the true state of affairs relating to the assessee 's accounts. [106G] 2.1 In the case of a nonresident assessee like the petitioner clause (a) cannot apply. The method adopted by the assessee for accounting years is really irrelevant. [107H; 108A] 2:2. The fact that the Indian company made a credit entry in the account books of the appellant does not amount to receipt of income by the asses sees. The mere fact that it maintained its accounts in U.K. in the Books on mercantile basis or mercantile system did not amount receipt of any income by assessee. [108B] 2 :3. In the circumstances, the method adopted for accounting regularly in respect o the said rent amount and determining the royalty amount payable to the assessee in its Books of Indian Company does amount to its receipt by assessee and is accordingly taxable and that it is immaterial when it did actually receive it in UK. In this view of the matter, it must be held that in the circumstances of the case, it was necessary to express ourselves on the view expressed by the High court that in case of non resident assessee like appellant clause (b) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains their accounts on mercantile system or mercantile method. [109C D] 2(a) The fact of the method followed by the Indian assessee for the relevant accounting years was really irrelevant and did not affect its validity. [111D] (b). In the present case, there is no dispute that the assessee had received the royalty in U K.K., but merely crediting to the accounts of the respondent in its book the books of Indian company does amount lo its receipt. The assessee has not shown that it was maintaining any particular method of accounts regularly in regard to the said payment. [112E] (c) In the absence of any evidence on record, it cannot be held to be a case where the assessee maintained its account on mercantile method or mercantile mode. [114F] (d) The High Court was right in holding that the amount of royalty should be taxed only on its actual receipt under section 5(2)(b).

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but on appeal by special leave, Held, that the evidence of the approver is no corroboration of the accomplice 's story which would be sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder. The conviction of the first accused upon a confession made by him to whom Deoba had made a confession was not illegal. The fact that the knife was got prepared by the appellant did not affect his reliability and it was unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. The evidence of an accomplice is no corroborated in material particulars and qua each accused. It cannot be doubted that under section 114, illustration (b) of the Indian Penal Code, an accomplice may not be said to be a rule of practice but it has been used for the purpose of corroboration of his approver 's testimony alone and so far as the appellant is concerned he was entitled to rely upon his evidence in material respects. The statement of the accused recorded under section 342 Of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, that he had made the confession of his participation in the crime, cannot be called in aid in the circumstances of this case. The Court would not ordinarily interfere with an order of conviction on the uncorroborated testimony of an approver unless it is shown that there was some evidence to corroborate him. In the present case the High Court was right in holding that the appellant could not be convicted on the sole testimony of the witness and that his evidence was corroborated by other independent corroboration of each accused 's version which would lead to the conviction of both the appellant and the High court.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case against him was that he took a bribe from one of his employees and gave it to the appellant who was a public servant. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been able to prove that he was a "public servant" within the meaning of section 21(12) of 'the Act. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the prosecution for taking a bribe under section 161 Indian Penal Code did not require sanction under section 197 of the Code and acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the conviction of the accused could not be sustained because he was not acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the Act, (ii) the High court had erred in holding that the appellant was a person performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of the Works Manager who was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21 (9) of that Act and therefore a public servants within the definition of that section could not he deemed to be a "Public servant" under the Act. HELD: (i)(a) The appellant was an Officer in the 'service or pay ' of the Government and he was attached to the office of the Superintendent of the Salt Department. He was, therefore, an officer within the protection of section 2(12), Indian Penal code. [695 B] (b) The words "public servants" include every officer in a service or paid of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or a Government company as defined under section 617 of the . All members, officers and servants of the Board shall be deemed to have been, when acting or purported to act, in pursuance thereof any of these provisions of this Act. [795 C D] (c) The word "public" in section 2 (12) means a person who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. Therefore, an "officer in the services or pay" of the corporation as defined by section 21, cl. (12), of the Indian Penal ' Code and therefore, a public officer within that definition could not claim any immunity from prosecution under section 6(2). [696 D E] (d) The expression "public service" in the definition is used to denote a service which is rendered or to be rendered by an officer. Therefore a person taking a gratification can not be said to be in the employment of the State Government within the terms of section 1(12).

The appellant was convicted for contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 1,000/ . The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him in respect of contravention of el. 3. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) is within the powers conferred by sub section (1) of section 3 of Defence of India Rules 1962; that the rule is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act and therefore, the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of forfeiture. HELD: The High court was right in holding that r 141(1) is not within the power conferred by section 3(1 ) of the Defence of lndia Act. [273 G] The rule is within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the defence of India Act and must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [274 C D] In the instant case, r. 142(2), which prescribes various matters on which rules can be made, but this is without prejudice to the generality of the powers given by sub s.(1) Of section 3. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provided for proof of judicial proceedings in the fact published.

The appellant was convicted by the Additional District Magistrate, Allahabad for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Sessions Judge had erred in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant had been rightly convicted by him. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) There is no evidence on record to show that the deceased was not in any manner concerned with the deep seated enmity between the appellant Sia Ram and his associates.
