The fact that the young Dubey had a standing but of 2 years in the District when he was supposed to have appeared for the complainant in the particular case, does not necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous designous. [87 B C] (2) There are several infirmities in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses which make it highly doubtful whether the appellant was present at the time when he made the attempt to test the claim of Om Prakash Dubey in order to hold that he was not known to the witnesses and therefore he should be put up for identification in an identification parade. [88 C D] (3) The High court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. [89 E F] (4) There were serious infirmities from which the conclusion of the High Court could be drawn that the evidence was not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the appellant.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him under section 303, read with sections 149 and 147 of the said Code but convicted him under sections 302 read and 34 of that Code. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that when three of the four named accused were acquitted either on the ground that one or more of them might have participated in the commission of the offence, the result would be that they did not conjointly act with each other and that the High Court should not convict only one of the accused on the basis of constructive liability. HELD : (i) The judgment of the High court cannot stand. It is well settled that when two or more persons are acquitted either by the trial court or even by the High, Court in appeal, the acquittal of some of them does not automatically follow unless there is a single observation to indicate that other persons also participated in it. [683 E] (ii) The fact that one of several named accused was acquitted by the Sessions Judge and the other by the State did not mean that they acted conjointly with each others, would not necessarily displace the charge under section 149 of the Code. [684 G H] In such cases either the trial Court or even the High Courts in appeal may be able to come to the conclusion that the acquittal was read in the context of the whole judgment, it would be clear that the learned judges meant to hold that other than the acquitted accused conjointly acted with the convicted accused. [685 B C] (iii) The effect of the acquittal is that they do not conjointally act with the accused. There is no evidence in this regard. It may also be that the charge disclosed only persons; it may also contain other evidence, which may disclose the existence of named or unnamed persons other than those who composed the unlawful assembly but who have not been identified and so have not even been identified.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron and steel products, was granted licence for import of iron & steel products under the Import Trade Control Policy, 1981. The licensing authority issued import licence No. 29598 for Rs.20, 12,729 in favour of M/s Industrial Cable India Ltd., Rajpura. On 11th May, 1983, the licensing authority transferred the same in favour o f M/S Industrial CableIndia Ltd., Patiala. The licence holder transferred the goods in favour Of M/ s Industrial Cable Corporation Limited. The petitioner filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution before the Central Administrative Tribunal, which was dismissed. In the writ petition filed by the petitioner under Article 226 of the Constitu tion, it was contended that the licensing authori ty had no jurisdiction to pass the order permitting clearance and loading of the goods for exportation under section 51 of the . The petitioner 's writ petition challenging the validity of the order of the Central Adminis tration was dismissed by this Court. In appeal to this Court, it is contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the licensing au thority had no jurisdic tion to pass an order permitting the clearance and the loading of goods for exportsation under Section 51; (ii) the licence holder had transferred the said goods in his favour by transferring the same to M/o Industrial Cable Industries Ltd., Lahore, which is a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. Dismissing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order permitting exportation and loading are not valid and legal. [628D] 2.1 The petitioner has no fundamental right to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. Whenever a person complains and claims that there is a violation of law, it does not automatically involve breach of fundamental right.

The appellants were the sons of one of the brothers who was a minor. The father died in 1947 leaving behind his widow and two daughters, three daughters and four daughters. The son of the first appellant was the eldest son of his second wife. The first appellant filed a suit for partition of joint family property on the ground that the debt was avyavaharika and therefore the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the debts of their father. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed it. In appeal by special leave, Held, that where the pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and the pious duty of the sons continues and consequently there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property, the right, title and interest of the defaulter must be regarded as one of his personal rights and interest. The liability of a father who is a managing director and who draws a salary or remuneration incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyabaharika debt as it cannot be termed as repugnant to good morals. A Hindu widow has no right, inter vivos, to make an offer to discharge her debts of her father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality. The pious obligation of the son continues and there is only a difference between the mode and enjoyment of property. In the present case the pious duties of the father continued and consequently the sons did not pass to the auction purchaser.

The petitioners, who were lawyers and police officers in the Delhi Administration, filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the orders of the Delhi Adminis tration. The Delhi Administration passed an order on 29th June, 1988 directing that the Committee should submit a report recommending suspension of the D.C.P. Kiran Bedi. The petitioners challenged the said order by filing Writ Petitions in this Court contending that the D .C. P. Kiran Bali and Jinder Singh S.I.S. Police Post Tis Hazari were not competent to investigate into the conduct of any person and that the petitioners had no locus standi to file the writ petitions. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1. The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 B of the Act before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined at the beginning of the inquiry. [517B] 2.1 In the instant case, the Committee had clearly observed that it had to examine the conduct and other material before the Committee in asking them not to be cross examined till the end of the enquiry. The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section 8 C of the . [518D E] 2:2.1 The Committee shall examine its witnesses first as provided by rule 5(5)(a) of the Rules referred to above, and then give evidence before the committee. If three persons referred to in that sub rule are examined at that end of inquiry there is no justifiable reason to deny the same treatment to the petitioners. [525G] 2 :3. The D.P., Special Branch, D.S., Tiswal, Delhi Administration and its police officers shall fully cooperate with the Committee so that the committee may complete its work as early as possible.

The petitioners, who were registered dealers under the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, challenged the validity of the provisions of the Rajasthan Goods and Goods Tax Taxation Rules, 1959. The petitioners contended that the Act was ultra vires the provisions Of section 3 of the Act as it imposed a tax on fares and freights being a different tax, the notification issued thereunder did not violate article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the notification in question was valid and the petitioners were entitled to challenge it. The tax was levied under the Entry and the notification was valid. The provisions of section 3 were not ultra vires. The Act was not discriminatory or violative of article 14. The notification issued under section 8 did not offend article 14 Of the Constitution, because it imposed an unreasonable restriction on the freedom of trade guaranteed by article 301 of the constitution. The State of Rajasthan vs Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga and Others, ; , followed. The word 'tax ' in section 3 is wide enough to include taxes on passengers and goods and not on freights. The words 'taxes on fares ' and freight ' are used in the sense of tax on passengers or goods and they are not confined only to taxes on goods but also to taxes which do not cease to be a tax. The expression 'tax on passengers ' is wide in its amplitude and includes all taxes on the passengers and property. The levy of tax under section 3, therefore, was not unconstitutional. The proviso to sub section (3) of section S, in terms, speaks of the charge of the tax "in respect of all passengers or Goods" but only lays down what the amount of freight or freight is measured by the fares and the freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory. The fact that the tax is levied on passengers does not cease merely because the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan. The taxation on passengers is a Union subject, and is not available to the State Legislature.

The appellant workman was dismissed from service by the management of the respondent company. The Labour Court directed reinstatement with full back wages, permitting him to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The appellant challenged the award in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The only question is whether the Labour Court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back salary. [567B] 2.1 The Labour court has directed reinstatement without back wages for the limited purpose of arriving at a just decision on the question whether the workmen should be awarded full back wage. This Court does not envisage this Court to be a regular Court of appeal but it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia, against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. [568C D] Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman, Calcutta, ; , referred to. 2.2 The Labour Courts have no discretion in the matter of awarding full or partial back wages and the relief of reinstatement must follow. It is no more open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the workman continues to be in service. [569D] 2:3 The only limited question is what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full and partial back wage, attempted to re open the controversy concluded by the order of this Court while granting limited leave that the retrenchment was inevitable in view of the mounting losses and persistent power shedding. It may well be that in appropriate cases the Court may, in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry direct scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too. [570E F] 2(a) The only point for determination is whether even where reinstatement is found to be an appro priate relief, what should he the guiding consideration for awarding Full or partial return. This question has become final. [571F G] (b) In appropriate cases, the Court can exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where Awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or discloses such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this court or disclose such other special or special circumstance which merit considered consideration of the Court or disclosed such otherspecial or special reasons which merit consider consideration of that Court or disclosesuch other exceptional and special circumstances. [575G H] (c) In the instant case, the only question for determination was whether the appellant should be granted full back compensation in the aggregate amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ . The Labour Judge has also awarded full wages to the workman on its finding that the retrenched workmen were entitled to the relief. Once leave against relief of reinstate is declined, the employer could not shirk his responsibility of paying the wages which the workman had been deprived of by illegal or invalid action of the employer.

The accused was charged with murder of his wife Churi deceased. The prosecution case was that the accused, in a murder case, had come at the residence of the Naib Tehsildar and the police was wanted there. The accused stated that he was with Churi, deceased in the house during the day but at 6 p.m. when the deceased was going to his house, the accused came to the house of the deceased and enquired from him about the father of the boy and the son of the accused. The deceased told the Head Constable that the latter had come to see the film at Kotkbai on that evening and that he would not have insisted upon Churi. The police then went to the residence and reported the matter to the police. The statement was recorded by the Magistrate and was signed by the accused as well as by the Sub Inspector of Police. The Sessions Judge convicted the accused under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the evidence on record established beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the husband of the appellant had been recovered after the accused had visited the house and made a report to the Police regarding the father 's father of his boy and that the deceased had gone to see film at the house when she was murdered. HELD: The evidence on the record establishes beyond any reasonable doubt that there was nothing to show that the police were aware of the murder of Churi by the appellant. [319 C] In the present case, the prosecution has established beyond all manner of doubts that the body of Chururi deceased was recovered after he had visited his house and that it is difficult to believe that he should have insisted on Churi for staying with him without the child. The evidence shows that the appellant was aware of murder of the wife of Chula deceased before the visit of the respondent to the place of occurrence. [20 E] In view of the fact that the relations between the accused and the deceased were strained, it is not possible to hold that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond any doubt that a person who was responsible for the murder was murdered by the act of the appel lant. The circumstances referred to above clearly point to the conclusion that it was the accused who suspected fide the fidelity of Chri deceased and believed that Joginder had been born to her as a result of her adulterous conduct.

The plaintiff, who was the owner of certain properties in Calcutta, instituted a suit against the defendants for recovery of the amount due and payable by them to the defendants on the basis that each of the three mortgagors was liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The plaintiff 's remedy is under section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82 of the Indian Contract Act and not under section 93 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [181 D] (2) The rule that a suit shall be instituted in a mortgage suit shall not apply to a mortgage decree is well settled. In the present case, the plaintiff had asked for a mortgage money decree up to a limit of Rs. 40,000 and also made an application under section 90 of the Act praying for a declaration that the properties mentioned in Schedule A were liable to be attached to the mortgage amount. The suit was therefore not maintainable. [182 F G] (3) The suit must fail on the ground that the relief claimed by the plaintiff was in substance asked for by the defendants and the suit must be dismissed. [183 E] (4) The declaration of charge standing by itself is superfluous Order XXXIV, r. 2(1) does require that the decree in a suit should be drawn up in the usual way affording either the right to redeem the whole of the balance of the property to which a subrogee would be entitled under the Transfer Act.

The appellants applied for the posts of Assistant Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. The selection was to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and in the interview. The appellants were selected and appointed as Asstt. Engineer (Civil). The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by way of special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violationof the judgment of this court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R. 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State o.P. & Ors, [1988], Sup.S.C., 657. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. The Rules do not contemplate any such practice being followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. [495B C] Ashok Kumar & Ors vs State Of Haryana & Anr., ; , referred to. 1.2 In view thereof, the appellants were bound to be selected on the strength of marks secured by them in interview calculated on the method of converting the same to 15% of the total marks and in case the marks for interview were kept at 15%, they would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants. [498D E] Ashok Yadav & Anr. vs The State of Punjab & Ors.; , ; , followed. 1(a) The Rules, therefore, are clearly violative of the judgment in Ashok Yadav and Ors. v State of Rajasthan & Ors.[1988] Supp. S C.R., 657 and the candidates selected have already joined the posts, and there was no allegation that any malafides on the matter. [594B D] (b) The appellants had not approached the High Courts for redress in time. They were vigilant in making selections according to the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for all the last 16 years and There is no allegations of any malafide in the matters of the said selections. Therefore, the selections made by the Selection Committee are clearly violation of this judgment. [500E F] Ashoka Yadav & ors. vs Govt. of Haryana and Ors., ; ; , applied.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial; (ii) the prosecution has relied upon the allegation of conspiracy, confession and other features to establish the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector; (iii) the High Court had erred in holding that the confession was voluntary and that it could be used as substantive evidence. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of the co accused cannot be treated as substantive piece of evidence against the coaccused persons in a trial. [413D] 2.1 In dealing with a case against an accused person, the court cannot start with the con fession of a Co accused person; it must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the other evidence. [414E] 2(i) The High court was right in holding the appellants guilty of conspiracy. [408F] (ii). The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadananda at the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. The mere fact that some other person was present when the deceased was taken into custody did not make any difference. [416F G] 2.(iii) The evidence of the prosecution is highly interested in the success of the case and it is difficult to accept the criticism of counsel for the appellant that if the wife had been called she would not have supported the version that she met her husband P.W.4 on that day, the story of bribing the jail officials has been introduced. [411A] 3.(iv) The prosecution case that the appellants were regularly visiting Sadanand at the Jail for meeting Sadanand is true and it cannot be said that they had an interview with his wife that day. It is a fact that a set of witnesses who, according to the prosecution, were present when Yadav was taken in custody following the incident, had not spoken about any confession. [409E] 4(v) The mere circumstance that some others were present at the Police Station would not make it unsafe to rely upon the evidence of such a witness. It may be that if there is no direct evidence against all the accused persons, the Court cannot start from the con struction of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegationof conspiracy cannot be accepted.

The appellants, who were working as clerks in the clerical and subordinate staff of the respondent company, were charged with having committed misconduct in respect of a number of years. The Tribunal found that there was no evidence to show that the total wage packet of the appellants had been manipulated or that the workmen had not been paid wages for any particular period. It also found that the Tribunal had taken into account the fact that the appellants were working in different departments and had made comparison for clerical and supervisory staff, and that the tribunal had adopted a uniform method of fixing the same scale of dearness allowance as it was applicable to comparable concerns. The High Court on appeal held that the Industrial Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowance with respect to clerical and superior staff and that there were different scales of dearness allowances prevalent in comparable concerns, and therefore, compared with the total pay packet of comparable concerns it took into account. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had not specifically considered what the total wages packet of each category of factory workmen was necessarily higher than 15 months ' which was usual so far as manufacturing concerns are concerned. [375 B] (ii) The Industrial Tribunal has gone wrong on the basis that there are different scales in the region and in fixing the scale of wages and, therefore, comparison had to be made with comparable concerns in other industries. [376 C D] (iii) The principle which is applicable to industrial adjudication is that the employer should have regard to all relevant circumstances including the nature of the industry, its capacity to pay and dearness allowances, the extent of financial loss caused by misconduct in case of dismissal for misconduct, the number of days during which the workman was in service.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa, executed a mortgage deed in favour of the mortgagees and for placing the mortgaged property in his name. The mortgagees applied to the Mamlatdar alleging that the mortgaged properties had redeemed themselves by virtue of the provisions of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, and prayed for the cancellation of the transfer in favour Of the mortgagees. The appellants pleaded that the Rajinama was a complete relinquishment of their interest and that as Shiddppa alone was the registered occupant, the Raj inama was valid and binding on him. Held, that the appellants were entitled to redeem the mortgage by adverse possession. The Rajinamama was not a complete transfer of title from the mortgagors to the mortgagees, and therefore, operated upon the entire occupancy and amounted to a relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers Shiddaiah and Annappa. The words "all occupants other than the registered occupants" in section 74(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, are wide enough to include all persons who have no interest in the occupancy. The word "occupant" in the context of section 73(1), is not used in the sense of a tenant or a person who has no interest therein but only as a tenant. It is true that where there are more occupants than one, the notice of relinquishment must be given by the registered owner; but that does not mean that in the absence of any specific pleading and cogent proof, that a notice of relinquished must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than tho registered occupant. The concluding paragraph of section clearly recognises that a relinquishment may be in favour only of more persons than one. It does not imply that in case of an occupancy the notice must necessarily have been given by registered occupant; but it is not necessary that the occupant should give such a notice without reference to the other occupants so as to effect their interest in his occupancy.

The respondent assessee was a dealer in carbon paper. The Sales Tax Officer, Kanpur, assessed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to March 31, 1967 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment order but the revision petition filed by the respondent was dismissed by the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. In a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution the High Court quashed the levy on carbon paper at 6%, and directed the Sales tax Officer to assess the turnover at the rate of 5% prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates of 7%. The appellant contended that carbon paper does not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon is a part of the typewriter so as to attract tax as per entry 18 of the Second Schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper generally understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing writing or printing or for drawing on or for packing or for preparing or for making or for fixing, on or in respect of, or for bringing on or covering the walls etc. does not mean that carbon papers are to be considered in the light of what is meant by a typewriter in the sense that people conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [838 D E] 1.2 The word ' paper ' has not been defined either in the U.P. Sales Tax , 1948 or in the Act, and as such, it has to be given the meaning which it has in ordinary parlance. Paper, as understood in common parlance, is the paper which is use for printing, writing or packing purposes. [861 E] 2.1 In popular parlance, the word "paper" is understood as a sub struction which is employed for printing and writing. It is not necessary that carbon sheets should be used for printing or writing. The word "popular sense" in common legal parlance means paper which has been used for carrying out printing, publishing etc. [862 G] 2(a) In popular law the word is understood to mean paper other than hand made paper. It may not be possible to out any type of paper but it may not he possible to mention in any type. The mere use of the word paper as a particular word would not make it a part and parcel of a typewriter so as not to attract sales tax as contemplated by entry 18. [863 G] (b) In the instant case, carbon papers were not paper as envisaged by Entry 2 of the aforesaid Notification. Just as aviation petrol is not a part or aero plane nor a diesel is a component of a motor car which is ordinarily used for the printing, printing etc.

The appellant was employed by the respondents 1 to 4 as clerks in a sugar mill at Bulandshahr. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager of the appellant Mills ordered the transfer of the respondents I to 4 from the appellant Mill to the new factory and the respondents were employed by them on that date. The appellant filed an application before the Labour Appellate Tribunal under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act for setting aside the order of the management and directing reinstatement of the workers in the new mill. The Tribunal held that the management had no right to transfer the respondents to any of its concerns in any place and the question that arose was whether in the circumstances of each case the transfer from one concern to another was valid or amounted to victimization. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant was not entitled to a writ under article 226 of the Constitution as it did not give rise to any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Act and that the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside the finding of the State Industrial Tribunal. The only connection between the two is in th identity of ownership and, but for it one has nothing to do with the other. It was not a condition of service of the employees either express or implied that the employer had the right to transferred them to another place where the business of the employer in the same line was situated unless there was an express condition to the contrary in the contract of employment. The essential distinction between that case and the present one is that the parties have the inherent right to the transfer their employees to another, place where they chooses to start (4) a business subsequent to the date of their employment. It does not prevent the employer from transferring an employee to another. The employer in such a case has the inherent power to transfer his employee to any place where he chooses to commence. The distinction between cases where there is no express condition and the facts of each particular case are different. In the present case, the two factories are distinct entities situated at different places and the records clearly indicated that transfer was one of the ordinary incidents of service in the Bank. The two factories were distinct entities and the record clearly indicated the fact that transfer of one concern was one unit and the documents clearly indicated a transfer was by the management with a view togla him and that it amounted to alteration in the conditions of employment of the two concerns.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948 and its registered office was situated in Ahmedabad. The State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in the case of factories or establishments situate in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V are in force. Section 28 of the Act provides for the payment by the principal employer of a special contribution which shall be in lieu of the employer 's contribution payable under Chapter V A of the . The appellant company, a registered medical practitioner, was assessed to pay special contribution under Chapter VI A of Part V of the , on the ground that it had been rendering service for more than 12 years. The appellant 's contention was that the contribution payable by the company for the period May 31, 1969 to March 26, 1973 was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payments. The High Court held that the contributions were not a fee but a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The payment of special contribution is a fee under Chapter IV A of part V of Part VI of the Constitution and it has been so laid down in the Act. [1088G] 1.2 The nature of the contributions contemplated by Chapter VA of Part VII of the constitution is that Parliament has enacted the . In the vary nature of things, it would have been impossible for the legislature to decide in what areas and in respect of which factories the Employees ' State Insurance Corporation should be established. [1188B] 1:3 The payment made by the employer under Chapter Ill A of Chapter V of part VI of Part IV of the Constitu tion is not a tax, fee or a fee within the meaning of section 28 of Act No. 53 of 1951. [1108C D] 1 :4 The fact that the appellant had been paying special contribution to the fund known as Employees ' Insurance Fund which was to be utilised for the benefits to be given to its employees under the Act and the payment of Special contribution is entirely borne from the aforesaid fund only, does not mean that the payment made under Chapter III A ofPart V of that Constitution is a tax. [1019G] 2:1 The fact of payment of contribution directed to be made by employer under chapter V A is no bar to its being treated as a fee or fee in respect thereof. It is pursuant to the power entrusted in respect Of entries 23 and 24 of List III, of their own force, empower Parliament or the legislature of a State subject to conditions with which we are not concerned, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List llI. [1009G H] 2.2 In the instant case, the contribution was made by it under Chapter VII A of that Part V and it had also been so provided for. The fact is that the employer has not paid special contribution as a tax or fee under the provisions Act. Therefore, the special contribution was, to be viewed as a levy and its incidence is illegal as it does not contemplate the rendering of any service. [1029G; 1019A] 2 :3 In the present case, there is no dispute that services and benefits are indeed meant to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer in due course when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. The payment under Chapter Il A of this Part V is not for the benefit of the employees but for the purpose of the scheme. [1039C D, G] 2(a) The fact remains that the employers have paid special contributions to the Fund known as the Employees State Insurance Fund and are governed by the Act in respect whereof they are not required to pay any contribution under the Scheme.

The petitioners demanded regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands are of regularisation and equal pay for equal work on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as regular workers. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order of termination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there were no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they were not doing any work for a short time. Hence this special leave petition. Allowing the special leave petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of daily rated workers is purely on humanitarian grounds so far as the daily rated employees are concerned. [54G] 2.1 It is not possible to absorb the petitioners immediately as regular workmen. There being no vacancies available or work in the Establishment for absorption, they cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purelyon humanitarian grounds. The principles of regularisation do not arise. [55A B] 2:2. In spite of the clear findings supported by evidence that there are no vacancies/ work available to the establishment, for absorption the petitioners, and that for some time they have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work for them, they are not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay. [655B C] 3:3. The doctrine of regularisation does not arise because the daily wages is paid to regular workmen only when the daily wage workman is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed in spite thereof or not absorbed. [557D E] 4.2. It is well settled that regularisation of a daily rated worker does not make any distinction between the daily wager and regular workmen and that it is only when a regular workman arises only when he is doing work as a regular worker that he is entitled to be absorbed against the same or not, even if there are vacancies available for the regular workmen in spite there being an vacancy available. [53F G] 3. The concept of regularisation has no application to the case of the petitioner and it cannot be said that the dailyised workmen have been continuously on rolls for more than some time. [57A B; F] 4:4. In view of the offer made by respondent No. 2 in his counter affidavit, the respondents are directed to consider the claim of regularisation in accordance with law and pass appropriate orders within a period of three months from the date of receipt of this order. [586B C].

The appellants purchased certain lands from the respondent No. 1 and sold them to the respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4. The respondent No, 1 filed a suit for recovery of possession of the properties in execution of the decree obtained by the appellants against the appellants claiming title to the property. The appellants contended that when the sale was effected in execution, the mortgage decree obtained against the appellant would be binding on them as full owner and the sale in court auction in execution would be illegal. Held: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the transaction was not a real one but only a portion containing the description of the parties and the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by them under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act. (ii) The appellants had failed to prove that the property conveyed by exhibit 12(i) was not the full owner of the property under the lease granted in 1928, by reason of the entry in the revenue registers which they obtained under exhibit 12 (i). (iii) The words "as full owner" in section 41 were not printed but only the portion containing description of parties and co heirs. The High court was right when it held that the sale under exhibit 13(i), though executed by a co heir, was not conclusive as to the nature of the transaction and the question whether the co heir had consented to put him forward as the ostensible owner of his property with the result that they were estopped therefrom from questioning its validity. (iv) The fact that the appellants did not raise any specific ground touching their right to this share, nor was any argument addressed to the High Court on this point could not be accepted as frivolous.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the provisions of sections 207A and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with, and as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. The omission was curable by reference to section 537 of the code, as no case of prejudice has been made out. The word "shall" occurring both in sub section (4) of section 207A is not mandatory but only directory, because an omission by a police officer to fully comply with the provisions Of section 173 should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. The words "shall", occurring in sub sections 3 and 4 of section 209A are mandatory but not directory, and only because an addition by a Police officer to comply with those provisions of section 173(4) is not directory. The use of the word "may" in sub s.(4) Of section 207 A in order to simplify the procedure in respect of inquiries leading upto a Sessions trial and at the same time to safeguard the interests of accused persons by enjoining upon police officers concerned and magistrates before whom such proceedings are brought, to see that all the documents necessary to give the accused persons all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. The fact that the accused got the necessary copies of the depositions of the witnesses in the Sessions Court before they were produced before the Magistrate, does not affect the validity of the trial unless it is shown that the omission was due to a complete failure of justice.

The respondent Municipality was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling oil. The appellant, a manufacturer of oil, used to manufacture oil from outside the State of Bombay. It applied for permission to use the oil for the purpose of manufacturing it. The permission was granted subject to certain conditions. The respondent Municipality filed an application before the Special Officer under section 153A of the Act for permission for the use of the oil in a factory and the appellant objected that the respondent Municipality had no jurisdiction to deal with it. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that if the requisition in the notice was objected to, the objection included not only the allegation of the existence of a nuisance which was purely a matter for subjective satisfaction of the Municipality but also to the direction as to the manner in which the effluent should be discharged. Held, that the scheme under section 155A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction Of the Municipality and not the existence or absence of a vacancy in terms of sub section (1) of section 153 A. The scheme under the section is to permit the Municipality if it is satisfied that a nuisance in the terms of the notice given does not deny the existence thereof. The Special Officer was bound to enquire into the dispute and make its report both as to whether a nuisance existed or not. If the existence was assumed because that was a matterfor the subjective opinion of the municipality, then it would not require a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire and report only as to what the manner therein the effluent shall be discharged and report merely as to how the discharge of the effluent in such manner as may have been previously approved by the Government and as mentioned in the notices so that rendering saline or corrupting the water of wells, tanks, ponds or other water receptacles, or prejudicially affecting the fertility of theoil in the surrounding areas may be stopped.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case was that he had purchased the scrap from someone who had no authority to do so and that the goods were not meant for use in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles seized belonged to any particular railway administration and that they were used or intended to be used in the constructions, operation and maintenance of railway. HELD: (i) The prosecution was not called upon to prove the articles belonging to a particular railway. It was only when the burden in respect of this was discharged by the prosecution that the article belonged to the railway administration that it had to establish that the properties were the property of a Railway Administration. [192 D] (ii)The prosecution was entitled to lead evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. The burden in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about identifying the marks on goods or certain peculiarity, peculiarity or importance of the articles not to he found in case of non Railway goods. [195 A B] (iii)The appellant had failed in proving that the items mentioned in his report were used for the construction operation or the maintenance of the railway.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the respondents on the ground that they had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The trial court decreed the suit and the first appellate court reversed the decree of the trial court. In second appeal, the High Court reversed the findings of the courts below and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act, introducing a clause (vii), thus, makes it clear that the heirs of the tenant of residential premises do not enjoy an estate or interest in the tenanted premises governed by the Act and also subject to the rights in favour of the respond ent created under section 13(1)(a) to (k) and other provi sions of the Act. [10F] 1.2 The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs in respect of commercial tenancies on the death of the tenants after termination of the tenancy, as has been done in the case of heirs of such tenants is not heritable on the demise of the statutory tenant and the heirs are entitled to enjoy the protection under the Act subject to their rights in the demised property governed by section 13 (1)(b) to(k). [10G H] 1:3 The mere circumstance that in a particular case the heirs have been evicted after termination, does not make any change in the status and legal position of the landlord. [11F G] 1 :4 In the instant case, the appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in a lease hold right of a demised premises governed under the Rajasthan Premises Tenancy Act, 1956. The tenancy rights are heritable and the successors of the appellants are entitled for enjoy ing the protection afforded to the tenants under the Rent Acts as amended from time to time. [12F] 2:1 Section 13(2) of that Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, a contractual tenant on the termination of tenancy shall continue to be in possession even after determination of his tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles him landlord to get an order or judgment for eviction is passed against him. [13F] 3:2 The appellants succeeded in September 1966 to the estate of the respondent without any hiatus and restriction on the heritable rights in their tenancy right held by them. They continued to remain in possession as on the date of the suit as statutory tenants.

The appellant Board maintained a Contributory Provident Fund in respect of its employees. The Employees Provident Fund Act, 1952 was amended by the Bihar Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1964 which came into force on 25th November 1966. Section 59 provided for the payment of interest on loans advanced to the Board and section 64 provided that where no such loan is outstanding one half of the balance shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of the State. The appellant Board was unable to pay the provident fund amount in respect thereof. The employees claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Funds Act. The Industrial Tribunal held that the Board was entitled to the benefit of the Provident Fund Scheme and directed payment of the interest on the loans. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Board that (i) the employees of the appellant were not liable to be transferred from one establishment to another; (ii) the Board had no power to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Funds to all workmen other than those who are covered by the Act and therefore it would bring about serious injustice if they were deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. HELD: (i). The employees of a company are not liable for payment of provident fund and gratuity. They are entitled to get interest on such loans. [47C] (ii). The Board is not bound to pay any Provident Fund to its employees in accordance with the provisions of the Act. It is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. The contribution to the provident Fund is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open tO the employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of payment of gratuity and provident fund can be met without undue strain on the financial condition of the employer, that burden will have to be borne by the employer. [48D E] (iii) The Board 'is not bound by the provisions contained in the Act or its rules. It has no power under the statute to extend or modify the terms of the scheme. The Board may grant such directions as it thinks fit for doing so.

The appellant wife filed a petition for maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 against the respondent husband. The Magistrate dismissed the application on the ground that the husband was impotent and unable to live with her husband merely because she refused to live in her husband. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and held that the wife having been found to be impotence for refusing to live With her husband, the appellant wife could not refuse to live at her husband 's residence. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 clearly provides that it is incumbent on the Magistrate to consider the grounds of refusal and to make an order of maintenance if he was satisfied that there was just ground for refusing not live with the husband as the one which he has in the present case, no legal effect to the legislative intent and will appear to have been given by the aforesaid decisions. [710C D] 2. The High Court was right in holding that no evidence of cruelty could be admitted in a proceeding under the section to claim maintenance from her husband even though she refused not to live. [811E F] 3. In the instant case, the ground of impotency which had been held by a number of authorities under the Hindu law or other laws is not a just ground as contemplated by the proviso for the wife 's refusal to live and the conduct of the husband from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife. [1110B] 4. The appellant wife was impatent and was unable to discharge her marital obligations, this would certainly be a just reason as contemplated under the proviso to section 125(3) for refusing the wife to live without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [1105C] 5. The husband having been granted maintenance by the Magistrate, he was not entitled to claim any maintenance from his wife. He could not have been compelled to live separately from his husband. [10D E] 6. The respondent wife had been granted a maintenance of Rs. 2,000 per month. She was unable even to maintain herself and hence she was entitled to maintenance from the husband. This would certainly amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a reasonable ground for refusal to keep her husband with a cause of action for refusing her to live as the husband, in a situation where her husband refuses to live, this will not be a proper ground for the respondent wife ' to refuse to maintain her husband and hence the wife is entitled to get maintenance from him according to his means. [611D E; G] 7. The order of Magistrate dismissing the application filed by the appellant under section 127 Cr. P.C., was set aside and the case remanded to the Magistrate for fresh disposal in accordance with law. [1210E F].

The plaintiff respondent Municipality filed a suit for declaration of its title and for possession of the suit property described in the plaint. The Trial Court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the vesting of title by the State Government in the Municipality was not intended to be vesting in its full amplitude but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the State to dispose of the land, that the State of Gujarat had no authority to transfer or assign the title to the plaintiff. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit is for possession based on title to a property and not vesting of the title itself in the municipality. [222B] 2.1 The suit was filed by the plaintiff respondent under Order 39 Rule 3 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff had also not claimed that he was formally handed over the land in question, that its right over the property was never recognised by the Union of India or the State Govern ment and that the possession was handed over by the Government of India to the State Gov ernment only on 7th July 1952 for use. [223C D] 2:2. The High Court has rightly held that the plaintiff had not shown possession of suit property within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was instituted and that he had not alleged adverse possession. [225G] 3:3. The Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January 1948 was intended to vest in its entire amplitude but meant only a vesting in it of title itself. In fact, the resolution No.37 dated 19.1.1948 was only a right or an authori ty to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of that title in the Municipal records and even in the suit they did not claim the structures as belonging to the Municipality. [226B] 4:4. The resolution No 37 dated 29th February, 1948 was merely a right to sell and take income therefrom shall be enjoyed by the Municipalities subject to the condi tions mentioned in the letter of the Government dated 10th August 1965. [227D] 5. In view of the above discussion, it is clear that what was conferred on the Municipality under Resolution 37 dated 1st January 1948 by the order of his Highness, Bhavnagar Municipality on 7.7. 1952 for " use" was only an "right or an Authori ty" to sell land as represented the Government and not a vested title in them.

The appellant was a lessee of a village who had undertaken to keep an account of its forest revenue and pay certain proportion to the Government, keeping the remainder for himself and the question arose whether such a person was an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. The Judicial Commissioner held that the appellant was not an "officer" within the definition of section 2(9), Indian Penal code but was performing the duty of a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was thus performing a public duty. He accordingly convicted him under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947. The appellant contended that he did not fall within the terms of the last portion of cl. (9) Of section 21 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as he was employed to exercise certain functions and duties in certain circumstances. Held, that an " officer" within a meaning of that term in section 21 (9), I.P.C., is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some pulice duty. The words "any person" in cl. 9 Of section 1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, are wide enough to include all persons employed to do public work and pay of the Government. The word "officer", in cl.(9) means a person who is employed to perform certain duties immediately auxiliary to those of some one who was an office or paid by Government to do private work. The expression "any other person" is not defined in the Act, but it is used in its ordinary sense in section 2 (9). The words 'any person ' and "any officer" in el. 9 of section 1 mean a person employed to discharge certain duties of another who is performing those duties immediately on his appointment. The fact that the word "office" is used as a term of employment in cl, 9 of the definition shows that it is not necessary that a person should be in the pay or pay of Government but is also performing a duty of the government and is therefore an officer of the State within the scope of section 3(1) of that Act. The High Court was right in holding that the words "an officer" were wide enough in that they meant only those persons who were employed to be paid wages or were paid by the Government to the employees of the Works Manager who were also performing the duties of a public servant within the expression "a person employed in connection with the execution of any work which is necessary for the discharge of such functions". The words used in cl., 9 Of the definition are wide and they do not include all those persons employed in the execution or pay. The mere fact that a particular person was employed in some other office does not make him an officer. The only meaning given to the word 'officer ' is that he must be in charge of the service or pay, but is certainly performing a governmental duty. It is not enough that a public officer should be entrusted with the performance or perform of some specified duties immediately and it is sufficient if he was performing a certain duty.

The Respondent, who was a tenant of the liquor shop in Punjab, filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,50,000/ from him on the ground that he had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69 under clause (c) of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The Trial Court decreed the said suit holding that the portion of the building in which the liquor shops were situated was exempt from attachment and sale under clause(ccc) and that the Respondent 's half share was exempt under clauseccc of the Proviso to sub s.(l) of Section 60 of Code of Criminal Procedure. The First Appellate Court, however, allowed the appeal holding that since the portion in which liquor shop was situated was exempted from attachment, sale and sale, the Respondent was not liable to attachment and sales in revenue recovery proceedings under the said Act. In second appeal, the High Court held that the remaining portion of a building was exempt as it related to the portion occupied by the Respondent and therefore, his half share in the property was exempt. Allowing the Appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The opening words of sub section(1) are "such attachment or sale" in the proviso refers to the attachment and sell mentioned in sub section 1 of section60 set out the properties which are not liable 'to attachment and/or sale in execution of a decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under that Act for recovery. " The opening phrase "such attached or sale", in the said proviso refers only to attachment, and sale mentioned in subsection (1), namely, sale. [848F G] 2. Section 60 sets out the property which are liable to be attached and sold in execution. The words "such attach or sale ' in the aforesaid proviso refer to the sale and the said clause refers to attachment of and sale in revenue Recovery proceedings other than in execution proceedings under any decree of civil court. [884C] 3. Section 61 sets out properties which were liable to attach and sell in execution and sale. The property, if any, which are exempt from attached and sale is not exempt from the attachment or sales in execution, of a money decree. The provisions of section 59 set out properties that are liable for attachment and sold under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. [881D] 4. Section 58 sets out all properties which may be attached or sold in the execution of the decree. It is clear from sub section 2 of section 61 that it applies only to execution of decrees of civil courts and declares what properties are liable "to attachment, or sale in any proceedings other then in execution". [849F G; 851A] 5. The language of sub s (1 ) of section 58 sets forth the properties that were liable for attached and sell. The attachment levied on and sold is also under the provisions of the said act and the sale which was notified as also under sub section 60 sets forth all properties, which were exempt from attach and sale and in execution thereof. [850C] 6. Section 59 sets out what are liable or to be sold in any proceeding other than execution of any decree. [854D E] 7. The word " attachment" is not defined in the Code. It includes attachment and selling. The expression "such property" has been used in sub s. (1). The words 'such attached ' and "sale" are wide enough to include sale, or delivery of possession. The said section does not apply to an attachment and Sale under any other law made expressly inapplicable thereto. The provision of section 63 sets out how the properties are exempt. [864F G].

The respondent, a displaced person, filed a suit for recovery of certain lands which were acquired by the Government under section 59(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had not issued a notice under s.61 of the Act on the basis that such right to compensation survived and it was that right which was being prosecuted by the heirs of the deceased and Land References were sought by them and the same were pending in Civil Court at the relevant date; (ii) the impugned notice did not represent their correct market value which was clear from the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court under its decrees in Land references and, therefore, such property had escaped assessment to duty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the respondent merely accepted the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Special Deputy Collector did not representing their correct valuation of the lands on the date of death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable inasmuch as the respondent himself had merely accepted that value of his acquired lands. [319B C] 2. The impugned notice issued under s,61 of Act on a wrong assumption that the acquired land still formed part of the state of the respondent which passed on his death, that the valuation for those lands adopted on the earlier occasion which was on the later occasion which is on the subsequent reassessment made in pursuance thereof would be clearly illegal and unsustainable inasmuchas the extra compensation awarded to the respondent by the civil court taken with the original assessment had been undervalued in view of the glaring enhancement enhanced compensation granted by the High court. [330C D] 3. The expression "any other sufficient reason" occurring in section 61(a), which is not defined in the Act, must be given a liberal construction so as to advance the object and purpose of the statute. It cannot be said that when the original assess ment was made it was the duty of the respondents after scrutinising the Account filed and examining the materials produced before him, to value the estate of the original assessing authority. [332D E] 4. The word "reason" in section 63(a)(b) of Act means a reason which is capable of being communicated by any communication or other means to the person making it. It does not mean that when an order is made under section 62, the person affected must be deemed to have known the reasons for making it and such communication or notice must be regarded as a "reason". [321B C; 331D] 5. The words "reason to believe" in s.63(a). are wide enough to include within their ambit all matters which can fairly and reasonably be said to be communicated by communication or otherwise. It is not necessary that the reasons must be communicated to the affected person personally or by any other means. [333E F] 6. The language of section 63 (a) is wide enough in its amplitude to cover all matters relating to the determination of compensation. The object and purposes of the section are different from those of the one which are intended to be taken into consideration in determining the amount of compensation payable by a person who has been deprived of his property under an award or settlement or award. [336F G] 7.

The appellant, a member of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank, was elected as Director on 18.8.1986 and he was elected on 18th August, 1986. The election of the appellant was challenged by him in an election petition before the Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur. The Deputy Registrar dismissed his revision petition under section 154 of the Act holding that the appellant had not been able to prove that he had committed default in payment of the loan and that the provisions of section 73FF were not attracted. The appellant 's revision petition was also dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar on 30.8,1989. In the writ petition filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution, it was contended that the impugned order removing the Assistant Registrar from the Committee of Directors was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant ' s election as a Director and that procedure having not been followed the Assistant Registrars could not have acted under section 78(1) of the said Act. The High Court dismissed the writ appeal holding that section 73F of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 was without jurisdic tion inasmuch as it prescribes a different procedure for called in question. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the State of Maharashtra that the disqualification under section 73G of the Co operative Societies Act 1961 ceased to exist on 12.5.1986 when he was declared elected as the Director and his seat already fell vacant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant having repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 77(1), he was surely not a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice and the provisions contemplated such a default and the appellant having continued to be a Director on account of his having committed default. [616C D] 1.2 The special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two maxim generalia special non derogant non derogata non derogative general words do not derogate from special words do general words does not derogatefrom special words. [680D E] 1:3 In the instant case, the appellant has already ceased to be Director and he is still a Director. The impugned order of removal was passed by the Assistant Regisrar Cooperative Societies on 18/8.86 and hence the appellant could not be treated as a defaulter under that section.

The respondent was in the service of the State of Maharashtra as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. The State Government issued orders reducing the pension payable to him by 50 per cent. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order reducing the amount of pension payable by 50% to the respondent by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court quashed the State Government 'S order reducing his pension by 50%. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was in service or after the completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government servant depend upon the good conduct of the government servant. Granting of pension by taking proceedings against a Government Servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. The validity of Rule 189 envisages withholding or withdrawal of a pensioner or any portion of it, if the pensioners are found guilty for grave misconduct either during or after completion of service. [35E F] 1.2 In the instant case, the State had power to reduce the pension granted to a government servant even after he had retired from the service. The Government ' power to withhold or withdraw any part is not questioned either before the Court or before this Court. Rule 189 does contemplate withholding or withholding of a part of the pension. [34F] 1:3 In the present case, there was no dispute that the respondent had retired in service and the reduction of pension was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against him. The proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. The orders were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. [33G] 1 :4 In the circumstances, the reduction in pension by50 per cent was too high harsh and arbitrary to the extent of Re. 1 per month be made the State Govern ment.

The U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, was enacted by the U. P. Legislature in exercise of its powers conferred on it by section 3 of the Act. The Act provided that before a District Magistrate grants permission to the landlord to sue his tenant he shall issue notice to the tenant and give him an opportunity to represent his case before the application of the landlord was dealt with on merits. The appellant 's suit for ejectment against the respondent was dismissed by the trial court but the High Court in appeal reversed it holding that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) was invalid, and so he came to the conclusion that the appellant ' suit was incompetent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 2(3). That is why it must be held that the District Magistrate has acted illegally or with material irregularity or has wrongly refused to act. [563 C] (ii) The provisions of section 3 (4) are clear and unambiguous, and they indicate that the jurisdiction of the Commissioner only to cases where irregularity or illegality was bad been committed by the District Magis trate in granting or refusing permission. The words "any order" occurring in section 16(1) do not mean that the Commissioner can deal with the legality, propriety or regularity of proceedings held before him, alter or reverse his order, or make such other order as may be just and proper. [562 D E] (iii) The word 'jurisdiction ' is used in a wide sense to include all kinds of jurisdiction which are exercisable by a civil court in relation to orders passed under the relevant provisions of the statute. It must be construed in its popular sense, that it includes all kinds or categories of jurisdiction that may be exercised by a Court in relation thereto. The word "jurisdiction" is used generally in contradistinction to the power conferred by section 6(1). [562 E] In the present case, the Commissioner could not deal with any matter which he was not bound to do under the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. He had no jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether a permission has been properly granted or refused by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the provisions of Act.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as an Assistant Registrar of the State Public Service. He was promoted to the post of Deputy Registrar on May 13, 1983. The appellant challenged his appointment before the High Court by way of a Writ Petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had not been able to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt and that he had been falsely implicated in the charge of assault because he had incurred the wrath of the Chief Minister of Punjab and the hostility of the Chairman 's husband and that it would be impossible for him to prove the case unless he was allowed to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 317(1) of the constitution provides that subject to the provisions of clause (3), the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commis sion may be removed from his office only by the order of the President on the ground of misbehaviour and ought to be removed. [640C D] 2. Article 318(1)(a) is not subject to this condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the Chairman, or any member of such a Public service Commission can only be removed on such ground. The danger of such an action is said to be that if a full opportunity is given to the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial it is an idle complaint that the evidence has been examined and found upon by some body or authorities. That article provides that, subject to clause (1), the chairman or any person of a public service Commission shall only be removal from his appointment on the grounds of misbehaviour. [643B C] 3. The expression "the Chairman or such other member" in Article 317 is not used in the sense of "may" but in its widest amplitude. It includes the Chairman and any other members of a State Public Services Commission. [641C D, E] 4. The word "may", in Article 318 (1) is wide enough to include the Chairman. There must be some other person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court. If a full hearing is given, the Judge may write to the Registrar of this Court immediately after the entire evidence is recorded. [652D] 5. The fact that the witnesses have filed affidavits before this Court may be summoned or requested by the learned Judge to attend his Court for the purpose of cross examination. The mere fact that a witness has been produced and found on behalf of the appellant, the charge sheet of misbehaviour is made out and whether the misbehaviour is of such nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his position, is in direct opposition to the plain words of article 317(l) of Constitution. [633E F] 6. The question which then arises for consideration is as regards the procedure which this Court should adopt in a Reference made by the President under Article 317 (1). The danger or of such action is that if the Chairman has reported to the President that the Member or any of other member, as the case may be, ought on any such ground to be removal. [466C D; 644A] 7.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. VIII of 1939) for the recovery of an amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ from the defendant respondents on the allegation that they had been rendering services to the deity and were using the temple for the maintenance of the temple. The appellants plaintiffs alleged that the endowment was a private one and the idol installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the dedication was not a private or personal trust and that the mere fact that members of the public were allowed to worship by itself would not determine the nature of the endowment. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants plaintiffs it was contended that the approach made by the High court was wholly incorrect and it had misconstrued the evidence and documents produced in the case to show that the endowments were a private and the intention of the founder was merely to instal a family idol in the temples. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere fact of worship would not fix the nature or character of the dedication. [830E] 2. The concept of a public nature has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be of universal application. This being the essential distinction between the nature and the nature, of a private endowment, it follows that one of the crucial tests to determine the character of apublic or a private trust is whether an endowment is of a purely charitable and religious nature. [ 832F] 3. The question as to whether the temple is of private or of a Hindu nature has been decided in several cases by this Court. In the instant case, the High Courts have not correctly appreciated the evidence led by the parties and have overlooked the important circumstance that the founder of the trust did not make any stipulation for taking offerings from members of public to worship in the Temple. [823C D] 4. The fact that the members of a family used to come to the temple with out any hindrance or donations to be made by members of their community or their descendants, the endowment would be of a personal nature. The High Court has rightly held that the trust was not of a religious nature and that it was a public trust. [824E F] 5. The contention that the evidence on record showed that the temple in question was a Hindu private one is without substance.
