It is manifest that whenever a dedication is made for religious purposes and a deity installed in a temple, the worship of the deity is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the idol. [825G H] 6. The circumstance that members were allowed by the public to perform all the work on the members or their ancestors, the endowments would be an important intrinsic circumstance to indicate the private nature of endowment. Some of the extracts of this document which are undisputed, clearly and conclusively show that there was any stipulation in the deed to dedicate the temple merely for the benefit of the members and their descendants.

The appellant Bank was working as a contractor to the military and other authorities. The agreement between the parties provided that the respondents would pay out of the specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities, the amount due under the bill be attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained against him. The document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts and the appellant Bank claimed that it was an assignee of the biLl and that the document was bring into existence. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the power of attorney was irrevocable and that there was no equitable assignment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power of Attorney was expressed to be irrevocable. The relationship of the two parties, Malhotra and the Bank was that of borrower and lender and that document was bringing into existence a particular fund in connection therewith. The power coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 created an interest in a specific fund and was irrevocable. There was thus a sufficient equitable assignment of a specific Fund in favour of the appellant. [775 B C] (ii) The agreement was not an equitable assignment but only an equitable assign. It was an equitable transfer of the money to the borrower. The amount due was to be paid out of a particular Fund of the lender in the hand of the authorities. Under the contract, the borrower had an interest and the power to attorney was expressed as an equitable assignedman of the fund by way of security. [777 E F] (iii) The document dated July19, 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant bank out of specific fund in the shape of security for the contracts issued by the Government in various departments on conditions mentioned therein. The letter of the power coupled and endorsement on bill dated 7th July, 1948 constituted an equitable assigningmen of the Fund by way Of security. The words "in other words" in the document were not intended to be used as an implied assignment of the debts or fund but only to enable the borrower to pay off his assets in his hands. [779 E F; 778 A B] (iv) The words 'in other cases" in section 7(1)(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, are wide enough to include a contract of agency between a debtor and creditor. The expression "in any other case" in that section is wide enough. [780 G H; 778 C D] (v) The word 'security ' in section 2(g) of that Act means security for money advanced by the debtor or an order given by him to his creditor upon a person owing to the lender, and includes a contract for the payment of money secured by the creditor. [781 E F]. (vi) The expression 'in any case" is wide in its amplitude and must be construed as including all other kinds of security which may be advanced by a debtor or by an order made by him. In construing the power Of attorney it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of two parties was, Malhotra, the lender and the borrower continued to be the owner and the lender was merely authorised to act as his agent. [771 D E] (vii) The powers of attorney coupled with endorsement on a bill dated 19th July 1948 created a equitable assignment and was unconditional.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gilland Arbuthnot & Co., Ltd. The said company had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not a recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. He also levied interest on the amount of his own contribution to the fund. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. In further appeal to the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary, the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). The High Court answered the reference in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17 has nothing to do either with deductions or with exemptions. [440 D] (2) The receipts of Rs 27,947/ by M/ are exempt from tax under section 56(1). [441 E] (3) The sum of Rs, 27948/ was undoubtedly an income as defined by section 17. Section 16 has nothing in either with deduction or with exemption. As the income in question is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on securities income; perty, profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains it has to be considered a "income from other source" and brought to tax under s.56.

The petitioners who were dealers in buffaloes, bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) of the State of Bihar challenged the validity of the Bihar Act on the ground that it contravened article 19(1)(g) of their fundamental rights under articles 19(i)(g), 19(6) and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned Acts were valid in so far as they prohibit the slaughter of buffaloes of all ages and calves of cows and calve of cows, male and female, but that it was constitutionally valid in its so faras it prohibited the slaughter Of those which are useful and useful as milch or draught cattle. The ban on the slaughter was not justified by reason of article 19 (6) of its Constitution. The impugned Acts did not contravene any fundamental rights of the petitioners under articles 14, 19(2), 31 and 31. The provisions of the impugned Act were therefore valid in law. The Bihar Act was constitutionally invalid as it contravened the fundamental rights guaranteed to the petitioners by article 19 of the constitution. The State of Bombay vs R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala, ; , followed. The restrictions imposed on the right of the dealers to carry on their trade and business under article 19 were not reasonable restrictions within the meaning of article 31(6). The impugned Act was therefore valid. The petitioners were entitled to the protection of article 14 Of the Constitution as it was not a law imposing unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right guaranteed by article 301 of the Constitu tion.

The respondent company was a public limited company. The Company was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh and its Manager was the manager of the Company. The company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, with effect from April 1, 1956. The respondent company had been carrying on business as an agent of the company. In accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act the company was to be deemed to have been incorporated in respect of the period between April 1 and May 31, 1957, and the date of its incorporation. The appellant company was registered under the Companies (Court) Act, 1950, and its managing director was appointed as an officer of the respondent company by the Government of Madhya Bharat. The management of the affairs of the said company was taken over by the State Government on April 1 , 1956. On March 31, 1956, the Company filed a suit against the respondent for damages for wrongful dismissal and for damages. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondent was not an 'employee ' as defined in the Indian . In appeal to this Court it was contended that the finding of the High court on the question whether the Standing Orders applied or not to the respondent, though he was an employee within the meaning of that expression in section 2(1) of the local Act, was correct and on a proper construction, inclusion of the name and ticket number in the departmental muster was an essential characteristic of an ' employee ' as contemplated by the Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Order NO. (g). Held, that the word 'employee" in section 3(1)(d) of Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, includes a person employed in any office, department or other establishment of the employer and does not include an employee who is employed in such a post. The essential content of the definition of an employee is employment in the office, Department or other establishments of the employers and doesnot include an 'workman ' as understood in the Bombay Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, nor does it include an "employee" within the definition clause in Standing Order (g) of section 2 of the Indian ,. The word 'employer ' in section 4(1), includes a 'workman who is engaged in any business or profession and does include an apprentice employed in that office. The words 'employer and ' do not include 'any person ', but only those persons who are employed in the department must be regarded as workmen within the expression in Standing Orders No. 2 of Standing Orders. The definition of "employee ' in Standing order No. 1 of Standing order NO. 2 is an inclusive definition and not an essential feature of an employer 's employment. The distinction between an employee and a workman is that who is appointed to do some work or other kind of work, but that does not mean that all persons employed in an office are workmen within that expression. The primary object of the Act is to provide for the establishment of an industry by providing suitable machinery for its employees and for matters connected therewith. The Act provides for the appointment of a committee consisting of representatives of employers and employees and the terms of reference thereto, and section 30(1). The Board of Directors of the appellant company which was constituted under the Act was to consist of representatives from the respondent Company and its Managing Director and the representatives of the employees. The Board was to function as an independent body for the purpose of carrying on the business of the companies. The functions of the Board were to be exercised by a representative of the workmen employed in connection with the affairs or business of companies, and it was not necessary that the representatives should have been present at the meeting. The provisions of section 30 of the Bombay Act did not apply to the appellant as they were not employees within the scope of the Standing orders.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961 and it went into production in the years 1964 65. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The Industrial Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained and so that no bonus was payable until this Project itself earned profits, or from the sixth accounting year following the year following that year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because alloy steel Project was owned, controlled and managed by Hindustan Steel Ltd., it had to be treated as a separate unit for purposes of section 16 of the Act; (ii) the proviso to sub section (2) of section 6 of the , did not apply in such a case. HELD: The Tribunal went wholly wrong in assuming that merely by virtue of the proviso, alloy Company was owned and managed in controlled and controlled by one single company and consequently, no bonus could be payable until it came into existence for the purpose of computation of bonus under the Act. [628 B] (i)(ii) The Tribunal was right in holding on the basis that only the employees of all the units on the strength of consolidated profits of all such units were treated as separate establishments and not separate units. [625 C D] (iii) The proviso to section 3(2) does not apply to the separate units for which separate accounts, separate balance sheet and profit statement are maintained. The proviso is only applicable in respect where there is no separate profit and Loss account and separate profit & loss statements are maintained; but that does not affect the principle to be applied to separate units of a company like Hindustan Steel Limited. [650 D E] (iv) The Explanation to sub s.(2) Of section 16 does not stand in the way of this claim because there is only one unit which is owned and controlled, controlled by the other single company. Therefore, the calculation of bonus on the foundation of consolidated accounts was Justified.

The appellant company was manufacturing sugar from sugarcane juice. The factory of the company was closed down on 30th September, 1989 and the factory was closed on 30.9.1989. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the Cess Act, 1976 on the ground that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products" and that the cess was payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corresponding entry in column II thereof as the Central Govern ment may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. The appellant company filed an appeal before this Court against the judgment and order of the High court. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'vegetable ' has been used in Entry 15 in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and since the entries are to be given a wider meaning sugar industry would be covered by the Act. Construction of words and the meaning of vegetables which people conversant with the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it, and so construed, it denotes those classes of vegetables who are grown in a kitchen garden or in a farm and are used for the table. [517B C] 1.2 The word "vegetables" has been defined in Entry 2(f) of Schedule I to the Cess act, 1976 as meaning any industry specified in Schedule I. It is not possible to define the term 'veleable product ' in the context in which it is occurring and to the fitness of the matter to the statute. [525G H] 1:3 The word vegetable in Entry No. 15 has to be understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense that sense which people dealing with the statute would attribute. It cannot be said that the term "veleables" is used in the sense in which the word 'vesleable products means something more than what they are known as vegetable products or make them known to the market. [500A B] 1 :4 The word `vegetability ' has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. It has a wider connotation. The term "creaming" is generally understood to mean that agriculture is an industry for certain purposes and vegetables are not understood as understood in commercial parlance. [617D] 1(a) In order to bring an industry within any of these entries, it has to he seen what is the end product produced by that industry. If the botanic meaning of the word "vesleables", as used in entry 15 is given some more then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule 1 would also be brought within Entry No 15. [417E] (b) The word edible in Entry 16 has to take its colour from the context and purpose of the statute in which they are dealing. It does not mean that agricultural products are not included in the expression "animal". If the end products produced by the botsanic is understood as meaning of vegetable products, it would be a different commodity. [450G] (c) The term 'agricultural product ' has to receive its popular meaning and must be construed in common sense. It must be interpreted in common understanding and not in commercial or industrial parlance. In order that the word vegetable should be understood as "analogic" it must mean something more like a vegetable product or make it known to market. The word is used for a limited purpose, but it has a wide connotation.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the practice of the profession was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a) (iii) and therefore, the respondent could not seek eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. The High Court in revision held that the use of the expression 'business ' in the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 did not mean any profession or trade within the definition of section 10(1)(a)(iii). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent tenant that the word 'business " in the context of the Andhra Act includes a profession. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression ' business ' in Section 10 (3) (a) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of an Advocate and that the meaning that the legislature of law is 'business within the term 'business" in the said phrase cannot be of any assistance in determining its meaning in Section10(3))(a). [14B] 2. The word ' business occurring in the Act includes the practice, profession or vocation of a person who is carrying on the date of the application, or (b) for the purposes of a business which he is carryingon the date on which the application is made, or, (c) for any purpose of a profession which he was carrying on. The words 'business in Section 2(1) are used in the widest sense so to include all professions and do not include any profession. [14C] 3. The term 'profession ' has been defined in section 2(2)(a), (iii), (iv) and (v) of the Act to mean a profession or calling for the performance of any of the following things, namely: (i) the carrying on of any business which is carried on by a person on his behalf; (ii) the doing of any other thing in relation to the business of which he has been engaged. [15D E] 4. The definition of 'business of an advocate ' in section 10 (1)(c) includes a trade or calling and also includes any profession, but does not include a profession as defined in the Indian Penal Code. [16F G] 5. In the instant case, the expression business occurring therein is used by the respondent landlord in the definition clause. The use of 'trade ' in that clause cannot be equated with the practice which he carries on the business. It would indeed be an activity which brings about nuisance to the occupiers of the other portions in the same building, securing alternative accommodation of alternative accommodation by the tenant and denial of the title of the landlord. [17F G; 18A] 6. The respondent landlord bona fide proposes to commence his profession in the city of Hyderabad. It is not right to give as to what he has done.

The respondent was a debtor to the appellant. The appellant filed a suit on 16 May 1953 against the respondent for recovery of Rs. 4,00,000 from the respondent as a banker and along with interest from time to time the amount of Rs 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed it. In appeal to this Court by certificate, HELD: (i) The appellant was not bound by the agreement between the parties as a result of which the respondent became the creditor of the firm of the appellant and the appellant could not have sued for recovery on that account. [575 D] (ii) The fact that the respondent had to be put on a footing of financial stability by giving the use of the appellants did not make any difference because the history of the transactions between the appellant 's firm and the respondent showed that the appellant had to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills. The transaction was between the respondent and the appellants and the transaction was, therefore, between the partners of the firms of the respondent. [574 E] (iii) The evidence on behalf of the parties shows that the history for the obvious reason that the transactions were between the appellants ' firm and Lakshmi Ratan Mills and that moneys were lent and advanced by Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills to India Supplies from time lo time and all that happened in that place was that in place of Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills and India Supplies. The correspondence showed that there were advances which were in the nature of deposit and were not covered by the award. [576 H] (iv) The history of transactions between M/s India Supplies on the one hand and Lakshmi Rantan Cotton Mills show that the appellants had to deposit with the traders the sum of Rs, 4,000 in its account with the respondent thus reducing the indebtedness of Lakshmi Rants from Rs. 2,00.000 to Rs. 1,00 lakhs.

The petitioner 's husband, Shital Kumar was detained by an order passed under sub section (1) of Section 3 of the COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention were served on him on February 28, 1986 and he was remanded to judicial custody on April 27, 1986. On his return from jail he made a representation to the Government of India against the order of detention. The Advisory Board considered the same and passed an order of deten tion under sub s.(1) on May 15, 1986 confirming that the petitioner ' husband had been in jail for at the time the order was served. The petitioner challenged the order by filing a writ petition in this Court. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The detaining authority was aware of the fact that the detenu was already in custody and yet he was sub jectly satisfied that his detention was necessary. [845G] 2. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, it would not be proper to hold that summons under section 108 of the Customs Act was in existence. [861A B] 3. The fact that a person is already in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order for preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining author ity was aware that the detenue was already neces sary and yet the detenu has been remanded to jail custody, the order being passed for preventive deten tion would not detract from the order having been passed for detention. [862B C] 4. The mere fact that an accused in deten tion is likely to get bail does not necessarily imply that he should be released on bail. It may also mean that if a person already in jail is already under trial or has been acquitted, the appeal is pending and in re spect of which he may be granted bail may not in all circumstances entitle an authority to direct preventive detention and the principle enunciated by the aforesaid decision must apply but where the offences in respect of which the detenu is accused are so interlinked and continuous in character and are of such nature that they are ofsuch nature that it would affect their continuous mainte nance of essential supplies and thereby render them likely to be prejudicial to the maintenance of public order, then sub jected detention would not necessarily amount to an order under the National Security Act. [863C D] 5. The detenu is al ready to serve the State of West Bengal as a full fledged criminal prisoner. He may be released from detention in accordance with law. [873D E] 6. In the facts and circumstances of the present case there is suffi cient material to show that the Detaining Authority was aware about the fact of the detenu being in custody when the order is made, yet he had been sub jectively satisfied, that his order of bail was necessary before he was actually released from custody. [872F] 7. The question whether a detention order can be passed against a person in jail has to be determined on its own facts and not by the Court. In this case there was sufficient material to indicate that the deten tion authority was unaware of the facts that the husband was already under detention and yet had been remanded, it is difficult to hold otherwise.

The petitioners were working as Casual Labour in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of the scheme on various grounds, namely: (i) The scheme was not prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, increments, pension etc., which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly; (ii) The petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are mostly engaged in digging, carrying and other similar types of work. They also contend that since the petitioners belong not to the categories of casual labourers or temporary employees for an unreasonably long period of time, where is any justification to keep persons as casual labourers for an unduly long period, their wages paid to them are very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to regular employees of the Posts & Telegraphs department at the rates equivalent to the minimum pay in the pay scales of the regularly employed workers in the Telegraphs and Telegraph Department at the rate equivalent to minimum payin the pay scale of semi skilled/skilled labour who strictly conform to the job content of corresponding regular posts in scales of Rs.210 and Rs.260, as the case may be; (iii) The benefit of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to the semi skilled or unskilled labourers who have worked continuously for more than six months; (iv) The benefits of increased rate of daily wage will not he admissible to casual labourers/s skilled unskilled labour in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period of more than 6 months; and (v) The respondents shall pay the same salary and other benefits as are being paid to the regular employees in accordance with this order. The Union of india has filed counter affidavits opposing the writ petitions.

The appellant was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1950 51 and 1952 52, but the Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on January 5, 1950, stating that he had submitted a return under section 23(3) of that Act. The appellant filed a revised return before the Income Tax Officer on January 6, 1950. The Income tax officer rejected the contention and held that the appellant was entitled to make a voluntary return on the date he did, and that as he had not submitted a " voluntary return" within the time fixed by the notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 24(3). On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. The Tribunal held that since the appellant had submitted his return under s 22(3), it was not open to the department to proceed under section 34(1) of Act for a voluntary statement showing an income below the taxable limit and that the Department ought to have issued a " Voluntary return" under section 33, and directed the Income ' tax Officer to issue a notice to the appellant. The High Court in reference held against the appellant on the ground that the department had failed to give a proper return before making a voluntary assessment and that it was open to him to make an application for a reference under section 66A of the Act. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the Incometax Officer had no jurisdiction to issue the notice under s.22(2). The expression " voluntarily" in section 22 (1) means voluntary return and not voluntary return. The word " voluntarily ' is used in the sense in which it occurs in section 34 (1)(a) of Indian Income Tax Act, but in its ordinary sense it includes voluntary returns. It is well settled that a voluntary and true return must be filed before the end of the assessment year and if no return was made within the period allowed by or under sub section (1), or sub section(2), the department should have issued notice to him requiring him to furnish a revised returns, but it could not issue a " involuntary return" when filed in response to a notice tinder section 22. The general notice under that section must be given before assessment is made.

The Reserve Bank of India, a nationalised bank, was constituted under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970. The Central Government issued an order dated 23rd August, 1982 appointing the representatives of the employees as well as the non union representing the interests of the bank as a whole and not of any special class of persons. The Reserve Bank, however, appointed one of its employees as Director of the nationalised bank. On 16th September, 1983, the Central Government made an order appointing the Directors of the said nationalised bank as Directors. The said order was challenged by the employees in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same on the ground that the Act did not provide for any machinery for the purpose of ensuring proper administration and control of the affairs of the Bank. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Reserve Bank that the scheme would not be even more defective if sub clause (c) was to receive the same construction as sub clause(b) so as to restrict the choice of appointment to the three persons specified in the Act, and that the Scheme would not suffer from any legal infirmity. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme is a matter for decision by the Central Govern ment and it is open to the Central Gov ernment to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for conducting an appropriate election. [857C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Reserve bank was constituted in the year 1973 under the Act. It was not a party to any scheme framed by the Reserve Govern ment. The scheme was made in the public interest and it was open to it to make provision for election in the manner chosen by it so as tO restrict the power of appointment of the representatives to the various categories of employees specified in section 9 of the Act so as not to restrict their choice in the selection of their representatives. That means, it would be perfectly in order for the Central Govt.

The respondent was a Income tax Officer. He filed returns for the assessment years 1964 65 to 1965 66 and claimed exemption from payment of income tax under section 24(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Income tax officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not produced any evidence in support of his claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner but the Tribunal held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. On a reference, the High Court held that section 254(5) of Act did not empower the Appellate Tribunal to stay proceedings relating to the recovery during the pendency of an appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of the provisions of the Act and the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal Rules 1963, powers have not been expressly conferred upon the Appellate Assistant Commission or the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner in exercise of administrative power could give the necessary relief of staying recovery to the assessee but that can hardly be put at par with a statutory power as is contained in section 220(6) which is confined only to the stage of pendency of appeal before the Appellate Authority. HELD: The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power of stay by the Tribunal. It could well be said that when an appeal is pending before the Income ' tax Officer, but the Act is silent in that behalf when an appellate authority is pending, it impliedly grants the power Of staying recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in disposal of appeals by the Appellate Tribunals. [69 E F] The Appellate Tribu nal must be deemed to have exercised its powers in proper cases to stay all proceedings relating thereto pending before it. It is needless to point out that the power under stay can be spelt out from that provision. When an appeal has been filed before the appellate authority, but when an application for stay of recovery of tax or penalty payable by a person is pending at the stage when an order for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal being rendered nugatory or rendered nugatory by allowing the recovery proceed ings to continue during the course of the pendency or appeal, it would be difficult to hold that such power can be exercised by the appellate Tribunal.

The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental enquiry. He was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with misappropriation and corruption in that he had on nine occasions, particulars of which were given in the charge, accepted bribes. The Superintendent of Police forwarded to the police for inquiry report and submitted a report to the District Magistrate. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the respondent was charged with committing cognizable offences and therefore sub paragraph (1) of para 486 of the Regulations did not apply to him as he was officiating in the Police Station, and quashed the order passed by the Superintendent of police. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Governor exercised his pleasure through the Superintendent Of Police, and as the Police Regulations were only administrative directions, the non compliance therewith would not in any way affect the validity of the order. Held: (i) The Governor exercised the pleasure through a Superintendent of the police in respect of the same matter which was the subject matter of the disciplinary trial. The Regulation providing for investigation in the first place under chapter XIV of the Criminal Procedure Code was only directory in nature and inasmuch as no prejudice was caused to the respondent, the Inspector of police could not proceed with the departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph 486 of Regulations. (ii) The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries did not affect the question if substantially the subject matters of the magisterial inquiry and the departmental proceedings were the same, could not affect its validity.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialists Grade II in the Central Government on February 8, 1971. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 9, 1971 and was confirmed in that post with effect from November 1, 1972. The appellant challenged his promotion before the High Court by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution contending that since he had been promoted as Specialists ' Grade II on March 31, 1973 he should have been promoted from that date and that the promotion of the said four respondents was not valid. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion from the date on which Dr. Sen was appointed to super time grade II. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the post in question was converted into a specified post and the strength of Specialists grade ' grade ' posts was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 posts added to super Time grade II was required to be filled in, it could only be filled by promotion from those belonging to specialists ' grade and (ii) since there was no substance in the contention that when unspecified Specialists posts were converted into specified posts 'as a specified cadre ' posts 'were converted into 'a specified post ', the appellant could not have been considered for the post which was deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The promotion of four respondents should be set aside. [53 B] 2.1 The appellant was fully qualified for being promoted to Supertime Grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists grade and added to Super time grade 11. He could not be considered eligible for promotion to super speciality ' grade II because his refusal to accept promotion at Simla was never superseded by any one junior to him in his speciality. [54 C] 2(a) The appellant had been given a chance to be promoted to the post of Director of Health Services, Manipur and he should be considered on that basis. He would be eligible for being considered for such promotion from that place. But since his refusal was never supersession by any person junior to the appellant in his specialists Grade ' grade, he could not claim the benefit of the rule. [55 G] 2.(b) The word 'recruitment ' has been used in a wide sense and it is not possible to lay down any precise definition of the term 'recruits '. It is, therefore, clear that when a post from amongst unspecified specialists is converted into one specified post it can only be filling in, by promotion, that would only be from amongst those belonging originally belonging to Specialists ( grade) category 'C ' and not some one who is on top of the general seniority list in Specialists. [56 D E] 2:2 The appellant could have been given an opportunity to be heard before he was promoted as a specialist Grade II.

The first respondent, a small holder of land in Punjab, purchased the same from his father. The first respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant and the second respondent on the ground that he had acquired the lands in excess of the permissible limit. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Act; (ii) the Collector ignoring the transfer of 167 bighas of land by respondent No. 1, and transferring the bighas of lands by respondent Nos. 2 and 3, was not hit under section 10 A and section 7B of Act; and (iii) the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The gift in both the appeals fail in the face of section 19 B. [632D] The gift by the first respondent to his father was saved from utilisation by the State. The purpose of the saving clause is cumbersome but the sense and is, having regard to the conspectus, can only be that although in the hands of the propositus, it is surplus land, if among the heirs it is available, it was not surplus land. [732F] (a) Section 19 B does not contemplate a transfer of any surplus area by inheritance or bequest from the tenant so settled. The provision is intended to give some time to the heir to ascertain the assets he has inherited, make the choice of his 'reserved area which he likes to keep and make the necessary declaration. [167A] (b) Section 20 B does nothing about the transfer or devolution of any land by inheritance. It only provides that if a person is a small owner, it can acquire lands by gift or bequest or bequest in favour of another person. The language of section 20 B clearly indicates that the surplus area must be at the disposal of the State Government for utilization under section10 A [167B C] (c) Section 10 A confers power on the State to make a declaration of his lands within a prescribed time. It is not possible to lay down any inflexible rule as to how an owner can acquire land by gift, bequest or gift from a person to whom he is an heir. The words "in the prescribed manner" in section 19A are wide enough to include within their sweep all transfers and inheritance made by a person who has no interest in the land acquired by him. [168C D] (d) Section 7B confers power upon the State Govern ment or any officer empowered by it in this behalf to utilise any surplus Area for resettlement of tenants ejected, or to be ejected under clause (a). The words 'in the manner prescribed ' are wide and they are not intended to take in their sweep every transfer or bequest made by the person who is an owner. [166E F] (e) Section 16B confers powers on the Government or any other officer empowered in this regard to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the section. The power conferred upon the Government under section 19C is a plenary one and it cannot be exercised so as to confer arbitrary powers on an authority which has no power to do so.

The appellants, who were the descendants of a joint ancestor of Amarshah, executed a will dated December 8, 1950, in favour of the respondents. The respondents claimed that they were entitled to receive compensation on the death of their father and that the appellants were entitled only to the estate devised in their favour by Amarshh. The appellants contended that the respondents had no right or title upon the property and that as the will set up by the appellants was genuine, the respondents were not entitled to claim the compensation payable in respect thereof. Held: (i) The High Court was in error in reducing the amount of mesne profits payable to the plaintiffs. The decision of the Governor in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be the successor on the deceased of Amarhah was binding upon the appellants and that it could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date. (ii) The decision in Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become binding and conclusive against the appellants because no suit was filed by them for setting aside that decision. (iii) The respondents were entitled under the will to receive compensa tion in respect of Malguza lands which belonged to the joint ancestor. The High court was in wrong in reducing this amount of compensation to the appellants. (iv) The order of the Compensation Officer became final and conclusive and could not he reopened in proceedings for setting up the estate.

The appellants were tenants of the respondent in a suit for eviction filed by them. The respondent raised a preliminary objection that the suit was barred by limitation as it was not maintainable on the date of service of notice on the tenant. The trial court dismissed the objections and held that the tenancy was governed by section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. On appeal the High Court took the view that the provisions contained in section 12 (3) (a) were not applicable to the suit, but that the suits were governed by the provisions of section 12 and therefore the suit is governed by sections 12(2)(b) and 12(4). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had taken a contrary view and held in Ambalal 's case that the dispute as to standard rent was to be raised within one month from the service of the notice on tenant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The provisions contained by sections 11 and 12 of the Act do not apply to the suits. [629 B] (2) The High Court in Amalbalal vs Chimanlal Nagindas held that section 12 of Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1948 applies only where there is a dispute as regards standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under the order made by the court. [ 630 E F] (3)(i) The expression "any other Court" in section 11(4) of Act means the High court which has jurisdiction to decide whether a suit should be filed within one year from the date on which the notice is served. The expression 'such Court ' in section 10(2) of Bombay Rent Control Act means a court having jurisdiction to entertain and decide whether the suit should have been instituted within one calendar month of the service or within one hundred days of the date fixed for the service. [625 G H] (ii) In the instant case, the notice terminating the tenancy by raising a dispute was not in accordance with section 12. The notice did not give any cause to the tenant to raise the dispute at all. The suit was therefore governed by Section 12(1)(a). [630 A B] Amballa vs Cholaram Nagindras, ; , referred to.

The respondent company was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant was a shareholder of the respondent company and its directors were appointed by the Aluminium Company to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the company, the Aluminium company nominated three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondents company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the appellant company at All ordinary or special general meetings and as such had "a controlling interest" in the shares held by them. The respondent company, which was then the appellant before the Tribunal, was a director of the said company nominated by the company to vote on behalf and on its behalf. In the assessment year 1943 43 the Income tax Officer included the amount of excess profits tax for the years 1939 to 1943. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the directors of respondent company had controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940 read with section 66(1) of that Act and therefore, according to the principles laid down in that case, they could not be said to have "a Controlling interest" within the meaning of that expression in section 2(21). The Tribunal held that there was no room for doubt that the respondent Company which was the appellant prior to the date of the assessment was a company controlled by it and as between them and the shareholders, they were the shareholders. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The words "a managing interest" must be understood in common parlance and not in popular sense. It is well settled that the word "interest" means the interest which is acquired or received by a person for his own benefit. [192 E] Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs B. Glasgow Expanded Metal Co., Ltd. ; , followed. (ii) The directors of a company may well be regarded as having "a control interest" when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority of shares which, under the articles Of association of tile company, are the shareholders and as both the shareholders are the registered members and the right to vote is vested in them although between them. [195 C D] (iii) The word " interest" means a fixed or fixed interest in the capital of the business of the Company. It includes interest which has been acquired or obtained by a company for its own benefit, but does not include interest which may be acquired or acquired by a public company for the purpose of earning profits. [196 E] (iv) The controlling interest remains vested in the Aluminium Corporation and is at no time vested in Mr. L G Bash. G. L. G Ahibowd vs Commissioners of Inland Reve (I.L.R. , referred to.

The respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. On 1st October, 1957, some persons junior to him were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. The respondent opted for the service under the Electricity Board and became an employee in the said service. He was promoted as Accounts Superintendent on 30th December 1966. Some persons junior t he respondent were promoted to that post with effectfrom that date, but no promotion was granted to him. On 30th January 1970, some of the persons junior ly were promoted. The appellant Board issued a resolution dated 19th May 1969 promoting some persons senior to the respond ent as Accounts Superintendents and promoted them on their completing the period of probation. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the resolution. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the resolution was not applicable to the allottees, but only on the ground of inordinate delay and laches. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Board that the Resolution dated 19st May 1969 and 5th January, 1970 were invalid as they had been passed without complying with the require ments of passing the examination and passing the examina tion. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The resolution dated 20th May, 1969 is not applicable in the present case as the Regulations framed by the Board under section 79(c) of the Electricity Supply Act are not applicable. [510B] The Resolution dated 5th Jan., 1970 does not apply to the allotment of the respondents. It is not possible to infer from the Resolution that the allottees were exempted from passing the Departmental Examination I and Kannada language test for the purpose of earning increments and for promotion. [511E F] The resolution also does not have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Govern ment referred to in the Resolution itself.

The petitioner 's son, a minor, was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No. 6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police of Jarai Police Outpost under Police Out Post under Police Station Bisra, Distt. Cuttack. The petitioner ' son, who was the mother of the minor, filed an application before the District Magistrate for compensation to be paid to her. The District Magistrate awarded compensation to the petitioner. The State Government appealed against the order of the District Judge and the High Court dismissed the appeal. In the Special Leave Petition it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the award of compensation in a proceeding under Article 32 or 226 of the Constitution is a remedy available in public law based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private law. Dismissing the Special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The compensation is in the nature of exempellary damages awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public duty and is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the private law in an action based on tort. [610D] 2.1 In cases where the court finds that grant of such relief was warranted, it may award compensation in appropriate cases, where that is the only practicable mode of redress available for the contravention made by the State or its servants in the purported exercise of their powers, and enforcement of the fundamental rights under Article 21 of the constitution. [ 610E] 2:2. The Court is not helpless and wide powers given to this Court by article 32 or226 would be available in Public law for enforcement of a fundamental right guaranteed under Article21 of the Constitu tion. It is only when there has been an infringement of the constitutional right that it can award compensation. [625E] 3:3. The relief of monetary compensation in proceedings under Article 226 of tho Constitution seeking enforcement or protection of such rights, and such a claim based on English law, is independent and of the right available to a aggrieved party for compensation under Article 22 of the Con stitution. It cannot be said that this Court has no power to grant relief in exercise of its jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 of Constitu tion in proceedings relating to compensation for breach of public duty. [650B C] 4:4. The compensation in the instant case is in respect of a claim for compensation for contravention Of fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 21, of the Consti tution and is based on the strict liability of the citizen.

The petitioner, a convict of the Indian Penal Code and two of his children Billa was convicted by the Chief Reporter of the Hindustan Times for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of the Chief Minister rejecting his petitions on the ground that the President had no power to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be allowed to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga, who were under a sentence of death. It was contended for the petitioner that the two prisoners had been sentenced to imprisonment for life and that the petition filed by them to the President of India for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment was rejected by the President. The Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner, inter alia, (i) that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right nor does it confer any right on the Press, to have an unrestricted access to means of information; (ii) that in the instant case, the petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners as they are willing to be interviewed and, indeed, if it were to appear that the prisoners themselves do not desire to be interviews, it would have been impossible for them to be heard and therefore, there was no reason why newspapermen who can broadly, and we suppose without great fear of contradiction be termed as friends of the society be termed, as friends. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The petitioner has not been asking the Superintendent of Jail to allow her to interview a condemned prisoner. [1186F] (2) Rule 549(4) of Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi provides that every prisoner under a sentenced of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends or legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press. [1108G] (3) Rule 559A provides that all reasonable indulgence should be permitted to a condemned prisoners in the matter of interviews with relatives, legal adviser and approved religious ministers. It does not provide that no newspapermen will be allowed. The presence of a Free Press does neither imply or spells out any statutory obligation on its citizens to give information to them. [1086B] (4) Rule 561A provides for a search of the person who wants to interview, the prisoners jointly and for not more than one hour on the whole. There is no reason how newspapermen can broadly be termed friends of society be called as friends or newspapersmen. The provisions contained in the Jail Manual do not imply nor does they mean that they can always without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview any condemned prisoner.[1186C] (5) Rule 556A provides a special procedure for the interviews and the rules contained therein are applicable to all persons who desire to interview. [1287D] (6) The Rules do not contemplate or spell Out any legal liability on the citizen to supply the information to Press, such as, for example, rule 552A provides in that every person under a sentencing of death should be allow such interviews. It is not necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview should be given the same facility of interviewing the prisoners. [1194E] (7) The provisions of Rule 559 A do not indicate or spellout any legal obligations on the public servant to supply any information to him. The only thing which is required to be done by the Press is that he must furnish information to his relatives and friends, legal representatives and legal advisors as the Superintendents thinks reasonable and in accordance with the rules governing the interviews.

The appellant mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s Das Bank Ltd. for recovering the amount due under the mortgage. The respondent 's application for appointment of a Receiver was rejected by the Subordinate Judge, Agartala on December 18, 1959. On appeal, the Subordinate judge held that the appellant was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire and dismissed the objections. The Subordinate Judge allowed the respondent ' s application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22, 1956. The High Court in revision set aside the order of the Subordinate Court and directed that the damages awarded to the respondent be recovered from the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Subordinate Judges who tried the suit were incompetent to enforce the surety bond executed by the appellant as he was neither the successor nor the successor in office of the Receiver; and (ii) under the terms of the bond, the appellant became liable for the losses caused to it. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i)(a) Under the terms and conditions of the bonds, the respondent rendered itself liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the Court. [360 G] (b) The appellant rendered himself liable as surety for his performance of the condi tions imposed on him personally liable under the conditions of bond. By virtue of section 150, the District Judge was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of enforcement of the surety bonds as the District judge himself. [361 B] (c) The Subordinate judge was not competent to enforce a surety bond. The appellant became itself liable for loss caused by fire. [362 C D] (d) Under section 145(c), the Subordinate judges were entitled to have the same power in the matters of enforcement and enforcement of a bond as the district Judge himself. The surety bond had undoubtedly, to be construed strictly but it was impossible to accept the contention that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of the tea estate and since the Receiver 's default had been caused due to the Receiver`s negligence in the performance of his duties the appellant is liable to make good the loss occasioned to the Tea garden by the fire. The bond was executed six months after the tea plantation was damaged by the Fire. [363 D E] (e) Under sections 145(a), 146(c) and 146(b), the District Court is entitled to take all such steps as are necessary for securing the execution of a decree. But the Subordinate Courts were not competent under section 150 to enforce an surety bond against the Receiver. The proviso to that sub section provides that where any person has become liable as the surety for fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of Court in any suit or proceeding consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed against the surety to the amount to which he has rendered himself personally liable in the manner provided for the execution. The sub section is not intended to apply to cases where the conditions are satisfied. [364 G H] (f) Under Section 145(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Sub Judge was competent to execute a bond against any person who had become liable under an orders of the Court in a suit or proceedings consequent upon the decree of the court. The Sub Judge could not be said to have acted without jurisdiction in executing the surety.

The appellant, a dealer in foodgrains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. Wheat Procurement (Levy) Order 1959, was selling to the State Government 50% of the wheat held in stock by him at the commencement of the Order. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U P. Wheat Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat sold by the appellant and the excess amount payable by it. The appellant contended that the sales were not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the expression in section 2(h) of the Act, that the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not liable to tax. The Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable because there was neither sale nor a receipt by the dealer to the Controller. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (1) the transactions were not exigible to sales tax as they did not amount to "sale", and (2) the sales made to the Central Food Controller under the provisions Of the UP. Sugarcane Procurement Order, 1959 were sales within the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 3(10) of that Act. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was a contract between the assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the term "sale". [538 D] (ii) The supply of wheat by the assessee to the Food Controller did not fall under section 2 (h) because steel products were supplied pursuant to directions issued under a Conciliator Order.

The petitioner was detained under the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him on June 23, 1986. He was released from prison on June 24, 1986 and he was informed that his case would be considered by the Advisory Board within three months. On August 7, 1986, the State Government passed an order under section 3(2) of the Act directing that the petitioner should be detained for a period longer than three months unless the Advisory Boards had reported within the period of three months from the date of detention. The petitioner challenged the said order in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the report of the Advisory board was more than three weeks after the detention, and that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the question as to whether there was sufficient cause for the detention of the petitioner. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of detention is illegal notwithstanding that it is within three month from the dale of the second order of deten tion. If the report is to be obtained within three weeks, it is not answer to say that the representation though not made within three days was disposed of before the hearing of the case. [206C D] 2. The Advisory Board in existence to whom a reference could be made under section 11 of the Gujarat Act and whose report could be obtained as required by the Constitution has to be obtain ed before the expiry of three weeks from the detention order. If there were no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry o f 3 months after the date on which its report or beyond the period Of three months after it is received, was not answer. [207D E] 3. The Court cannot assume that the Advisory Commis sioner had applied his mind to relevant materials before passing the order of preventive detention. If he has applied his own satisfaction, the Court would be justified in taking into account all the facts and circumstances of the particular case. But if the report was made after the hearing was over, it would not be a sufficient answer to show that the delay was so long as the Advisory Committee had reported that there was no adequate cause for detention. [208E F] 4. The detaining authority must have applied its own mind before passing an order of Detention. If it is satisfied that there has been sufficient cause justifying such detention, the order would be illegal notwithstanding the fact that the detenu may not be detained in view of the provisions of section 3 of the . [207F G] 5. In a habeas corpus proceeding, it was not only the report but also the opinion of the Board that there had been sufficient ground for detention of a person when the order was made.

The respondent filed an application under section 17 of the for setting aside the award on the ground that the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. The trial court rejected the objections and dismissed the application. The petitioner preferred a civil revision application against the judgment and order passed by the trial court in Special Civil Suit No. 145/77. The High Court allowed the respondent 's revision application and set aside the decree passed in terms of the award under section 18 of the . In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and signing the award, both the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to the arbitrator. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The conduct of parties that the parties have agreed to referring the disputes in writing to the arbitration of the named arbitrator is not a proper arbitration agreement in terms. [537B] 2.1 In the instant case, it is clear from the narration of facts that the respondent had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20th January, 1977 in respect of which award there had been continued objections but now they have agreed that neither of them had re affirmed the acceptance of the Award. [437C D] 2:2. The contention that the High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did is without substance. It is clear that both the sides agreed to reference the dispute in writing and signed by both the par ties. But in the present context, it was clear that the evidence of the respondent was not sufficient to warrant a finding that the agreement between them had been duly executed. [540E F] 3:3. The question whether the suit was barred as res judicata is essentially one of fact and has to be decided on its own facts. In the light of the facts and circumstances of this case, the High court was right.

The respondent mortgaged a property in favour of the appellants for a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 and the appellants were put on auction. The respondent 's bid was accepted by the Subordi nate Judge who held that the transaction amounted to a "proceeding" within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act and dismissed the suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the Sub judge but granted a decree for redemption on the ground that the respondent had not received notice of the mortgage and was therefore entitled to exemption under proviso (ii) to sub section (1) of section 36 of the Transfer of Property Act. The appellants came up in appeal by special leave against the judgment of the High court. Held, that the expression "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after the 1st day of January 1939" in section 2 (22) Of the Indian , is wide enough to include a proceeding in execution for any purpose mentioned in clauses (a) or (b) of sub section(1) and therefore it must be construed strictly. The expression "all the rights of the original mortgagee are not assigned to the sub mortgagee and that the mortgagee still retains a legal interest in the original mortgage even when the mortgage was in the form of an English mortgage, and therefore the respondent ' s decree must be taken to have been passed "in a suit to which this Act applies" with the result that the appellants claim exemption under the proviso (i) to section 36(1).

The appellant was his concubine since 1945 till his death on February 22, 1949. He transferred to the joint family properties and for allotment to him of their respective shares in consideration of past cohabitation with her. The respondents filed suits against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents executed without consideration or for the transfer were void. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transfers under exhibit A 1 and A 2 were not supported by any consideration by way of cash or delivery of jewels. They were invalid as they were made in consideration for past cohabitations with her, such past cohabitance was the consideration for the subsequent promise to transfer the properties to her. [45 B C] (ii) The High Court rightly held that the transfers under Ex. A 1 were not valid and the subsequent severance of joint status between Venkatacharyulu and his sons could not validate them. [46 D E] (iii) The past cohabitated transactions were invalid, and the alienations were without consideration. The past contracts were invalid. The previous cohabitation was the considered for the earlier promise to sell the coparcenary properties. In the alternative, the appellant did not make any such gift. The subsequent severance in 1947 could not invalidate them. The transfers were by way Of gifts and not in consideration.

The respondent, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business as an investment company. The company had its registered office at Bombay in the year 1948 and it had its head office at Baroda. It had its Head Office at Baroda in the years 1949 to 1960. In the assessment year 1961 62, the Income Tax Officer issued a notice under section 226(3) of the Income tax Act, 1961 on 5 12 75 for the recovery of the amount due from the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice and the order withdrawing the notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice was not made by the I.T.O. within the meaning of section 244 of the Act, and that it was not necessary for him to make the requisite statement on oath under clause (vi) thereof. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the award of interest in the present case was not governed by Section 244 of Income Tax Act, 1922; (2) the notice issued under section 227(3), which led to revocation of the earlier notice under clause(vii) thereof, was without jurisdiction and was therefore invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the notice under Clause (vi), which was served on the respondent, was in fact made after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by section 226 of the 1961 Act, could be raised only after the filing of the requisite statements under clause 5(vii). [114B] 2.1 In the instant case, the award was passed on 5 5 1275 and it was incumbent on the L.I.C., in the open court to make a statement on behalf Of the respondent that the sum demanded by the notice dated 5 12 74 was not payable to the assignee of the policies to whom the payment thereunder had to be made even according to the stand of the L I.I C. [114D] 2:2. The delay in making the requisite declaration under section 225(3)(vi) of Income tax is a matter which can be agitated before the High Courts and it cannot be said that the delay was not due to any fault on the part of the respondent or that it resulted in the denial of its liability to the assessee. [115E] 3:3. The fact that the appellant had made the requisite disclosure under clause 4(vii), which is a condition precedent for making the application under section 22(3). does not mean that the omission to make such a statement was not a mere technical defect.

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of sugar. The appellant 's father who had been carrying on the business as an agent of the respondent, filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain sugar cane from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the first appellate court dismissed it. In second appeal the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that the appellant had failed to prove that he had paid the price fixed by the respondent for the sugar cane purchased by him. The High Court also held that in view of the provisions of cl. (2) of article 173 of the Limitation Act a period of limitation was prescribed for an appeal under section 115 A of that Act and that, therefore, the suit was barred by time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had proceeded on the basis that section 29(2)(a) applies only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law; and that as in the present case the First Schedule to the Limitation Acts prescribed a period different from the period prescribed therefor by the First schedule, the provisions contained in section 29 (2), sub section (1) of section 29 would apply even to a case where the First Scheduled to the Act prescribes a period for an Appeal or application by any special or Local law. HELD: The High Courts have proceeded on a correct interpretation of cl.(2) and held that it is governed by article 156 of the First Schedules to the Constitution. [144 D] The first limb of sub section(2)of section 29, sub section 2 of section29, provides for an application or appeal by any local law prescribing a period within different from that prescribed therefor. It does not make any difference whether a suit, appeal or application under a particular local law is of a kind similar to one for which a period Of limitation is provided in the First and Second Schedule. [145 D] In order to deal with the second ground given by the High 'Court it is necessary to reproduce the provisions Of section 29 sub section 3 of that section, sub s.(2), of section 28, sub sections (1), (2A) and (3) of that Schedule. The first part of sub secs.(2A), which deals with proceedings under special or other local law for which period a period is provided therein, provides that the provisions thereof shall apply to such appeals as if they were prescribed therefor in that Schedule and for the purpose of determining any period of time limit prescribed for any suit, Appeal or an application by the special orlocal law. The second limb of subs.(2B) of sub s(2), which is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, is that proceedings of the kind, that is, proceedings under Special or local laws for which limitation is prescribed in the first schedule because it is enough if the special law prescribes for such an appeal a period. [146 D E] The High ' Court was right in holding that in the instant case the Act provides a period shorter than what has been prescribed by the first Schedule because it does not fall under article 156.

The appellant, a private operator, was providing transport service in the District of Mathura. The Regional Transport Authority, Mathura, issued an order under section 76 of the Act directing that no area as a bus stand shall be used for any purpose other than the purpose for which it is provided or set down by the statute. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as bus stands under section76 of the . Aggrieved, the appellant has preferred this appeal after obtaining special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 76 of Act confers wide powers on the State Government to make rules for the purpose of the Chapter. The power conferred on the District Magistrate by section 76 is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stand which can only be notified by the Regional Transport Author ity under section 68(2)(r) of the , and therefore, rules could be framed by the State Govern ment regarding the said subject under section 63(2) (r) thereof. [713C D] 1.2 The power to issue a notification fixing a bus stands vested in the Regional Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. It only authorises the District magistrate to exercise the powers under section 77A by the state Government regarding the same subject under Section 68(1) of Act. [774E F] 2. The word 'control ' has been defined in Section 3(g) of 'the Act to mean control over all transport vehicles and includes any other vehicle used for the pur pose of carrying on any trade or business. It is not disputed that in the instant case no order had been passed by the District authori trate to determine the area in question as a Bus stand and the power to impose a bus stood vested in tho Regional Transport authority having jurisdiction. [777G H] 2:1 The word "control" has been used in Section 76(2), which is in Chapter IV of the Indian Act, with the object of establishing a bus Stand. It also authorises the State Transport Authority to exercise powers under Section 76A by issuing notification fixing the places for the bus stand and to start from there and to get out of their buses at that bus stands. [779G H; 778A] 2(a) The word control ' has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. It has only been used to denote control over transport vehicles. It does not mean control of transport vehicles which are carried on by the public. It cannot be said that the power under Section 77A is vested in a Regional Transport Officer. [780B C] 2.(b) The Regional Authority, Agra, had no authority to fix places for bus stand or halting places within the Town Area of Baldev (Mathura). The District Magistrate could not exercise the power of fixing a Bus stands under Section76 of Act and that could be done only under section 67(2 ) (r), which contained the provision relating to parking places.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the , and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The High Court set aside their conviction and sentence on the ground that there was an attempt on the part of the appellants to transport paddy outside the State of Punjab in this case. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) There has been no export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order 1959. [667 B] (ii) The sufficiency of the act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt is different from attempt to commit it. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempt to committing it, he must first have an intention to commit the offence and secondly to have done an act which constituted the act constituting the act. [669 C] (iii) The adequacy of the acts which constitute the act of export is a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it.
