[670 D E] (iv) In order to bring an offence into existence, one must first be shown first to have an intended intention to committing the offence, and secondly, to have doing an act with intent to commit that crime. The sufficiency is not a question as to whether there was export of the paddy within or outside the meaning Of Para 2 (a) or para 2(b).

The appellant was the Managing Agent of a company which had been incorporated in 1946 and was carrying on business as Managing Agents. The managing agency agreement provided that the remuneration payable to the Managing Agency shall be paid by the Company to the Company at the end of each calendar year, and that the Managing Agents shall pay the remuneration for the entire period during which the commission was expected to be paid. The appellant claimed that the managing agency commission should be deducted from its profits in computing the taxable income of the company under section 10(2) (vi) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it stood at the relevant time. Held, that the agreement between the Company and the Managing Agencies was a composite contract for a whole year 's remuneration on the completion of a whole of the year 'S work and the commission thereof as remuneration, for purposes of convenience, the true nature of the functioning of the Managing agency, and the remuneration therefor as well as clauses I and 3 of the managing Agency Agreement show that the assignor and the assignee are to be treated as one entity and that in this respect it is to be treat as an income bearing asset. The terms of the agreement clearly implied divisibility of contract and of the remuneration, but by the very terms of its Managing Agency Agreements it could be referred back to the period in which it was earned and the portions of the commission actually earned by them or which had accrued to them under the terms of their Managing Agency Agreement which were thus transferred to them would be their income and no part of such income could ever be said to have accrued to the Sassoons. The case of an assignment of managing agency is not one entity but one entity, and it is the profits and gains of the business carried on by the assignee, when a fact he stepped into the position of the assignee, as if his name had been inserted in the Managing Agreement from the beginning, and, therefore, the remuneration received for the whole year would be the income which had fallen due after the date of assignment. The word "income" is not defined in the Act but it has to be understood in its ordinary sense in its popular sense. It is a well known rule of construction that where an agreement between two parties is one, the terms are capable of two meanings, the meaning of which may be different from the words used by the parties in the agreement. In the present case, the agreement was not one of sale but one of transfer of property and it was the profits or gains of business carried out by the assignors. The agreement between them clearly implied that the assignment or the assignee would become the Managing agent only on some date in the course of the accounting period.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be. HELD: (i) It is implicit in the concept of "confession" that something meant only "something stated". The mere fact that the accused had been overtaken by some persons would not necessarily lead to the conclusion that he was guilty of the offence. [89 E F] (ii) The confession, whether it is extra judicial or judicial, must be in the first instance fully established. It is an extrajudicial confession and it is implicit therein that something stated is that something said is that anything said is not necessary before "sthing that is stated" is that nothing said is "anything said". [89 G H] (iii) The evidence of P.Ws. 11, 13 and 15 shows that they clearly heard the accused saying when he opened the door of the house and came out at 60 'clock in the morning of the fateful day that he had "finished Sunderpatti" his daughter in law, and thereby finished the daily quarrels. [90 E F]. (iv) The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be in first instance clearly established. All the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the appellant and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the proved guilty should be Of a conclusive character and tendency. [91 G H; 92 A] (v) The mere circumstance that the deceased was sleeping in the house at about 6 a.m. on that day would not by itself lead to his conclusion that the appellant had committed the murder.

The appellant, a registered owner of an existing insurer, was appointed as an officer in the respondent company. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Manager (Rationalisation) and he continued to hold the same post till his retirement on June 30, 1976. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of termination of his service. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant 's services were terminated by tendering one month 's salary in lieu of notice and also a direction to pay all the allowances upto that date including the period of his suspension. In appeal, the Division Bench held that the termination of the respondent 's service was not justified as he had been given an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken against him. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee 's Service whether permanent or temporary" in Rule 5 and without conducting an enquiry or giving an opportunity, indicate that the Board may unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there is no need for the services of a particular employee, in consequence of the service of the officer/employee. The words 'in the case of the society not having an further need ' of any employees 's servant whether permanent, temporary or temporary, which shall be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days notice in writing for termination of service or in lieu thereof pay such employee a sum equivalent to his salary in full without any notice or pay in lieu therefor. [225B C] 1.2 The words `in the circumstances ' occurring in Rule 9 of the Rules of the Delhi Transport Corporation Regulation, 1976 are capable of two interpretations. The first interpretation is that the word 'in 'may ' should be interpreted to mean 'shall ' and not 'shall. '. If the provisions of law or the rule are construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the Rule unconstitutional, the rule unconstitutional, and the rule is interpreted in such manner as would render it consistent With the constitution. [226D E] 1:3 The expression 'in any case ' occurring therein must be construed in its ordinary sense and not in a narrow sense. It should be understood in its popular sense. The word 'may" has been used to convey the idea of the rule of service jurisprudence. The rule is intended to serve as a guide to the interpretation of statutes. [227D] 1 :4 In the instant case, the Board of Directors had to take a decision whether the need to continue the employee ' s service which would be based on the relevant material.

The Orissa Excise Act, 1915 was enacted to provide for the regulation of the grant of licences and the imposition of a fee on the manufacture or sale of country liquor. The State Government issued a notification dated August 19, 1970 under section 22(1) of the Act directing that the licence granted to the petitioner for the manu facture and retail sale of ' country liquor shall be cancelled. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that (i) the High court erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector was not for the grant or privilege of manufacture and sale of liquor; (ii) the Collector had no authority to issue a notice under section 5 of the Amending Act of 1970 and the Collector bad no authority in law to issue such a notice; and (iii) the State Government had no power to issue the said notice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court erred in taking the view that as sections 2 to 5 of tho Amending Act were not made retrospective in operation, the effect of section 6 amounted to a direction by the Legislature to the State disregard the decision in Ajodhya Prasad 's case that the amount realised by auction was illegal and that section 6 was therefore ultra vires the powers of the legislature. [718C D] 2. The impugned judgment of the High Courts is set aside and the writ petition No. 1855 1863 of 1972 is allowed, the impugned judgments of the Orissa High Court dated May 15, 1970 are quashed and the Writ Petition No. 1302 of 1972 stands dismissed.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to one of life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that there was corroboration in regard to accused No. 3 and that the High Court had wrongly come to the conclusion that there were no corroboration in respect of accused No 2. It was further contended that the evidence of the tailor 's shop was not sufficient to connect him with the crime. HELD: The High court rightly came to the finding that there is sufficient corroboration of the evidence and it was proved that accused No 1 and 3 went together for the sale of cycle to Rupvate. [628 B] In view of the fact that there had been no corroboration, in regard, to accused Nos. 2 and 3, the High court was right in holding that there could be no corroboration. [625 C D] The evidence of Dinkar and accused No,. 2 clearly showed that accused Nos 1 and 2 were responsible for the crime and that they were rightly convicted. [650 F G] In the present case, the evidence did not show that accused nos. 1 and 4 had any motive to commit the murder of the deceased. There was also no corroboration as to the fact of recovery of articles in the godown of Takalkar. The evidence showed that the tail or 's shops were purchased by accused No 3 for Rs. 2,000/ . The evidence did show that the shop of Takkar and he had kept a bag of utensils in his godown and gave the key of the godown to accused no. 3 who afterwards returned the key and gave it to accused nos 1 and3. [600 C D; 600 A] In this case, there was nothing to connect accused No1 with the murder. The discovery of articles did not amount to an admission by accused Nos 2 and3 that they had kept the bag in his own godown for Rs, 2,500/ . There was no evidence to connect them with the commission of the crime as the tailoring or 'grade of the articles were not identified by the witnesses.

The appellant was the owner of an original plot. The Town Planning Officer made a declaration under section 64(1) (f) of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1958 that the value of the original plots exceeded the total value of their original plots and directed the Town Planning officer to make a scheme for the area in question. The appellant challenged the validity of the declaration on the ground that the Town planning Officer had no jurisdiction to determine the market value of each plot. In the writ petition filed by him under article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court held that the declaration was not appealable and quashed the order of the Town Improvement Planning officer determining the amount of compensation in the appellant 's case. The present appeal is against the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the decision of the town planning Officer determining the compensation in appellant 'S case was not an appealable order. [84 E] (2) The principle for determining the difference between the total values of original plots included in the final scheme and not the final plot is well settled. In determining the market price of each Plot, whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not compensation is payable on the basis of the market valuation of the plot at the date of declaration of intention to make the scheme. [851 C] (3) The Town planning officer has a duty under clause (viii) to calculate the increment to accrue in respect of each plots included therein in the provisional scheme and partly to the general public, which shall be included in costs of the scheme, and partly from such person as the Town Development Planning Officer may in each case determine.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama Iyer who died in 1934. He had a brother Seetharamma Iyer and his two daughters surviving him. The appellant filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court held that the testator intended to give the selection to the daughter and that as his brother had died without making the selection he was entitled to the properties in question. Held, that the will was not void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89 of the Indian Succession Act. The intention of the testator was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees making the selections in order to make it certain. The testator intended that the daughters should get their lands after taking into account good and bad quality of the land. The gift cannot be said to be void for uncertain within the mischief of section 90, for it can be made by selection of the daughters and is not so uncertain that it is impossible to say on the construction of a will that the legate must get their properties after taking in consideration the good and good quality of land. Held further, that where the testator wanted to select a house himself he intended that he should get the area of land devised to take them into account the good, bad and bad standard of living. The test for determining whether a will is void was whether it was intended to be acted upon or not. In the present case, the testator had given the right of selection to his brother Seetharamma in the case of the property which he was bequeathing to his daughters; but there were no words in the will that would lead to the inference that the legatee intended that his daughter should get her lands after take into account bad and good standard of maintenance. The will did not show that it was a gift which could be made for uncertainty. The fact that the widow had died before making the appointment showed that the daughter was given the power of selection.

The appellant, a co sharer with the respondents, was allotted plots in dispute. The respondents filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the plots in their favour. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the District Judge reversed the findings of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal the High Court held that the appellant 's name was clearly recorded as co sharers with the defendants and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The High Court, however, found that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the respondents were in joint possession of plots in question and they had absolutely no concern with them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The findings of fact recorded by the District judge are not sustainable in law and the judgment of the High court cannot be allowed to stand. [867F] 2.1 The finding of the District Court that there was no evidence on record to prove that the plaintiff was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the name of the plaintiff as a co holder in law would be deemed in law to be the possession of respondent No. 1 and the right of the appellant would be protected by the trustees. [ 867F G] 2:2 The High court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the Act.

The petitioner, a member of the Council of Minis ters, was appointed as Prime Minister of India in 1951. He was later promoted to the post of Deputy Chief Minister on May 1, 1985. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 by filing a writ petition in this Court contending that he was still functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath register was administered to him as Deputy Prime Minister and that he had been still functioning in the Council for 1950. He also contended that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. The respondents contested the writ petition contending that the petitioner was not a member in accordance with the oath in accordance to the prescrip tion of the Constitution; and that the practice which has been followed eversince the Constitution came into force has been referred to. Disposing of the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A is that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [319C] 1.2 In view of the clear statement made by the Attorney General that Respondent No 1 is just a Minister, along with his other submis sions, it cannot be said that he has been described as Prime Ministers. He is merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. [320D E] Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., ; , referred to; 1.3 The requirement in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirement of article 75(4) of the Constitu tion is only for a Minister of the Union and there is no separate form even for the Prime Minister. [322G] Virjibhai Ram Sutar vs Natraj Premji, Bhavadia and Ors., , referred tO. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minis ter as Prime Secretary and all other ministers sign as Ministers. It is not necessary that he should be a member belonging to the Council or the Legislative Assembly of the State. [323B] Virjji Ram vs Natal Premaji Bhavadia, ; , relied on. 1.4 The requirement for oath under Article 173( read with form VII A was that the candidate taking the affirmation will bear true and faith allegiance to India and uphold sovereignty and dignity of India and maintain the integrity and integrity. [324C] Virrai Ram Sutari vs Natwaral Premjibhai Bhavadia; , ; , applied. 1:2 The requirement under Article 174 read with the Form VIIA was that a person taking oath or makes the affirmation shall bear true allegiance to, and uphold, the sovereignty, integrity and sovereignty of India, and is not merely descriptive but also contains the Sub stanial part. [326D E; 327B] 1:3 The requirements of Article 174 are only descriptive of persons and of their nomination as candidates. It does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers along with other subse quent parts. He takes the oath as Prime prin cate, while being sworn into office, he describes himself as Prime Prin cates. [328D E]. Virji Premji Ram Gujari vs Drhalalji Bhavlia & Ors. ; , followed.

The appellant company was a private limited company. It carried on the business of manufacturing and selling textiles. The workmen were employed by the company as its employees for a period of 12 months in the year 1948, but they did not work for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a day 's leave. On the 3rd November, 1948, the appellant company closed down the strike and gave notice that it would not be entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act. The workers were asked to report to the management about the stoppage of work on 1st November, but the management did not do so. On a reference made by the Government of Madras under section 10(2) Of the Industrial Disputes Act, the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the continuity of service was broken by the illegal strike and that as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 hours in tho course of the day ' leave was granted to the workers who participated in such strike. The appellant company appealed to this Court. Held, that the stoppage on 1 November, 1949 amounted to an illegal strike within the meaning of section 49 A of the Act and the provisions of sections 49 B and 49B were not attracted to it. The closure of work by the workmen was a concerted action on the part of the workers and that several workers in their own individual capacity wanted leave on that date. The stoppage of the work on the 1st, November, and the cessation of work at that night would not amount to an unlawful strike so as to amount to a break in the continuity in service of the workmen concerned.

The appellant, a film producer, was convicted by the trial court under section 292 I.P.C. for using his language as a means of communication to the public exhibition and for preventing him from performing his duty in the matter of exhibition of films. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors acting within their jurisdiction under the Act thereby sanctioning the public exhibit of the film, which was offensive to section 292 1 I. P.C., and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) The combined operation of section 5A of the Act and section 79 I.p.C.; is based upon the combined operationof section 5 A of the Penal Code. [517B] (2) Section 79 I P. C. prescribes a maximum as a matter of interpretation, which is that if the performance of the act which constitutes the offence is justified by law, i.e., by some other provision then section 79 exonerates them at least in view of their bona fide belief that the certificate is justificatory. [525G] (3) The test for determining whether a certificate granted under section 5(A) of the is valid or not is whether it is merely certified as suitable for show by a law, namely, by someother provision then Section 79 exonersates them from the operation of that provision. If the offender can irrefutably establish that he is actually justified by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason Of a mistake on his belief in good faith, believes himself to be justified by Law, it may amount to justification within the meaning of section 79. [511B C] (4) The certificate issued under section 4A(1A) is conclusive evidence that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 293 I.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader in the Patna District, was given short shrift by the High Court in a laconic order. He filed a writ petition in this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of the Bihar State Legislature 's laws on the ground that his client 's claim as the sole representative of Government Pleader was not a legal cover for seeking lucrative land acquisition, as part of the professional estate of a Government pleader. The petitioner contended that his clients ' claim as an independent and responsible person of Government pleader was not covered by Article 136. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the petitioner 's case was covered by article 136. [760C] 2. The State Legislature has a constitutional duty to protect public interest from frivolous litigation. It is for this reason that it is not possible to lay down any rigid or inflexible rule of universal application. [764B C] 3. In every suit or proceeding to which the Government is a party, it shall be the duty of the Court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible to do so consistently with the nature of the circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [765C] 4. The time has come to examine the quality of the product or service or the control, price control, floor to ceiling, the price control and price control. The Court must also be satisfied that having regard to the various functions and duties to be performed by him in the due exercise of that office, most of which are of an independent character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of quo warranto proceeding. [763D E] 5. In the instant case, the petitioner was admittedly the Government Pleader for the Patna district and the High Courts have not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf, for the sake of the lucular practice of a single government Pleader by applying the provisions of Article 136 in suits to which Government is an agent. [762G] 6. The Government Pleader, in a sense, was only an agent of the Government and his duties were only to the Government who are his principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a Public office. [761C D] 7. The fact that the Government pleader is employed by the State Government in the matter of administration of justice, does not mean that the Court has the power to appoint a counsel to assist him in arriving on a settlement. It may also be that the State Legislature may have appointed a counsel for the petitioner or the counsel who is engaged in the litigation. [759D] 8.

The appellants held shares out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the respondent Bank of which at an extra ordinary general meeting held on May 6, 1948, a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the bank and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in proportion of one third of the shares held by them in this company. The appellants applied to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act for an order directing the respondent to pay up the excess amount of Rs. 100 as dividend. The High Court, on a reference, held that the distribution of the right to apply for the shares of a Bank of the Baroda was not a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act and consequently the distribution was not taxable under section 12 of the Act. On appeal by certificate: Held, that the High court was right in holding that the distributed right to the Bank Of India shares amounted to a distribution within the definition of "Dividend". The word "dicend" in section 2 (6A), as used in the Indian Companies Act, 1913, means "divend". It is not correct to say that the word "cividend", in the definition includes "dilend". But by the form of the resolution sanctioning the resolution for distribution of dividend, it took the form Of a resolution for the distribution and distributed the proceeds among the shareholders. The resolution did not purport to distribute the right amongst the shareholders as dividend; it did not also take the form or distribution of a resolution of the true character of the Resolution. The shares were indisputably the value of the new share which had a monetary value. The mere fact that the shares were offered by the Bank to its shareholders amounted to distribution of their shares in the proportion of the share held by the shareholders, did not mean that the right was transferred to the shareholders and the transfer of the rights could not be regarded as dividend within the extended meaning of that expression in section.

The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant on various grounds including that he had committed corrupt practice under section 123(1)(a) and (b) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt and that the allegations made against him were not proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the requirement of section 87(1) of Act was mandatory and that it was only when the election petitioner sought permission from the High Court to examine witnesses or to produce documents without applying for summons under Rule 1A that the party may bring any witness to give evidence or to adduce evidence if it is of the opinion that the evidence of such witness or witnesses is not material for the decision of the petition or that the person tendering such witness was doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had not been able to produce its witnesses without applying under Rule IA. [534B] 2. The requirement of sub rule (1) and who can be produced without the assistance of the Court is imperative on the party to procure presence of a witness by issuing a summons through the Court or otherwice which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring the attendance of a person whose name is not shown in the list filed under sub rule(1). [535C] 3. The expression "the Court" has been used in the Representation Act to include the High Courts and the Supreme Court as well as the High courts. It is, therefore, apparent that the obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub r.(1) was in respect of witnesses whose presence the assistance could not be obtained without the aid of the court. [435D E] 4. The obligation to give the list under sub section (1), and who could be produced by the party, without the help of the High court, is implicit in Rule 1 A. [506B C] 5. Where the party wants the assistance from the Court to procure attendance of witnesses on being summoned through the court, it is obligatory on the part of the party in the case to produce their witnesses without the assist of the trial court by issuing summons through a process or otherWice which normally the court will not extend to procuring the presence of such a witness. [511E] 6. The Court has no jurisdiction to refuse to examine the witness who is present when the evidence is being recorded and is not closed, and the Court has any jurisdiction to decline to examine such witness, Rule 1. A copy of the said application shall also be delivered by the respondent or his Advocate to the said party at the same time it is made to the Registrar. [635F] 7. Where a party wants to produce some witnesses without application for summons, under r. 1A, the party would be entitled to examine those witnesses and to produce them through the witness without the permission of the Judge. But if on the date fixed for recording the evidence, the respondent is able to keep his present despite the fact that the names of the witnesses are not shown In the list, the Court may still extend its assistance for procuring presence of the witness by issue a summons by issuing the same through the District Court or anotherwice where ordinarily the Court would not extended for procuring attendance of the person whose names are mentioned in the List.

The appellant was appointed Principal of a private college in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The management of the College issued an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant on which appointment of appellant was made as Principal. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said appointment and also prayed for a direction that the Committee of Management be directed to appoint him. The High Court held that the radiogram had no effect on the validity or appointment of the appellant alleged to have been made on May 1, 1981 and therefore the appointment of Principal was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the management that if the appointment was otherwise valid and power to make appointment notwithstanding the fact that its power to do so had suspended or withdrawn its power, the State Government could be said to have rescinded that order and that the appellant 's appointment was not valid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of appointment made by the management in contravention of the provisions of the Act is invalid. [982C] 2.1 The order contained in the radiosram had nothing to do with the validity and continuance of the appointment. It does not say that the appointment could be terminated or withdrawn at any time without giving an opportunity of being heard to the management. [986F G] 2:2. The State Government was bound to hear the appellant before making any consequential order. But as there was no power of appointment, it could not be said that the State had no power to pass the appointment and hence the appointment continued. [987B C] 3:3. The letter dated May 1. 1981 which has been extracted hereinbefore shows that on April 7, 1981 the order contained therein clearly shows that the date on which appellant was appoint ed Principal, the Committee had the power to set up a Selection Committee for selecting the candidate for appointment as Head of an Institution in contravention thereof. [985C] 4:4. The appointment of a Head of the Institution and the Director in the case of appointment of Head of Institution and of the Director could issue appointment order on April 27 1981 to appellant and the appointment would be by a body not authorised to make the appointment, and hence ineffective though ineffective and if it may not be invalid. It is well settled that the power conferred on the Committee under section 9(4) of the has been given to the State Govern ment without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind any regulation in respect of any matter. [984D E] 5:5. The power to appoint and withdraw or revoke an appointment is conferred by the regulations. If the order was valid and powers to make appointments were not suspended it would have no difficulty in upholding the appointment as such. But if the power was not suspended, it would not be open to the Selection Committee to make an appointment. [983F G; 982A] 6:6. The Board of Management had no authority to make any order or issue appointment and therefore, the appointment made could not he said to be invalid though ineffective. [988D E; 983G] 7:7. The fact that the order dated May I, 1981 was not otherwise valid, although ineffective and it may be ineffective though inoperative does not mean that the Board of management had no jurisdiction to make such appointment.

The petitioners manufacture "a textile" consisting of rayon threads in the warp and cotton threads. The petitioners state that the manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "a Textile" and also that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately go into the manufacture of a fabric. The question whether the product for which the Delhi Cloth Mills claims exemption is a textile fabric or not was a disputed question of fact. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the goods sought to be taxed were not the "end product" and, therefore, could not be taxed under section 4(1)(d) of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: The expression "textiles" in the definition of "textile" is used in a wide sense and includes all kinds of textiles which are capable of being described as "woven fabric". [501C] The word "yarn" has been defined in section 2(f) to mean any fabric consisting of or containing any fabric, whether wholly or partly, of the fabric. It is not necessary that the term "taple fabric" should be given a wider meaning so as to include all kinds and varieties of textiles. [502D] The expression 'textiles ' has been used in the sense in which it occurs in section 4 (1) (d). The word 'yarn ' has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. It has, therefore. to be understood in a broad and popular sense. [504D] In the instant case, the High Court was right in holding that the products for which exemption is claimed are "totton fabric" manufactured by it were woven by its purchasers "into a fabric". The High Court had rightly held that the taxing authorities should be left to determine whether the "tyre cord fabric" is more readily capable of having been described as a fabric or merely as corded merely as an corded to pass off as ar textile fabric.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal on the contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied work. The respondent No. 4 was a Senior Supervisor in the Company 's establishment at Dhanbad. He was a Junior Supervisor in a company 's Establishment at Dhanbad, and doing allied and incidental work. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Government of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view to the difficulties expressed by him to attend the labour court, Dhanbad since he had been residing at Hajipur and it would be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court, Patna. The Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs, New Delhi, issued a letter dated September 8, 1988 to the petitioner company stating that it would not be difficult for him to attending the labour Court Dhanbad since the petitioner had been living at Hajpur and it will be convenient to him if he case is transferred to Labour court, Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which it was so transferred. The petitioner company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the transfer order of the Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government had no power to transfer the case from the labour courts, Dhanbad to the Labour Court and transfer it for disposal to another labour court or Tribunal. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The procedure prescribed in Section 33B of the Act is not followed in the instant case. [297D] 1.2 The procedural rules which are implied by the duty to act fairly have been explained by Lord Pearson in Pearln Binjraj and Anr. vs Union of India ; , and Bihar State Electricity Board vs Ram Chandra Singh, ; , relied on. 1.3 In the instant cases, the respondent No 4 was not denied the documents annexed to the Special Leave Petition, nor seriously disputed the factum of his residence in the colony at Dhanbad and it is not seriously disputed that the factum o f residence in a colony at Patna is also not seriously dispute. [298E F] 1(a) The procedural requirements which are implicit by the duties to act judicially as to act reasonably have been observed by the respondent. The procedural standards which are expressly implied by duty to acts fairly, cannot be said to be arbitrary or capricious. [299F G] (b) The procedure for transfer of cases under section 5(7A) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is not prescribed in the Rules of natural justice. It is only when the authority concerned has reason to believe that the conditions laid down therein are satisfied that it can transfer the cases from one Income Tax Officer to another without affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the assessee. [300G H] (c) The requirement of section 5 (7A), which makes it obligatory to record reasons in making the order of transfer after affording a reasonably opportunity of hearing to the asses see, is not so much to writing as would be subversive of the principles of natural Justice. [301H; 300A B] 1.(d) The provisions of section 33B are mandatory and they do not require that the reasons given by the Government for transferring the case should be communicated to the party affected. [302C D] 2(a). The requirement is directory and not mandatory. It must be complied with in every case. In the present case, the order was quashed for not communi cating reasons to the appellant company.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948. The management of the Hotel Imperial, New Delhi and its workmen represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, was taken over by the Government of India under section 12 (4) of the . The dispute between the management of a hotel and its employees was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the reference was incompetent as it did not indicate how many of the 480 workers working in the hotel were involved in the dispute, but the reference made by the appellant company under section 10 (1) of ' the Act to make a reference of the dispute to a tribunal for adjudication was incompetent. Held, that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the reference and it could not be said that the references were incompetent merely because the reference did not become incompetent merely on the ground that the workmen were responsible for the dispute. The fact that the dispute which was referred for adjudication related to retrenchment or reinstatement does not affect the competence of the order of reference. The question whether the reference is bad simply because in the order dated August 7, 1955, it refers to a workman of a trade union which he is a member of the trade union itself, does not arise merely because it is mentioned therein that the workman will be represented by an officer of a Trade Union of which he was a member. The dispute which is referred for the adjudication is clearly specified in the terms of reference and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction under section 11 to make the reference incompetent. The word "person" in section 10(1) means a person who is engaged in any trade or business of a company. It does not include an individual workman. The expression "any person" in the definition of "workman" in that Act includes a person employed in any industry, profession or vocation. The words "any other person" are wide enough to cover all persons who have been employed for wages and benefits of labour. The definition of the word "workman ' in section 2 (k) of Act is not exhaustive but it includes an individual who has been dismissed or retrenched by the employer. The appellant company, a trade Union of workmen, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cinema talkies. It had its own establishment at Delhi and had its head office at Delhi. Its employees were employed in the Hotel and the hotel was situated at New Delhi. The employees of the hotel who were working in that establishment were not taken over as employees of any other company or body. The workmen employed in a hotel were taken over under section 6 of the Act by the management. The company was not taken into possession of any office, nor was it taken over and the management took over the management under section 7 of the Delhi Act. The Government had no power to make an order referring the dispute for adjudication as it had no authority to do so. The reference made to the Tribunal was therefore incompetent.

The appellant imported rod bushes and camshaft encroaching upon the internal combustion piston engines. The Customs authorities, however, held that the Heading No. 84.06 was not applicable to the parts of the engine or engines in question and therefore, the benefit of exemption under Notification No. 281 Cus/76 granted by the Collector of Customs was not available to them. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the parts referred to in paragraph 2 of column (2) of the Table must be all the parts constituting the engine and engines, and that even assuming that the bushes and bearings are not identical articles but they are distinct and separate yet there is no material for holding that the Consumption, which have been imported by the appellant, are parts of such engines. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Notification No, 25 Cus./76 dated 14th February, 1976 exempts parts of a engine or engine in question from payment of Customs duty in respect of articles specified in column (1) of column 2 of the table annexed to the Notification. [227D] 2. The words "part thereof" and "parts thereof" are not defined in the notification. They have been used in the sense of "part" but also in the context of the Notification, and therefore the parts which must be included under Heading No 84.04 will get the benefit as provided by the Notification irrespective of the fact that they or any some of them have already been included under heading No.84.06. [228F] 3. The word "part ' has not been defined in Notification No., 25 C.E. dated 14 2 1976. It includes parts of engines, but also parts thereof. So although the parts are not mentioned under Heading 84.07, they will get exemption as provided in the Notification and in the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect only parts of parts of engine or chassis mentioned under heading 84.05, such parts will get benefit of the exemption as stipulated by the notification irrespective of fact that these parts are parts. [229F G] 4.

The plaintiffs, who were the descendants of a Muslim Law, filed a suit in the High Court for a declaration that their father and mother had lost their right by ouster from the property of the Dargah and also for a permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with the management or offerings of the property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High court dismissed the appeal holding that the plaintiffs were not entitled to any right in the management of thewl and even if they were entitled to claim any right or claim the same was barred by limitation. In the Second Appeal, the defendants contended that the High COurt had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the said judgment and decree were res judicata or binding on Fathima Bee and that the said judgments and decrees were not binding on the plaintiffs. The High Court dismissed the second appeal holding inter alia that the right of Fathita Bee was a co sharer in the right and management of Dargah according to Muslim Law. Hence this appeal by the defendants. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A perusal of the pleadings show that the defendants are claiming ouster on the basis of expressed denial of Fathaima Bee 's title at the time of the judgment of the High Courts in 1909 and another ground taken is that neither Fathida Bee nor the plaintiffs had at any time received a share in the offerings. Thus, the plaintiffs who were claiming through Fathua Bee had lost her right by ousting from the enjoyment of any share in Dargah and even though she had got any right, the same had become barred by ouster. [526D E] 1.2 The defendants are seeking ouster on account of their own assertion that they had asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoy ment to the knowledge of Fahima Bee. Thus the plaintiffs have not at any point of time ever received a part of the hundial collections or offerings in the Dargah. [525G] 1:3 The defendants were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not enti tled to any share or claim in the Management or offerings. They had asserted their hostile title and possession coupled with an assertion to the fact of ouster of F,athima. This clearly goes to show that relations between Fathma Bee and her brothers were cordial and as such there was no question of any knowledge to Fathila Bee. [ 526A B] 1 :4 The defendants had asserted that they were carrying on a mistaken belief that their ancestors were not in possession of the offerings or offerings made by them. They also asserted that the suit property was not their exclusive property but only a part thereof. It is clear from the pleadings that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand taken that the rights of Fakhima Bee had become extinguished by ouster and as Such there was denial of his Fathula Bee ' 's right or interest in the property and that she was expressly ousted out from the management and offerings.

The appellant was the owner of a house in Bombay. He had been allotted railway quarters by the respondent to his wife and children. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to get house rent allowance as part of his wages from the respondent 's husband. The Authority appointed under section 15(1) of the Act, allowed the claim of the 1st respondent on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from him 's wages inasmuch as the respondent had been allocated railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowances. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which allowed the appeal holding that the house rent was "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of tho Act, and that the appellant was not enti tled to withhold the house Rent allowance. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The rules in question were framed under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and the appellant could not claim any house allowance from the Government. (ii)The rules did not make the grant in such absolute terms. The rules contemplated the grant of house rent to every employee of a particular category but the rules do not make it the grant In such absolute term. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceases to be entitled whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. (iii)The rule in question was inconsistent with section 7(2)(b) and section 11 of the Bombay Rent Act. The rule did not create any absolute right in the employee to the house rents allowance and that allowance ceased to be "wages".

The petitioner was detained under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA by an order dated February 15, 1980 purporting to have been made under section 2(d) of COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention were as elaborate as possible, that the substance of the statements, of which copies were asked for by the detenus, had been incorporated in those 'grounds which were served on them after undue delay on March 25, 1980 and were actually received by the detenu on April 3, 1980. The detaining authority, however, called upon the detenus to furnish the material relied upon by them in the grounds of their detention to enable them to make an effective representation against his detention. The petitioners challenged the validity of this order on two grounds: (1) that the order of detention was vitiated because the Minister concerned of the State Government never passed any such order and under the rules of business framed by the Governor under Article 166 of the Constitution, he had no authority to pass the order; (2) that there was a violation of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply of the earlier statements, all the basic material relied on or referred to in those "grounds" must be supplied to the detenu with reasonable expedition and (3) that in any event, the 'ground ' served on the detenus after undue delayed delay on the direction of the Central Government was not adequate to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The detention order was vitiated by the failure of the detaining authority to supply the copies of the statement and documents relied upon or referred in the ' ground 's of detention. [349B] 2. The delay of more than a month in supplying the copies to the detenus was not unreasonable. It is obvious that the supply was on receiving a direction from the Central Govern ment that the copies were supplied. In fact, it was on receipt of a direction by the State Gov ernment that the copy were supplied to them. The failure to supply these portions of the ' grounds of deten tion vitiates the detention. There was thus an infraction of the Constitutional imperative that the State Govern ment should withhold the supply. [350C D] 3. In the peculiar facts of the instant case, the detaining authori ty without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies supplied to detenus after great delay on a direction of this Court, made an order under clause (6) of Article 22 of the Constitu tion withholding the supply and conveyed the same to the petitioners. [352D E] 4. The State Government had not applied its mind properly to the facts of each case and had not taken into consideration the nature or character of the document which was relied upon in the "ground" of detention, all these basic material documents and documents were supplied by the petitioners to them after a delay of nearly three weeks. [353E] 5. The supply of those portions of 'ground ers must be furnished to the petitioner with reasonable diligence to enable it to make effective representation. [351F G] 6. In view of the fact that the representations made by the petitioner were considered and rejected, there was no reason why the State should not withhold the supplies of these portions. [354G] 7. The order of the Government is vitiated because of the infraction of constitutional imperative. The liberty of free supply of material to the detenue has been taken away in the instant cases.

The respondent was tried for offences under sections 302 and 307 I.P.C. The Sessions Judge acquitted all the accused persons but convicted him on the ground that there were no eye witnesses to the occurrence, and that the evidence of the eye witnesses did not support the prosecution case. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the acquittal was unsustainable in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the High court had erred in holding that the trial court had failed to take into consideration the fact that the respondent had been acquitted at a joint trial and that there was no evidence to show that he had been falsely implicated; (ii) the acquittal of the respondent was not based on any legal evidence, and (iii) the judgment of the High ' Court was wrong in holding the joint appeal to be maintainable. HELD : The Full Bench decision of the Gujarat High Court was erroneous in holding a joint appeal by several accused persons jointly tried and acquitted at one trial must be upheld. [259 B] In the instant case, it is not possible to negative the maintainability of a joint 'appeal by the state against more than one accused person convicted at a Joint trial by a common order acquitting several persons jointly charged with various offences. The High Court had rightly held that there could be no doubt that the decision in the present case was erroneous. [260 C] In re: Harris Jadav, , referred to. (i). Section 419 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is against the maintainability or a joint prosecution by the trial Court by a separate order at a single trial. The question of competency of a Joint appeal by various accused persons tried jointly and acquitted several persons at a trial must also be held not to be contrary to any provision of the code and therefore not legally prohibited. [ 261 D E] (ii).

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in foreign countries. The assessee was assessed to income tax under the 1918 Act, and the Income tax Officer treated it as an assessable income of the year of assessment. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business as such was not assessed under section 3 of the 1918 1922 Act but only receipt of the income in British India and therefore the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. On further appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee could not be deemed to have been charged under the provisions of the 1919 Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the assessee from foreign business itself. The High Court in reference held that in respect of the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year account, the assessee 's income tax was levied on that income under the 1949 Act and not on income derived from business. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the foreign business of the assessee must be held to be charged under section 23(3), because what is taxed was that there was an assessment to tax on the foreign profits and gains of business, profession or vocation and therefore, the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 (VII of 1918) applied. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the Indian income of a foreign business cannot be deemed as charged under that section. [912 D] The assessee is entitled to the relief under s 25(1) of 1922 Act with regard to the rental Income from house property owned by it and as the income received by it from foreign firm, which was stopped in the account, is on receipt of income in the British India. [980 E F] Commissioner of Income tax vs P. section Rajagopalan, ; , referred to.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of bricks to the said department for the construction of the Capital Project. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent for the supply of lime to burnt bricks to its Department for the purpose of constructing the capital project. The agreement provided that the contractor shall give notice to the Executive Engineer or his Assistant, as the case may be, of the completion of the work and to supply materials at the rates mentioned in the contract. Clause 9 of the agreement provided for payment of the price of bricks by the contractor. Clause 10 provided for arbitration of disputes between the parties. The respondent filed a claim before the Sales Tax Officer under section 14A of the Act. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim holding that the transaction was a works contract. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was no concluded contract between the respondent and the Public works Department of Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not a works contracts. [164F] (2) The High Court erred in holding against the appellant. The contract was clearly of the opinion that it was a contract for sale and as such was not a contract. [165G] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs Chandra Bhan, ; , referred to. (3) The respondent could not sell bricks after manufacture. Clause 13 of the contract provided for settlement of disputes by arbitration. The High court was wrong on its construction that there were no concluded contracts between the appellant and the public works Department. [166A] (4) The essence of the Contract was entirely of the assessee. The essence was entirely entirely of 'the assessee. [167B C] Chandra Kanta Gosain 's case, ; referred to; (5) The essential ingredient of a contract is that the materials should be supplied at his own cost and in the event of failure of the contractor to do so within such period as may be named by the Executive Engineers or his assistant, the said officer may have rejected such material removed at the contractor 's risk and expense. [168C] Chandra Bhushan Gosain & Ors. vs Chandra Kanta Goswami, ; ; , followed. (6) The appellant was not entitled to any compensation for any loss that might accrue on account of the collection of the materials or engagements entered into. Clause 18 of the Agreement provided for the payment of price of brick by the Contractor at his risk and expenses. [169D] Chandra Mohan Gosain and Ors. etc. vs C.I.T., Bombay & Anr.

The petitioner, who was a member of the Lok Sabha and had been elected to the Rajya Sabha in 1977, challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on March 25, 1971 by which he was declared as the President of India. The petitioner contended that the two Proclamations of Emergency were validly issued and the proclamation of Emergency dated March 25.1975 was either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation on 26th August 1975 because the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament approving the two resolutions of the House of Parliament were either ultra rites or had not been published in the official Gazette. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Proclamation dated March 3, 1971 issued by the President acting as the Vice President by his proclamation dated March 26, 1975 had ceased under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 83 of the Constitution and since the two proclamies of Emergency had been duly published in their official reports of the two Houses of the Parliament; (ii) the two Acts of 1976 and 1976 were either intra vires or had become void on account of the fact that they were passed by the House after the expiry of the period of one year; (iii) the provisions of Article 352(2) and (3) of the Constitu tion were not ultra vires as they were in operation at the time when the resolutions were moved in each of the Houses of Legislature. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The two Procamations dated March 23, 1971 and January 25, 1975 were duly published by the Governor General in the Official Gazette. They were duly revoked by the two proclamations of Emergency on March 26.1975. [448B] 2.1 The validity of both the Acts of 1974 and 1976 was not challenged before this Court. The validity or otherwise of both these Acts had to be judged by reference to the provisions contained in Article 352 of the constitution which provided that the period during which a Proclamation of emergency was in force under the Proviso to clause(2), shall continue from the date appointed for its first meeting in relation to the present House of People. [441C D] 2:2 The two Acts were validly passed by Parliament and they were duly notified in the Gazette. It is not possible to say that both these enactments are intra vires. They are merely prospective in operation. But the question whether the two statutes operate prospectively or retrospectively does not arise for consideration in this case. [442E] 3:3 The validity and otherwise of each of these Acts depends upon the interpretation of Article 359(1) of Constitution. It cannot be said that both the enactments operate prospectively unless there is a clear intention to confer power on Parliament to make laws with retrospective effect. [444F G] 4:4 In the instant case, the two provisions of the first Act are not ultra rites and they are merely declaratory in nature. They have no application to the State of Jammu & Kashmir. The second Act is a law relating to preventive detention and not a law dealing with preventive detention. It does not operate retrospectively unless there has been a clear indication that it operates prospectively. [443G] 5:5 In the present case, both the Proclemations of emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions of Parliament until they were validly revoked by two Proseclamments of Emergency. The Legislative Assembly passed the second Act on March 24, 1975 which was duly published and approved by the resolutions.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the premises in question constituted a temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The property belonged to the family of the appellant and was an alienable private property of the family. The property was not a public temple. It was not capable of valuation as it could have either in no case market value or was incapable of valuation. [157 D] (ii) The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that the property belonged exclusively to the appellant. The question whether the property was the private property or a public trust did not involve directly or indirectly a claim or question respecting property of value of Rs. 20,000/ or more and therefore capable of a valid transfer. [158 E] (iii) The subject matter of dispute has to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property is the private properties of the said family capable of alienation, the High court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to them the property itself was not inalienable. [156 A B] (iv) The question as to whether the appellant was a public or a private temple could have no market value and therefore incapable of valuing the property under 0. 1,126 C.P.C., is not correct. [155 D E] In the present case, the subject matter in dispute was the property which was the personal property of one of the members of the plaintiff family. It consisted of a house and a building. The appellant 's ancestor was also an alienantable private owner of the property. The suit was therefore not maintainable.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent company. On an industrial dispute between them, the respondents raised two items of claim for cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements made at present by the appellant. The appellant claimed that they should be given cash allowance for the period of their re employment and that the respondents should be paid the same. The Tribunal held that the practice started by the appel lant was not based solely on humanitarian grounds, but it had ignored the fact that the re employment of retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was introducing a wage structure in respect of the reemployed personnel which is definitely inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the company by the award , and cannot be permitted under industrial law. [571 G] (ii) The fact that some of the retrenched persons have been employed and correspondence between the parties on this subject shows that the policy adopted by the company in re employing retired personnel was not solely based on humanitarian considerations, but there are some other factors in relation to this problem of re employment which cannot be ignored. [572 C] (iii) The question posed by the respondents 's demand must be considered. The fact of reemployment which could not be ignored is a relevant circumstance. It is in the light of these facts that the question posed was whether the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by them. [573 E F] (iv) The Tribunal has overlooked the fact of the correspondence between parties on the subject and had overlooked the importance of the matter introduces a serious infirmity in the appellant 's case as it was presented before this Court.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in sterling was to be made in sterling. The Union of India then applied for removal of attachment on the ground that money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that attachment was "illegal" and without jurisdiction. The respondent contended that the money represented Provident Fund money and could not be attached as he had no interest to maintain the application for attachment. Held, that the High Court was in error in holding that the amount in the hands of the Reserve Bank of India had ceased to be provident fund. The order of attachment passed by the High court was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the . The respondent could not claim immunity from attachment on account of the money being converted into sterling and was liable to be attached. The High Court rightly held that the moneys in the hand of the Bank were not liable to attachment under section 3 Of the , as the amount lying with the Reserve bank was not the agent of Browne to receive the amount on his behalf. The Bank had no independent interest to keep the application pending for attachment and could be attached only if it was made out of the funds of the Imperial Bank. The Reserve Bank was, as already stated, the agent Of the Railway Administration was the agent and the money remained at the disposal of the Railway administration. The fact that the respondent had not authorised the ReserveBank to receive payment of his money on behalf did not affect the liability of the respondent to attach.

The appellant, a pump manufacturing enterprise, issued a notice ending the employment and offering one month 's pay as authorised by the relevant Standing orders. The management did not file any counter affidavit nor did it even file a counter affidavit. The Labour Court held that the action was regarded as punitive and dismissed the appellant 's application for reinstatement. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The order of termination simpliciter is not conclusive and the tribunal can go behind the form of the order in such a case is not decisive and the Tribunal can go back and set aside such termination. [495 C] (2) The power of the Tribunal to intervene and set it aside may be exercised judicially. But if the exercise of such power is challenged on the ground of being colourable or mala fide or an act of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have the jurisdiction to intervene. [498 D E] (3) In the instant case, the appellant did not even file any Counter affidavit nor filed a counter affidavits and the counsel for the Union agreed that the order of dismissal was not a camouflage to cover up what was really an order of victimisation. The Tribunal could go behind this form of order in the absence of the workman 's own showing that it was not bona fide or colourable exercise of power by the management. [594 C D] (4) In view of the fact that the appellant had not filed a Counter affidavit and the Counsel for the respondent Union agreed, that the impugned action so regarded as victimisation or illegal labour practice was wholly unjustified and that it should be tested on its own merits.

The petitioners, who were victims of a fatal accident, filed a Writ Petition in the High Court for quashing the order dated 9.2.1988 passed by the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Kotputli, District Sant Kabir Nagar and directing the State Government to initiate appropriate action against those responsible for tragedy. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition on the ground that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 32 of the Constitution. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the State had no jurisdiction to issue the writ as the fundamental rights of victims were violated by the action taken against them and that the High Courts had erred in holding that the victims were acting pursuant to and under the authority of the Government and that on the doctrine of the State action, the activity must be reckoned as that of the state itself which must be computed as thatof the State itself which is liable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The factual foundation laid before the Court and the limited scope of proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine. [255B] 2.1 In the instant case, the factual foundations laid before this Court and in the limited application of the principles of natural justice have been overlooked by the High courts. The State itself has not taken any steps to prevent the tragedy from being committed. It is unfortunate that some of the victims who were acting under and under authority of Government and had been acting pursuant thereto, had been paid a sum of Rs.5,000.00 by the State Govern ment. [256C D] 2:2. The petitioners have not been able to make out any case for interference with the order passed by this Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Consti tution. [257D E] 3.1 It is true that the Supreme Court has held that the fundamental right of victims to life and liberty is a basic feature of our Constitution and it cannot be said that they are not entitled as of right to life or liberty. But, in this case, there was no dispute about the fact that the compensation payable by the petitioners had been received by them. The amount shall be deposited with the District Judge who shall arrange to dis tribute the same in accordance with the procedure adopted at the time of administration of interim relief.

The petitioners, who were members of a Samiti, challenged the action taken by the State Government under Section 3 of the Assam Rashtrabhas Prachar Samiti Act, 1984 (Assam Act No. XXIII of 1984) and section 1(ii) of the Ordinance by which the said ordinance was replaced by the Assam Panchayat Raj Act No: XXIII of1984. The petitioners contended that after the passing of this Act, the State Legislature had no power to repeal or modify the ordinance and that the ordinance was repealed by the provisions of the Act as it disclosed title was a temporary measure and continued at perpetuity, and the Samiti was being run by its members having elected by virtue of emergency provi sions. The respondent State contended that since the ordinance came into force in 1984, the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution. Dismissing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Act does not provide for temporary transfer of management and control of the affairs of a Panchayat Samiti. It is also clear that although the Act talks of a temporary measures in fact, the Act does neither provide for as to how the temporary measures come to an end though from 1984 till today they were not allowed to function. [172F] 1.2 The argument that since 1984 when the Act speaks of a permanent measure in fact the Act did not provide as to what was contemplated in the Act and the notifica tion issued under Section3 of the said Ordinance taking over the management of the Rashtra bhahas Prakha Samiti could not be accepted to be in accordance with the Constitution, is untenable. [173G H] 1:3 The argument of the State that since 1985 when the ordinance talks of temporary measure in existence, the Government has no desire to restore it back to the Society but ultimately it appears that with considering the question and its constitutional aspects the reply came that the State has no intention to restore the Samiti and therefore the petitioners are left with no option but to decide and upholding the Constitution and the right of association conferred under Article 19(1)(c) of t he Constitution. [174A B] 1 :4 The argument is not tenable because the period of the Karyapalika and byabasthapika Sabha which was functioning in 1984 has come to An end although from 1984 until 1984 when this Act was passed and a notification appointing a Board was issued, the Govern ment had no desire t0 to restore back the Society. [175B] 1(a) The argument on behalf of the respondent State that the Ordinance came into effect after the coming into force of the ordinance is not correct because the Ordinance does not contain any provision for temporary or permanent transfer of the management and administration of a panchayat Samiti. [176D E] (b) The contention that since there was no provision in the Assam Act which provides for temporary transfers of management, the Panchayat had no right to continue to exist merely because the ordinance did not contain such provision is without substance. [177E F] (c) The State Government has not chosen to take any steps to restore a Samiti and it is only that the authorities appointed by the Board or the State Govern ment shall restore back all assets and properties of the Samiti to the Karyapika and the Byabastha pika Sabha duly elected are functioning and they have sufficient time to go on. [178G H; 176A] (d) The petitioners cannot be allowed to take advantage of their own wrongs. They have been denied the right to represent a party in the meeting of the Panchayat Samiti which was constituted under section 3 of Assam Act No 1 of 1984.

The appellants, who were the sons of one Sumitra Devi, made a gift of four houses at Asansol in favour of Kamala Devi. The deed of gift was actually executed and registered on March 10, 1940, some two years after the marriage. On the death of Sumitra Devi the widow of Sumitra, the first appellant, made an oral gift of the four houses to her daughter in law and to deprive the respondents of their right to make a gift. The appellants filed a suit for partition and possession of the properties on the ground that the gift was not valid as it was made by Sumitra Devi at the time of the marriage itself. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) A Hindu widow is entitled to make an oral gifts of a reasonable portion of her estate of her husband to her daughters as marriage. [461 B] (2) A gift made long after the date of marriage or not may be supported upon the ground of moral or religious obligation flowing from the ante nuptial agreement, even though the gift is made some two year after the said date. But it is not essential that a gift should have been made at the date when the marriage was performed and it must be done afterwards in fulfilment of which it was competent for the father to execute a deed of gifts in favour Of the daughter of a specified portion of the estate. [463 C D] (3) A mere acceptance of a gift by the husband does not amount to an acceptance at the stage of the final settlement of the family marriage. The fact that the wife made a "sankalpa" at the very time of her marriage would not make any difference in the matter of the question whether she made a 's sankalwa at the relevant time of marriage. It is open to Sumitra Devi to fulfil that promise as a religious act which conferred spiritual benefit upon her deceased husband irrespective of the consideration whether she makes a "paal" at or after the time when the parties to the marriage, but it may be made afterwards in fulfillment of which the same was competent to make the gift. [465 D E] (4) A person who has no right to dispose of his property without the consent of the husband is not entitled to any benefit under section 14(1).

The appellant filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh, respondent, for setting aside the election of Tej Singh. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by Tej Singh were established beyond reasonable doubt and that the election was not void ab initio. Hence this appeal by special leave.
