Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would now cast their votes in favour to Tej Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubt materially altered the result of the election. [419C D] 1.2 In view the very wide margin of voters (123), between Tej singh and Avtar, a presumption and chance that the polled votes in his favour would now be cast their vote in favour Of section Tej Singh is clearly established. The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubts that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of posters by Tej Kaur was done by or with the consent of Tej Kaur. Therefore, it is clear that Ex P 1 and P 2 which contained the appeal purporting to be of Ruplal were in fact printed at the instance of Tej singh. [416D E] 2.1 The allegations of the corrupt practices are clearly proved beyond doubt. The election petition filed by Tej Pal Singh was rightly dismissed by the High Court. [414E F] 2:2.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was alleged to have committed criminal contempt of Court. The respondent, who was then the Chief Minister of the State, was prosecuted for contempt of court on the allegation that he had committed criminal breach of trust and was guilty of criminal misconduct under section 409 IPC. The appellant filed a petition in the High Court for initiating contempt proceedings against him. The High Court dismissed the application holding that no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High Courts in exercise of its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. When a court is conferred with the power or jurisdiction to act in a particular manner, the exercise of jurisdiction or the power will involve the acting in that particular manner and in no other. Article 215 confers jurisdiction on the High court to punish for contempt. The jurisdiction of the High COurt under article 215 confers on the Supreme Court the power to punish by punishing for contempt, and not against any decision or order of a High Court passed in exercise thereof. [893D E] 1.2. When the High Cour ture does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High Commis sioner is made in the exercise thereof, such decision of the high court in not exercising its jurisdiction to punish contempt. But when a court has been conferred with power or jurisdic tion to act, in a specific manner, that is to say, by imposing punishment for contempt., the High Court cannot exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. [888E F] 1:3. The power of punishing for criminal contempt is not absolute and it is subject to the provisions of Article 215 which confers jurisdiction or powers on the court to try for contempt in appropriate cases. It does not, however mean that when a Court is conferred by the statute with the jurisdiction or authority to act or jurisdiction in a certain manner, its exercise of power or power will involved the acting or jurisdiction of a particular kind, the exercising of jurisdiction would involve the act or duty in a specified manner. [868F G] 1 :4. The right of appeal will be available under sub section (1) of Section 19 only against any order or decision of a high court passed in the exercising its jurisdiction to punish. But where a court, by convicting the contemnor is made liable in the performance of its juris diction, such order of conviction cannot be said to be exercising its power or authority as conferred by Article 216 of the Constitu tion. [878H; 893A] 1(a) The High COun ture has no jurisdiction or competence to punish the alleged contemner for contempt and it does not confer any right of Appeal on the petitioner for contempt.[893B C] (b) It is for the first time under that section 19(1) that under Section 19(i) of the Act, a right of appeals will be provided. After furnishing such information he may still assist the court but it must always be borne in mind that in a contempt proceeding there are only two parties, namely, the Court and the contemnor.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in Poona. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he had fallen to 1013 his share and that the lease was therefore determined under section 111(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as amended by the Bombay Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1929, which came into force on 1st April 1930. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal reversed it holding that the provision in the rent note that on non payment of rent the rights of the tenant would come to an end was a clause of nullity and not merely a clause Of nullity and that therefore the lease could be terminated, did not apply to leases made prior to 1st March 1930. Held, that the High court was fully justified in finding that in second appeals it would not interfere with the discretion of the courts below in refusing to grant relief against forfeiture. The principles of justice, equity and good conscience are well settled principles of equity and justice and must be held to govern even agricultural leases made before 1st May 1930, and to leases executed prior to 31st March 1929. In the present case the High Courts were fully justified on the facts of the case in refusing relief against the forfeiture. Held further, that section 111 (g) as amended in 1929 which was applicable to leases for agricultural purposes did not make a distinction between leases made after 1st October 1930 and those made prior thereto and those in respect of non payment or tender of rent under section III(g). The rule embodied a principle of justice and good faith and must, therefore, be held not to govern leases made subsequent to 1nd April 1930, the principle of equity is applicable.

The respondents were employed as a driver in the appellant 's factory. The appellant was charge sheeted and after enquiry, the Enquiry Officer found him guilty of misconduct and imposed punishment on him by an order dated September 9, 1970. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the enquiry was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the respondents and that in the alternative the interference with the punishment of dismissal in respect of Rama Shanker and Barmapradhan was erroneous while another writ petition (Misc. 17) requiring a second opportunity being given to a workman at the conclusion of the enquiry into his misconduct and before inflicting upon him the punishment on the other hand, it was not disputed before this Court that if no such second opportunity is contemplated by it then the only ground on which the inquiry has been held to be invalid by the Arbitrator and the High court would disappear and the Arbitrator could not have entered into merits of the case or interfered with the penalty of dismissal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The first part of the Standing Order read as a whole does not warrant any such assumption and therefore it cannot be said that the second opportunity contemplated by para 3 was not given to workman at all. [368C D] (2) The second part of paragraph 3 of the S.O. says that "all orders shall be passed by the Manager or Acting Manager who shall do so after giving the accused an opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment of dismiss ment". This part of para 3 does not contemplate any such inference and therefore, it cannot possibly be said to have been made in the matter of punishment. [369F] (3) The High court has rightly held that the first part deals only with the punishments of dismissal and for that last part deals with two different stages concerning disciplinary proceedings against a delinquent, first holding of a departmental inquiry into the charges but refers to further opportunity being afforded to the delinquent to show his cause against punishment of removal. [370A B] (4) The third part of Paragraph 3 does in no way warrant any inference and it cannot therefore be said, that the fourth part deals merely with the procedure for imposing punishment of dismissing a workman after he has been found guilty or the opportunity spoken of is the opportunity to meet the charges. [371F G] (5) The words "any order" occurring in para 3 of S.S.O., do not mean any such order which is passed by an officer who is subordinate to him and the second part deals mainly with the disciplinary proceedings. It does not refer to the opportunity of meeting the charges nor refers to the further opportunity to be given to him to show that he was guilty of the misconduct. [ 371F G H] (6) The word "any" in para 2 of S, 3 means "anything done or omitted to be done by an authority subordinate to it". It does refer to a person who is entrusted with the duty of performing any particular thing or doing something which he has no control over that thing. [372A B; 371B] (7) The expression "any such thing" in the first paragraph means anything done or purported to be performed by an employee in his capacity as a servant or otherwise. It is not necessary for the second paragraph to refer to any other part of it. The word 'any ' in the second para means something done or intended to be used by an employer in his capacities as a master, servant or servant.

The appellants were tenants of certain lands in Malabar to which the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 was applicable. The respondents filed a petition under section 7D of the Kerala Tenancy Act, 1964 before the Tahsildar for ejectment of the appellants on the ground that they had acquired title by adverse possession and that they were entitled to get protection of the Act. The Tahsildar dismissed the petition holding that the appellants were not tenants within the meaning of the said Act. In appeal, the District Judge confirmed the order of eviction. The High Court in second appeal held that the respondents were tenants within section 7F of the Madras Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 and that the lands were not liable to be ejected under section 5A of the Abolition Act. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 7D(2) of the does not require that a person who has been in continuous occupation of any land for not less than ten years immediately preceding the 11th day of April, 1957, on the basis of an oral permission or an unregistered deed purporting to be a lease deed purporting t he to be registered deed purportingto be a sale deed purporting under section 6 of the Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1960, shall be deemed to be tenants if he or his predecessor in interest was continuously in occupation of such land for less than 10 years immediately before the 11 th day of the April, 1955 or which was unsurveyed on that date, shall he deemed to have been a tenant if he had not actually transferred possession of the land to the landlord. [111D E] 1.2 The respondents were in continuous possession of lands for more than ten year immediately preceding such commencement of the Amendment Act. Certain persons who surrendered lease hold rights but continued in possession of such lands till the commencement of this Act, such deed shall be presumed to be valid and such person shall be entitled to possession notwithstanding the expiry of the term fixed under the varam arrangement. Certain land holders who had paid amounts for occupation of land shall be regarded as deemed tenants if they or his predecessors in interest were continuously in posses sion of such property and have ob tained a receipt described as M.R. receipt described the payment as modavaram or modavasam or modvashtavaram, or modivasam, or the receipt described in the deed surrendering their leasehold right to the land. Certain lands holders who surrendered leases hold rights, but continued to be in possession notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law or in any contract, custom or usage or in force, or in a judgment decree or order of court, where on or after the 11st day of March, 1957 a tenant holding land less in extent than the ceiling area had executed a deed surrendering his leasehold right. Certain tenants who surrendered leasehold rights but continue in possession were not deemed to hold any tenancy under section 4A of that Act. [112E F] 1:3 The respondents are entitled to claim protection under section 3(1) of Kerala Land Reform (Amendment ) Act, 1968.

The appellant was found in possession of certain goods on 21 4 1967. He was prosecuted under section 135(a) and (b) of the Act for having committed offences punishable under section 13(1)(d) and 135(2). The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 114(d) read with section 114 of the Evidence Act. On appeal, the High Court confirmed his conviction under section 11 of the , but reduced the sentence to six months rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the goods in question were actually smuggled or brought into India without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory; and (2) that, the appellant was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, The conviction under s.11 of the is not sustainable. [541 B] In the instant case, there was no evidence to show that the goods were legally brought into the country without payment or at a later stage of importation. Therefore, the mere possession by the accused of such goods could not enable the prosecution to apply section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act when the appellant could not know where the goods came from or when they were imported, or that duty, if leviable was not leviable on them. [542 D] Gian Chand & ors. vs The State of Punjab, ; , followed. (2)(a) In the present case, the goods had been in possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually came to be; and the appellant did not admit the possession of the goods at all. Therefore there was some evidence to enable the Courts to come to the conclusion that the appellant knew that the imported goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. [543 E F] (b)(i) The appellant had not produced any evidence to establish that the articles were legally imported or brought in India without paying customs duty. Therefore the mere fact possession by him of the offending goods could no enable the Court to come into the conclusion whether the goods must be smuggled or not. [544 B C] (ii)The appellant had failed to produce any evidence showing that he knew that he was an innocent receiver of such articles without knowing that they were illegally imported or that they might have been imported or imported into India. The fact that the gold was seized from his possession on 21 5 1967 could not make him liable for confiscation under section 111(d). [541 E F]. (iii)The burden of proving that the offending articles were smuggled goods must fail on the appellant. It is immaterial that the appel lant knew that they had been illegally imported into or brought to India without any payment of Customs duty at the time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. [540 G H] (iv)The fact that gold was recovered from his person does not make it a case of fraudulent evasion of customs duties. The appellant did neither admit the posses sion of the articles at all nor did he admit the same in evidence.

The appellants were the President of a Association registered under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The Association was dissolved in February 1948 and its members were paid their share capital. The decree directed by the Court to render accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar was not binding on the Association as it was formed for the purpose of carrying on business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a company under the Vindhya Pradesh State Companies, Act, 1948. The appellants contended that the Association was not a legal association within the meaning of section 4(2) of the Rewa States Companies Act and that the appeal must fail. Held, that the contention must fail and the appeal should be dismissed. Section 69(3)(a) of that Act provides that an unregistered firm shall be registered if it is formed in pursuance of a Charter from the Durbar. The memorandum of association which was dissolved under section 4 of the said Act is not a contract between two or more persons but one of them being a member thereof and the other being a partner thereof. The suit for accounts must fail on the ground that the appellants had a right to bring a suit for account of an illegal association which had been dissolved in March 1948. Held further, that under section 69(2), an unregistered partnership is not illegal merely because it is constituted in pursuance Of a Charter between the Durarbar and its partners. The contention must be negatived. Where a plaintiff comes to Court on allegations which on the face of them show that the contract of partnership on which he sues is illegal, the only course for the courts to pursue is to say that he is not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the Courts cannot adjudicate in respect of contracts which the plaintiff is compelled to rely so as to make out his right to what he asks.

The respondents were prosecuted for an offence under section 9(1) read with section 10 of the . The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence on 8.6.1986 and issued process against them. On the same day, the respondents filed a complaint before the Judicial Magistrate, Chaibasa, taking cognizance of an offence punishable under section 190(1)(b) readwith section 190 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. The Judicial Magistrate took cognisance of the said offence on 9.6 .1986 and ordered issue of process against the respondents. On 8.7.1986, the Judicial Magis trate issued process to the respondents for their appearance before him on that day. The respondents filed an application under section 482 Cr. P.C. in the High Court for quashing the proceedings contending that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of offences against them as he was not satisfied with the allegations made in the complaint and prayed for a direction to the police to register the case against them on the basis of the complaint filed by the respondents, and that the learned Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the provisions of section 210(1), Cr.P.C., 1973 were attracted and quashed the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that: (i) the allegations in the present case concern the specific act of killing an elephant, all ad that such an offence at all events falls within the overlapping areas between sec. 42 ' IPC and Sec. 50(1); (ii) the complaint as framed by the Magistrate was not maintainable; and (iii) the Magistrate acted beyond his jurisdiction in passing the process under section 561 Cr. The contention of the respondents was that the allegations were made in a cognizable offence and, therefore, the cognizance of such an offi cial offence could only be taken on the complaint of the officer mentioned in that section. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that the complaint is not maintainable as the provisions contained in sec. 561 A Cr. Procedure Code are applicable to the proceedings before the Magistrate. [463C] 2.1 In regard to the first ground, presumably certain provisions of the "Act" in regard to cogniza tion and investigation of offences under any other law, the High Courts will be justified in quashing the proceeding at the stage of the Magistrate taking cognizance on an offence. [465D E] 2(i) The words "where such contempt is an offence" and "the same offence" are not defined in secs. 2(3) of Cr. It is well settled that when the High court is empowered to exercise jurisdiction under section 483, one thing, however appears, is clear and it is that when a High Court can upon exercise to exercise its jurisdiction to quash a proceeding at an earlier stage of a Magistrate taking cognisance, the Court will be entitled to quash the proceedings in exercise of its powers under section482. [467E F] 2.(ii) The word "any other offence" in sec tion 9(i)(b), which is used in its widest sense, includes all offences punishable with imprisonment for life or fine. It does not say that there must be any act alleged to constitute such an act. In the instant case, the allegations are made in respect of a cognizable offi cer and not in law. The complaint as originally framed by a Magistrate was therefore maintainable under section 195 Cr. [466D E; 466A] 2:2.

The appellant, a poor man, was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had been in jail for over 20 years and that he had been released on bail in his favour. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant 's criminal appeal pends in this Court and he has obtained an order for bail in this court. He is prevented from contribution to the preparation of his defence; and so, the merits of that matter do not have to be examined now. [345 A B] (2) The best guarantee under section 437 Cr. P.C., is that the accused should ordinarily be released on his own bond without sureties. It is a well settled rule of criminal jurisprudence that bail covers release on one 's own bond, with or without sureties and in other cases it is not the only deterrent but there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against fleeing justice. [346 C D] (3) The Court should always bear in mind that monetary security or release on his bond cannot be a deterrent against fleeing Justice from justice. In one case the poor accused is fleeced of his moneys by touts and professional sureties and sometimes has even to incur debts to make payment to them for securing their release; then, an accused in judicial custody, actual or potential may be released by the court to further proceedings.

The assessee, a manufacturer of textile mills, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 52 on the ground that it had earned profits in its business during the previous years. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle, Amritsar, disallowed the claim of the assessee to include the amount advanced to 'Castle ' in the computation of capital employed by it as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the assessment of the capital employed for the purpose of section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim on the view that the business was not a separate entity. On appeal, the Tribunal modified the assessment and directed that in clusion of the amount of Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to the assessee, the latter concern should include the sum of Rs, 3, 21,460 in the capital invested for the purposes of section 14C of Indian Income Tax Act,1922. The High Court declined to direct the Tribunal to state a case on the question whether the business called 'Cartle ' was at Bombay ' and that the constitution of both the undertakings being the same, the same were the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the assessee that (i) in the previous year to the year of assessment 1951 52 the income from 'Ctle ' had not been computed and included in the assess ment of the assesee; (ii) in any case the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to direct a reference to the High Court under section 66(2); (iii) the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the finding of the Tribunal on matters of appreciation of evidence could not be regarded as a finding of fact, if there was some evidence to support the finding; and (iv) the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner had acted without jurisdiction in arriving at its findings. HELD: The High court has the power merely to advise the Tribunal upon questions of law arising out of the order of the Tribu nal refusing to state the case on a question of fact even if on a review of the evidence the Court might have arrived at a different conclusion. [419 G] In the present case, the Appellate Tribunal had considered all the relevant matters before arriving at the conclusion and in refusing to record its finding, it assumed the only fact on which its conclusion was founded and overlooked other relevant matters on which the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner relied in support of his conclusion. The Tribunal has therefore misdirected itself in law in arriving At its finding.

The respondent State of Punjab issued a notification fixing the seniority of the engineers in Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. The Minister concerned was also directed to file his personal affidavit. In the writ petition filed by him, the Minister concerned had stated that he had deviated from the normal procedure while passing the impugned order dated February 18, 1975. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the impugned notification. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was impleaded as a party to the writ peti tion. [972 D] (a) The High Courts were in error in directing that the Minister be impleaded as party. [983 A] (b) The direction for impleading of the Minister as a respondent is not a necessary or proper party. It is essentially for the Minister to decide in the light of the allegations made in the petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. [992 C D] State of U.P. vs M/s. P.D. Sharma, ; , followed. (c) The Secretary of the Department was also given a direction that the respondent be impleaded. [963 A B] (d) The order made by the High Court in so far as it has directed that the minister concerned should file his affidavit is set aside. [952 C] (e) The State Government should file an application for impleading the Minister in the writ proceedings.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The rent in respect of the land was fixed at Rs. 650 per month. On January 7, 1960, the respondent filed an application under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 260 of the Act on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The trial Magistrate held that the respondent was not liable to pay the rent and dismissed the application. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and convicted the respondent for an offence under section 258 of the Indian Penal Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the proceedings before the Magistrate were not one under the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore neither could a reference be made by the Sessions Judge to the High Curt under section 438 of the Code. HELD: The words "rent on land and buildings" in section 259(1) are wide enough to include rent or fee which can be recovered under summary provisions of that section. [347 D] In respect of rent of land or building under the management of the Cantonment Authority falls to be recovered, resort could be had either to a suit or to summary proceeding as provided in the section. The words 'rent on lands and buildings ' are wide and comprehensive enough to cover all kinds of rents and fees which may be recovered from the owner under section 256. [346 E] In the present case the proceedings were not before the magistrate but only under the lease in respect Of rent of the premises or building. Therefore, the provisions of section 259 will apply.

The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman in the State of Rajasthan. The respondent company sold its product to various dealers appointed by it in the area of each section salesman. The appellant was employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company 's products in his area. The salesmen were employed by the company in order to canvass and promote the sales. The company was required to supervise the work of the local salesmen appointed in the areas of each Section Salesmen. The services of the appellant were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The employees of the respondent company were appointed as salesmen and local salesman for certain number of local sales men, a number of Local salesmen, and local Salesmen appointed for certain numbers of local Sales men, and the local Salesman. On these facts found, the Labour Court held that the appellant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. The Labour Court also held that there was no dispute as to whether the termination of the services of respondent company was legal and justified and if not to what relief he was entitled to. In appeal by the Management, the High Court held: (1) that the termination itself was illegal; (2) that it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promotion in the Area of his operation as well but it was merely incidental to the main work of canvassing, promoting the sale of the product of the Company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The object of this enactment is to provide for the establishment of a Tribunal for adjudication of disputes between the parties. [474B] 2.1 The object and purpose of this Act is to ensure that the Tribunal should not be an "workman". It is not necessary that the dispute must be referred to a Tribunal. The Tribunal has to determine the facts on evidence adduced before it. If the Tribunal finds that the evidence adduced by the parties is not sufficient, it can refer the matter for adjudication to the Tribunal. [473C] 2(a) In order to come within the definition of workman under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's service was terminated, the employee has to be "under the employment to do the work" of one of the types of work referred to in the Section i.e. manual, skilled and/or clerical in nature.

The appellant company was a Government lessee under section 181 of the M.P. Gwalior Dairy Ltd., Gwalior, which had been granted by the State Government to it for a period of 10 years from 1.10.1977. The Company had been paying rent regularly and in terms of the lease deed dated 30.6.1975, the company was given the right to continue in possession of the land till 31.3.1978. The company filed an application under section 182(2)(i) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, Samvat 2007 for eviction of the Company from the land in question on the ground that it had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under the MP. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Sambandh (M.P.) Act No. 66 of 1950. The Additional Collector held that the company had not been a Government lessees within the meaning of section 181 read with section 2(h) and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms thereof. The order of the Additional Collector was confirmed by the High Court in Second Appeal. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Company had not acquired the status of a Gair Maurusi tenant under section 185 of the Code as it had become an 'pakka ' tenant under Section 182(1)(2)(ii); and (ii) the company could not be evicted by summary proceeding provided for under that section. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that the Company was not a `pakkka ' as found by the Additional Collec tor dated 1. 10.1977 in Case No. 67 of 1975. [179G] 2.1 Section 181(2) of Madhya Pradesh Act 66 of 1953, which is the law in force till repealed by M. P. Land revenue and Tenancy (Messrs. Amendment) Act, 1978, clearly shows that the Additional collector was well justified in recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 183 of the code. [180A] 2(i) The finding of the High court that the land was not an 'Pakka tenant ' is set aside.

The Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1965 was passed by the State Legislature of Orissa in exercise of the power conferred on it by article 31(2A) of the Constitution. By section 1(3), the Act came into force on July 1, 1949. The petitioners who were holders of land in the erstwhile United State of Orissa challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it was inconsistent with article 3 A of the Constitu tion and was not saved by article 3A of the Consti tution. The High Court held that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 of 1965 which provided for compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent was in consistent with article 31 (2A). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Orissa Land Reform (Amendment), Act 14 of 1965 is a law in force when the United State was formed. The notification issued under section 1 (3) on the date appointed by the Government by notification dated October 17, 1960 was not law in existence at that time and since no notification was issued before Ch. IV of the principal Act was repealed there was no ceiling limit applicable to the landholders under any law for the time being in force. [15 B C] (ii) The second proviso to article 31A is a piece of legislation which provides for compensation for the property so acquired and either fixes the amount of the compensation or specifies the principles on which, and the manner in which, the compensation is to be determined and given. The second Proviso to article 3(2 A) enacts that where any law makes any provision for the acquisition by the state of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within the ceiling limit applied to him under any Act for the purpose of acquisition by, the State of any Estate and where no land comprised in the estate is held in a person on his personal cultivated, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within that ceiling limit. [16 D E] (iii) The notification dated November 17, 1965 issued under the second Proviso was not in law in operation when the Act was passed and the Act brought into force. The Act was therefore a law which provides that notwithstanding that it deprives any person of his property, notwithstanding that the same is within its ceiling limit, applicable to him tinder any law providing for the compulsory acquisition or requisitioning of property, there is compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market price of that part of the surplus land which is within tho ceiling limit under the principal act. [17 E F] (iv) The Act does not provide for the transfer of ownership or right to possession of any property to the State or to a corporation owned or controlled by the Govern ment. It is only when the land in question is within a ceiling limit that the owner has to pay compensation which is not less than the market valuation under any laws providing for acquisition by tho State. [18 G H] (v) The provisions of Ch. V of the Orissa Land Revenue Act 14 Of 1965 are not inconsistent with the provisions of article 31 A and therefore the subsequent legislation seeks to restrict the ceiling and to vest the surplus lands in the Government under section 45 as amended. [19 E F].

The widow of her husband 's estate had been declared an absolute owner by a will executed in her favour by the widow. The widow was not given any right to alienate the property and she could not be divested of it except under a will which she could make a surrender. The question for decision was whether the widow could make such a surrender, if the reversionary interest of the alienee had been extinguished by adverse possession against her. Held, that the widow 's title to the estate in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death, must be deemed to have been extinguished and the reversioners ' interests would not be affected by the will. The reversionary right of a person who has acquired an interest by adverse Possession against his property is not lost by adverse posses sion on the part of the widow, but it is only when the reversioner does not derive any title from her. In the present case, the widow was under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate and she cannot be deprived of it merely because she had made herself a surrender; but as has been said already, she could be incapable of derogating from her own grant and disputing the alienation which she had himself made; but she did not derive her title from any lawful authority. The mere fact that the reversioner was under an obligation to give possession of the property during the life time of the reversioner would not make her a surrender by adverse pos session on the death of the reversioners. The right of the reversional interest in the estate is not affected by any statutory provision which may be applicable to the case.

The appellant, a Textile Company, was appointed as the managing agent of a company. The management of the company was taken over by the State Government under section 5 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958. The Board of Directors of the Company resolved to treat the said notice as a special notice under section 284(2) and (5) read with section 190 of the Land Revenue Act read with Section 5 of that Act for appointment of a Receiver in respect of the shares of the Polytex Company held by it since it was likely that one or the other member might raise it as an issue at the next meeting. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton Mills Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the polytex Company by reason of the appointment of the Receiver under the Land revenue Act readwith section 5 thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the special notice was not properly called since it had not validly been called since there was no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, and quashed the order of the Collector. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the extraordinary General meeting had been validly summoned since the cotton Mills Company ceased to have the rights of a members under section 169 of the Act; (ii) the Board of directors had obtained an equitable right in the shares in question and there being no other or equitable or equitable interest which would be prevail over the Cotton Mill Company, the Cotton Company had lost its right to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under Section 169 of that act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order under the English Law is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of any Receiver under Land Revenue Code. [877C] 2.1 The High court was right in holding that there was a contravention of section 172 to the Indian Contract Act inasmuch as the Board had no power to appoint a receiver in respect thereof. [864D E] 2:2. In view of the foregoing, the pawnee in the instant case could not be treated as the holder of the share pledged in its favour. The resolution of the Board dated February 1, 1985 was therefore invalid and inoperative. [875B C] 3:3. The fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh would also not make any difference Sections 172 to 178 A of the deal with the contract of pledge. [884C D] 4.2. The word "property" is used in section 172 of the Indian Penal Code and it has no bearing on the question whether a particular property is liable to be attached or not. It is only when the property is attached that the property can be attached. In other words, the property cannot be attached by the Government without any legal or lawful right which could have been acquired under section 172. [854D] 4:3 The word 'property" in section 171 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has to be construed as including all rights and liabilities of a person who is entitled to receive the property. It does not mean that the ownership of the property must vest with the Government. In the instant ease, the Board was appointed only as the Managing Agent of the Cotton Textile Company. The sale proceeds of the sale proceeds were distributed amongst the members of the family.

The petitioners filed a suit in representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others. The Panchayat in the course of its written statement inter alia pleaded that the suit property along with certain others had no sort of right in the suit and that the same had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat. The petitioners also filed an application under Order I Rule 8 for a mandatory injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering their possession. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the issue involved in the Suit was merely one of title to the suit, and that it was not necessary to decide whether the suit was shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not. The revision petition filed by the Panchayat before the High Court came to be allowed. Hence this special leave petition. Dismissing the special leave Petition, the Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 provides that any person claiming right, title or interest in any land vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act, or claiming that any land has not so vested in it shall submit to the Collector within such time as may be prescribed. The Collector is empowered by or under the Punjab Act to determine" Section 11 of the Act provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction (a) to entertain or adjudicate upon any question whether any property or right to any interest in or any property is or is not shamlathy deh; (b) to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector under the Panchayat Act or in respect of any matter which the Commissioner is empowered or the Collectors is empowered under or under this Act to decide such claim in such manner as may he prescribed. [836E F] 1.2 The petitioners cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by drawing his plaint cleftly by draw their plaint, clever by drawing its plaint cletly by drawn their plaint and clever. They have not claimed that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat validly. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was sham or deh. [ 836F G] 1:3 The petitioners could by drawing the plaint cleatly by relying their plaint on the entries made in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the land.

The respondent Board issued a notification under Section 49(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply Act, 1948 for the supply of electricity to the appellants. The appellants challenged the said notification by filing writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no order of this Court adjudicating the rights of the Board on the consumer in respect of the validity of consumption security deposit being condition precedent for the grant of consumption and the supply thereof being statutory, the provisions under the provisions of the Act were not violative of Article 19(1)(f) & (g) of Constitution. The writ petitions filed by the appellants challenging the said notifications were dismissed by the High court. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect thereof since the money is deposited by the consumer with trust with the Board to secure the payment of consumption charges. [278E] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants have not challenged the notification dated 17th April, 1988 issued under Section 50(1). The appellants have failed to challenge the said Notification in this Court. Therefore, the High Courts were right in holding that the Board is a trustee and the appellants are entitled to continue to charge interest on the security deposit. [279F] 1:3 In the absence of any statutory provision or any rule framed under the Act, the Board cannot be held to be a trustee for the purpose of achieving the desired objective and to ensure that the intentions of Parliament shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates harshly on a small section of the public. [280A B] 1 :4 The object of deposit is to secure payment of the consumption charges, since it has direct bearing to the level of supply in consumption of electricity. It stands to reason that if there is a revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in consumption security deposits since it had direct bearing on the operations of the board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus.

The petitioners are working 1009 officers in the Telecommi nation Centre of Posts and Telegraphs Department. They were appointed as Deputy Directors, Assistant Director and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.1.1973. The posts of Deputy Directors and Assistant Directors are manned by the Transferred Field Officers belonging to the Indian Telecommunication Service Group A and Group B. The petitioners belong to this category. The direct recruits to which the category they belonged were not given any Special Pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Telephone Service Group B and Group C respectively. The Special Pay of Rs. 150 per month in addition to their pay scales in the grades of Deputy Director, Assistant Directors and Technical Officer Grade I was made under the S specifi cations and the Special Pay accordingly. The respondents who were directly recruited through the Union Public Service Commission after a rigorous competition test followed by an interview followed by written examination followed by interview followed for appointment to the posts of Assistant Directors, and Assistant Director, and Technical officers Grade I in the general line. The recruitment to the different cadres in the telecommuni cation Centre discharge same functions as the petitioners. In these petitions, the petitioners have raised two grounds, namely, (i) denial of promo tional opportunities to them on account of irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules and the second relating to violation of Article 16 of the Constitution by not grant ing them the same special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who are working in the Telephone Research Centre discharge similar functions as that of direct recruits; (ii) denial on account o f equal opportunity to the petitioners to get it at the same rates at which they were drawing the Special pay. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things as such quali cates, functions and duties are the same as between direct recruits and the transferred officials and that the transfer officials had to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay in addition thereto their scales of pay which was granted to them. [1010C] 2.

The appellant was employed as a contractor in the respondent company. The respondent company terminated his services on the ground that he had failed to comply with the provisions of section 42(4) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The Labour Court held that it was not necessary for an employee to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Court for relief under section 7 (1). On appeal by certificate, the High Court set aside the order of the Labour court and directed the Labour Judge to dispose of the application within six months. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD : The scheme of the Act is that disputes should be settled as far as possible through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side all by every step side by all this step. [737 B] The scheme is that dispute should be settle as far in possible through arbitration and conciliation agreement, It does not stands to reason to that reason that the employee should have been able to sides all by a direct reference to the labour court. [ 734 D E] The object of section 7(1) is to enable an employer to make an application for approval of the Commissioner of Labour in the prescribed manner and from time to time. If he does so, he can apply to any authority under sub s.(4) within six weeks from the date of the order or, if he fails to do so, the employer may apply to that authority for relief. [ 735 G H] The Scheme of the is that a dispute should have to be settled through conciliation, agreement and it does neither stand to ground that an employer should be allowed to side the all by all means. In other words, effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of matters covered by section 42.(1) or an employee desiring a change in regard to any order passed by the employers under standing orders which would of necessity include an order of necessity including an order for making such an application.

The appellants were occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. The respondents filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif claiming the right to contin ue in possession after 31. 7.1971 as tenants from month to month. The appellants ' application was allowed by the Munsif holding that in absence of a month 's notice under section 13(1), the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsiff and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The Judicial Commissioner confined his decision to deciding the issues between the parties and granting one month ' s time to the respondents for vacating the premises. The Munsif allowed the appeal holding that the appellants would have to make another application under Section 12(3) of the Act before the civil court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit for eviction under section 11 or making an application thereunder. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the respondents. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proceeding has to be treated as a suit and the judgment of the Munsif as a decree therein. [975C] 2.1 In the instant case, it is the Civil Court, Ranchi who is the proper court either under section 17 or under section 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure that both a suit under section II and an application Under Section 12 are to be filed. The question whether the petition which was filed by appellants as an application tinder section 12 should be treated to be a plaint and the impugned proceeding as one in the facts and circumstances of the case, is a most appropriate one for exercise of such power. [970E F] 2:2. In the present case, the proceeding has been treated as one under section 47, and the order passed by the court would have the effect of a final order under section 48 which would be appealable as a judgment and decree therein.[975F G] 3:3. The proceedings have to be regarded as a plaint, and judgment of a Munsif as contemplated in Order XXI Rule 58 must be treated in the same way as a decision of the court. [969G H; 974A B] 4.1 Section 12 is wholly inapplicable in the circumstances of this case because even on assuming that an application for eviction was filed before the High Court, it was the same court before which both a suits under section ll and an appeal and a second appeal would lie. The occasion for filing an applica tion under section12 of the is not one under Section 13(3). [970H; 975A] 4:4. In view of the provisions contained in Order XXII Rule 58, the Civil Procedure Code does not apply to the facts of this particular case.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain immovable property. The trial court decreed the suit and the first appellate court dismissed it. In appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and restored the decree. The appellant Society then moved this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the only remedy of the appellant is to file a fresh suit. If a party makes an application before the Court for setting aside the decree on the ground that he did not give his consent, the court cannot investigate the matter in exercise of its inherent power under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [237B] 2.1 In the instant case, the trial Court had committed several errors and required a recon sideration. The High Courts were, therefore, right in holding that the application of the Society was not maintainable. [236F G] 2:2. The jurisdiction vested in the High Courts under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code is a very limited one. It has been held by this Court in Hari Narain Swami 's case that the inherent power conferred on the High courts under section 115 of the C.P.C., is not an absolute or conditional power and it can be exercised only for the purpose of securing justice. [238A B] 3:3. The inherent powers of the High court are very wide in amplitude and they cannot be limited to those specifically mentioned in the statute itself. It is well settled that a superior Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with an order passed by subordinate courts or tribunals. [239B C] 4:4. In the present case, it is not disputed that Hari Narain Singh Swami was not its elected secretary and was, therefore not authorised to withdraw the suit under its inherent powers. The courts below were, however, right, in holding the application filed under section 1 of Code of Criminal Procedure a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. [240D] 5:5. In view of the fact that Hari Narayan Swami was elected as the Secretary of the society and had, therefore. not authorised him to withdraw, the suit is concerned, the same suffers from several errors. The Courts below were right in dismissing the appellant 's application as not maintainable, and the High COurt should have inter vened in its revisional power on the grounds that the trial courts had failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested by law.

The appellant was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction but on appeal, the Supreme Court held that the Ordinance did not cease to be in operation after April 1, 1946, when it was promulgated and that therefore the Ordinance ceased to have effect after April I, 1946. Held, that the appellant could not be convicted under section 304 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as he had been in jail for over six months from its promulgation. The Ordinance having continued in operation even after the declaration of emergency having come to an end was made on April 1 1946, and the Ordinance having ceased to be operative on April I 1946, there was no limitation of the period of duration of the Ordinance in question in any event beyond April 1. 1946, as it originally stood before the Ordinance had been promulgated. The words " for the space of not more than six months" in section 3 Of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, were all equated with the Acts of the Federal Legislature or the Indian Legislature, as the case may be assented to by the Governor General. The fact that the ordinance had been repealed did not mean that it was a law which was in force at the time when the Ordinance was promulgated. Held further, that under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, the words "for the space not more" were omitted from the section and the appellant was rightly convicted by both the courts below.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, on appeal, but the High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the High court had no jurisdiction to convict them because of the delay in the disposal of their appeals; (ii) the appellants were not entitled to any benefit of doubt as they were convicted by the trial court under section 304 Part II I. P.C.; and (iii) the sentence imposed on them was too severe. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. [1075G] 2. Section 354(3) of Cr. Pc., 1973 confers upon the court a discretion in the matter of the punishment to be imposed for an offence of murder and the court has to choose between a sentence of death and a sentence for life, irrespective of the gravity of the clime as the surrounding circumstances i.e. virtually abolish the extreme penalty. [1175A B] 3. The word 'special reasons ' in section 354(1) of Criminal Proce dure Code is used in contradistinction to 'special ' or 'reasonable '. In the instant case, the High Courts were justified in affirming the death sentence passed under s.34 I.p.C. [1107B] 4. The sentence imposed by the High Curt was neither unreasonable nor excessive. It could not be said that the award of death sentence to any of the two appellants was neither 'reroneous in principle ' nor 'arbitrary or excessive ', or excessive. [1275G H; 1176A B].

The appellant was a Income tax Inspector. He was suspended by an order dated 30th September, 1953, by the Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., Lucknow, on the ground that he had entered into partnership with others under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart in 1939, in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court which dismissed his first appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the appellant had entered partnership with other persons under the names of Gautam cycle Mart in 1941 and not in 1939; (ii) the enquiry in 1949, by Shri A Inspecting Commissioner into some of the matters mentioned in the charges, and about others in 1952 by Shri R. N. Srivastava, another Inspecting Commissioner, was void and inoperative; and (iii) the departmental proceedings were null and void as no charge had been framed against him on each occasion. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. Unless the exclusion of evidence is of a kind which amounts to denial of natural justice or would have affected the final decision it could not be material. [584 D] (2) In the present case, the questions raised by the appellant were not argued before the Division Bench and, therefore, the special leave petition was not heard. [585 E F] (3) The questions raised in the appeal were not raised before the Single Judge. The special leave application did not state that all the points sought to be raised were not urged before the learned single Judge.

The appellants are the owners of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The contracts between them and the S.T.C. were inter connected with the contract entered into by the M.M.T.,C. with their foreign buyers. The appellants, who were the agents of the S .T. C. in the course of export, entered into contracts with the respondent 's foreign buyer for the supply of manganese ores to them. The contract provided that the appellants would supply manganese ore at the rate of Rs. 1 per ton and that the contract would be governed by the terms and conditions of the contracts. The respondent ' firm was carrying on business in manganese ore. The sales tax authorities assessed the appellants under section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 for the year 1963 64. The appeals filed by the appellants were dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the contracts between the parties were not integrated activities in the nature of export and therefore the M/s.M .T., C.T.; could not be the last purchaser within the state, and therefore, the M;M. T.C.; could be the first purchaser within tho State, and, therefore, they were not the last purchasers of the goods within the meaning of section 3 (1) (a) of Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: The contracts entered into between the merchants and the Corporation are integrated contracts in the Course of export. If they are different contracts, as they are in the present case, the last purchase in the State is the last seller within the M .M.C., and the contract between the two buyers is one independent between the Corporation and their foreign buyer. The transactions between the appellants and the respondent were different contracts. [444B C] Serajuddin 's Case (supra) referred to.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October 1974 with immediate effect from 1st October, 1975. The appellant challenged the said termination order before the Labour Court which dismissed it in limine. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the termination of his service was not by way of punishment but a discharge of a temporary servant and therefore, the termination was illegal; (ii) the respondent had no right to be retained in service with all consequential benefits; (iii) the appellant was not on probation and assuming maximum in favour of the respondent that he was a temporary employee could not terminate his services even according to the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service of the appel lant was ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service without any break in service for a period of one year. [529 B] 2.1 In the instant case, on principle and precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of sub section (1) for a particular period. If he has worked for 240 days in a period exceeding 12 calendar months, it is not necessary that he should have been in the service of employer for one whole year. Therefore both on principle as well as on precedent it cannot be held to be illegal especially where there is an ineffective order of retrenchment. [525 C D] 2(i) The termination was abso lute and inoperative. A declaration follows that the workman concerned continues to remain in service even according t he date of retrenchment, and a decree declaring that he continued to be a temporary workman would be null and void. If the workman is in service, for a specified period, he shall be deemed to be continuously in service. [540 G] 2.(ii) The appellant was in continuous serv ice for a number of years even though he had rendered service for 240 working days within a period Of 12 calendar month preceding the date of termination with reference to which calculation is to be made, in case of retrenchment dates, and that declaration follows. The conditions are that commencing the date with reference tO which calculation was to bemade, in cases of retrenchment date, if in a year of retrenchment the date for which calculation has actually worked under that employer for not less than 240 days. [541 B C] 2:2 In the present case, the appellant had rendered continuous service for more than 240 working hours within a specified time and therefore his case fell within section 25(2)(a) and he was deemed to have been continuously in serv ice with all attendant benefits.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by the Settlement Officer, Bhatinda. He was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement officer 's report the appellant was not dismissed or removed from service. The appellant applied to the High Court for a writ under article 226 of the Constitution quashing the order terminating his services on the ground that no reasonable opportunity had been given to him to show cause against the order of dismissal and that the order was in contravention of article 311(2) of the constitution as no reasonable opportu nity to show that he was a probationer. The High Court held that the appellant 's appointment was in the nature of an order of punishment and that it put a stigma on his competence and thus affects his future career. Held, that the enquiry made by the Enquiry Officer was not in accordance with the rules governing the conduct of public servants for ascertaining whether the probation of the public servant concerned should be confirmed. The enquiry held by the officer was in respect Of the alleged misconduct, inefficiency or other disqualification which may appropriately be regarded as one by way of punishment. The order terminating the services of the appellant did not carry with it "any evil consequences" such as forfeiture of his pay or allowances or loss of seniority etc. and therefore there was no stigma affecting the future career of the respondent. The termination of the service of the appellants was in violation of article 31(2).

The appellant State Government issued a notification dated November 15, 1968 inviting applications for the posts of Professors in the colleges. The Commission invited applications from candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The appellant was one of the candidates who had applied for the post. The respondent No. 1 was selected by the Commission and appointed as its Chairman. The State Government published a notification on November 15. 1968 inviting objections from candidates interviewed. The Selection Committee recommended the names of four candidates, including the appellant, and the other two candidates, and recommended their names to the State Government for appointment. The Government thereafter issued a Notification dated November 30, 1968, appointing the appellant as its Member. The Public Service Commission was consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another. The notification further stated that the selection of four persons for promotion to the post of Professor should be made by the State Public Service Commis sioner, and that the appellant should be given a chance to appear at the interview. The High Court allowed the writ petition filed by the appellant and quashed the order of appointment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Commission had consulted the Commission under section 133 of the Constitution; (ii) the Public Service commission was consulted only in regard thereto, and (iii) the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed that the Commission was consulta tion either in regard ties to the principle to be adopted in making the promotions to the posts and posts of Professor. [875 B] 2. The expression "in respect of" in sub section (2) of section 133 means "in relation to the affairs of the State". It is not provided by section 133 that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed or any of the candidate, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. [ 874 C D] 3. The word "in" in section 133(2)(b) is used in contradistinction to "in connection with the affairs" of the Government. It is a well settled rule of interpretation that unless there are words in a statute which are capable of two constructions, one construction should be preferred and the rest should be so construed as to advance the object of the Act. [864 D] 4. The words "in any particular case" in the section must receive their plain meaning and it is only when they are clear that the legislature intended that the word "shall" should be read as "may". It would not be correct to say that the Legislature intended that a word should be interpreted in its ordinary sense, but it must be construed in its popular sense. [884 E] 5. The object of section 132 is to enable the Commission to make recommendations for the appointment of persons to posts and appointments to Civil services and post and to make promotions and promotions from one Service to another and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. It would be a matter of construction that the words "may" in clause (b) of sub section(2) should receive their literal meaning and not merely because they are used in some other sense. The scheme of the section is that the Government may make recommendations to the Commission for the selection to posts of teachers, but that does not mean that the State has to act according to its own sweet will or volition. [854 G H; 875 A] 6. The fact that the Public Services Commission was not consulted in respect of the principles laid down by this Court in Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia vs State of Bihar, ; , is not a ground for quashing the selection.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the Bihar State Legislative Assembly and was declared elected. The petitioner filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election on various grounds, inter alia, (i) that the House of Commons had no privilege to prevent publication of its proceedings ; (ii) that it had the privilege to prohibit the publication of the proceedings directed by the Speaker to be expunged; and (iii) that in any event the petitioner was entitled to succeed. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i)(a) The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the provisions of article 194(3) of the Constitution. That clause provides for powers, privileges and immunities of a House of the Legislature and of a member and the committees thereof must be such as may from time to time be defined by the Legislature by law. That cl. (b) of that Article provides for the power, privileges, immunities and immunities which a House or Committee of a Legislature of such State has also a similar privilege or power and it can exercise notwithstanding the fact that it infringes the fundamental right of a citizen. [639 D E] (ii)(a). The privilege to restrain publication of proceedings is subject only to the limitations imposed by article 194 (3) and cannot be restricted to cases where the Legislature has no power to take action in respect of the said publication. It follows that cl. 2(b) which provides for privileges, privileges etc., of a house of the legislature of a state and of its members and committees at the commencement of this Constitution is not made subject to article 19(1)(a), and therefore, if the House has formally rescinded the orders from time lo be expunged, it cannot be said that the Legislature had no power under cl. 3 (b). [640 F G] (b)(i) The petitioner 's fundamental right under article 19 (1) is preserved despite the provisions Of article 194 and the rules of this Court should so construe the provisions as to give force to both the provisions. [ 636 B C] (iii)(a)(ii) The Legislature has the privilege of preventing publication of their proceedings, and at any rate of the expunged portions by the House or committees of a Legislative Assembly upon many occasions have declared the publication thereof without the authority of the House to be a breach of privilege, and the House had never formally rescinded its orders from which time to be deleted.

The appellants, who were working as Readers in different faculties in the private college, were appointed as Reader by a circular of the Government on March 9, 1971. The Government issued an order dated July 30, 1970, appointing them as Reader in the said College on the date of taking over. The appellants challenged before the High Court the validity of the said order and the High court allowed their writ petitions holding that the teachers were drawing salary more than Rs.600/ per month or more in the scale of pay Rs.6100/ and that they were entitled to be appointed as Readers on the basis of the recommendation of the Public Service Commission. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court erred in directing the Government to take into account, as experience, the service of the respondents while they were in the college after taking over the management. That action based on the salary under the said circular had to stand. [777G] (2) The fact that the appellants were drawing a salary exceeding Rs. 600/ on the dates of takingover was not decisive of their suitability for appointment as Reader. [779A B] (3) The Government Circular dated March 23, 1971, alone was in controversy in the High Courts and the reason is obvious that these were not relied upon by the State in connection with the appointment of the Respondents as Readers. [778B C] (4) The appellants are eligible to be referred to the Public Services Commission for consideration of their ap pointment for appointment.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 A) of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 for plying their passenger vehicles on routes which were notified by the State Transport Authority. The applications were rejected by the Regional Transport Authority and their appeal to the State Government was also dismissed. In a writ petition filed in this Court it was contended that since the scheme had been prepared and published under section 69C of Chapter IV A of the Act, the Corporation alone could not grant temporary permits to any one else. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Regional Transport Authorities or the State transport Authority as the case may be, in exercise of power specifically conferred upon it by section 68F(1A) merely means that even though there are 7 vacancies and the Corporation applied for only 3 temporary permits, once the Corporation made an application for temporary permit not for the full strength but something short of it there was no power left in 985 the State Road Transport Authority to grant temporary permit. [987 F G] 2. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court fell into an error by interpreting section 68 C(1) C of the . It is incumbent upon the State or the Regional transport Authority, as the ease may be to fix or increase the number of vehicles that may operate on the route for which the scheme is published till modified or modified. But if the Corporation was unable to provide service by obtaining all requisite temporary permits and ply vehicle because in respect of the remaining strength there would be no application by the Corporation and section 68 G(1 C) would squarely attracted. [986 D E] 3. The High Court and the State Appellate Tribunal fell into error by construing section 68C(1). But if it was unable, to provide vehicles for the optimum strength fixed by the Transport Authority, then the remaining permits will have to be granted to any other person willing to obtain temporary permit and ply vehicles because in case of a temporary permit the Corporation had applied for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining number there would not be application by it and section68 F(l C) will be squarely attracted.[986 D] 4.

The appellant was the son of respondent 10. The property inherited by him from his maternal grandfather 's estate is the property in his hands ancestral property qua his own sons. The appellant claimed that the property inherited from his paternal grandfather was ancestral property and not ancestral property. Held, that the decision of the Full Bench of the Punjab High Court in Narotam Chand vs Musammat Thakri (I.L.R. , approved. The Privy Council decision in Muhammad Husain Khan 's case (1) was binding on all courts including the High Courts and the Supreme Court. It is well settled that a decision of a Full Bench cannot be treated as good law merely because it is erroneous. A Full Bench decision of this Court in Mst. Lehna vs Musamat Thakari (I L.R., , approved, relied on. The principle of stare decisis is applicable to the present case and not to cases where the decision was rendered by a Full bench of the High Court without following the earlier Full Bench decisions of that court. The doctrine of stare overruling is applicable in the instant case. The question as to whether the property owned by a Hindu from his descendant is ancestral property or that such property in the hands of a daughter can be described as ancestral property between the appellant and respondent 10, was not decided by this Court. Held further, that there was no force in the contention that the doctrine of obiter decisis was applicable in this case. A decision of Full Bench which had been followed by the Privy Council in Muhammad Hussain Khan ' case (I) L. R. , should be treated to have been overruled.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, they came there and while one of them struck him and pressed his chest and hands, Matiullah inflicted an injury on his neck with a dagger. He also gave an injury to his neck which resulted in his death. The appellants contended that no charge under section 307 read with section 34 of the Penal Code was sustainable in law. Held: (i) Section 449 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not applicable to cases where murder has been committed by a number of persons, jointly it can have no application. But once it is decided that the act is done by a series of persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act.
