The distinction between the two classes of cases is that if one is convicted and the other is acquitted, he would be guilty of murder. In such a case, it will be proper to say that he has committed the offence punishable with imprisonment for life or to commit any offence punishable under section 302 read with s 34 of Indian Penal code for injuring Ebrarian Ali with the dagger on him. The position is in no way different when Matiulla is not acting alone but he several others are acting jointly in furtherance and the common object of all of them to kill Ebeman down while one used the dagger in him on his person, each of them becomes punishable under s 307 of the I Penal Code for injuring Abrar. (ii) The offence committed by the appellants was not an offence punishable within section 302 of the IPC but only a charge under s.307 read with 34 of that Penal Code and so they became punishable under sections 449 and 451 of the code.

The appellant, who was the son of a Brahmin of Gurdial, was the last male holder of certain properties in suit. The respondent claimed that he had been excluded from inheritance by the collaterals up to the fourth degree with respect to ancestral property and contended that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial at all, that the custom in favour of the daughter 's self acquired property of her father had been varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter which was binding on the parties. Held, that there was no force or basis for the contention that even if the presumption as to the correctness of the Riwaj i am was weak, the respondent had not cited a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collateral 's from succession to self acquired properties of her husband and had therefore failed to discharge the onus that lay on him by producing the evidence in the Rwaj iam of 1913. The presumption as regards the correctness Of the Rhi am was not conclusive or reliable. It could be rebutted by proof of a special custom which excluded the daughter from inheritance to selfacquired property of the last female holder from succession. Held further, that where a person dies before the death of his father and the question whether he is entitled to succeed to the self acquired estate of her deceased father arises only after the presumption is raised in favour Of the collateral, the onus shifts on him to prove that the general custom was not displaced by the special custom. The burden of proving the special customs of the district of Gurdaspur which was compiled by the respondent was not discharged by producing any evidence in support of his claim that the village of Kingarian was a non ancestral one and that according to the custom prevailing in the Gurdaspur District, a daughter was entitled to succeeds.

The respondent was a Managing Agent of several Companies registered under the Indian Companies Act. He executed a deed of sale in respect of certain properties and on behalf of himself and his wife, the managing agents of the companies. The deed provided that when the instrument fell under two or more of them were liable for the duty specified in the Schedule, the duty payable was the highest payable on any one of them, that is, the highest paid on any of them. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant and his family members for a declaration that the deed was not binding on him as he had no power to execute it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the document was not a sale within the meaning of section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 and that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect thereof. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the question whether a power of attorney relates to distinct matters or is one which is capable of forming one matter must be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. The words "distinct" must be construed as having reference only to the capacity of the executant as trustee, executor and so forth, but in respect Of every transaction entered into by him in his personal capacity, the expression "distuminct" is not sufficient in its opinion to constitute one instrument comprising each or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities of the donor are concerned. The word "distribution" in section 5 means that when a person executes a powerof attorney in respect only of all matters in which he could act, it should be held as a matter of law and without regard to the contents of the instrument, that whatever the nature and extent of the authority conferred thereby would fall under article 48(a) in whatever capacity it was executed. The fact that the power of executes itself in different capacities is not enough in my opinion to constituted one instrument consisting of several acts which can be done by the donor himself, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys and cannot be split up into separate instruments comprising each and relating to distinct matter, so far the different characteristics of the donee are concerned, and that it is within the very nature of the general power of Attorney executed in favour of the donees constituting the doneies his attorneys to act for him in all the capacities which they enjoys.

The assessee, a company carrying on business as an investment company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1949 50 and 1950 51. The Income tax Officer treated the depreciation allowance as allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but disallowed it on the ground that the depreciation had been allowed in computing the written down value of the assets. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to deduct depreciation at the written off value of its assets for the purpose of calculating the written up value. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal took a different view and held that this expression "or which would have been allowed if a proper claim had been made and substantiated, assuming the Indian income tax Act 1922, was in force in the past" did not permit the Income tax officer to make any deduction under this section. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative but gave a certificate that it was a fit case for appeal to the Supreme Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, as the written back value had been computed by deducting depreciation which would be allowable under that section. Held: (i) The words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order, 1949, are apt and sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. The words used are not sufficient to give effect or to give it effect to the intention. They are not enough to express their meaning. (ii) In considering whether a particular provision is necessary for the purposes of the Income Tax Act, the Court has to consider whether the intention of the legislature was that the intention should be gathered from the words used in the statute and not from the language used. The word "may" in section 13(5)(b) of that Act means "shall have been reasonably allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income Tax and super tax on business ". The words 'any law corresponding to income taxes on profits ' of business ' in paragraph 1 of the removal of Difficulties order, 1949 are apt.

The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent Corporation for supply of certain essential commodities to be supplied. The contract was to be completed within a period of six months from the date of the agreement. The appellant failed to complete the work within the stipulated time and, therefore, the respondent was liable to pay the balance amount due under the contract. The respondent Corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on various grounds including that the pre requisites for supply were only the three conditions set out in para I of the N.I.T. and that the details called for in para V could be supplied at any time before the final award of the contract, that the appellant had failed to comply with the requirements of para I and that even if para V was not applicable, it would have been possible to supply the essential commodities within a stipulated period. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the conditions set forth in para 1 were only for information and were such they could be met before consideration of the tenders. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that para I provided for prequalifying conditions to submit a tender for the contract; that the clause did not require the tenderers to satisfy the prequali fication as stated in para II and that only para V set out the pre conditions of eligibility to submit the tender. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that the condition set forth was only for the information and was not material in assessing the capabilities of the tenderers as well as their eligibility as their ineligible as well. [239A B] 1.2 In the instant case, the conditions laid down in para III of the said agreement were merely for information. The clause did require the applicant to satisfy these prequalities and that it was not possible to furnish the document by the time stipulated but would have applied for the tender documents only because it thought it would not be able to produce the document at any stage before the decision of the con tract. [240D E] 1:3 The High court has rightly held in favour of the respondent. The non compliance with para I was a serious irregularity and that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice. [243F G] 2.1 In the absence of any specific provision in the NIA Act, it is not possible for this Court to interfere with the decision.

The appellant was the Custodian of Evacuee Property, and the Custodian General of Evacuee property. The Custodian General made an order under section 27 of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Evacuee Properties Ordinance 1949) directing that the evacuee property should be disposed of in accordance with sections 5A and 5B of the Act. The appellant challenged the said order by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the Custodian had no jurisdiction to pass an order which was made by him in 1948, and that the order of confirmation passed by the Custodian was not subject to appeal or revision and it was specifically declared to be final and conclusive. Held, that the application for confirmation pending on the date when Central Act XXXI of 1950 came into force was not competent to an order passed by Custodian under section 5A of the , as amended in 1948. The order of the Custodian declaring the appellant to be a evacuee was not open to appeal nor revision but became final and decisive. The orders of confirmation were therefore subject to revision and could not be challenged on the grounds that they were made without jurisdiction or that the orders of the custodian General were ultra vires. Held further, that having regard to the clear findings of the High Court that the appellant was in the nature of perverse exercise of revisional power, the order passed in 1952 would clearly be subject to the revisional powers of the Central Government under section27 of the . The order passed under appeal was one passed by virtue of wide powers of revision vested in the CustodianGeneral under section 10(4) Of Act XXXI Of 1950 and that clause (c) thereof must be construed as referring to matters ejusdem generis with clauses (a) and (b).

The appellant company was a textile mill. Its workmen were employed by the respondent company as its employees in its mills. The dispute between them related to bonus for the relevant four years, and the Industrial Tribunal made short shrift of the jural stream. The claim for bonus for these four years was founded on custom or condition of service. The appellant company claimed bonus for three years, but it did not include any other item in its claim. The respondent company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the claim for Bonus was based on custom and conditions of service and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The Industrial Tribunal was called upon by the terms of reference, dealing with bonus based on conditions or conditions of services of service, and in that light, the demand pertaining to the practice prevailing in the establishments before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. [612 B] (2) The Tribunal was asked to consider whether the claim of customary bonus based upon conditions of employment or those based on condition of services could be sustained either as a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees creating a term of employment for payment of Puja bonus, or that even where no express agreement can be inferred, it may be inferred. [625 C] (3) The claim of bonus based purely on custom is not a matter which has to depend on the content and terms of that custom or the tradition on which the claim is made. It is true that if the Bonus Act is a complete Code and is exhaustive of the subject, whatever species of bonus, there may be a bar, but that it is quite conceivable that the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which other types of bonus are left untouched. [650 D E] (4) The Bonus Act does not bar claims to customary bonus or those founded on conditions of serv ice. It does not provide for those categories of bonus and confines itself to profit based bonus, nor a deferred wage, and that where wages fall short of the living standard and the industry makes profit part of which is due to the contribution of labour, a claim for payment thereof as an implied condition of service cannot be sustained. [600 G H] (5) The Act does nothing in its nature or character, but only deals with bonus. It has no application to bonus based solely on conditions and conditions laid down by the industrial law.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were direct recruits to the Superior Judicial Services of Punjab and Haryana. They were appointed as Assistant District Judges on August 25, 1976 by the State Government. The High Court issued a notification fixing seniority of the promotees and direct recruits appointed to the Higher Judicial Service of Punjab. In the meanwhile the Governor amended Rule 12 in 1972 providing that the seniority of members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by the length of continuous service on a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation. The petitioners who were directly recruited to the High Court challenged the validity of the said notification and contended that the retrospective effect was given to the rules from April 9, 1976 for the mere reason that on August 26, 1976 the High court had issued a Notification fixing seniority as the promotees appointed to Higher Judicial Services in the Superior judicial Service. The State Government contended that recruitment to the higher judicial service was governed by a rule of rotation and not by the rule of quota; therefore it was not open to the Court to give an arbitrary date of confirm to the promotees. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 12 of the Punjab Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 is in two parts. The first part deals with seniority of officers appointed or promoted to the judicial service and the second part deals only with seniority. The rule of seniority is not a part of the control of the High Courts which is vested in it by Article 235 of the Constitution. [1055G H] 2.1 Rule 12, as amended by the Haryana First Amendment Rules, 1972 provides that the members of service, either direct recruits, or promoted officer shall be determining by the date from which their seniority is to be determined with reference to the dates of confirmation and until that is done, promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. [1155A B] 2(a) The High Courts have not given any arbitrary date for confirmation. It is only after the amendment that the rule was amended that the High courts could re draw the seniority from the dates on which the rules of the Superior Court had been amended by that amendment.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B.S.N. Swamy and G.A. Swamy were appointed as Junior Assistants in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board on various dates between 1.1.1986 to 31.3.1987. The respondents Nos 4 &5 were promoted as Junior Assistant in the said Board on 22.2.1988. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated 22.10.1989 and the consequential orders issued by the State Government on 16.11.1989. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants for Adilabad and Warangal Divisions was illegal, contrary to order issued in G.O.Ms. No. 1342 dated 15.12.1989; that the appellants were not entitled to any relief on account of their promotion as Junior Assist ants and Senior Assistant; that they were entitled to be promoted as Assistant only after the respondents Nos 1 & 2 had been given the benefit of the said order, and that the respondents No. 4 and 5 were also entitled to get the benefit thereof. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal filed by the appellants against the judgment of the Single Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The creation of an integrated division and maintain separate seniority is illegal, as the case may be. [574G] 2.1 The State Government has to place necessary material before the President for organise classes or classes of posts in a civil service of the State into different local cadres for different parts of the state in the manner provided therein. No such order was issued by any authority subordinate to the State Govern ment nor was it issued by an authority subordinate thereto. [575A] 2:2 The creation, composition and maintaining of separate seniority are illegal, inconsistent with the order issued by Government under G.Os.Ms., No. 1242 dated 1.12 .1989. [576B C] 3:3 The State Govern ments have to place before the Presi dent the President and the President alone has been given power under proviso to para 3(1) of the Order, which requires the State Gov ernment to organise classes of civil services in a local cadre within the local cadre in respect of such category in the State. [577D] 4:4 The creation or maintaining separate inter ests for different cadres for various parts of tho State in the form of subordinate cadres is illegal and contrary to orders issued in that regard requiring the State Govt. to organise the local cadres in relation to any class or classes or civil posts under the State in a manner provided thereunder. [578E] 5:5 The President alone had been conferred power under Proviso to para. 3(i) before the expiry of twelve months from October 20, 1975.

The appellant mortgaged his property to the respondent for a sum of Rs. 1,000/ . The mortgagee 's mortgage was later transferred by the mortgagor to the Bank. The mortgagee instituted a suit against the mortgagor for recovery of possession of the properties on the ground that he had no right to sell the mortgaged property and that the mortgagee had no power to grant a permanent lease of the mortgaged properties so as to bind the mortgagee. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed it. In appeal by special leave, Held, that the mortgagor was not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and so long as nothing took place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. The mortgagor could thus in the usual course of management create a tency from year to year in the case of agricultural land or from month to month in the ease of agricultural lands or from months to month and so that nothing took,to impair the valuation, or hamper the operation or impede its operation or obstruct the operation Of the mortgage. The mere fact that the mortgagors had no such power could not affect their rights under the mortgage unless it was shown that they were entitled to have the property sold for a period of time. The words "in possession" in section 65 A of the Transfer of Property Act, which dealt with the mortgagor 's power to lease while lawfully in possession of a mortgaged property, indicate that the lessee could not be permitted to exercise his right of redemption by making an express provision in the mortgage deed for a limited period. The expression "in such circumstances" in the section means "to hold it". It is only when there is something repugnant in the subject or context which would render the words "construed" meaningless that the legislature intended that the intention should be given effect to. In the present case, the mortgagor had no authority to deal with the property in the normal course of the management by the mortgagee and so he could not have exercised his right to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of sale. The fact that a mortgagor was entitled to alienate the mortgaged land for a fixed period, did not affect its rights under section 65A of the Indian Transfer of property Act. The only relevant consideration is whether the mortgagor in possession had power to create a lease of an immovable property in his management by making the mortgage and this could be done only if he had exercised his powers under section 64 Of the Transfer Of Property Act.

The petitioner, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for execution of certain works. The work was to be completed within 9 months from the date of completion of the work. The petitioner sent notice on November 28, 1989 to the respondent demanding payment of the balance amount due under the contract. The respondent filed its claim before the arbitrator and the arbitrator made a reference to the arbitration. The arbitrator gave his award on December 12, 1979. The award was challenged by the petitioner in the High Court. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the petitioner had not been able to prove that the work was completed within the period of 9 months. Hence this special leave petitions. Allowing the special leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary, cause of action shall be deemed to have accrued in respect of any matter at the time when it should have accrued but for that term in a contract to provide that an arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference referred. [362B] 1.2 The provisions contained in Section 12(2) (b) of the Act would not apply to proceedings before the arbitration, and the courts below had justifiably exercised their discretionary power, jurisdiction under sections 5 and 12(3)(b) to permit the respondent to rescind the arbitration agreement and declared that the arbitration clause shall cease with respect thereto. [363C] 1:3 The provisions in Section 14 of the 1963 Limitation Act apply to arbitration proceedings, and like interpretation was given to section 14 of 1963 Limitation act. [364D] 1(a) In the instant case, the petitioner has not been unable to prove the existence of any period of limitation for commencing an arbitration. It is also open to him to approach a Civil Court for reference to arbitration. [365E F] (b). The provisions under Section 14 are in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of Section 12 of the . [364F G] (c) The provisions relating to arbitration are contained in Sections 5 and 6 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. They are intended to apply to all proceedings before a Civil court including arbitration proceedings. The provisions are intended for the benefit of the parties to be protected by limitation under Section 12. [366B C] 1.(d) In these circumstances it is open to the parties who have substituted the arbitrator for a court of law to arbiter their disputes or differences. It would, therefore, be clear that the provisions contained under Section 5 and section 12(1)(b), are in derogation to the provisions relating thereto. The proceedings before arbitration are like civil proceedings before an arbitrator within the meaning of Section 14. [367E F; 367A] (e) In view of the express language of Sections 5 & 6 of 1963 Act, the proceedings before arbitrator are like Civil proceedings before him. [368B C, 370C] 2(a). The proceedings under Section 8 of the Arbitration Act are like proceedings before civil courts and like construction was given in section 14 to permit a party to rescind arbitration agreement. [369D E] (f) In cases where the claim is not to be brought after the expiration of a specified number of years from the dates when the claim accrues, as also in the case of arbitrations, the claim cannot be put forward after the expiry of a period of specified number. [370F G; 369A B] 3(a)(i) The proceedings are like criminal proceedings before arbitrators and like interpretations were given to Section 14 to enable them to plead in the proceedings that they should not have been instituted within a certain time or not at all, and going on to provide, that if an arbitration is not so commenced the claim concerned shall be barred.

The appellants mortgaged their lands to the State of Bihar for a sum of Rs. 1,000 and odd. The mortgagor 's case was that the mortgagor had no right to mortgage the lands in question. The mortgagee filed an application under section 47, Civil Procedure Code, for setting aside the sale on the ground that the execution was barred by res judicata. The executing court held that the objection raised by the judgment debtors was barred because the execution proceedings were barred by the principles of res judicata and further held that it had no merits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions contained in section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, are not applicable to a mortgage decree holder. [910 B] (ii) Section 4(a) provides that "no suit shall lie in any Civil Court for the recovery of any money due from such proprietor whose estate has vested in the State" or tenure holders and so it would be reasonable to confine the operation of section 4 (d) only to claims made against the estates which have vested in, the State. [10 C] (iii) The object of the Act was to provide for the transference to the state of the estates as specified. But in construing section 4, this Court has not intended that the legislature should be given a restricted meaning and it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the statute do not fall within the protection of the said Act. [11 D] (iv) The words "so far as they are consistent with" in section 6(d), are wide enough to include all claims made by a proprietor or tenure holder and so, it would cover all claims which have been made against him by the notifications issued under section 3.

The respondents, who were allocated to the Indian Police Service (Cadre) Group A ' and were eligible for promotion to the post of Deputy Superintendent of Police in the Indian Audit & Accounts Department, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the C.S.E. (Main) Rules, 1989. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the second Proviso to Rule 3(2)(b) of the said Rules was not applicable in the case of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes candidates and that the respondents were within the permissible age limit and had succeeded to be given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17. The Union of India preferred an appeal before this Court against the decision of the High Courts. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to improve his efficacy of selection to higher civil service, a candidate who has already been allocated to a service on the basis of the next Civil Services (Main), Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal for the Civil Services Examination in 1988 or1989 and have succeeded, are to be granted benefit of the success subject tO. to Rule 17 of the Central Services Group 'A '. [586E F] 1.2 In order that a candidate may be allowed to sit at the next C.D.S., IFS & Central Services, Group A, Group B ' and who has been permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to do so will become eligible to appear in the next examination subject to Rule 16 of the Rules. [59G] 1(a) The second proviso thereto provides that a person who has once been allocated under the Cadre to a Service Group A or to a Central Services group, Group 'B ' shall be eligible to compete for promotion. The words "may be allowed" in the first proviso are not intended to convey any idea of the fact that the said proviso is intended to apply only to candidates who have been allocated earlier to the service and who were permitted to rejoin the Service to which they had already been allotted. [60H; 61A] (b) The words 'may be allow ed to sit ' in the C D.S, IFS and Central Services are not meant to convey an idea of a fact that a particular candidate has already got himself allocated to another service or to any other service. It is only when the proviso to the said rule expressly states that the proviso will apply to such a situation that it would be necessary to give effect to the plain meaning of the proviso. [61D] (c) The expression 'may allow to sit" in proviso (b), however, does not mean that the word 'shall ' shall not be construed as conferring an arbitrary or uncontrolled power on the Government to make a rule which is intended for the benefit of all persons similarly situated. [62E F; 63A] 2(a). The expression "may allow" in Proviso (b)(i) of Rule 4 has been used by this Court in several decisions. In the instant case, the proviso does not contemplate that the Government should have allowed the candidates who had been allocated and to be allocated to any service on a particular basis. [63F] 3(b). The second Proviso thereto provides for an opportunity to appear at the examination if they are unable to take training with their own Batch. Those applicants who have already been transferred but not having to resign from the service to which them were allocated nor would he lose their original seniority in the service, to which the they are allocated nor will they lose their respective original seniority. [64G] (d) The third proviso to rule 4 of C.P.S.(Main) Rule 4 is intended only for the purpose of enabling a candidate to appear before the next competitive examination. It does not restrict it only with regard to the preliminary examination as now contended by the respondents.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The grounds of detention were that on 25th November, 1986 while he was in his custody, he had been engaged in smuggling goods and had been transporting smuggled goods. He was also charged with offences punishable under sections 120B, 468, 471 read with section 34 IPC. The detaining authority rejected the representation of the appellant by its order dated 25th January, 1987. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that since the detenu had no statutory right to be represented by a lawyer before the Advisory Board, he could not have been allowed to assist him in the proceedings before the Board; and that the failure to do so would render his detention invalid. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The detaining authori ty or the Government takes the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser for permitting assistance of a friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer. [792C D] 2.2 In matters like the proceedings of Advisory Boards, whosoever assist or advises on facts of law must be deemed to be in the position of a Legal adviser. The Advisory Board has to be careful in permitting assistance to a friend before the detaining authority or the government to appear before the Government to appear and to assist the detenu when he was produced before the board. [789D E] 2:1. In matters relating to preventive detention, the detaining author ity is not required to consult the Advisory Boards with the aid or advice of a lawyer engaged in the smuggling of goods. The Board has no power to permit the detenu to be assisted by a legal Practitioner. It is for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of denial of such opportunity. [788F] 2 :2. In cases like the present, the detention order was passed without affording any opportunity to the appe lant to be heard before the order of detention became vitiated. The detenu was not afforded legal assistance in proceedings before tho Advisory Board and the refusal of such assistance to the detenu was justified. [ 789A B] 3:3. In view of the position that the detaining au thority or the Govern ment takes the assistance of the legal advisers before the advisory Board, it cannot be said that the refusal by the Advisory board to permit him to be engaged in any other proceeding is vitiated. [781F G] 4. The order of the High Court is quashed and set aside. The appellant shall be released forthwith from detention.

The appellants were the owners of certain goods and requisitioned them for a period of three years from September 30, 1946. The requisition orders were served on the managing agents on September 30. 1946, under r. 75 A(2) of the Rules framed under the Act. The appellants filed suits in the High Court against the Union of India and the Mills for possession of the goods. The High Court decreed the suits but the suits were dismissed by a single judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the requisition orders did not bind the managing agent, and (2) the delivery orders were not properly served on them as required by r. 74 A(1). Held, that the services of the managing agency were properly served and the appellants had no right to be heard in the suits. The delivery orders did neither bind the appellants nor could they be said to have been served on their own behalf. The services of requisition were not validly served on it as required under r 75 A (2). The delivery order was not properly addressed to the managing Agents and the delivery order did not represent the delivery of the delivery Orders. Held, further, that in view of section 18 of the Act the title in these cases had not passed to the holders of pucca delivery orders on September30, 1946, for the goods were not ascertained till then whatever may be the position of the holders or the delivery ordered. The service of the requisition order was also good service in the case of orders of requisition and notices of acquisition were valid and binding on the respective defendants.

The assessee, a Private Limited Company, set apart a sum of Rs. 4,50,000 from its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. Out of this amount an amount of Rs 4,51,000 continued to remain and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that no action could be taken against the assessee under Section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922. In reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of Revenue and against the asses see. Hence this appeal by the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that no order levying additional tax under Section23A was made on or before the relevant date to the relevant assessment year 1963 64. [112E] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc. vs Commissioner of income Tax, A.P., etc. , distinguished. 1.2 The assessee itself called it a provision and not a reserve. It did not call it a reserve nor was set apart or appropriated as a reserve and was not set apart as a reserves. [114F] Metal Tubes Ltd. vs Their workmen, ; and Commissioner of Incometax, Andhra pradesh vs Vazir Sultan & Co., , referred to. 1(a) The distinction between a provision for a reserve is stated in the following words: "In other words, the broad distinction between provision and a reserve has been made against anticipated losses and contingencies and charges against profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts. [115G] Metal Corpn. of India Ltd. etc. Vazirad & Co.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as temporary Assistant Engineers (on a later point of time) in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I. They were informed that six of them would be absorbed into the Indian Railways Service of Engineering Officers (Class 1) every year, this figure in the subsequent years was increased from time to time when in 1975, the figure as increased stood at 25 per year. The petitioners in their writ petitions challenged the classification of temporary Assistant Officers separately from the Indian railway Service of Class I and contended that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis of half the total period of continuous service in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The distinction between two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case specifically said that relief of equality was being denied to the petitioners because of the history, origin, and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed however as to the validity of the given weightage of half of the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, because of its being questioned elsewhere. [1027B C] 2. The principle of constructive res judicata is based on sound principles of law and not upon abstract doctrine. It is well settled that in order to be valid, it must be shown that there has been complete absorption of the personnel into one service or that their length of continuous services was such as would adversely affect them. [1127C D] 3. The concept of equality before law enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution is not a static concept but a living concept. It has to be applied with all its rigour and it cannot be extended to all situations which may arise from time immemorial or even by way of amendment. [1228D E] 4. The doctrine of constructive Res judicata is founded on sound principle of law. It does not require that the decision must be given on the question of constitutional validity of a statute, and it should be applied to all cases where there has already been complete absorbed of the persons in the service. [1102B C; 1127A] 5. The principles of constructive constructive resjudicata are well settled. It cannot be invoked by a party to a litigation between two rival parties or between them. A dispute raised before this Court is not one which is directly and substantially in issue in a proceeding between the same parties but between the parties. [1012C D; 1128A] 6. The State is prohibited to create separate channels of service and create discrimination by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotional avenues reasonably falls to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by direct Recruit 's cases specifically said. [1003D E; 1129F] 7. The difference between two Services was well advised in Kattyani Dayal vs State of M.P., ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted by the Special Court under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, for offences under sections 9 and 11 of the Indian Penal Code read with sections 109 and 109 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to try the case as the provisions of the Act were not applicable to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 5 (1) Of the WestBengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949 (No. XLIII of 1949), which authorised the State Government to direct any class of cases or classes of offences to be tried by a special tribunal constituted under the Act, and that the delegation of such power to the State Govern ment to direct "offences" was beyond the competence of the legislature and was, therefore void under article 13. Held, that section 11 of Saurashtra Ordinance No. XLII of 1949, which authorised a State Government not to direct 'offenses ' or classes thereof ' to be try by a Special Tribunal constituted under that Ordinance, was ultra vires article 13 Of the Constitution and was void under articles 14 and 19 of the Constitu tion. The notification issued by the State of Saurashtra in exercise of its executive power under section 3(1)(c) of that Act, authorised the Government to make rules for regulating the procedure of trial of offences or classes or classes by Special Courts constituted under it. The State Government was competent to make a classification on the basis of a proper classification and the notification issued thereunder offended against article 14 Of the Constitu tution and as such void under section 11 Of the Act.

The appellants were convicted under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the evidence of P.W. 1, who was undoubtedly present in the eastern kotha of the house of the deceased could not be relied upon because he had intentionally made improvements in his version about the occurrence; (ii) the prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily and beyond all reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the appellant for the offence under section 395 I. P.C., was not justified; (iii) the High Court erred in holding that the evidence was corroborated by the evidence on record and that it could not have been relied upon as a piece of evidence to convict the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High court for rejecting the evidence are totally untenable. It is well settled that in an appeal against acquittal, the Supreme Court would normally interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the trial court unless there are compelling reasons to do so. [901 B] 2. In the instant case, the prosecution had proved the charge beyond all doubt and beyond any reasonable doubt. The evidence of the eye witnesses was corroborated in material particulars by P.Ws. 1 and 7 who were undoubtedly present at the scene of occurrence. There was sufficient moon light at the time of the occurrence and it is not improbable that P. Ws. 1 to 7 and 8 could have seen some of the offenders and that their evidence could not he relied upon. [964 C D] 3. The prosecution has established the case beyond all shadow of doubt and the conviction under section 302 I.p.C.[964 E] 4. The motive for the crime is the presence of P W. 1 at the place of occurrence and the accused having been found broken open, it is difficult to accept the evidence that P Ws.1 to 7 had witnessed the incident. [963 G H] 5. The circumstances of the case show that PWs.1, 7 and8 were injured in the house and that they could not identify them. There is sufficient moons light at that time of occurrence which has taken place and must have sufficient opportunity to indentify with the help of lantern which was burning, the appellants who were previously known to her and not strangers.

The appellant Corporation created under a State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to appoint its employees on probation for one year. The services of the respondents were terminated by an order dated June 30, 1981. The appellant Corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of their services and also sought a direction that they should be paid wages at the rate of Rs. 500 per month from the date of termination till the date on which their services were terminated. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the termination was bad as it amounted to retrenchment and for non compliance with the provisions of section 25F of the (Disputes Act ' for short) the termination is bad, but set aside the Award of the Labour Court and directed reinstatement of the appellant Corporation with back wages. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Corporation that the High Courts were in error in holding that termination of the services of a workman on ground of unsuitability amounted to 'retrenchment ' as defined in section 2(oo) and as used in section 25FFF had no wider meaning than ordinary accepted connotation of the word; it means discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service of a probationer would also amount to retrenchment. [793G] 2. The effect was that every case of termination of services by act of employer even if such termination involved any consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking was to be treated as 'retrench ment for the purposes of notice, compensation etc. ' and not contrary to the scheme of the Act. [788A B] 3. The words 'termination of service for any reasons whatsoever" in section 26F(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act are wide enough to include termination of a service of an employee on the transfer or retrenchment of the Undertaking. The consequence was that each case must be of termination simpliciter and not of service simpliciter. [789C D] 4. The word 'retrenched ' in section 3(oo)(a) of 'the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 has been used in a wider sense than the ordinary accepted meaning of the term. It means discharge or retrenchment by act or conduct of employer. [ 788A B; 789B C] 5. The expression 'ret retrenched ' must include every termination of employment by an act of the employer even though such termination is involved in transfer or termination of undertaking. The intention was that the word 'termination ' should be understood to mean discharge or termination simpliciter of service and not merely termination of an existing service. [ 789F] 6.

The assessee, a dealer in textiles, was assessed to sales tax for the four quarters ending March 1959. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sale effected by the asses see was a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The revision application filed by the appellant before the Board of Revenue was rejected on 27th January 1960. In the revision petition to the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, the Board held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assesses and that the assessee was a 'dealer ' under the Act and therefore liable to assessment under the said Act. The High Court also dismissed the revision application. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The activity of so disposing of the goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of disposal so disposing off the goods remains un claimed. [782G] 1.2 In the case of the asses sees South Eastern Railway, what were sold were unclaimed goods. The Railway was a carrier of the Goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained uncovered for a number of years, it could not be said that the business of so disposed of continued to remain unearth ered. There could be no dispute that the activities of so dispose of were adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of goods. It was an activity, which may he regarded as integral or ancillary for its business. It could not therefore be said to be an activity of a "business" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940. [781A B] 1:3 The activity so disposing is an incidental or subsidiary to its main business as carriers of goods and if on the stage it remained unear thorised material lying with it. It may be an act which may incidentally be regarded by necessarily ancillary or incidental to its 'business as carrier, of thegoods. It would not therefore, be correct to say that the transaction of so disposal of the said goods remained an integral part of the main activity of carriage of the same goods.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of conspiracy to cheat and fraudulently misappropriate Government securities. The prosecution case was that the appellant had entered into a contract with the Bank of India, Bombay, for the purchase of certain securities and for the payment of the same to the Bank. The appellant was convicted under section 409 read with section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal the High Court acquitted him but on appeal by special leave it was contended that the contract for the sale of securities had taken place on September 16, 1955, and that the money had been paid to the Union Agencies when funds were needed and also providing funds in the Insurance Company 's account with the Chartered Bank, Bombay. Held, that the transaction was not a mere ruse to show that the moneys were received by the appellant from the Insurance company or the receipt of the cash or other transactions, his role having begun according to the prosecution after the offence under section409 I. P.C., after the commission of the offence tinder section 409 I.P.C. and after consultation with the Central Government, was a mere device to cheat the Bank and thereby misappropriate it. The transaction was one in which the appellant was acting as the Director of the latter company and not on his own behalf. The money had to be paid by the Bank to the appellant for the purpose of meeting its losses. The fact that the amount was received in cash did not show that it was a case where the appellant acted as the Managing Agent of the Bank or that he had no knowledge of the passing of the money from the funds of the Insurance Co. Ltd., and that therefore the transaction could not be said to have been entered into by the Managing Agents with the appellant. The presumption under section 4 Of the Indian Contract Act is rebutted by the evidence on record. Held further, that there was nothing in the terms of the contract which required the Managing Agency to make a profit out of the funds and to invest it in securities. It was really on the basis of his paying the money out of its Insurance Company to the Central Agencies as he had nothing to do with the movement of the securities held by the Insurance Companies to the Exchange Agencies, as he bad nothing to doing with the diversion of the fund of the insurance company to the Corporation Agencies. The Bank was not entitled to invest the moneys in securities in the Bank 's accounts and it could not therefore be said that the Bank had acted dishonestly or fraudulently.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. They were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the new State of Bombay and later in the State. The appellants were allotted the ministerial services of the Secretariats of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States respectively. By a notification dated August 19, 1966 issued under section 115(7) of the Government of India Act, 1935, the appellants were transferred to the Secretariat for being posted in the Secretariat. In pursuance of this notification the appellants filed a petition before the High Court challenging the order of transfer on the ground that the transfer was illegal and void as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellants had been transferred to their Secretariat by the State Government under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1947 and that the order was not in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The proviso to section 115 (7) is intended to ensure that conditions of service shall not be changed except with the prior approval of the Central Government. Transfer of the ministerial staff from the States of Saurashtra and Saurashtra to the secretaries of the erstwhile Saurashtra State and were allotted in connection therewith to servein connection with affairs of another State. [522 B C] (2) The appellants are transferred to Secretariat of Gujarat, but they were not absorbed in the Ministerial service of their Secretariat. They had been allocated to serve as Secretary of the Department of Public Service in connection With the affairs and affairs of a State. In view of this rule the appellants could not be deprived of their statutory right under section 116(7). [523 C D] (3) The order of the transfer made by the Government was valid and binding on the appellants.

The petitioners who were dealers in cotton and other goods filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of section 5(2)(a) (vi) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that since the tax was levied, whether on sale or purchase at the first transaction, the stage was fixed and that the dealer could always claim exemption under section 5 (2)(b)(vi), that party is liable to pay sales tax and would have also paid the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that since a tax has been levied, both in respect of declared goods and taxable turnover, the State Legislature had no power to levy tax at more than one stage; that the Act itself did not indicate the stage at which the tax is to be levied and because under section 15(1) of Central Act there could be no liability for payment of tax unless this stage was so stated in the Act or the rules thereunder. HELD: (i) The contention must fail. Section 5(1)(a), as it stood before its amendment, provided that such tax shall not be levied on the purchase or sale of declaredgoods at more then one stage and that for purposes of section 15, the tax could be collected only at one stage. [539 B] (ii) The Act itself does not indicate that the stage is fixed and it is not enough for the State to say that a person who is not liable to tax must nevertheless pay tax, must nevertheless be pay it in the first instance and then claim refund at a later stage. It is clear from section 5 that if a dealer has purchased cotton and sells it after the period provided for in section 5, he must nevertheless, pay it at one time and then claims refund at once. [511 C] (iii) The tax could not be said to be higher in the case of goods liable to purchase tax.

The respondent mortgaged his properties to the appellant for a sum of Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition under section 47 and O. XXI, r. 2, Civil Procedure Code praying that as the amount thus deposited together with the payments already made completely wiped off the amount due under the decree as scaled down by the High Court in favour of defendants 2 to 7, full satisfaction of the decree might be recorded exoner at Rs. 1,05,000 and odd. The respondent contended that the amount payable by him under the mortgage decree was a debt scaled over in accordance with the provisions of the Act and as such he was liable for the entire amount of the mortgage debt. Held, that the subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of the execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release the interest of defendant No. 2 and that by defendants 3 to 7 separately on payment of certain specified amounts by them together with their interest would not be liable to be sold. The subsequent agreement was a contract for sale of immovable property and it was only an execu tive one and in substance it was a mortgage debt and the security had been split up into two groups of defendants 3, 7 and 8. The earlier agreement between parties arrived in course Of the execution proceeding by which decreeholders agree to release interest of the respondent would be sold for the entirety of the mortgaged property including their interest.

The appellants were tenants of the respondents. The City Civil Court, Bombay, in a suit for possession of the premises, granted a decree for eviction against the first respondent on the ground that he was a tenant within the meaning of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as amended by Act No. XLIII of 1956. The appellants contended that the City Civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed it on the view that there was no lawful subletting by the first plaintiff of the property to the second respondent. Held, that the High Court correctly decided that the suit filed by the appellants in the City civil Court was one relating to possession of premises where the relationship of landlord and tenant admittedly subsists between the parties, jurisdiction to try such a suit was exclusively vested in the courts specified in section 28 and no other. The provisions of Part 11 of the Act applied only to suits or proceedings between a landlord and a tenant relating to the recovery of rent or possession of any premises to which the provisions of the Part II of the Indian , apply, even though they may be in the nature of a title to the premises. The Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1948, did not confer jurisdiction on the City Court to entertain suits relating to eviction of tenants and the right of the landlord to evict any of the defendants was only with regard to possession and not with regardto the tenancy rights of the parties. The High Court rightly decided that a suit in the city Civil Court was not one between a tenant and a landlord because the defendants of this suit did not admit that the plaintiffs were the tenants of premises within the definition of section 2(6) of the City Rent Act, and no more.

The respondent, a private limited company, was incorporated under the name of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., hereafter called the Company. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba transferred his business to the Company and on July 7 , 1955, an appointment by a director of another person as the managing director of the Company by the will of Dadoba was void. The company then appointed the appellant Govind as the Managing Director of the company by the said will. On August 7, 1956, the respondent filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that he had been appointed as the manager of the appellant company and for a decree for possession of the premises in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the appointment of the respondent was void under section 312 of the new Act. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the proviso to section 86B of the old Act did not help the appellant and the respondent could not claim to have a say in the appointment Of his successor by a Director intending to absent himself from office. The proviso to s.86B of old Act does not help him because the word "assignment" would include an "appointment". It is only when the section expressly excludes the appointment or appointment of a person as managing director that section can be invoked and the proviso applies. In the present case, Dadatar had power under the main part of section 86 B of the Act to appoint a person to be the managing directors in succession to him, and in exercise of that power he appointed the respondent as the "assigned office" by a company intending to do so. The word "his" would not include an appointment of his successor but it did not include appointment of any other person as a director.

The respondent landlady filed a eviction petition against the appellants and one another firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart. The appellants contended that they were unlawful sub tenants and that their tenancy was not terminated by the respondent. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully sublet the shop to M/ s. Adeshwar glass Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction petition was not maintainable at all. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent subletting the said shop let out to the said firm and one other partnership firm, M/S Adeshwar Tub Mart without join any of their partners. The High Court in revision held that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appel lants had unlawfully sub tenants. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction peti tion was filed against the firm and another partnership firm and the other partnership firms were also joined by the respond ents as respondents in the eviction Petition on the ground that they had unlawfully, without the permission of the responden ts. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The law is well settled that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. [420B] 2.1 In the instant case, though in a wrong name, the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business at the said premises even for some time during which the appellants con tained firm had not ceased to carried on the said prem ises. The partnership firm was carried on by the partners themselves and that firm was carrying on the same business even for sometime during which they firm had no ceased to do so. [422D] 2:2. In the case of Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm is carried on in the said Premises even for a number of time during when the appellants ' firm had cease to carry out the business. The partners of M /s Adeswar Glass Mart were carrying on their business at premises even during which their firm had discontinued to carry it on the aforesaid prem ise. Therefore, there was evidence to show that rent was received by the appellants from M/o Adeshwarace Glass Mart without joined any of them as respondents. [416E] 3:3. The contention of Mr. Nayar must fail. There can be no doubt that the partners are before the Court though in wrong name. In this case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a period of number of years. [414F] 4:4. The appeal must accordingly fail.

The Andhra Pradesh Urban agglomeration (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for imposition of ceiling on land situate within the urban agglomerations. The Andhra Pradesh Act came into force on 1st January 1975. Section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Central Act defined "family unit" as meaning a person who held land in excess of the ceiling area and includes a person holding land in an urban agglomeration. Section 3(f) defines "family" to mean a person, who held or was deemed to have held land under the State Government for the time being in force in any part of India. The Act came up for consideration before this Court on several occasions. In the State of Andhra Pradesh there were two separate Acts, one relating to the ceiling areas and the other relating to urban agglomations. Section 4(1) of that Act provided that "all lands situated within the limits of a municipality shall be deemed to be land situate in any area which is not an urban or agglomeration" and section 5(2)(a)(ii)(b) provided for imposition by the State Legislature of ceiling area on land situated within such area. The two Acts were challenged before this court on the ground that (1) the Andhra Pradesh Legislature had no legislative competence to provide in respect of the land situate outside the urban or uncultivated agglomeration and since the concept of agglomeration defined in section 2(p)(A) (ii) was an expensive concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified as an urban Aggomeration under section 2 (n)(a) (i) of tho Central Act but until it is so notified it would not be an urban cultivable agglomerating or a land within the ceiling limit would be liable to be determined as on 1.1 1975 under the Andhra Act and (2) since the definition of "family units" in section 3(j) was amended by the Andhra Nadu Urban agglomerated Lands (Ceiling & Regulation) Amendment Act, 1977, it could not be said that the Andhra Legislature had legislative competence in enacting the Andhra State Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Andhra Land Ceiling Act, 1961 and the Andhra pradesh Act are valid. [1157C] 2.1 Section 4 (1)(A), as amended by Act No. 11 of 1977, provides that "any land situated in any urban aggl yard" shall be liable for the payment of land revenue to the State. The land obtained by the divided minor son on partition would be entitled to remain with him. [1102D] 2(a) The Andhra Act was enacted with a view to provide ceiling on lands situate within its limits and the provisions of that law were made applicable to such areas. The Land in question is not covered by the definition in section 4(i)(A).

The respondent workmen were dismissed from service by the appellant company on the ground that some of them were near Burnpur and might have joined another, but they did not report for duty. The Company filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of dismissal on the grounds (1) that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to give relief to the workmen because the Standing Orders did not contain any provision for giving them leave; (2) that there was no evidence to show that the workmen were nearing Burnpur or might have been working in a particular area and that the Company had failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence, and (3) that it was not possible to proceed on the footing that the respondent workmen did not join or before the Industrial Court. Held, that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide whether the charges were proved and the Industrial Tribu nal should have interfered with the decision of the Company. The Industrial Tribunal was justified in refusing leave to the company when it held a regular enquiry in which Samar Sen was said to be suffering from blood pressure and Surcharge on workmen. The Tribunal was not justified in interfering with what really was a finding of fact. The question whether the workmen had been given permission to dismiss Chattoraj was one of fact and the Tribunal could not interfere with that decision unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. Held further, that though the Industrial Tribunals were wrong in refusing to give leave to all of them for a "more or less indefinite period", they had jurisdiction under article 136 of the Constitu tion to interfere with the award of the Tribunal and the High Court could not substitute its own opinion on the question of fact for the decision. The jurisdiction of the Industrial Courts is limited by the provisions of article 136 and the powers of the Supreme Court under article 142 are very wide, but in exercising their jurisdiction under articles 226 and 227 of the constitution they have to act judicially and not arbitrarily or capriciously. The power of the High Courts under article 227 is a very wide one and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or without any just cause. It is well settled that the Supreme court can interfere with an award only when there is some legal error apparent on the face of the record, or if there are no special circumstances or where there are exceptional circumstances which warrant interference by the High court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226. The Supreme Court cannot interfere with findings of fact recorded by Tribunals unless it finds that they have been arrived at without any evidence or is based on irrelevant considerations or has acted perversely or otherwise improperly.

The appellant University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 6(4) of the Rajasthan Universities Act, 1974 put a restriction that no teacher in any university in Rajasthan shall be appointed except on the recommenda tion of the Syndicate which was subsequently extended to one year instead of six months. The appellant University issued a resolution dated 10th July 1978 for selection of the respondent No. 1 Dr. Urea Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list as Professor in Bot any. On the basis of the said resolution, the Selection Committee recommended the name of the appellant Dr. Nathawat on 3rd December 1983. The respondent No 1 Dr., Ureakant challenged the validity of the Resolution before the High Court by filing a writ petition in the High court which was dismissed. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The very purpose of preparing a reserve list is to remain valid upto six months from the date of approval of the syndi cate. Thus no fault can be found that the incumbent recommended in the reserved list by the Selection Commis sion Committee which is constituted for selection Of a teacher in the university. Thus any fault can he found that there was no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve List alive for a long period of one year. [419B C] 1.2 The High Court has arrived to the conclusion that the Committee constituted for the selection of a professor in Botsany was proper and in accord ance with the provisions of section 6 (4) clearly provided for preparation of reserve list to the extent of 50% of the vacancies in the post caused during the validity period of the reserved List. [420F] 1:3 The Selection Commit tee constituted for selecting a teacher or officer for which the selection committee was constituted had approved and recommended the names of the appel lant Dr. Lila Kant who is already selected. Thus, no fault could be found with that view taken by the High Curt. [416D] 1 :4 The very object of preparing reserve list would be defeated if the view taken in the earlier case was accepted that once a person selected by the selection Committee has joined that post then selection made by the committee is exhausted and the reserved lists are not available and becomes extinct. There was no reason or purpose for keeping the reserved select list alive for long period. [414E] 1 (a) The Selection Board constituted under Section 6(1) of Act, 1975 put a ban on the appointment of Dr. Kathawat as valid on the post created during the period of reserve List, and numerous appointments had been made in the last decade from the reserve lists. Thus there was nothing wrong with the view adopted by the University that once the person selected is accepted that he has joined the said post then the selection made in accordance with law would be frustrated if the decision taken by it is accepted. [413F] (b) The purpose of preparation a reserve List is also adjudged by the selec tion Committee which was constituted for selections of a teacher and officers for which selection committee is constituted. Thus the Selection Board has not only the candidates selected by it but also the candidates kept in reserved list.

The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of sections 4 and 11(3) of the , on the ground that they were violative of articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31 (2) and 31 (5) of Constitution. The petitioners contended that the provisions of section 9 of the Act violated article 14 inasmuch as they contravened articles 14 and 19(6) of 'the Constitution. Held: (i) Section 4 of the impugned Act was violative of article 14 because it infringed articles 14 or 19(2)(f). It was not a law relating to acquisition of land for public purposes under section 7 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The provisions of sections 3 and 11 of the Central Act were not violative of Articles 14, 31 (1) and (5), as they were not in conformity with the provisions Of the Act. (ii) Section 9 was not violative either of articles 19(f) or 31(2). (iii) The scheme of section 4 of Act was that the local authority could not delay acquisition of any land designated for public purpose under section 3 of the . (iv) The procedure prescribed by sections 4 to 16 was not followed in making a declaration under section 10. (v) Section 11(4) was violative both of articles 31 and 31(5). (vi) The provisions were not discriminatory as they violated article 19(i)(f) and were therefore violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 14. (vii) The provision for compensation for acquisition of property under section 17 was not discriminatory because it contravened article 14, because it was a law providing for acquisition for public pur poses. (viii) The power had to be exercised by one of the highest officers of the local authorities intimately connected with the preparation of the development plan and that the rules framed thereunder complied with. (ix) The preparation of a final development plan was nothing which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the Local authority. If the provisions were borne in mind and the rules made thereunder complied, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was little or no scope for the local authori ty acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the Acquisition Act.

The appellant company was incorporated in the United States of Saurashtra and was a part of India. The Government of India, by an agreement dated August 18, 1948, appointed the United State of Saurashtra as the sole authority to deal with the affairs of the Company. In pursuance of this agreement the Company entered into a contract with the Government of Saurashtra for the supply of certain goods to the Company and the Company was to supply certain quantities of goods to it at its own cost. The agreement provided that the company would supply certain quantity of goods at its disposal, and that the Company would pay the price thereof at its sole cost. In accordance with this agreement, the Company agreed to supply some quantity of the goods at their disposal. The Company was also to supply the quantities mentioned in the agreement. The appellant company made a claim for the difference between the prices of the materials supplied by it and the rates at which the supplies were made. The claim was rejected by the Government on the ground that the dispute was not settled by arbitration, and the award was confirmed by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award did not purport to, nor does it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. It is not evidence of the fact that it was part of the Great Rann of Kutch which formed part of Pakistan. [303 B C] (ii) The Award does not purport lo, nor do it operateas giving rise thereto an obligation or to an implied right to supply any goods at all. The award does not merely purport to give rise to a liability to cate, an obligation in respect of the territory of India and does not operate as conferring rise to such an obligation. [304 D] (iii) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that the disputes between the two States were concluded by the award of the Tribunal which was binding on it. [302 B C].

The mortgagor was the proprietor of a five annas share in Mauza Bansjora, eight annas share. The mortgagee executed two deeds dated June 18, 1946 and August 27, 1922, whereby he mortgaged his interest in the Zamindari property to certain lessees for an annual royalty of Rs. 2,000 payable in two equal instalments. The mortgages were confirmed by the Collector on April 7, 1937. On July 12, 1946, the mortgagor sold his interest to some other persons who had no interest in that property. The mortgagees filed a suit against the mortgagor and others for recovery of the amount due by sale of their interest in Mauza Bahldih which was dismissed by the trial court. The High Court held that the claim was within limitation because the mortgage was partly simple and partly usufructuary and partly simple but even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest after the mortgagor had parted with his interest, part payment will not extend the period of limitation for the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922 was a usufructuary mortgage and not a usufructuary one; (ii) the mortgagee having lost his interest therein in Mauzas Bansjor, Simitanr and Bahaldih prior to the payment of Rs 600 by the mortgagor on April 1, 1937, as evidenced by the endorsement on the first mortgage deed, the plaintiff 's suit to enforce the mortgage dated August 27 , 1922, was barred by limitation because (i)(a) the mortgages were not hit by article 120 of the Limitation Act and (b) the suit was within time. HELD: (1) The High court rightly held that in any event even if Mauza Bahalderih was one of the mortgaged properties, the mortgagee must be deemed to be in possession till the mortgagor 's interest in this property was sold and under section 68(1)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act dispossession of the mortgagee from Mauza Bahdih or part payments of principal and interest after him had parted in his interest. [644 D] (2) The suit filed within twelve years from the date of dispossession was within period of time. The decree passed by the High Court will be set aside and there will be a decree in favour of the plaintiff only in respect of the mortgage on August 27,, 1922, from the original mortgagor ' s interest in village Bahlderoh which was decreed against the mortgagee.

The appellants were carrying on business of transport of passengers. They were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for the transport of employees from Chinchvad to Villagevad and back. The appellants contended that they were not liable to pay any tax as also the penalty. The Commissioner rejected their contentions and held that the challenge to the tax sought to be realised by the Revenue was not tenable and the appellants were liable to be taxed. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner.
