In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the transport service provided to the employees by the company would be a public service vehicle; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, and (2) that such passengers must be carried for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a public Service vehicle. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [362B C] 2. The word 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the statute it is clear that vehicles which could not be termed as public service vehicles fell within the ambit of the charging Section. [363D E] 3. The words 'public services vehicle ' have not been used either for any purpose or by any method of reasoning. It has not by any means of reasoning, stretch or imagination be said to include persons of aprivate company who were given facilities as not members of public but holding special status as the public. [361F] 4. The transport provided to employees by them could be apublic service vehicles in any sense of the term. [364E F] 5. The expression 'public property ' has been defined in section 2(7) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958 to mean a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which carries passengers for hire and reward at different fares paid or by individual passengers, either for whole journey, or for stage of the journeys. [365B C; 366A] 6. The definition of 'public ' in section 3(7), therefore, clearly indicates that the tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public services vehicle. [366C D] 7. The object of the legislation was to impose tax on certain classes of public service Vehicles which could by any system of reasoning be deemed not to include members of private company which were given facility not as member of the Public but holding a Special status, viz., employees of the company who have been given facilities for providing transport facilities. [367E F; 366B] 8. The preamble clearly indicates the dominant object of this Act was to levy tax on passengers carried by road and (3) that the transport provided by the appellants could be public service motor vehicle in any view of the Preamble. [368F G] 9. The main object of section 2 is to impose a tax on all passengers carried on public service. It does not by itself create any difficulties because having regards to the preamble of the enactment it is clearly indicated that vehicles, which could be termed 'public Service vehicle ' are not 'public goods '. [369B C]. 10. The legislature has used the word 'Public property ' in its widest sense and has used it in a wide sense.

The appellants, who were the owners of a cinema house in the State of Madhya Pradesh granted a licence for a quasi permanent cinema by the State Government under Rule 101 of the M.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1972. The appellants objected to the grant of no objection certificate and the third respondent, who had objected to it, filed an appeal against this order before the State Govt. which was dismissed in limine. In a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants, the High Court held that the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there was a mosque, and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence having been re opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema houses with a temporary 'temporary ' licence. The High Court also held that since the appellants had objected, they could not now be permitted to plead a right to oppose the grant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the detailed provisions for the grant were invalid as there was nothing in the Act or the rules which required the licensing authority to invite objections before granting of a "no objection certificate" and (2) the order granting no objection Certificate was violative of the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The detailed provisions relating to the granting of licence at three distinct stages by the licensing authorities in the process of licensing a cinema House, viz., (i) no objection certificates specifying therein whether the application is in respect of a permanent Cinema or a touring cinema. Rule 6 provides that without prejudice to the right of the licensing Authority to refuse or to grant a 'no objection Certificate ' when that grant was under consideration, the State Gov ernment may, with the previous permission of the Government, grant a "No Objection" certificate specifying therein either the application being in respect thereof whether the applicant is in regard to a permanent theatre or a tourist cinema. The Rules do not contemplate any such permission. [897B C] 2. Rule 3 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas Regulations Rules,1972 relates to the issue of a 'No objection certificate specifying the site on which the cinema house is to be built and does not confer any right of appeal on a person who might have raised objections before the licensing authori ties under Rule 102. The Act does not impose any right or appeal on persons who may have raised objection before the Licensing Authority at their back and thus the decision was rendered in violation of the principle of natural Justice. [997C D] 3. The order granting the no objection is violative of principles of Natural justice. It is not a fit case for interference under Article 136 of the Constitu tion. [986F G] 4. The appeal must fail.

The appellant entered into a contract with the respondent for mining of iron ore. The respondent agreed to assign the mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekan Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and claimed specific performance of the contract. The appellant contended that by virtue of this contract and the earlier contract dated August 3, 1957, he was entitled to remain in possession of the mining area. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the respondent had agreed to transfer his leasehold interest under a contract dated September 2, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the agreement was concluded by an oral application for shares and the service of a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons were not necessary; (2) the communication of an acceptance was not necessary because the respondent did not accept the offer either orally or by any letter sent to him before November 6, 1957; (3) the appellant had not agreed to purchase the mining leases and that the agreement could not be unilaterally altered. HELD : (1)(a) The plaint in O.S. 46 of 1957 was not an acceptance of the offer but was intended to be an acceptance. It was not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint; nor it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy Of the plaint through the medium of the Court. [584 B] (b) The High Court was right in holding that there was no concluded contract between the parties. [585 C D] (c) The respondent had not offered to assign a mining lease. There was no agreement at all. The communication of the acceptance was communicated to the appellant before November, 6,1957. The offer was made and communicated to him after November 6. 1957. [583 E F] (2)(a). The correspondence between the appellant and the respondent showed that the appellant 's offer was accepted by the respondent on September 2. 1957 and that it was communicated in the letter dated September 1, 1957 to the respondent before November 7, 1957 and this acceptance was conveyed to the parties after November 7. [58 C] (3)(a)(i) The correspondence did not show that the communication was made or communicated to any of the parties before November 9, 1957 when the appellant filed the suit for specific performance. The letter dated August 2,1957 addressed by the appellant to the respondents showed that it had been communicated to them before November 11, 1957 but this was not done.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1948 for selling sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The complaint was registered against them under sub rule (3) of rule 3 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order 1955 read with section 7 of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay the price of the sugarcane purchased within the period prescribed. On appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution was not maintainable and quashed the complaint. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the Bihar Sugarcane Control Order, 1955, was ultra vires the State Legislature as it did not provide for any regulation of the price at which sugarcane may be bought or sold; (ii) the Central Government had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State; and (iii) the State Government was also well within its powers in issuing the Sugarcane Control order, 1955 in the manner it did because all this was in exercise of the concurrent power of legislation under Entry 33 of List III. HELD : (1) The Bihar Sugar Mills Control Order 1955, which is a part of the Indian , is within its legislative competence in issuing and distributing foodstuffs. [677 E F] (2) The State Legislature had no power to enact the Act and hence the power conferred on the Government under section 2nd of the Essential Commodities Act was not invalid. [676 G H] Ch. D. Chamarbaugwala vs The State of Bombay, ; , followed. (3)(a) The Central Government was well within the competence of Parliament to enact a law relating tO the control and sale of foodstuffs. It is well within that competence of the Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs; [677 G] (b) The Act does not provide anything to the contrary. The State legislature had no legislative competence to pass the Act. [674 C D] (4) The power conferred by section 3 of 'the Act is within exclusive legislative competence of a State. The Central Legislature was well in its powers under Entry33 of List I and therefore the power given on the State to legislate under Entry 32 of List II cannot be challenged as invalid. The contention that the Parliament had no authority to enact law relating lo the control or sale of food crops is not tenable because the complaint made before the police does not disclose a cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of that complaint. [679 E F; 678 A] (5) The fact that the State legislature has no competence under Entry 3 of List 11 to enact an Act relating to control or sell foodstuffs cannot be a ground for challenging the validity of the legislation. [678 C D].

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage industrialisation and that, in pursuance thereof, the Government had on 30th November 1966, indicated the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order dated 12th January 1977. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th June 1969 when the order of 30th September 1969 came into effect and before 949 the order was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industrial units requiring investment. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of Mysore that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30th 6 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. In these appeals, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the principle of Prom promissory estoppel could not apply to the facts of the case since the benefit given to the new industries was being utilised for industrialisation. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory Estoppel is not applicable to the present cases because the benefit granted by the earlier order dated 29th June, 1969 did not specify the power under which it was issued. [950G] 2.1 The doctrine that a benefit given by an earlier order should be treated as a fresh grant or reduction as permitted by section 8A of the Act is in effect, the benefit is granted in the nature of an exemption from the payment of sales tax or reduction in the sales tax liability to the extent stated in the order. [ 950C] 2:2 The doctrine cannot be invoked for determining whether the doctrine is applicable to a case where the earlier orders were made by way of refund of sales Tax paid to the old industries and not merely certain words used out of context. In order to test the validity of the order, it is clear that in effect the benefit was granted in respect of the benefits granted to the existing industries. [ 951F] 2(a) The doctrine has been evolved by this Court in several decisions of this Court. It is well settled that a rule of law cannot be applied to cases where there is an express provision in a statute which would make no difference because such a rule can be applied only if the words used therein are clear and unambiguous. [948B] (b) The principle of promissory estoppel is not attracted to cases of this kind. It has been repeatedly held that the benefit conferred by an order cannot be taken away unless it is shown that there was something in the statute which makes it retrospective or that it was intended to affect any rights already acquired or accrued. [949C] (c) The mere fact that the order passed on 30.6.1969 did not mention the power of the Government to provide for the grant of refund does not mean that the Government has no authority to provide the grant. [946D E] 2.(a) It is clear from the language of section 8 A and the relevant provisions of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957 that the concession granted by an Order dated 30.06.1969 was being misused. The benefit given in respect thereof was being used for industrialising new industries which required investment of huge funds and it was not necessary to hold the Government 's promise or assurances.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148 and 323 I.P.C. for causing the death of Madda Lakshamandas in a road accident on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 holding that he was not guilty of the offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 I. P.C., but convicted him under Sections 148 and 302 readwith 149 I.I.P., for causing his instantaneous death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 148 and on applying the principles laid down in the case of State of Punjab vs Ajaib Singh, ; , held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted A 1 to A 3. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction under Section 147 I.p.C.; but it set aside the conviction of the appel lants under Sections 302 read and 34 I P. C. and maintained their sentence of imprisonment under Section 323 read with 149 IP.c. [803B] 1.2 The High court clearly fell in error in convicting the appellants for offences under Section 326 I.PC. [883C D] 2.1 A person who is liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of all, must be a member of the unlawful assembly and not merely a member. The members of the assembly are entitled to be convicted under Section 304 read with 34 IP C. [873D] 2:2.1 In the instant case, there was no question of forming an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.C.[803E] 2 :3.2 A person is liable for the offence of murder if the evidence discloses commission of any offence in pursuance of the same common intention. The appellants were only three in number, there being long standing enmity between the parties. There was long standing dispute between the par ties and there was long enmity between them. The prosecution case that the appellants formed an unlawful mob alongwith some unidentified persons is satisfactorily established. [863G] 2(a) In the present case, the prosecution has failed to establish beyond reasonable doubts that the common object of the accused was to kill the deceased. It is in evidence that all the accused criminally inflicted injuries on the deceased with their respective weapons. The High COurt was therefore right in convicting them under Section 7 I.

The respondent assessee was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. The Income Tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500/ as capital gains on the basis that the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains, the fair market value of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assessee by an amount of not less than 15% of the value so declared. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. In a writ petition filed before the High Court it was contended that the provisions of section 52(2) were mandatory and that the notice issued under section 52 (1) was invalid as there was no provision in the Act for making a reference to the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the assessee had failed to prove that the amount of consideration received by it exceeded the value declared by it. [644C] 2.1 Section 52(3) provides that where an assessee transfers a capital asset and in respect of the transfer two conditions are satisfied, namely, (i) the transferee is a person directly or indirectly connected with the assessee and (ii) the consideration has been stated under or other words, the consideration actually received by the assesee is more than what is declared by him. [643B] 2(a) The expression "transfer" in section 52 means transfer of property in goods. It does not mean transfer of a right to possession but it includes transfer of an interest in the capital asset. [641C D] (b) In the instant case, the assessee was not a person who had received more than 15 per cent of the consideration as declared by his predecessor in interest and therefore could not be said to have accrued to him. The transaction was one of transfer of the right to possess the capital assets. [651D E] (c) In view of the well recognised rule of interpretation, a fair and reasonable construction of section 53(2), which provides that when an assessee sells a capital assets and in the case of a bonafinde transaction where the full price of the goods is not disclosed and the consideration declared in respect thereof exceeds the full amount of the sale consideration declared, it would be difficult to determine and prove the exact quantum of the suppressed consideration.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two months. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been given any opportunity to explain his conduct in the course of investigation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the evidence of the Food Inspector did not corroborate the version of the food inspector and that the appellant had no opportunity to cross examine the Food inspector; (2) the High Court erred in holding that the evidence did not support the prosecution case; (3) the presumption under section 114A of the Evidence Act was rebutted by the statement of the accused which was more probable because it was supported by what the appellant 's explanation was more credible, and therefore, it could not be said that he was prejudiced. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The evidence of a Food Inspector is admissible under section 24 of the Act. It is true that the presumption of innocence in favour of an accused person is ordinarily used for human consumption but this presumption does not mean that the accused must be given an opportunity to rebut it by cross examining the witnesses produced by him. But this rule is subject to the exception that where the evidence is of a circumstantial nature, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should in the first instance be fully established and all the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the person accused. [330 B C] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration ; , followed. (b) The presumption under s 114A is not a rule of law but it is an exception to the general rule that where two views are possible, the benefit of doubt must be extended to all persons charged with the offence. In the present case, the appellant was convicted by the trial court and sentenced by the High court. He had no right to cross examination the Food Inspectors. Therefore, the conviction of the appel lant under section 13(i)(a), read with section 7 (1), is not sustainable. [329 C D] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Adminis tration, ; , referred to.

The plaintiff 's suit was dismissed by the Collector on 13th of January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966 on the plea of limita tion. The plaintiff 'file second appeal before the Divisional Commis sioner was also dismissed on 30th September, 1966 holding that the order of dismissal was bad and he continued to be in service. In the second appeal by the State Government, a Single Judge of the High Court held that the suit was within time and dismissed it on 31.8.1966. The Letters Patent Appeal filed by the plaintiff was also rejected by the Division Bench. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Article 58 of the Constitution is not applicable to orders of departmental tribunals. It does not apply to orders made by administrative authorities and it is only when the statute prescribes that it commences from the date of accrual of the cause of action that there is no getting behind these words in spite of apparent inequity of applying the same.

The appellant, who was the decree holder of a mortgage executed in favour of one D and his brother, filed an appeal against the said decree. The appellate court dismissed the appeal holding that the decree passed by the trial court did not amount to affirmance but variation and that it was not a decree of affirmance. On appeal the High Court held that the word 'decision ' meant the decision of the suit by the Trial Court and not the grounds stated in support of the said decision. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the expression 'decision" in article 133(1) should mean not a part of the decision or the grounds given for it but the decision on that part of a dispute between the parties if the appellate court makes a variation in respect of the order as to costs such a variation cannot affect the character of the decree which would in law amount to a variation. The word ' Decision ' in article 136 means not only the judgment or decree of the trial Court but also the decision thereon. In considering whether an appeal is one of affirmness or not, it is necessary to consider the nature of the appellate decree and its effect on that question. It may be necessary to make it clear that if an appellate decree confirming the decision in the trial of the case does not affect the nature or character of a decree which will in law have been withdrawn such variation cannot affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is made in favour or the part of, the decree has been withdrawn. The expression ' Decisions of the High Courts in article 134(1)(c) should be construed as meaning the whole of the judgment and not merely the decree of a affirmance and it would not be correct to say that the words 'decisions of a trial court are intended to convey the same meaning as is given to them by the Privy Council. The words ' Decision of the Supreme Court in article 141(1), which are used in the context, must mean the whole judgment and cannot be construed to mean that it is not a judgment or an order of affirmation but only makes variation in regard to it. The difference between the two concepts is that if the appeal court makes an variation in the decision, the appellate Court can make a variation even though the variation may have been made in respect thereof. In the present case the variation was made in the decree and not by reference to the whole or part of it.

The High Court of Allahabad, in a revision petition filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, held that the revisional jurisdiction conferred on the District Court by section 115, Civil Procedure Code, was not available to it. The High Court, however, dismissed the revision petitions filed under Section 115, and remanded the case for consideration afresh. In the meantime, the U.P. Legislature passed the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 which came into force on 1st February, 1977. The Act was amended by the Amendment Act of 1978 whereby section 115 was amended and section 115 as it stood before that date was substituted for the original section 115. The amendment made in 1972 added a proviso to section 115(1), which declared that in relation to any case decided by a District Judge or Additional District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes, the revisional power under section 25 would vest in the High Court. In view of this amendment, the High Courts had exclusive jurisdiction under section 116, Civil procedure Code, to entertain revision petitions against orders of the District Judge under section 24. The State Government appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. A revisional order passed under section25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, is amenable to the revisional powers of the High court under section 100, Civil Laws (Amendment) Act. [38B] 2.1 The High Courts have jurisdiction under Section 25, Provincial Provinces Small Causes Courts Act by a district Court. [39C] 2(a) In the instant case, the District Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the revision petition under section 114, Civil Rules. [40E] (b) A revisional application under section 26, Provincial or Small Cause Court, is not amenable to revisional jurisdiction of the high Court under section 20, and no question could have arisen of invoking the revisional revisional power of the State under section 23, and a revision application under Section 116, C.P Code, against an order of the district Judge under that section, would vest the High 'Court in its original form.

The respondents were owners of certain land situated in Jaipur City. The State Government issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Act for acquisition of their lands situate at Jaipur and notified the same to be acquired by the State Government under section 53 (l) of . The respondents filed objections before the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur. The Special Officer held that the alleged need of the respondents was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. The respondents preferred an appeal before the Division Bench which allowed the same holding that the proposed notification issued under section 51(1 ) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 was not a colourable exercise of the process of Court. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the acquisition of the land in question was not bona fide as no notice had been given to them before the acquisition proceedings were initiated and that the entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition was within the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court at Jaipur Bench. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The entire cause or action culminating into the acquisition is within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the jurisdiction of Jaipur Bench of the Patna High Court. [605B] 2. The High Court 's order under article 226 of the Constitution is set aside and proceedings before the Land Acquisition Officer, Jaipur are quashed and the proceedings before him are restored.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant from the premises in dispute on the ground that the building was constructed by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court, accepting the finding of the Additional District Judge that the construction in question would be deemed to have been completed on 1st October 1971, the date of assessment of house tax and water tax held that the appellant building was not ten years old on the date when its construction was completed. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the suit was barred by section 20 of the new Rent Act because the building in question had been constructed by co operative societies and the respondent landlord had acquired it from a society and, therefore, the new rent Act had no application to the building. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the premises which were not ten year old on 1 October 1971 could be deemed as completed on the dates of assessment. [337C] 2.1 Section 20 of new Rent Acts provides a bar to a suit of eviction except on the specified grounds as provided in the section. The new Rent Control Act is manifestly erroneous and without any basis. [336D E] 2(a) The new rent law will not apply to a building during the period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. [333F G] (b) In the case in hand the building had not become more than ten years on the day of assessment, the landlord or deposit in court the entire amount of rent and damages for use and occupation of the building due from him, such damages for user and occupation due from the appellant, such damage for use & occupation of building duefrom him, Such damages for using and occupation by the building pursuant to the notice issued under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act would be payable. [332D E; 336A] (c) The High court was right when it held that it was the date from which its constructions was completed on 16th June 1967 and not on the 1st of October 1971.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of a building contractors. The respondents entered into two contracts with the appellant company and the appellant was to execute the agreement on behalf of the Governor General in Council. The terms of the contract were that the contractor would be entitled to carry out the work as per the agreement and that he would be liable to pay the bills if they failed to do so within a period of one month from the date of the receipt of the notice. The appellant company filed a suit for specific performance of the contracts on the ground that the respondents had committed breach of contract by not executing the agreement, and that the agreement was void as it was not executed in accordance with the provisions of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the arbitration clause did not comply with the requirements of section 176(3), and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that (1) the agreement for reference did not contain any arbitration clause, and (2) the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 12, in which case he would not be competent to execute it. Held:(i) The agreement dated February 6, 1948, was executed by a person who was authorised to do it by the Governor, and in consequence there was a valid reference to arbitration. (ii)The agreement did not mention that the arbitrator had been authorised to execute its agreement. It was not necessary for the present case to decide whether the agreement contained an arbitration clause or not. The question whether the award which was sent by the arbitrator to the court was the original instrument or a copy thereof, could be decided only on the basis of the provisions in section 175 (3) Of the Government Act, and not on the merits.

The appellants were working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab. They were charged with offences under section 120B, 468 and 471 IPC read with sections 109, 468, 471 IPC and sections 5(2) (d), 5(1)(e) and 5(3) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that the appellants had demanded illegal gratification from the complainant for doing so and that they were not given any bribe. The Trial Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that the prosecution was barred by limitation under section 468 Cr. P.C. The High Court quashed the First Information Report as against Kailash Nath, respondent in Criminal Appeal No. 422/88. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2.2 cannot be interpreted as laying down an absolute or general embargo on prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein; and (2) the second proviso to rule 2.3 is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit Rule has been framed. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The third proviso under clause (a) of rule 2 cannot be construed as laying out an absolute embargo on the prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. This purpose can be achieved if the said rule by adopting the rule of reading down is to mean that even if a government employee is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause or action which took more than four years before such institution, as has been held by the High Court can be treated to be a rule regulating the condition of service of such a person. [920E F] 1.2 The third Proviso to clause(b) is in nature of an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing or withdrawing pension of a retired government servant contained in clause (c) with regard to pension of such Government servant. This provision can be invoked by the respondents in support of their interpretation of the third Proviso under clause(a) with respect to pension. [936B C] 1.(1) The third and the third provisos to rule 3.2 are in the form of a beneficial legislation and cannot be read as laying off an embargo on Prosecution of a Government servant on his expiry of a period of four year from the commencement of the departmental proceedings. This is not to place an embargo upon prosecution of the Government servant if he conditions stated in clauses (b), (c), (d) and (e) are satisfied.[936D] 2.(2) The second proviso cannot be understood as laying over an absolute bar on prosecution. It does not help the respondents. [945E F; 920A] 3.1 Rule 2(2)(a) is a rule providing for the benefit of a public servant who has been prosecuted and convicted in judicial proceeding instituted against him in respect thereof for prosecution in respect whereof a cause of an action which arose or an event which took place more than 4 years before the institution of the proceedings as has be held by this Court. The third sub clause (e), therefore, cannot be said to be laying down any absolute bar to prosecution of such government servant. [946B C; 921A] 2(a).

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. 1,000 each. The authorised share capital of that company was 8,000 shares and 2,000 equity shares of the face value of the shares. The respondent company acquired and carried on the said business in the name of " Amrutanjan" which was marketed in the trade name of Amrut Ranjan. In September 1936 the respondent company purchased and carried out the business in its name "Amritanjan". In September, 1936 the authorised capital was 7000 ordinary share and 3200 preference shares were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. The Income tax Officer held that the respondent had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23 A of the Indian Income tax Act for any of the three years and on that footing he answered the question in the negative. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which the public are substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such shareholders acting in concert, the company would be regarded as one in which public were substantially interested. HELD: The Explanation to section 23(1 A) is in reality an illustration which defines a company in which it is substantially interested, having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty one per cent or more of the voting power are held by a single individual or a group of individuals acting in combination of persons acting in joint concert. The Explanation has raised a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of a company carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the share are vested in the public. But shareholders who are entitled to the fixed rate have to be excluded.

The first appellant was the purchaser of certain bales from the respondent. The goods were delivered to the purchasers on behalf of the latter. The first appellant paid the price and the second appellant received a sum of Rs. 4,000 as earnest money. The respondent filed a complaint against the appellants for an offence under section 138 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellants contended that the transaction was not one which was in the physical possession of the first appellant but was only a sale by him to the purchaser and that the property in the goods had passed to the buyer on behalf Of the latter and that as the respondent had not delivered them, the property could not be sold. Held, that the appellants were rightly convicted under section 141 of the Act. The transaction was one which did not fall within the definition of sale in section 2(g) of the Sale of Goods Act and the first two were sales by the purchaser to the respondent who had received the money for them from the appellant. The property in goods had been passed, and so the first respondent was liable under section 3 Of the Act to pay the price. The fact that the first sale was made by the respondent did not make it a sale within the meaning of section 2 (g) Of the Sale. It was not necessary for the purchaser who received the amount for delivery to prove his title. The mere fact that he had paid the money in advance did not mean that the goods were not delivered to him. The words "any other person" in the entry meant only those goods which were intended to be pledged without permission or that they were not intended to pass on to others. The word "person" in section 3(g)(i) of 'the Sale of goods Act means a person who has been authorised by the owner to sell, whether by way of sale or otherwise, any goods which are intended for the purpose of being pledged without the permission of the owner. The expression "any person" is not defined in the Sale Of Goods Act but it is used in the sense in which it occurs in section 4(1) of that Act. It is well settled that a person cannot be said to have purchased any goods from another person for valuable consideration and so he must be deemed to have sold them as such without his permission or with the consent of the purchaser. The definition of "sale" in article 366(29A) of Indian Sale of Property Act, means a transfer of property in execution of a decree or order of a court or tribunal to another person who is not a party thereto but has been permitted by the Court or authority to do so. The Explanation to section 2 of the Sales of Goods (Control of Trade and Commerce) Act, 1950, does not exclude the first purchaser from the definition. It merely says that goods which have been sold are intended to remain in the possession of a person for a valuable consideration. The second appellant was not authorised by him as the agent of the respondent to sell them. He had no authority to sell the goods and the sale was therefore illegal.

The respondent was a public servant. He was charged with offences under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case against him was that he had committed the offence of criminal misconduct in the discharge of his official duty and that he was guilty of corrupt practice within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. The High Court held that the respondent was not a public officer but was merely an officer in the service or pay of the Government or was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of a public duty. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The use of the word "obtains" in clause (d) of section 3(1) of 'the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is not decisive and it would be reasonable to put on clause (a) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. [325 F G] (2)(i) The word "public servant" in cl. (d), Twelfth clause after the amendment made in 1964 under the twelfth clause, was wide enough to include a public servants who were employed for the purpose of any public duty by the Government. It would be unreasonable to say that if a public Servant were to take money from a third person by corrupt or illegal means or otherwise abusing his position as a public service he had not committed an offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. [326 A B] (ii) The words "obtaining" in the first clause are wide enough and include a person who is employed for performing any public function, but it would not be correct to say, that if the public servant were to carry on his duties as a teacher he had no other means of livelihood. [327 C] (iii) The abuse of position as public servant was clearly implied. It could not be said that there had been any abuse by him of his position in a position as an examiner. [328 D E] (iv) The respondent was guilty under section 120B read with s 5(2) and the offence was committed by him.

The petitioners in each of these applications under Article 32 of the Constitution are engaged on terms of casual labour for varying periods between 10 140 days and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Northern Railway. The petitioners alleged that notwithstanding the fact that each of them has put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, has not treated them as temporary servants and has applied discriminatory rates of wages. They have asked for a direction to treat them at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked For their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Railway Board and the Northern Railways. The Court directed that seniority of project casual labourers should be combined for the purpose of screening and forming panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in. This Court directed a scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. In the Signals and Construction Organisation under which the petitioners are working, according to the Railway administration further privileges of being regularised in permanent service are affirded by giving them access to their regularisation against permanent vacancies which mostly occur in open line acquire temporary status on completion of 120 days of continuous employment previously. The Railway Administration is required to take steps to screen such casual labour who acquire temporary Status, will not, however, be brought on to the permanent establishment unless they are selected through regular Selection Boards for Class IV staff. The Railways are directed to take immediate steps to prevent the casual labour from being absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line acquired temporary status.

The Forward Markets Commission was constituted under the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956. The Forward Markets Act, 1955, came into force on January 24, 1956, and the Forward Markets Com mission was constituted in exercise of the powers conferred by section 12(1). By a notification dated February 7, 1956 issued under the Act the Forward Marketing Commission was appointed to function as the Forward Market Commission for the period from April 1, 1957. The appellant who was a member of the Forward Co operative Society filed a petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution inasmuch as it conferred arbitrary powers on the Central Government to make bye laws under section 12 of the impugned Act. The High Court held that the Forward Committee was not competent to frame a bye law with retrospective effect, but only empowered the Central Govern ment to make a bye laws in respect of certain matters specified in section 11 and that the power of the Central Gov ernment to make such bye laws could be exercised only by the Association. The appeal to this Court was confined to the question whether the Forward Com mission constituted a 's authority ' within the meaning of article 12(2) of Schedule I of the constitution, as amended by the impugned notification, and whether under section 4 (f) Of the Act, the Forward com mission could exercise a power delegated to it under section 11 in regard to the framing of bye laws. Held, that the contention must fail. The power conferred on the Government by section 13(1) of Act to make rules under section 10 of the , is co extensive with the power to make the bye laws and not with retrospective operation. The powers conferred on a body by section 11 are co extensive in nature and can be exercised by the Central or State Governments only if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for its failure to exercise that power. The impugned Act, therefore, falls within the words "under the Act" and not under article 12 of Schedule 1.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company which comprised salami and premia received by it as consideration for grant of long term leases after 31st March, 1948. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the assessee for the grant of Long term leases was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assessee from other sources. On reference, the High Court answered the questions in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) on the facts and in the circumstances of the case distribution to the assessee of the amounts attributable to land acquisition received by him as consideration of grant of short term leases without taxable as dividends, was not a receipt of income in the hands of the asses see; (ii) the distribution to him of the capital gains was taxable. HELD : (i). The scope of enquiry in this group of cases is more extensive. In view of the form of questions, in view of Explanation to section 2(6A), capital gains arising after 31 st March 1948 were not part of accumulated profits of a Company. Prima facie receipt of compensation for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gain. Primafacie receipt of compensa tion for compulsory purchase of land is capital gain and whether any part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2 (6A) of Income tax, 1922, was taxable as income. [737 D E] (ii). The High Court had to decide on the fact whether any amount of salami was capital gains or not. If that be so, then the question is answered in favour Of the Revenue.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of cutting wood from a forest by using it as an exudation from living trees in the forest belonging to the family of the Dipterocarpucoae trees whilebow oil is a bye product fromika (Santalalum Album) by industrial process. The trial court acquitted the accused on the ground that the forest produce was not 'wood oil ' as defined under section 2(f)(1) of the Act. The High Court in appeal affirmed the acquittal and convicted the appellant under Section 3(2)(i) of Kerala Forest Act, 1963. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word 'wood ' should be given a narrow meaning so as to defeat the object and purpose of the legislation. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'forest produce ' in Section 2(k) of Act means 'Sandal wood '. It must also be construed in the context in which it is used and the purpose sought to serve the tribals in the Forest area. [164G] 2.1 The restricted meaning canvassed by the counsel would defeat the purpose of legislation. The restricted interpretation given to the word wood oil ' should not be extended so as not to defeat or frustrate the principle and object of the legislature. [165A B] 2:2.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court acquitted him but on appeal, the conviction was set aside by the Sessions Judge and the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal; that the High court should not have interfered with the findings of fact unless there are substantial and compelling reasons justifying interference with the conclusions of the trial Court. Held: (i) The High Courts should not set aside an order of acquittal unless there is substantial and cogent reasons for doing so. In the present case, the evidence in the present ease was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn. (ii) The judgment of the High ' Court does not disclose any such reason justifying interference. Held, further, that the evidence of the doctor P. W. W., who had examined the deceased at 5 p.m. on the day of occurrence was highly interested and partisan and it was unsafe to accept his testimony as being of any great value which is still more diminished by the finding as to the innocence or guilt of the accused. The judgment in the case of a dying declaration made by a person who is not examined as a prosecution witness, must be disregarded unless there were substantial and compel reasons for so doing. In such a state of affairs it cannot be a sure foundation for maintaining the conviction if the statement of the Hazari the sole eye witness is disregarded, as it must be ignored in this case; because ordinarily a dying declarations of the kind which the prosecution has relied upon are by itself insufficient for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder.

The appellant company was an all India complex having its own establishments in different parts of the country. The dispute between the management and the workmen represented by the Indcox Labour Union, Jamshedpur, raised a dispute for adjudication. The Industrial Tribunal held that the constitution of the said Indcoox Labour Union validly amended its constitution so as to extend its membership to the company 's other employees in other establishments, inasmuch as the disputes referred to it were only those set out in the said agreement and the said statement was made by the General Secretary of the Indusco Workers Union. The Tribunal held against the appellant company. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Industrial Tribunals had no jurisdiction to entertain the dispute raised by the union. [539 D] (ii) The Tribunal 's conclusion that the union 's constitution was duly amended either on January 6 or 21, 1963 or that, therefore, the/ndian Oxygen Workers Union represented the workmen of the company at Jamshedpur and not the workmen employed in the appellant 's factory at Jamshedpur came to be known by the Industrial Tribunal as a dispute between two Unions. [553 D] The Tribunal was right in holding that the reference made by it was incompetent. [554 E F] (iii) The award is operative in respect of the workmen in the company. [552 A B] (iv) The appellant ' union had not filed any statement to show that the Industrial Tribunals constituted under the Act were only concerned with the dispute referred to them and they had agreed to refer those disputes for adjudication by the Tribunal. [555 E F].

The assessee firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939. In 1934 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement of partnership to carry on in the name of M/s Hakam Malani Tani Mal which was originally carried on by the undivided family. The Income tax Officer assessed the firm under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1943 44 and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed that order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the firm of M. Hakam Lal TaniMal was dissolved before April 1, 1939, when the assessee was dissolved and on that account the assessee could not be said to have been carrying on business at the commencement of the Act 7 of 1939. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the assessee commenced business immediately after the dissolution of the firm Messrs Hakam Mall Tani Lal Tang Malani Mal. It must therefore be held that the business of Messrs. Hakan Mal Tanimal Mal which continued till the midnight of March 31 1939, on the 31st of March 1939, was not entitled to the benefit provided in section 25 (4) or 25(2) of that Act. [646 B] The assessee was constituted to carry out the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1 1939 and all the partners have become separate from the 1st of April 1939. It is not necessary for the assessee to prove that the partnership was dissolved by reason of the fact that the partners had been living separately. [650 C D] The mere fact that a partner has been living apart from his father or mother does not make him an owner of the property. The partnership deed of 1932, which was executed on April 1. 1939, did not show that the partner was a separate firm. It was only in the absence of other evidence that the agreement constituted a separate partnership of the assessee.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Shimkot via Shinoga. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. On April 25, 1967, the Secretary to the Regional Transport Authority, Shimkatoga called upon the appellant to produce the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that the Secretary, to the State Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1945 (old Rules) after a lapse of such long time from the date of grant of the permit and that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The High Court also dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the old Rules which was applicable to his case, for the issue of a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional transport Authority granting the permit; that the issue was made beyond the prescribed period of time and therefore the appeals before the State Government were not competent. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The appeals before this Court are not competent under section 64 of the Act to the District Transport Appellate Tribu nal against an order issuing a permit. [189G] (2) The appeal before the High Court is not competent as there was a period of limitations under rule 115 of the new Rules which prescribes the procedure for appeal to the various authorities. There is no dispute that section 64 is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of a permits and other matters with which we are not concerned here. [188B] (3) The provisions of the rules framed by the State Govern ment under section 68 of the were in force and rule 151 was replaced by new Rules.

The appellant was the successful candidate for election to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in the State of Hapur. The respondent, who was a sitting member of Parliament, challenged the election on the ticket of the Republican Party on the ground that the Congress election meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February 1967 and there was no discussion of the entire evidence and secondly, that there was an attack on the office of the appellant with regard to the attack on his election agent. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the meeting was not held at any time in accordance with law and that the appellant 's witnesses were not present at the meeting. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the meeting which was held on 7 2 1967 did not mention or refer at all to any meeting on behalf Of the appellant; (ii) the reports which were lodged by the supporters of the Respondent with regard tO the attack upon the office and the appellant were not mentioned in the newspaper ' news item in the newspapers ' published on 7 3 1967; (iii) the report of the Joint Secretary of the State Government to the effect that there were no meetings at Hapur and no election meeting could be held at Meerut on 7 4 1967; and (iv) the allegations in the petition about the appellant having been assaulted by the workers of the Appellant with regard lo the attack against the office bearers of the Federation on 7 1 1967 did amount to an offence under section 123(1)(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i). The oral evidence of PW 18 is in support of the rival contentions that the speeches made by the appellant and his supporters were not published with the consent of the Congress Party. The evidence of DW 1 is corroborated by the oral evidence on behalf o the appellant. [895 D] (ii). The evidence regarding the assault on Elahi, a worker of the appel lant was not proved as to the truth of the contents therein. In the present case, annexure KK had not been established to be published with his consent. The oral testimony of DW I is in respect of the attack made by PW 18 on the appellant on the date of the incident.

The respondent purchased the property in auction on July 17, 1980. The sale was confirmed by the District Judge on July 16, 1980 and the decree holder filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property purchased by him. The application was dismissed by the executing court on December 12, 1980 holding that in view of the provision of Explanation I to Section 47 of the C.P.C., an application for setting aside the sale could be made within a period of 12 years from the date of decree irrespective of the date on which the decree had been passed and all questions relating to the delivery of posses sion of the said property would be questions relating thereto. The respondent filed an appeal against the order of the executing Court, which was dismissed in limine by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of Section 47 read with Article 136 of the . when a property is sold in execution of a decree, an application filed for setting it aside the auction sale may be made under Rules 89 or 90, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the Civil Procedure Code by the person and on grounds as mentioned therein. Such an application is not one as contemplated by Rules 89, 90, 92 or 91. [368E F] 1.2 In spite of such settlement, the respondent decree holder having filed the application for delivery o f possession in July, 1980, that is, within one year from July 21, 1979, it should be held that the application was quite within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 134 of the Limitation Act. [369B] 1:3 The expression "any other sufficient reason" occurring in Section 47(1) of the is not defined in the Code but has been used to denote a substantial reason which would render the application an application within the meaning of Section 43, Civil Procedure code, as amended by the Code. [370C D] 2.1 The expression 'any other reason ' occurring in section 47(2) of C. P.C. is not confined only to the grounds mentioned therein but also those specified in the said Rules. In other words, an applica tion for setting up a sale can also be made after the decree is put into execution within the time of limitation prescribed by article 134 of t he . [370D E] 2:2. The expression `any other reasons ' occurring under Section 47 (1) is not restricted to the ground mentioned in the proviso to Section 43(a). In other terms, an appli cation for setting at naught the sale becomes absolute on the dissal of the application of the judgment debtor 's claim for setting t aside the same. [371F G] 3:3. The words `any reason ' used in section 48(1)(b) are not restricted only to grounds mentioned in sub clause (a) of Section 48(2). In the instant case, the application filed by the respondent was within one month from July 22, 1979 and that is why the application made on July 21. 1979 was beyond time. [372F G; 371A] 4:4.

The appellant, a voter in the constituency of Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattan Constituency No. 14 P and 15 P, was declared elected to the Kerala Legislative Council from the said constituency on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The appellant challenged the election of the first respondent on various grounds including the ground of corrupt practices under Section 123 (4) and (5) of Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appellant 's election agent. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that in order to prove an allegation of corrupt practice under Section 100(4), it must be proved that the offending poster was affixed prior to the election by the workers of the candidate with his knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition. [766C D] 1.2 In a case where the allegations are of a general nature, the burden is on the person who alleges them to prove such facts. But where the allegation is that the particular poster was not affixed prior ted to the date of election by any one and there is no evidence to show that it was affixed before the date fixed for the poll, the onus shifts on the party alleging it to prove that the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus. [764C D; 770A] 1:3 In a given case, where the election petition does not disclose any particular fact, the court may presume that the allegation was true and that it is for the petitioner to prove affirmatively that the allegations made in the election are true. But when the allegation of the general nature is not supported by evidence, the Court cannot presume that it has been so stated or proved. [774C] 1 :4 In a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court must be satisfied that the petitioner had failed to prove the allegations in the plaint and that the petition was liable to be dismissed. The burden of proving the allegation rests on the petitioner who seeks to support it. [754D E] In the instant case, the appellant has not only examined witnesses in connection with the pasting of the poster but also produced a copy of exhibit P 1 which is an admission made by him before the election tribunal. He had also admitted that he did not see the wall posters together with exhibit P1 being pasted near the wall poster. Therefore, even if it be assumed that the publication was intended to create an impression and did create an apprehension that the incident of murders had taken place a previous day, it is difficult to understand as to how this witness could have seen the wall pamphlet together with the poster directly named the first appellant as the murderer of four victims. [765E F] 1(a) The publication by a candidate or his agent or by any other person with the knowledge and approval of the petitioner 's candidate or by some other person, with the intention of causing it to be believed is not an election action within the definition of section 123(1)(c). It is only when the allegations disclose that the candidate has committed corrupt practices within the mischief of section 100(1) (c) that the burden shifts on him. [777G H] In a matter where the petitioner alleges that the first Respondent had committed an offence of harbouring the accused in murder, it may be necessary to prove those with special knowledge of the extrinsic facts were likely to interpret or understand the words alleged in a defama tory sense, in an election proceed ings. [779A B] (b) The High Courts must not be satisfied about the existence of any particular ground which would justify the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitu tion.

The respondent No. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for construction of a five star hotel on the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corpora tion rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference, as a recreation ground with appropriate internal network and directed sanction of the revised development plan. The respondent No 2, however, rejected the proposal on the ground that the land was proposed for recreation ground in the draft revised development Plan. The Municipal Commissioner accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order of the respondent No 1 granting sanction of building plan submitted by the respondent Nos. 5. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellants. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order granting exemption should be quashed as there was no such revised development scheme in the sanctioned plan and that the said plot was included in the residential zone and no proposal to exclude it therefrom in the proposed revised development plans had been published. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order granting the exemption should not be quashed on the grounds of challenge to the order granted by the Government to the respondent. [922D] 2. The appellants are only interested in seeing that sufficient area is kept reserved for a park or recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public. They are not, in our opinion, concerned with the question as to the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by Government to respondent No 5. [ 924F] 3. The permission granted to the res pondent No. 2 for construction was only a provisional sanction and could not be withdrawn on the basis that it had been issued without any final approval. It is, therefore, apparent that in granting sanction to the plan, the Municipal Commissioner was not justified merely relying upon a proposal for revision of draft development plan, but also on the view that even the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors. [980G H] 4. The State Government had no power under section 46 of the Act to withdraw the sanction granted by it. It was not open to the appellants to challenge the validity of the order dated April 30, 1984 granting exemption to respondent Nos 5. No. 6.

The appellant union filed two complaints against the employers, two sisters and one of them for a declaration that they were guilty of unfair labour practice by imposing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. The Industrial Court framed an issue whether the employers had committed an unfair labour practices by imposing the lock out. The Tribunal held that the employer was guilty of committing unfair labour Practice by imposing lock out and that the old workmen were not being re employed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant union that (i) the industrial undertakings of the employers have never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that, therefore, the old workers are not being recruited; (ii) the employer will put on record an unconditional undertaking given on behalf by the employers by the learned counsel for the appellant Union which does not command us to and avoid any such error being repeated in future; (iii) the old employees would be re inducted in service as resumption of work is gradually expanding and that till all the old workman are re inducted into service, no new hand will be recruited. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The employer has imposed a lockout or has closed down the industrial undertaking. Therefore, the closure of the industrial establishment cannot be said to be illegal under the Act. [67F] 2.1 The employer is not guilty of imposing a charge of unfair Labour practice by impose a lock off or cessation of work or the refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him even though the business activity was not closed down. [68G H] 2(i) The employer cannot be held guilty of a charge which is illegal under section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [69A B] (ii). In the instant case, the issue whether an employer has impose a slow out or has stopped the industrial activity was a consequence of imposing lockout and permanent closure. The concept of lock out is the refusal of the employer to re open the industrial premises. It is not decisive of the matter. To accept the view taken by the Industrial Court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re opened, bonafide to re opening and/or claims to have closed down its industrial undertaking, and it was not a case of lockout but is necessarily temporary or for a period.

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which were set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause were set forth in el., I of the Memorandum of Association. The object of the company was to deal in investments but the case of the assessee company not only the Memorandum or Articles of Association gave power to the company to deal with investments but also the case on which the case was decided against the assessee Company. In the course of its assessment for the year 1962 63, the Income Tax Officer included the profits and losses made by the assessee in its books of account. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was a dealer in shares, securities and properties and dismissed the appeals. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (1) the assessee had relied on two basic facts, viz., the objects set out therein, namely, the objects setting out in cls. I, 2 and 16, and that because of the objects contained in the memorandum or articles of association the assessee could be treated as a dealer; and (2) that since the objects were not of an investor it was a case of pure fact but one mixed question of law and fact. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the Tribunal in reaching its decision on the point. [50 C] In the present case, the facts and circumstances of the case showed that the object set out was to invest the assessee with investments and properties. The question as to what were the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investment is a mixed question and fact and law. It is not necessary for the Tribunal to decide whether the profits or losses arising from the sale of shares, etc., are assessable to income tax. [51 D E] In re: Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay City I.T.R. , referred to.

The appellant was appointed as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, in 1935. He was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge on June 19, 1950, and was posted as Subordinate judge of Masuipatnam. In 1949 he was promoted as Subordinate Judges. On July 28, 1954, he was suspended pending enquiry into certain charges against him. The Government issued a notice to the appellant under r. 4(1)(a) of the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953. The appellant filed a petition in the High Court for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28,1954, and for a direction to the State Government to refer the cases of all. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant had a right to have his case referred to and determined by the Tribunal in accordance with r. 5(1) (a). Rule 4(i)(a), however, does not confer any such right on the Government servant. The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government, and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution, and it was only that authority which could dismiss or remove him from service. The word "dismissed" in r. 3(1), (a) and (b) of r. 6, refer to departmental enquiries against judicial officers and not to disciplinary proceedings pending against them.

The respondent, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1946 47 and 1947 48 on the ground that the said shares were not assessable to income. The Income tax Officer treated these shares as his personal income and taxed them in the hands of the legal representative of the deceased. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but the Tribunal held that the respondent was liable to pay income tax on the dividend so deemed to have been received by him or her before his death, and that the High Court answered the reference against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the expression "any tax which would have been payable if such person had not died" in section 24B of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, meant only those cases where the income was notional as under section 23A the legal personality of the assessee must be regarded as extended to the end of the year in which such notional income must be deemed to be received by the legal representatives; and (ii) that where the Income Tax Officer had not made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the estate of a deceased person, he could still be taxed as his income in the profits of the previous year. HELD: The expression "assessee" in s.2(2) means a person by whom income tax or any other tax or which would be payable under this Act if he had not expired. [597 B] Amarchand Shroff vs Amarchand Sharmasiklal, ; , followed.

The appellant was the Ruler of a State. He was recognised by the President as the successor of the Ruler and therefore, he became an ex Ruler. The appellant contended that he was still a Sovereign ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution and that the provisions of the Act did not apply to him as he was also a maufidar. Held, that the High Court rightly held that the appellant was an ex ruler and was entitled to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages. The fact that the village had been assessed to land revenue did not mean that the villages were not assessed to revenue but only a grant from the State or Ruler of the former. The effect of the Merger Agreement was clearly one by which factually a Ruler of an Indian State ceased to be a Ruler but for the purposes of the constitution and for the purpose of the privy purse guaranteed, he was a Ruler as defined in article 366(22) of the Con stitution. The High Court was right in holding that the expression 'maufidar ' was not necessarily confined to a grantee from a State or a Ruler and consequently a Ruler could not conceivably be a murfidar; but for purposes of article 366 (22) it did not make him a Ruler for the pur pose of the ,. The word "maufidars" in section 2(m) of that Act means a person who by or under the provisions contained in the wajib ul arz applicable to his village, had the right to recover rents or revenue and from persons held land in any village.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (U.P.) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. By order dated January 29, 1991 he was transferred to Pouri (U .P.). The respondent challenged the said order before the Central Administrative Tribunal which quashed the order of transfer on the following reasoning: "The guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been followed, while ordering his transfer.
