The guidelines contained therein are applicable to the case of the respondent. The Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order transferring. . . . The Tribunal had clearly exceeded their jurisdiction in interference with the orders of transfer. [434B C] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta ; , followed. In the instant case, the Tribunal has completely exceeded its jurisdic tion in interfering With the order dated 1.12.1990 passed by the respondent transferring him from Shillong. The order of the Tribunal is not an appellate authority sitting in judgment over the orders transferring. [ 432E F] Bank Of India vs Shamsher Singh Mehta, ; , referred to. In view of the facts and circumstances and findings it is clear that the guidelines issued by the Government on the subject are not followed, much less can be said to be arbitrary. The respondent was a Gardener in the office of the Director, Cotanic Survey ofIndia, Eastern circle, Shillong and he was posted at Shillong. He was transferred back to Pora (U.) by an order dated March 29,1991. The transfer order was challenged before the Tribunal which held that the respondent was liable to be transferred anywhere in India and directed the appellant to consider his case for transfer on merits. The said order of transferring him was quashed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfer order is vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does so merely because certain guidelines issued in the administrative instructions/guidelines contained in the Administrative Instructions issued by it are not follow, muchless can be done. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The orders of the transfer are set aside and the respondent is directed to consider the case for the transfer afresh on merits and dispose of the same within a period of three months from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. [ 433D] 2. The appellant shall consider the matter along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such promotion or any appointment in an all India service, the couple have to bear in mind this factor and be prepared to face such hardship if the administrative need and transfer policy do not permit the posting of both at one place without sacrifice of the requirements of administration. [ 435E F; 432A] 3. The administrative instructions issued by Government on this subject are applicable even where it is passed malafide or where it was made in violation of any statutory provisions, the Court cannot interfere with it. [ 434B C].

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of Jawahar. The prosecution case was that the deceased Jawahar had caused injuries on his person and that he died in the hospital. The Trial Court acquitted all the accused persons but convicted them under Section 304 Part 1 read with section 34, I. P.C., and sentenced each of them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal by A1, the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1 and A2. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such they could certainly have killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing simple and grievous injuries to him. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all first accused had remarked that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. The High Court while confirming the conviction and sentence of the appel lants under Section 325 read with 34, IPC convicted them and instead convict them under section 325 readwith Section 34, Cr. P., I.C.; but acquitted them under Sections 147 and 148, IP. C. [312B D] 2. The appellants shall deposit Rs. 7,000 each before the Trial Court within four months from today. In case of non payment of fine they shall undergo rigorous imprison ment for five year.

The appellant Bank was constituted under the Banking Companies Act, 1949. The Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1976 came into force on 1st April, 1976. Section 4(e) of the Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, usage or agreement, any sum due to a Corporation formed in pursuance of an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom or any special Indian law which is not in force on the day on which such Act comes into force shall be deemed to have been paid by the Bank to the appellant. Section 5(e)(ii) provides that the provisions of the Banking companies (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1976 shall apply to a corporation formed or created by any special law made by the Central Government. The appellant Bank, which was constituted in pursuance thereof, was incorporated under the Companies Act on 1.4.1976. Section 6(e), inter alia, provides that all laws in force in any State immediately before the commencement of this Act shall be repealed and reenacted as if they were inconsistent with the provisions contained in Part III of the Constitution. The Bank filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to it from its employees. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the Bank was not constituted under section 4(a) of Act VIII of 1969 and, therefore, the provisions relating to 'special law ' in section 4 (e) were not applicable to the Bank. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Bank that as the words `any Indian law ' refer to any action taken under the law and not by the law itself, it will not come within the purview of section 4 of the , as it stood on the date the Act was passed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression `special law" in section 2(e ) of the General Clauses Act includes a special law enacted by an Indian Legislature and not a corporation. [968E] 2.1 The words `in pursuance of ' and `by or under the ' but by using the expression `in respect of ' in pursuance ' refer only to a action taken by the Parliament, and not to a suit instituted by a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian Law. [986F G] 2(a). The words 'by orunder ' and ' by using ' mean ' in the context of the provisions made in Part I of the constitution. The words "by or Under" refer only when there is a law made under Part III, and the expression 'by ' has been used in that part. [987B] 2.(b) The word `in ' refers to a special statute enacted by the British Parliament as a piece of special legislation applicable to India. It does not mean that the general law enacted under the General Clause Act is a special one. The general law made in the instant case, is the Banking Company Act, and, consequently, it cannot be held to have become void as making a discrimination in favour of corporations created by British Parliament. [984C D] 2:2.1 In view of the language employed in section 3(27)(a) and (b), the word 'special ' refers only to cases where there is no special law under Part II of the Constitu tion.

The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that it was beyond the legislative competence conferred by section 3 Of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (Act 1 of 1955) and cl. 5 of the Order which provided for the control of production, supply and distribution of essential commodities in the interests of the general public. Held, that the impugned Notification was not ultra vires the powers conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Essential Supplies Act, as it did not authorise the Central Govern ment to fix the ex factory prices, and that there was discrimination between factories in other parts of India and the Union Territories in these three regions. The notification merely fixes the exfactory price and the ex depot prices are not arbitrary or unreasonable. The impugned notification merely fixed the ex depots prices and the prices are below the cost of production. The petitioners have not shown how the prices fixed by the Government were arbitrary or irrational. Nor is there any basis for such a clasification in effect by the fixation of prices in these two regions. There is discrimination between manufacturers in other States which are said to be deficit, and the contention that the factories in the other areas are left free to sell at any price is specious and does not merit a moment 's consideration. The Government was of the view that prices fixed for factories in Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar should be pegged at the level at which they were at the end of May, 1958, the prices were below the price of production and that no price below them would meet the cost Of production.

The appellants, who were working as clerks in the Calcutta Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta, represented by Bengal Chemical Mazdoor Union, represented a dispute between them and their employees represented by the Bengal Chemical Workers Union. The Tribunal held that the working class cost of living index was Rs. 344 1/2 per month and that the award was binding on both parties. On appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (1) the award dated June 21, 1951, was not terminated under section 19(6) of the Act as it had been made after the commencement of the Amending Act; (2) the previous award did not show that there was a change in the working classes of cost of the living index and therefore the reference was bad in law. HELD: (1)(a) The Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal, that the said figures relate only to working class menials and the corresponding entries in regard to the working Class cost of index do not indicate so much increase as in the case of menial class. [148 C] (b) The award dated December 21, 1956, was binding between the parties and therefore it should be mentioned; it was not necessary for the Tribunal to consider whether there was substantial change in its working class of cost. [149 D E] (c) The agreement replaced the earlier award by the Amending act of 1958. It did not provide that the rate was accepted by the parties as reasonable on the date of "the agreement" till there was no substantial change. [150 F G] (2)(a). The Tribunal rightly relied upon exhibit 3, the original award and the original document. In regard to matters covered by it, the Tribunal wrongly relying upon exhibit 4, corrected the basis on the information given in the Weekly Statistical Digest, WestBengal, that there were substantial change of the working conditions of the index in 1957.

The appellant was the Matadhipati of Sri Gavi Mutt which is a religious institution dedicated to propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The said management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act, was not disputed by the appellant. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the scheme framed under the provisions of section 63 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, was inconsistent with the relevant and relevant provisions Of the earlier enactment. Held: (i) that the scheme was framed under section 63 and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. The scheme was not a mere device to make it consistent with the provisions Of section 103(d). It was open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme on the ground that some of its provisions contravened his fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, and (ii) that since the scheme had been framed under an earlier Act which was valid when it was enacted, it could not be challenged on the grounds that some other provisions of that Act were inconsistent with those of the later Act. The object of the latter Act was to make provision for the better administration of the Mutt and its properties. The intention of the Legislature in enacting section 103 (d) was merely to make the scheme in question effective from the date when it came into force, i.e., the 26th January 1950. The provisions of sections 103(a), 103(b) and 103(c) were intended to give effect to the object of that provision and to make them consistent with those provisions. The purpose of the former Act was not to provide for the same but to make a scheme in respect of the same subject matter. The latter Act did not contain any provision for its own purposes, and it was only provided for the manner in which the scheme should be deemed to have been framed. The fact that the Executive officer had been given an opportunity to make his representation against the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation of the Scheme by legal proceeding and partly as such did not affect the validity or otherwise of the schemes.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in the school on ad hoc basis. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. The management of the school by its resolution dated July 6, 1987 decided that the appellant should be regularised in terms of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12, 1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appel lant was entitled to be regularised as Hindi Teachers with effect on July 12.1982 and directed the educational authorities of the State Government to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi teachers but no action was taken by the said authorities. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Validation Act does not arise because of the validation Act. [901C] 2.1 The validating Act does no more than validate a substantive vacancy because of an Validation Act. It is a piece of social legislation enacted with the obvious object of granting relief to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping them in short spell appointments like that day break and in the process denying them rightful dues and other service benefits. [995D] 2:2 The validating statute does not suffer from the vice of discrimination. It merely provides for a method of regularisation of services of persons appointed on ad interim basis. The validating legislation is, therefore, clearly covered by Section 3. [996E F] 2(a) The Validation Acts are valid and do not offend Article 14 of the Constitu tion. [993F G] (b) The validation Act does nothing more than regularise a substantive post but merely provides that the services of ad hoc teachers shall be regularised with effect retrospectively from July 1, 1982 in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Education Act and the Rules framed thereunder. [992B C] (c) The validating Acts are not valid and cannot be sustained. [ 993F G]. (d) The High Courts erred in denying the benefit of validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [999C] (e) The appellant is still continuing to serve as Hindi lecturer with effectfrom July 12 1982 and has been working with the approval of the authorities for almost 4 years with short breaks.

The appellant was elected as Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being a candidate based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, Non official Members ( Allowances) Rules, 1965, framed under the Act, was that he had been disqualified for being chosen as Chairman or Member of a committee of a Zila Parishad. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on various grounds including his disqualification. The High Court held that the allowances paid under rules 3 to7 were in addition to the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 7, and therefore, the office of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti was an office of profit and the appellant was disqualified for contesting the election. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the Tribunal; (ii) the order of the Tribunal was not vitiated by any error of law or procedure, and (iii) the Tribunal had acted without jurisdiction in interfering with the finding of fact. HELD : (i). The High court was right in holding that the allowance paid under r 7 to the Chairman of Panchayat Samiti at Rs. 3 per day and Rs. 100/ as a consolidated amount in lieu of the travelling allowance, daily allowance and any other allowances to which he might have been entitled in order to compensate him for expenses incurred in connection with the discharge of his official duties. [422 D E] (ii). The appellant had failed to establish that the payments under r., 3 to seven made the office as Chairman were an office under the State Government.

The appellant was a tenant of a building. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration, and that the tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin sheds marked by letter ABH G were constructed by him with the permission of the District Magistrate. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal, the first appellate court reversed the findings of the trial court and dismissed the suit holding that the roof wall did no constitute material alterations in the accommodation. The High Court also held that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent landlord was entitled to recover possession from the tenant. In second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the disputed construction which the High Court has found to be 'material alteration ' is a relevant consideration in determining the question of 'material alterations ' and that since two sides of the tin structure were resting on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion, the appellant merely extended that tin shed which did not make any sub stantial change either in the form or structure of the building. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the constructions have been made with the prior consent of landlord is a material alteration in the existing structure and they are likely to diminish its value. [975C] 2. The word 'materially altered ' in section 13(1) of the Act does not mean something which is likely to alter the accommodation or to change the structure of that building. It is the unauthorised constructions which brings about substantial change in the front and structure of a tenant 's eviction, but every construction made by a tenant in the building does not provide a ground for eviction. The material alteration consists of a partition wall of 6 feet in a hall converting the same into two rooms and a tin shed marking by letters CDGH had been erected by the appel lant with the sanction of the district Magistrate, but if the tenant, without the permission granted to the landlord, makes or permitted to make construction in which in the opinion of the court has materially altered the accommodation, it took care to use the word ' materially altered the accommod a tion. [964E F] 3. The essential element which needs consideration is as to whether the construction is permanent or temporary in nature does not provided a groundfor eviction; instead the constructions complained of must be of such nature and character as to alter tions, the structure and the extent to which they make changes in the rear and structure. [963G] 4. The object of the legislation is to provide for the prevention of unreasonable eviction of tenants from any accommodation except on one or more of the following grounds: (a) xxx (b) xxx xxx (c) xxx 5. (d) xxx 6. (e) xxx 7. (f) xxx 8. (g) xxx 9. (h) xxx 10. (i) xxx 11. (j) xxx 12. (k) xxx 14. (l) xxx 15. (2) xxx 16. (3) xxx 17. (4) xxx 18. (5) xxx 19.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. The High Court set aside the judgment of the trial court and upheld the passing of the ex parte order. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the summons in question was duly served and the respondent had no knowledge of the decree. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The meaning of clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of Order 5 which is meant for issue of service and summons on natural persons. [1032C] 2.1 In Rule 17 of Order 29 of C.P.C., it has been provided that "where the defendant or his agent or such other person refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the defendant, cannot find the defendant and there is no agent empowered to accept service of summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving officer shall affix a copy of the summons on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. [1132E F] 2:2. The language used in Rule 17 is "in relation to" and not "to". It is a well known rule of interpretation that where the words "Principal Officer" are used in a statute, they should be construed as meaning "as to what is meant by service on the Company itself. [11032G] 3:3. The word "Principal officer" has got a very wide connotation and it cannot be understood as including "to" or "to", but must be understood with reference to the context in which it occurs. [1012B C] 4.1 Rule 2 of Order 30 of CP. C. P.C. is meant to serve as summons on a natural person. The words "in connection with" and "to act" are not intended to convey a sense of meaning. They are used to denote the actual service of a summons on persons. It is only when the defendant makes or offers to do something which he does not intend to do, that he can be said to have done something which is not contemplated by service. [1003C D] 4:4.2 In Rule 2 it has got two meanings. The first is "to serve as a summons" and the second is "by whom the defendant normally resides or carry on business". It does not mean that the person who makes the summons must be deemed to have been served on him.

The respondents were prosecuted under section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code for having committed a breach of peace. The Magistrate recorded his reasons for his being satisfied that a breach existed at the time when the order was passed and directed the police to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145, the Magistrate passed the final order in favour of the appellant. The High Court found that there was an apprehension of breach of the peace and once he records his reasons, it could be presumed that the breach of law existed at that time and ordered the police not to file written statements. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The final order passed by the Magistrate must be set aside and the order of the High Court is restored. [94C] 2. The preliminary order drawn up by the magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a dispute exists as contemplated under section 146(5) Cr. P.C. requiring such a finding in the final orders. Once a preliminary order is drawn up, the High court in revision cannot go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the Magistrate was based. [952D] 3. The enquiry under section145 is limited to the question whether there is a breach and if so, what is required is that the dispute should be resolved by recording evidence. If the Magistrate has given a finding on this aspect of the matter, he must pass a preliminary and final order under sub section (4) and pass a final order. Once he is satisfied on these two conditions, section 145 is attracted and the enquiry under sub s.(1) and thereafter to make an enquiry under subsection (4). [953C D] 4. The finding of existence of a dispute likely to cause a breach must be recorded by the Court in the preliminary order itself. If it is not necessary that at the stage of passing the final Order the apprehension of the breach should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the disputed dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section(5). [963D] 5.

The appellant was a resident of Madras and had been assessed to income tax for the years 1942 43, 1943 44 and 1943 45. The Income tax Officer included in his total income the profits of the year 1942 43 and the appellant claimed that the profits should be taxed only if they were remitted to British India. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant was liable to pay income tax on the entire profits as well as the profits accrued to it both in the business and in the legal sense and that liability had arisen. On appeal, the Tribunal held that though the appellant sold its goods to the ultimate purchasers and received the prices there could be no question of benami between the appellant and the buyers and that the profit was apportioned to them by the Income tax authorities. The High Court on reference held that section 42(1) applied only to non residents and not to nonresidents and consequently it did not apply to non residents. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The finding of the Commissioner that it was not liable as it had not been treated as profits by the assessee and the profits had accrued to them both in their business and the legal effect of those findings is a question of fact. [722 B] (ii)The conclusion of the Tribunal on the facts found was one of pure fact and could not be challenged in a reference under section 66(1). The finding must, therefore, be an inference from other facts, when it is an inference to be drawn from the facts proved on the application of the proper principles of law. [774 C] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., ; , followed.

The assessee, a firm carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth, was appointed as an employee of the General Manager of the factory. The terms of appointment were that in case the profits exceeded Rs. 1 lakh, the commission payable to him would be Rs. 75,465. In respect of the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 76,465 paid as commission to the General manager on account of business considerations but there was some collateral reason. The Income tax Officer determined a sum of Rs, 70,465 as commission paid to the Managing Director and held that the amount of Rs 75,467 paid by him was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. In further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court held that a higher rate of commission was reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The principle of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out for the purposes of the profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(Xv) of the Income tax Act has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each particular case. [527 B] (ii) The High Court was wrong in taking this circumstance into consideration. The principle is that an employer in fixing the remuneration of his employees is entitled to consider the extent of his business, the nature of the duties to be performed and the special aptitude of the employee, future prospects extension by the business and a host of other related circumstances.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company (Private) Limited. The company filed an application before the Patna High Court under article 226 and article 227 of the Constitution for quashing the award on the ground that it had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and praying that the agreement should not be accepted and his agents should be heard before the disposal of the case. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting the appellant 's application for a writ. Held, that the appeal must fail. The scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act does appear to contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act when the same had not been taken up by the Union or a number of workmen. The necessary corollary is that the individual workman is at no stage a party to the industrial dispute independently of the Union which has espoused his cause. The question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman was taken up in proceedings before the Tribunal by an officer of that union, its Secretary Fateh Singh himself had made the complaint against the appellant which resulted in the order of dismissal must be decided on the basis of the reference. Held further, that section 36 of the Act does not contemplate that machinery provided thereunder should be laid in motion for settlement only disputes between an individual workmen and an employer cannot be an industrial dispute as defined in section 2(k) of the . The Tribunal committed an error in refusing to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the respondents on the allegation that they had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2, who had sub letting it out to defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the surviving plaintiffs could not have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in view of the provisions of O.XXII r. 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) A joint Hindu family is a creature of statute and it cannot be sued without its being brought on record. It can sue without its own name or without its name being brought in the record. The provisions of 0. XLI r. 3 of OXLI r. 1 of OYLI, r. 2 of OOXLI, r., 4 when the decree proceeds on a ground common to all the plaintiffs or defendants, if all the parties or defendants are appealing from the whole decree and there upon the appellate court may reverse or vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiff or defendants. The words "any one of the plaintiffs" in O. XLI, r, 4 when read with O. XXXII r., have to be construed as meaning "anyone of them". The word "any other person" in section 41 of the Act means a person who has been brought on the record and includes any one who has not filed any appeal or objection. The word 'any other ' in section 43 of the Indian , is used in the sense in which it occurs in section 42(1) of the . It is not possible to define precisely what would be the meaning of the words "other persons" in that section. The expression "other person" has been defined in section 2(18) as including a person whose name appears on the 'record ' and includes a person, who has filed an appeal or an objection under section 35A, and also includes a sub tenant of any other person who is not a party to the appeal. The definition of "other legal representative" in the Act does not include a person claiming through another person as a result of a decree passed by a court in favour or against him. It is only when an appeal has been filed by all the defendants or defendants that the appeal could be continued even after the death of Kedar Nath and the abatement of the appeal so far as he was concerned under O. XXII r, r 4 when his appeal by the surviving appellants was not a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent of the High court. The appeal by Kedar Nath had abated as all the appellants had a common right and interest in getting a decree of ejectment against defendant No 2 and such decree could have been on a common ground to all of them.

The appellant landlord sought to break through these defences by urging that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited by efflux, limited by duration thereby under section 111(g) or outside it. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the tenancy was not terminated by efflux and that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 is needed and further that the forfeited tenancy caused thereby sub letting according to the express condition regarding sub letting in terms of section 111 is needed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The statutory law as it stands today, does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and forfeiture clause and sufficient to satisfy justice, equity and good conscience. [920C] 2. The rule regarding forfeiture and notice to quit and notice terminating tenancy under Section 111(a) and no notice terminating a tenancy under s.111(g), as amended by the Amending Act of 1929, did not apply to the lease executed in Delhi and, secondly, if it does not, ipso facto, extinguish the tenancy but only executes the contract with the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the lease by giving notice in writing to the lessee. [1020D E] 3.

The appellants were convicted by the Assam and Nagaland High Court under section 302 I.P.C. for having committed an offence of murder. The High Court acquitted them on the ground that the evidence was insufficient to establish the charge against them beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The provisions of article 311(2) are not intended to be used as a safeguard against arbitrary action taken by the Government in regard to the security of the State. It is not necessary that the Governor should arrive at his satisfaction on the basis of evidence adduced during such inquiry. [490 B C] (2) The satisfaction under the unamended provision, therefore, that the Government was to arrive at its satisfaction on a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard thereto has to be given to the government servant and, under the proviso, the Governor 's satisfaction required is that in the interest of the security thereof it is not expedient to give the said person an opportunity. [488 E F] (3) The Government cannot be said to have arrived at its own satisfaction on any material or evidence adduced before it. It must act reasonably and rationally. If the Governor has arrived at his subjective satisfaction, he must act fairly and reasonably and in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. [489 G H; 489 A] (4) The Governor ' s satisfaction under unamended clause (2), therefore, is required to be recorded by that authority in writing. It cannot be doubted that the satisfaction under amended provision, namely, that it was not expedient for giving the government servants an opportunity of show cause against action proposed should be taken. [486 B C; 489 D] (5) The discretion conferred on the Governor under article 311 is a judicial one and must be exercised in accordance therewith. It has to act reasonably, fairly and justly. If he does not act arbitrarily or capriciously, he cannot be held guilty of any misconduct. [487 E F]. (6) In the present case, the High Court was right in holding that the enquiry under unamended section 311(1) was not justified. [485 B C].

The petitioners and respondents 5 and 6, who were the Shia Wakfs in U.P., filed a Writ Petition in the High Court of Allahabad challenging the validity of the Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board, declaring that plots and structures in question had been registered as Shia Waqfs for purposes of performing their religious ceremonies and functions thereon under section 3 (1) and (2) of U. P. Muslim Wakfs Act, 1936. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Notification issued under Section 5(i) of 1936 Act was not applicable to the disputed plots and structure in question and that the petitioners had no locus standi to file the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the petitioners that (1 ) the notification dated 26rd February,1944 issued under s.5(1), as well as the Notification in question were ultra vires the powers of the Sunni Boards; (2 ) the Notification under section 4(1)(a) of Act was ultra vires and void being violative of Articles 14 and 19(1); (3) the notification was not a law within the meaning of Article 31A of the Constitution; (4) the Notification was issued in violation of the fundamental rights guaranteed to the petitioners under articles 19(i), (f), (g), (k), (l), (m), (n), (o), (r), (s), (t), (p), (q), (w), (u), (v) and section 5 (1); and (5) the Notifications were ultra rites of the Shias to perform their religious functions and functions on the plots and buildings in question. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Notification dated 25th February 1944 issued by the Shian Board under s 5(l) of ' 1936 Act is not ultra vires Article 19(2) as it does not purport to regulate or restrict the rights of the petitioners and members of Shia community in respect of their customary rights to perform its religious ceremonies, practices, observances, ceremonies and other functions over the other plots and the structures thereon. [1135B C] 2. The notification dated 25rd February 1944 refers to mosque in question which has been listed as Shias Wakfs under the Notification of 15th January, 1954. In fact it was one of the contentions of respondents 5 & 6 that before the Allahabad High Court in the earlier litigation, the petitioners or members of the said Shia Community sought to prove their existing and established customary rights on plots and constructions thereon. The petitioners and respondent No. 7 have also filed their respective affidavits in the matter and have been heard through respective counsel. [1235D E] 3. The controversy whether the Notification is ultra vires or not must be decided by this Court in a pending litigation between the same parties. It is well settled that the Supreme Court will not interfere with an interlocutory order passed by the High Courts unless it is satisfied that the final decision on merits has been vitiated by some error of law or fact. [1335E F] 4. The Court cannot go into the correctness or otherwise of the decision of the High court in a writ petition where the question of title and the binding nature of the order passed are involved.

The assessee, a registered firm, had its business in the manufacture of textile products. The assessment year concerned was 1965 66 corresponding to the previous year ending 31st December, 1965 and the loss claimed by it was claimed by the assessee that when in the assessment year 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computation of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim for set off on the footing that when the assessment was made, the loss or set off was not really notional in nature and that the claim of set off could be allowed to be notified by the Income tax officer under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner also rejected the assessee"s appeal holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in character and that claim for setting off on loss on the ground that loss had not been determined as required under Section24(3), of the 1961 Act, was essentially accidental in nature. The High Court dismissed the assessee appeal by holding that the assessee had filed its return showing the loss and that it had merely computed the loss but passed an adverse order, the Income Tax Officer was not entitled to take advantage of his own failure and reject the assessee claim of carry forward and set off in accordance with the provisions of Section 74(1)(b) and Section 80 together. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The benefit conferred under Section 4 of the U.P. Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that claim of setting off was admissible in its view on a bare analysis of these provisions. [1164D] 2.1 The benefit of Section 24 of 1922 Act continued in force to be give effect to the 1961 1961 Act and notwithstanding anything contained in this Chapter no loss which has not been decided in pursuance of a return filed under section 139 shall be carried forward for more than eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment years for which the loss first computed under the Act or as the case may be. [1064E] 2(a) The benefit given under Section 34 of 1922 is to be read with Section 80 and not in any other manner. [1106B C] (b) In so far as it relates to capital assets other than short term capital assets, it shall be carry forward to the following assessment year and so on. [109D] (c) The assessee has a right to set off against capital gains under Section 72(1) of 1922. [111E] (d) The claim of the set off is admissible in law. [112F] 2.(a) In the instant case, the assessee has not filed its returns showing the losses and the Incometax Officer neither computed the same nor passed an order, which is clearly erroneous. [114B C; 115A] (2) The High Courts were right in holding on a plain reading of Section 80 that the benefit conferred by Section 24 was to be extended to the asses see.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production ( Air) (D & D) Directorate of Engineering and Production. The recruitment to the Defence Accounts Service was always to the Military Science Service and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of service. In the year 1979, the Defence Research Service was reconstituted into three units viz., Defence Science and Technical personnel. The respondent was appointed as a Junior Scientific Officer in the Department of Defence Production (D) on October 13, 1966. He joined the Defence Engineering Service as Assistant Engineer on November 12, 1967. On his appointment to the said service, he was promoted to the post of Director of Technical Education on December 24, 1985. In 1970, the respondent was again appointed as Assistant Director of Industries and Production in the Military Engineering Service. The services were initially recruited to the defence Science Service but later in the year 1980, the recruitment was made when the recruit ment was always in the service. The Respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said appointment on various grounds including that he had been appointed as an Assistant Director and Production by virtue of the order dated October 24,1985 issued under Rule 12(A) of the Defence Services Rules, 1965. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the respondent belonged to another unit viz. DAQAS and DQAS, since the said condition of service was not expressly provided for in the Service Rules. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order dated 10.2.86 issued under rule 12( A) of Defence Services (Pension) Rules 1965 is valid and there is no substance in the present appeal. [24B] 1.2 In spite of the decision of the Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the age of 58 years. The denial of the benefit of enhanced superannuation to the members of the other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution.

The appellant was declared elected to the Sangli City Municipality on June 3, 1967. The election of councillors to the Kolhapur City Municipality was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act 1965. The appellant challenged the validity of the election of the councillors to a local area on the ground that the procedure adopted by the trial court was wrong in that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the learned Judge had in the exercise of jurisdiction vested in him refused to issue summonses to them when he was asked to do so on August 21, 1968. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the trial judge had no power to interfere with the order of the trial Judge based on the evidence of these two witnesses called as court witness and that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June, 1967 that the second publication having been taken place at the 869 time the trial was wrong. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the procedure followed by the High Court was wrong; (ii) the trial Court had wrongly held that the witnesses who had been examined as Court witnesses were not examined and (iii) the evidence about distribution of the pamphlet was meagre and not beyond reproach. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i)(a) The election petition was rightly rejected by the Trial Judge on the sole ground that there was no proper trial of the two persons who were present at the time when the election petition had been filed. [975 B] (b) The High court was right in holding that there could not be any doubt that the appellant was guilty of trying to arouse religious sentiments of voters of the particular ward a majority of whom were Muslims. There was also a charge in that pamphlet that he had turned the Kabarasthan into a brothel and was trading in illicit liquor for which was alleged to have been convicted. [986 D] (c) The evidence about the distribution of pamphlet was sufficient and not within reproach, but this does not mean that everything deposed to by him should be rejected and when the trial Judges accepted the evidence with regard to distribution of a pamphlet was adequate and not fraught with any defect. [987 E F] (d) The allegations of corrupt practice were of a serious nature and if the appellant had been found guilty of a criminal offence, the period of five years ' disqualification would certainly not be inappropriate. [98 G H] (e) The allegation that the election petitioners were guilty of having published two pamphlet which cast serious aspersions on their character and conduct was highly improbable. There is no merit in this contention. The allegations about distribution were of such a serious character and if they were found to be out why there could be two publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period prescribed by section 21(1) of the Act, it would have been very difficult if not impossible for the Judge to have come to the conclusion he did.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute cloth. The petitioner challenged the validity of this notification by a writ petition under article 32 of the Constitution. It was contended that the impugned notification was ultra vires the powers of the legislature under Entry 54 of List II and that it was not saved by the Validation Act. Held, that the validation Act was intra vires and the impugned Notification was valid. The Validation Act was not ultra vires on the ground that it did not validate the impugned Act. It is a law in respect of tax on the supply of materials in a contract for the construction of works simpliciter on the footing of a sale of goods as recognised, and it is therefore a matter of policy and does not affect the competence of the Legislature under Entry 48. The validation Act is intra vires the power of the State to impose a tax thereon is plenary and unrestricted subject only to any limitation which the Constitution might impose and in the exercise of that power it will be competent to the legislature to impose the tax accordingly. The impugned notification must therefore be held to be within the saving of the Validation act. Held further, that there was no force in the contention that the Validation Ordinance was ultra rites. The State Legislature had the power to enact a law with retrospective operation and the validation of the imposition of sales tax did not affect its competence. The validating Act is not ultravires the powers conferred on the legislature by Entry 54, List II or List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and any other provisions of the constitution bearing on the question as to when such a tax could be imposed.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Court. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. In this appeal, it was contended for him that rape is violation of human rights and is violative of Article 21 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The sentence of imprisonment imposed on the appellant is not excessive. [22D] Sunil Batra vs Delhi Administration ; , referred to. 2.1 In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychicultural or criminal factors involved, given propitious social environs, brutalisation, criminal companionship, criminal accompliceship, brutalization, criminal plus murder, criminal commis sion and rape of a woman, in our conditions of barbaric sex, the young appellant has inflicted on his cousin 's wife snatching a tricky opportunity. [23F] 2.2 The offence is not cruel but cruel. The victim is a young man like the appellant. A man like him has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a hardened delinquent, thanks to the penal illiteracy of the Prison system. [24G H] Sunil Kumar Batra vs State of Delhi ; , followed. 2:1. In prison sentencing a convict on a potentially good person 'successfully processed into a young delinquent, given in his early twenties and murders reaching a new high places, the Court must restore the man. [25A B] 2:2. The appellant is a poor man like a man like that of a humanist. He has a young wife and a young woman who has a long prospect of committing rape. He is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, brutalised molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are socially and weaklyally disadvantaged. [26C] 2 :3. The sentence imposed on him is too severe. [27F] Sunil Dhingra vs Delhi Admn., ; , applied.

The assessee, a limited company dealing in land, maintained its accounts on the mercantile system. It maintains its accounts at the mercantile systems. The Income tax Officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assessee on the date of the award. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner reduced the amount of compensation payable to the asses see. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the amount received by the assessee related to acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assesee and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the asses sees. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court is right in the view taken by it and, therefore. a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax. [398C] 2.1 The High court was called upon to decide without the right to receive the enhanced compensation under the Land Acquisition Act accrued or arose to the assesses when he sought a reference under section 18 of the Act or when the award was made by the Arbitrator on July 29, 1955 enhancing the amount payable to him in terms of the Award. [399D] 2:2. The legal position was explained in Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Deputy Land Acquisition Officer & Anr., [1962] 1 SCR 676 and Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, ; , followed. In that case, though the award made by Arbitrator on August 29, 1956 enhancing the compensation accrued to an assessee only when the Court accepted the claim and not when the land was taken over by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment P. It cannot be forgotten that even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation there is a right of appeal by the State Government to the High Court, and the High Courts may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation. [397E F] 2 :3. The fact that the award had been made by an Arbitrator on September 29, 1957 enhancing the amounts payable to an asses see, does not mean that there is no liability in praesenti in respect of the additional amount of compensa tion which accrued or deemed to accrue, whether in fact or not. [395E] 4.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they had withdrawn all their defence to the application filed by them and for other reliefs in January 1968. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it holding that no decree for eviction could be passed except on one or more of the grounds mentioned in section 12(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the compromise was legal and was in accordance with the terms of the compromise; (ii) the suit was not maintainable because the compromise decree was not a compromise decree but was a nullity under section 12 of the Act; (iii) the trial court had no jurisdiction to pass a decree for possession on the basis of the joint compromise. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure are mandatory and do not confer any right upon the tenant to seek eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act. [881 D] 2. In order to get a decree or order for eviction against the tenant whose contractual tenancy is regulated by any rent restriction or Eviction control Act, the Court would refuse to record the compromise as it will not be a lawful agreement. If on the other hand, the court is satisfied on consideration of the terms and conditions of the agreement and if necessary, by considering them in the context of the pleadings and other materials in the case that the agreement is lawful, as in any other suit, then the Court will refuse to Record the compromise. [861 E F] 3. The protection of a tenant based upon public policy is inherent in the language of Order 3, Rule 23 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise the Court shall pass a decrees in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit". [861 B C] 4. The words "in any other case" in section 13(1)(f) of Madhya Pradesh Act, 1950 are clear and definite especially in the background of the pleading of the parties and in our opinion it squarely makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of section 12 (1) (f)of the Act on admission of the appellant. [862 D] 5. The Court can pass a judgment on the evidence that a ground for passing such a decree in accordance 'with the requirement of Order23, Rule3 when it states "where it is established to the satis faction of the Court that a decree has been adjustment by any unlawful agreement or settlement the court shall pass an order for possession in favour of the landlord without further enquiry". [882 E] 6. The meaning of paragraph 1 of the said compromise petition is clear and specific especially in view of the averments in the plaint. It makes out that on a perusal of the entire joint compromise it was found that the same is legal and is within the purview of the plaint.[861 B] 7. In the instant case, on the facts and in the circumstances of this case, the compromise decrees were clearly valid and executable.

The assessee company, a private limited company, was incorporated in the United States of America and its managing agency was transferred to it by the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The company had its registered office at Calcutta and its branch offices at Calcutta. In the assessment year 1964 65, the Income tax Officer included certain amounts of depreciation in the value of the shares of the company in respect of the capital loss incurred by it on account of depreciation. The assessee claimed that the loss was a capital loss because it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the Company and that the losses were not capital loss. The Income tax officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer but the Tribunal held that in view of the depreciation in respect Of those years in view Of the capital losses incurred by the company on account Of depreciation in its value of 83 shares held by it in Elphinstone Mills Ltd., section 23A(1) and levied additional super tax @ 4/4/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs. 12,00,000/ . The High Court answered the reference against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "having regard to the losses incurred" in the relevant accounting years are not used in the sense of "having regards" only to losses previously incurred by a company and to the smallness of profits made. [864 D] (ii) The word "having respect" is used in contradistinction to "having relation" or "having a particular meaning. It may be that the word "has regard" has been used in different senses but it cannot be said that the intention of the legislature was to prevent evasion of tax. [874 E F] (iii) The language of section 23 A(1), which is couched in very wide terms, leaves no doubt that the assessee had suffered a capital gain and the loss incurred must not be considered as a super Director. It is only when the Directors of a company have reasonable grounds for not declaring any dividend that it is not open to the Incometax Officer to constitute himself as a Super Director. [884 E] (iv) The expression "having respects" in section 23(1A), which has been couched in wide terms leaves no room for doubt that an assessee had received a capital asset and the losses suffered must be considered to be capital loss, if established by evidence.

The appellants filed an appeal before the District Judge against the order of the Civil Judge modifying the award. The District Judge held that an appeal lay under section 39 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1947 and that the Civil Court was not justified in modifying the decree. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) Section 37 of the Act does not apply to arbitrations referred to in section 37 of tho Act. The effect of section 37 is that all the provisions except sub sections (1) and (2) of section 12(4) shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of the . Further, the effect of s.46 and section 47 of the , read with sections 46 and 47 of , is inter alia to apply sections 15 and 39 of tho to the proceedings under the Act. [67 B C] (ii) The effect is that the decision of the arbitrator under sub section (4) of Section 12(6) shall he final. [68 E F] (iii) The consequence of section 46 and section 37, read with section 37 Of the Act, read together, is that in all other respects the matter referred to, i.e., the question of title referred to the arbitrator, in all respects the matters shall be decided in accordance therewith. [69 G H] (iv) Section 38 of the does not make the applicable provisions of section 15 of the to arbitrations under section 12 of the and if it is so read it is quite clear that what is made the decision is final. The consequence is that section 46, read along with sections 47 and 48 of the is in two parts. The first part deals with the procedure for making an award and the second part deals only with the manner in which the award is to be made. [70 E F; 71 A] (v) Section 36 of the provides for a statutory arbitration and section 38, which provides that the decisions of the Arbitrator under sub s.(4) or sub s(5) shall not be final. It does not provide for an appeal against the decision in an arbitration referred to therein. [72 E F].

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. The resolution passed by the corporation resolved to make 75 per cent of the posts of Superintending Engineers available to the executive engineers holding degrees and 25 per cent to the Executive Engineers who were diploma holders. This resolution was also not challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the impugned resolution passed in accordance with section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961 is discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification made on the basis of educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the cadre of Executive Engineers, be classified on the ground that the creation of selection grade in the same category on the same basis other than that in the case before them classified the same for purposes of promotion on a different basis other then they should be drawn from different sources. [753G H] 1.2 The classification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 or 16 of Constitution. It is well settled that for the purposes of promotions a valid classification can made among the members holding the same post on the foundation of their qualification which is not permissible in law though the creation by executive instruction finds direct support in Mysore state Road Transport Corporation vs Gopinath Gundacharacharjee, ; and State of Mysore & Anr. vs P.M. Gopinath Guondacharjee & Ors., [1971] 1 SCR 767, followed.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Judges of the High Court of Orissa. They were promoted to the post of District Judge on ad hoc basis and were confirmed in their posts by the State Government. The petitioners challenged the validity of the order of confirmation before this Court contending that they had been confirmed in the post without any blemish, and that the appointment was not a matter of public interest and that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the appointments were made by way of direct recruitment and by promotion from amongst persons who were junior to them; that the Chief Justice of India had no authority to appoint any person as a Judge in view of the fact that he was not an officer of the State concerned; that there was no consultation with the Chief Minister of the concerned States, and the appointment of the petitioner was made without any basis; that it amounted to discrimination against the petitioners; that in any case the appointments made by the Chief justice of India were violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Chief Justice is not a constitutional functionary having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Government. It is imperative that the role of the institution of the Chief Judge of India be recognised as crucial importance in the matter of appointments to the Supreme Court and the Chief Ministers of the States. That being the position, the function of the Institution of the Judges of this High Court is not to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. [460E F] 1.2 The Chief justice in the instant case has been entrusted with the task of making recommendations for appointment of Judges and it is incumbent upon the State Governments to make a reference to the Chief Justices of the respective States. It cannot be said that there is any violation of Article 16 or that the petitioners have been denied the opportunity of being heard before making their appointments. [459F G] 1:3 The question whether the appointment made by an authority in exercise of its executive power is arbitrary and violative of article 14 of our Constitution has to be decided on a consideration of all the relevant facts and circumstances. [461B C] 2.1 In the instant cases, the Chief Judges of Orissa are merely constitutional functionaries having a consultationative role, the power to appoint resides solely with the power and the powers of appointment reside solely and primarily in the State Govern ment. The matter is not, therefore, to be consider that the matter requires to be looked at again a reference only if the Chief judges of the said High Court or the Chief prin cise are experts in the field. [465D] 2:2.1 It is clear from the plain reading of these Articles that the Constitution has been enacted with the object of bringing about uniformity and integration of the judiciary, the independence of the Judiciary and the establishment of a high level judicial body. The independence of judiciary is not merely an executive function but also a part of the basic structure of the constitution. It consists of the various organs of the country including the judiciary. [455E F; 460A] 2(a) There are two important features which must be borne in mind while considering the question whether there should be a proper and adequate consultation with an independent judiciary. The first is that the independence and the judiciary should be so arranged as to ensure that the judiciary does not interfere with the due course of administration of justice. [463B C; 460D] (b) There is no provision in the Constitution which requires consultation with any other person or authority. It has been provided in article 124(1) that the consultation with a High Court should be made by a Judge of the Supreme court and the Judges who are to be consulted must be persons who have been appointed as judges of a High Courts.

The respondent was appointed as a Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Director on March 1, 1981. The respondent challenged the order of punishment by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the impugned order got merged in the appellate order, the initial defect, if any, stood removed and the subsequent defect, stood cured by the learned Judge 's order. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in quashing the impugned ordi cial order of penalty but because the technical plea of incompetence or jurisdiction of Shri U.B. Menon as an official of the bank could not be saved because both sides to the proceedings had not raised any objection to the continuance of the enquiry by the said Enquiry Officer and therefore the High court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry Officer. [199F G] 2. The order of dismissal having merged in an appellate order it should not have ordered payment of 'all consequential benefits. [200G] 3. In the facts and circumstances of this case, the ends of justice would be met if instead of directing 'all other consequential benefits ' to which the respondent would be entitled on superannuation. [201C D] 4. The ends of jus tice would be served if instead thereof the respondent had admittedly retired from service in 1986 and if the order imposing punishment is quashed he would ordinarily have to be paid his wages etc., upto the date of his retirement. [202E F] 5. In view of the fact that the respondent was not duped or not would be a different matter, it should have ordered him to pay '50% of the consequential benefits to which he would be enti tled on superannuation and if he had admittedly retire from service then in 1986, and if his order imposing penalty is quashed, he would normally have to pay his wages.

The appellant, a Zonal Development Plan for the District of Delhi, was sanctioned by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi under section 336 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act 1957. The Master Plan prepared under section 7 of the said Act provided that the proposed user mentioned therein would be the Central Business District of the Corporation and that the proposal should be forwarded to the Central Government for approval. The appellant 's objections were rejected by the Corporation. In appeal, the High Court held that the order of rejection was legal and justified because the Development Act did not contravene any provisions of the Development Acts or of any other law. It further held that since the plan submitted by the respondents did not violate any of the provisions of section 336 or the provisions Of section 340 of the Act, it was incumbent on the Commissioner to give sanction for the erection of a building or execution of a work unless such building or work contravened any of these provisions of sub section (2) of section 339 or section 340. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: The order of the Commissioner refusing sanction is legal and valid. [168 C] The appellant will have to establish that any land or part of a land of a zone has been dealt with in a particular manner by the Master Plan and that it is proposed to be used in a different manner. If neither of these plans provide for the particular use of any land adjoining that road is prohibited for an indefinite period, then section 14 will equally stand attracted because any user of a plot or part thereof is indicated in a Master Plan. [169 D] The reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 would naturally stand attracted if either of the Master plan or any provisions thereof are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of the proposed road, or that is so, there is no violation of either the Master plans or any provision of the development Act. [170 E] The purpose of section 14 is to enable the Commissioner, if he thinks it necessary, to give his sanction for such erection of the building or the execution of the work, and if he does not do so, he may refuse to give its sanction. If the Commissioner does not agree with the proposal, he can reject the proposal. [171 G] The provisions of sections 336 and 340 are intended to enable a person aggrieved by an order passed by him to prefer an appeal against the decision of the appellate authority. But if the order is made without any application of mind, it would be open to the Commissioner under section 337 to take action under section 339. [172 G] In the present case, the respondents ' lands were not in a manner indicated in the Master Development Plan and, therefore, there was no violation either of section 15 or of the Land Acquisition Act. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had failed to establish the existence of any such land or building in the area or zone concerned.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and Industries, Government of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant No, 2, a member of the Bar Council of India, was convicted under section 161 I.P.C., and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The appeal of the appellant No 1 was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to cross examine the prosecution witnesses and that the statements made by him in regard to the statement made by the appellant Nos. 2, 3 and 4 were inadmissible in evidence. Held, that the statement of the accused No. 2 was admissible under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and was therefore inadmissible in any evidence. The statement made to the appellant no 1 was not recorded under the provisions of section 164 Cr. P.C. and was inadmissible in law. The statements made to him were inadmissible under section 162 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, as it was not a voluntary statement made before the police authorities. The High Court erred in holding that the evidence given by the prosecution witness was admissible in evidence and could not be relied upon orally. Held further, that there was no force in the contention that the appellant had been prejudiced by any such tactics adopted by the executive authorities. Held also, that it is of the essence that public confidence in the independence of the judiciary should not be undermined by any tactics adopted or by the officers of the Government. The independence of judiciary is a priceless treasure to be cherished and safeguarded at all costs against predatory activities of this character and it is the essence of the religion that public interest confidence in independence of,the judiciary should be undermining by any methods adopted by executive authorities and became a limb of the police as it were. The Constitution has made a law relating to the administration of justice and its provisions have been enacted for the protection of the people against exploitation of the judicial system. The power of judicial review is not an absolute or unfettered power but is subject to judicial review. It is a basic principle of our constitutional jurisprudence that the judiciary must not be allowed to function in accordance with the rules of law and procedure established by law. It has also been recognised as a fundamental rule of law that the executive should not interfere with the due course of justice unless it is shown that there has been an abuse of power or that there had been violation of any principle of natural justice. The doctrine of audi alterem partem is based on the rule of audi alteram partem and it must be applied to all cases in which the rules are found to be arbitrary, reasonable and just. In the present case the appellant was a member and was charged with an offence under section 16 I. P.,C. for having taken a bribe or illegal gratification by the police officers. The conviction of the appellants No. I was therefore not sustainable.

The respondent was serving as a Police Constable. He was dismissed from service by an order dated 6th November, 1982. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant and two other constables for a declaration that he was permanently assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. The trial court decreed the suit but the first appellate court reversed it on the ground of limitation. The High Court allowed the second appeal in limine. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the other constables were convicted with him only for a short time and not for a period of six months. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules 1934 directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed, and this mandate cannot be ignored on the grounds that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. [824D] 2. The expression "other police officials" is used in Rule 16(2)(a) of Punjab Police Regulations 1934. The words "other authorities" are not defined in the said rule. They have been used to denote all persons who act as police officials and do not mean any person who acts as a police official. [825E] 2:1. In the instant case, the respondent was served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. The appellant had filed a regular second appeal before the High Court against the decree of the first Appellate court which was dismissed at the admission stage itself as the case is an old one. [826B] 2 :2. In view of the fact that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void, the High Courts should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself. [827C D] 3:3. The operation of the decree in favour of the respondent would not preclude the authority to award a minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions and the direction about the payment of the salary and other emoluments. After heat ing the learned counsel for the parties, this court is of the opinion that serious questions of law are in volved in this case and the High court should callfor the records.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea, filed its return of income under section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court in Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; and Commissioner of Incometax, Madras vs Bhuwalke Brothers Ltd., , relied on. In the present case, the transactions entered into by the assessee were mere sales of delivery orders or sales of goods so as to bring them to charge under section 4(1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that these transactions were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the appellant in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the assesee 's non speculative business. On appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no sale of goods at all and that the loss was allowable as a deduction under section 23(1)(a) of Income Tax. The High Court also relied on the decision in Commissioner of income tax vs Wadhwana, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 840, holding that the transaction involved mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods to the transferee.
