In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The explanation to section 30 of the Indian Income Tax is qualified by the first proviso which permits the set off of a loss in speculative business against the assessee 's profits and gains under any other head in that year. [184 D] Raghunath Prasad vs Commissioner Of Income tax; , followed. (2) In the instant case, there was nothing to show that the transfer of the P.D.Os was not followed up by actual delivery. The explanation is not to invalidate the transaction which were not completed by actual or constructive delivery of goods to a transferee. [185 E] Raghunathprasad Poddar vs Commis sioner of Income, tax, West Bengal, ; , referred to.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from a constituency reserved for Scheduled Castes. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice under section 123(1)(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Election Tribunal held that the respondent had committed "a corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (2) of that Act and dismissed the election petition. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the words " subscribed " in the General Clauses Act do not mean " signed " or " registered" in the general way prescribed by the Rules. The word "subscribe" is used in the sense of making a signature and the making of a mark is to be construed as meaning " signing", and it is equally clear when the Act is read as a whole along with the form in the second schedule that "subscribes" can only be used in, the sense in which the word " Subscribe" has been given to the word. The words " signed" in section 36 are not intended to convey any more than the meaning given to " sign". It is also clear from the form of a signature that " subscribed" means to write and do what is required by the Act. If the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by Rules. But if there is no signature of either a proposer or a seconder in any one of the four nomination papers, then it is not necessary that the signature should be attested. The use of the word 'subscribe ' in the context of section 36 is not decisive and the omission to record the satisfaction could only be sufficient for the purpose of satisfying itself about the genuineness of the signature.

The appellants, who were working as Labourers in the Company, were dismissed by the Company on September 19, 1972. The company sent separate communications to them asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the Company. On September 19. 1972, the appellants wrote to the Company that since "by not reporting for duty" they had confirmed their duty for not reporting on or after September 18. 1972 failing whereof their absence will be construed to be voluntary abandonment. The Company sent separate letters to the appellants and others intimating them that since the strike was called off by their union, they were no longer interested in continuing service of the company and had totally abandoned the service of its Company. The appellants filed complaints before the Labour Court under section 33(A) of the for adjudication of a dispute, 344 workmen of the appellant, who had been dismissed by it on September 26, 1972, but their absence was not explained to them. The Industrial Tribunal held that the action of the appellants in removing the names of the workers from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary and that the appellants were entitled to reinstatement with full back wages. On appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal upheld the order of the Industrial Tribunal. In the appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellants that (i) the action taken by the company in removing them from service was wholly illegal and without jurisdiction; (ii) the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the services of the respondent Company and had not voluntarily abandoned their service; and (iii) the impugned action on the part of the respondents amounted to a change in the conditions of service of their employees. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The action taken against the appellants was wholly without jurisdiction. [630E] 2.1 The action of removal of the names from the rolls of respondent Company was clearly illegal and unjustified. The impugned action of removing the name of the workmen from its roll on the presumption that they had abandoned service was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination be construed, as voluntary relinquishment by them of the employer 's service. [613B C] 2:2.1 In view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, the impugned actions on the basis of the said circumstance were manifestly illegal and invalid. The respondents had voluntarily terminated their services and they had not abandoned the company 's services. Therefore, their being no provision in the certified standing orders by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the services could only be in terms of the Standing Orders by virtue thereof the company would have retrenched the services. [730G] 2(a) The impugned actions were manifestly arbitrary and without any basis. The High Court was right in holding that there was no abandonment of the service on the ground of voluntary abandonment by the appellants. [625B C, F] (b) There is nothing in the surrounding circumstances or the conduct of the parties indicating an intention on their part to abandon service on their behalf. It is not necessary for the workmen to show that they were voluntarily abandoned or had voluntarily relinquished their services. The mere fact that the respondents had withdrawn their names from their rolls would not make them liable to be punished under section 25F(b) of Industrial Disputes Act. [650B C; F] 2.(a) There was no relinquishment of service on behalf of the employees. The Labour Court and the High Court were right in taking the view that there had been no abandonment.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under the decree and in an application for execution by the mortgage, the mortgaged property was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs. 89 0/ . The trustees filed a suit against the trustees for recovery of the amount due under a mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree on the ground that the appellant had failed to pay the instalment due under an earlier mortgage, and in any case, the decree was not executable. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) A judgment delivered by a Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court after due consideration of the points before it is liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the Full Bench for decision. [461 B] (ii) The Full Bench was not right in holding that a judgment delivered on a reference made on a question of law arising before it was liable to he regarded as relevant by judges of that Court on the same point. [463 C D] (iii) A Division Bench of a High Court, when exercising its jurisdiction under article 227 of the Constitution, does not act in excess of its powers under article 226 of the constitution. It is only when a Single Judge hearing a matter comes to the conclusion that a single Judge hearing it would be in error in holding otherwise. [465 D] In the present case, there was no order as to costs in this Court and in the High 'Court. The judgment of the Division Bench was binding on the appellant. [455 E F] (iv) A Full Bench hearing a case is not bound by the precedent because by following the precedent it would act contrary to section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act, and would also violate the oath of office taken by him when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution.

The respondent joined the Post and Telegraph Department as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He was promoted to the post of Telegraph Depart ment in 1954. The respondent challenged his promotion before the Central Administrative Tribunal which allowed the claim of the respondent for premature retirement under Rule 56(j) of the Liberalised Pension Rules. The High Court held that Rule 2(2) of Pension Rules could only be exercised to weed out those Government servants who have lived out their utility but there was no guide line provided in the rule to this effect. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under rule 2(1) of pension Rules can only be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. [802B] 1.2 The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitution of India and as such cannot be statutory. Para 620 of the Railway Pension Manual being executive instructions supplementing the statutory Rule 2046 has no parity with Rule 2 (2)of Pension Rules to interpret that rule. [800G H] 1(a). The memorandum is in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1 ) of the Constitu tion and as Such cannot be Statutory. Para 621 of the Manual being administrative instruction supplementing Rule 2047 has no relation to Rule 2. [ 800A B] 1.(b). The Memorandum dated November 29, 1962 is in nature of administrative instructions issued by the President of lndia. Para 6 of the Pension Rules is inconsistent with it. Para 619 of the said Manual being Executive instructions supplement ing the statutory rule 2046 of the Rules should be treated as supplementary to Rule 2045 of the rules. [702C D] 1 (c). The letter dated November 28, 1962 issued by Ministry of Home Affairs contained a provision that the Government has decided to retire an officer who has completed 30 years qualifying service and has not attained the age of 55 years. This will be in addition to the provisions already contained in Rule 2 of Pension rules to the effect that the power can only he exer cise of its executive powers under Article 73 of the constitution should be given due effect since there is no statutory provision or a rule framed under the proviso to Article 309. [781F G] 1:3 The memorandum issued by Minis lary in the names of President, India as well as the State Government on November 30. 1962 and April 8, 1964 are not statutory rules. They are merely administrative instructions supplement menting the Statutory Rule 2044. There is thus no legal or equitable ground to interfer with the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court and hold that Rule 20 46 having been framed under Article 310 of the Con stitution and being a compendious rule, the Railway employees are only g over 800 out those government servants who had lived out Their utility but they have lived their utility. [780C D; 803A B C] 1 :4 The memorandum in the instant case is in terms of executive instruction issued in favour of President as required by Article 77 (1) and (k) of Rule 2946 of Pension Rule to say that the Railway Servants who have worked out their useful utility but has not completed 30/ years qualifying serv ice, will normally be exercised loed out Those Government servants whose utility is only 51 and has completed thirty years of qualifying service. Any Government servant who has complete 30 years of service may be retired at any time after he has attained the 58 years of age. [783C D].

The assessee firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu, which was a registered firm carrying out the business of manufacturing and selling kateco, filed its return for the assessment year 1944 41 under the Excess Profits Tax Act 1940. The assessee claimed that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable accounting period from 1st April, 1941 to 31st March, 1943 should be allowed a set off in computing the excess profits for the chargeable chargeable accounting periods ending 31st December, 1940 to 31 st March, 1942 and 23rd November, 1942 to 31th March, 1944. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to a setoff only for the deficiency of profits during the chargeable period ending 31 st3, 1941 and 23th November, 1943 to 31rd March, 1941. In further appeal, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that as provided in the Act, the provisions of the Act would apply to every business of which any part of profits was made during the relevant accounting period ending on 31st 3, 1942, and as such there could be no deficiency of profit. The High Court held that since the chargeable account ing periods ending March 31st, 1941, 31st and 31st of March, 1940 were occupied with manufacturing activity alone and there were no sales, therefore, no part of the profits realised upon the sales from 30th May, 1941 could be attributed to the manufacturing activity between 28th OCtober, 1940 and 23nd November, 1944 and that such profits were not assessa ble to excess profits tax under the third proviso to section 5 of the Indian Income Tax Act. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The method of computation under section 7 of the Excess Profit Tax Act, 1940 must be on the basis of account of 'accounting period ' and after that the deficit in profits for that period should be computed on that basis and after set off carried forward to be set off during the accounting period commencing 31st3, 1942. [608C D] 2. The principle of apportionment of profits to which it had adverted to, the profits earned upon sales effected during the assessment period ending March 1, 1943 must similarly be apportioned between the manufacturing activities at Raichur and accused or arose at Raichur. Such profits were neither assessa ny for the relevant chargeable accounting year ending 31th December, 1941 nor could such profits be apportioned to those chargeable accounting years. [625E] 3. The fact that the chargeable accounts period ending April 31st 1943 and 31rd October, 1944 were occupied by manufacturing activity did not make any difference in the computation of the excess profit for the purposes of section 7. [650B C] 4. The liability to pay tax under third proviso of section 5 is on the accrual basis of ' account ing period '. The chargeable accounting date is the period from January 1, 1944 to 31.3.1944 and the deficiency or profits worked out on that date in respect of the chargeable assessment period commencing March 31, 1941 must be set Offi cially determined on that footing. [600D] 5. The expression "accounting year" in section 4(1) of the Income Tax is used to denote a particular accounting period and not to include any particular accounting year. It is only when the assessee has made an estimate of his income during that period that he can be assessed to tax under that proviso. [700E] 6. The word "account" in the second proviso to Section 5 of Income Tax, Act, 1922 must mean a particular assessment year and not a particular one. [701B C]. 7. The words "accounts year" occurring in section 3(1)(a) of Income tax Act, 1961 are wide enough to include all cases where there is no account of any excess profits during those periods. [643D] 8. The concept of "account '

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for the posts of Mechanical Engineering and Mechanical Engineering in Civil Engineering. The applicants were interviewed by a common selection committee and they were selected. The candidates who had qualified in Civil engineering and Mechanical Engineers 'C.A., were called for interview. The Selection Committee recommended two names, namely, (i) those who had appeared in the written test and (ii) those whose names did not find place in the final list prepared by the Public Service Com mission. The Government accepted the recommendations of the KPSC and appointed a common rank list. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the selection and the method of selection. The learned Single Judge allowed the Writ Petitions holding that the applicants who had been qualified in civil Engineering 'C ' and Mechanical engineering degrees could not rationally be included in a common list after interview held by it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i). the expression "the common list prepared" in clause (a) of sub section (1) of Section 3 of the Kerala Public Services Commission Act, 1961 should be deleted; and (2) the word "select list" occurring in clause(b) of subsection (1), should be given a wider meaning so as to include all cases where the selection has been made by an interview. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "seat List prepared by Public Service commission should be omitted. [748B] 2. The word "relect list ' occurring in sub section(1) should be interpreted in a broad and liberal sense so as not to include cases where there is no common list. In the instant case, the appellants were called upon to appear in the interview held on the basis of their examination already conducted. They had also participated in the viva voce test. The KP SC prepared the two rank lists for Engineering (Civil) containing names of 152 candidates and the other (Mechanical). The rank list for Engineering was prepared by a Public Service Commissioner. Therefore, the appellant will be entitled to a post if he has exercised his option in terms of this Court 's order and he is high enough in the common list for claiming the post. [750C D] 3. The Kerala Public service Commission is directed to prepare two separate rank lists one for Civil Judges and another for Mechanical Engineering graduates on the strength of examination already held. The rank lists prepared by it should be expunged.

The appellant filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and valuing at Rs.50,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on the ground that the correct value of the suit was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the suit is governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act and the plaintiff has the absolute right to put on the plaint any value he wishes to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under valued at Rs,50 only. (2) the valuation put by the plaintiff appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable; (3) the court is bound to accept that ' made on behalf Of the plaintiff before the Income tax department mentioned In paragraph 19 of the Plaint that it could be tentatively valued at RS.50 only; (4) the Court is bound not to accept the valuation given by the defendant before the income tax department, but it should have rejected the plaint in the light of the decision of this Court in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849 and (5) the plaintiff cannot arbitrarily and unreasonably under value under the relief claimed in the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit is covered for the purposes of court fee by section7(iv) of Court Fees act, 1870. [501B] 2.1 In a suit to set aside an valuation put on a plaint, the plaintiff must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate". It is true that in a suit of accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. [511E F] 2(a) The plaintiff cannot be arbitrarily and deliberately made on his behalf before the court and has no jurisdiction to examine the matter. It is well settled that in order to decide whether a valuation put in by the party is reasonable or not, it must be shown that the valuation is arbitrary or unreasonable. [601D] (b) The Court may reject such valuation if it is patently arbitrary or capricious. But it should bear in mind that the court has no power to reject such a valuation. In such a case it is not only open to the court but its duty to reject any such valuation. [ 511E F;511G] (c) It is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the litigation. The plaintiff, however, has not been given the absolute rights or option to place some valuation whatever upon such relief. [51F G] 2.(a) In a case where the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of a suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII Rule 11 of Civil Procedure Code.

The respondent assessee was a manufacturer of "traditional industries" which were set up in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The State Government issued a notification under section 12(1)(i) of the M.P. General Sales Tax Act, 1958 exempting certain class of dealers from payment of tax. The appellant company filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notifications and the High Courts dismissed the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the exemption granted by the notification in respect of the industries run by them were "trainedditional industries", they could not travel beyond the terms of the notification; that the exemption under section had to be given only prospective operation and not retrospectively, that the Director of Industries should have granted them a certificate (a) that the company was entitled to the exemption and (b) that he has not opted for the scheme of deferring the payment of sales tax under the rules framed for the purpose. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The notification in question does not set out the conditions on which, and the procedure in accordance with which the Director or Industries is to issue the eligibility certificate. [657D] 1.2 The exemption granted under section 17 of the Act is prospective only. It cannot be extended retrospectively. The exemption has been given retrospective effect from the date it was issued. [625E] 2.1 In view of this interpretation, the assessee claimed that they are eligible for the exemption. The notification does not state the conditions which require that the manufacturer should grant a certificate. All the conditions for exemption have incorporated the requirement of an eligibil ing certificate in accordance by which the Directorate of Industries is required to do. [650B] 2(a) The State has to satisfy itself that those condi tions are fulfilled; he cannot travel beyond its terms. [600C D] (b). The State can not be allowed to invoke the doctrine of promissory estoppel. [599D] (c) The exemption is prospective in operation and it can be prospective only prospectively.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were direct recruits to the Delhi Judicial Service. The High Court of Delhi by its judgment dated August 13, 1981 allowed the Writ Petitions and directed that the seniority of the promotees vis a vis the promotees should be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits had been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the service or substantive vacancies to which they were appointed in accordance with the qualifications laid down under Rule 7(a) and if they were not so appointed, by promotion from amongst the members of the Delhi judicial Service. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the seniority list prepared by the High Court was not based upon any rules framed under Article 309 of the Constitution; (ii) the Rules did not provide for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits and promotees who were appointed as temporary posts in the Service, while under Rule 17 they were recruited to substantive vacancies in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service; (iii) the appointments made by the Full Court of the High Courts and the promotees who are appointed in consultation with the High court from amongst members of Delhi Judicial Services who had not completed less than ten years of service in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the Punjab Judicial Service is appointed in substantive capacity to a temporary post of Additional District & Sessions Judge, cannot be said to be an exception to the quota rule; (iv) the rules do not provide that the first vacancy should be filled by direct recruitment and if there are no vacancies in any cadre then by promotion, the second vacancy should also be filled up by direct recruits. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The seniority list of promotees prepared by High Court is not based on any rules or regulations framed under article 309 of Constitution. [395B] 2.1 Rule 7 of the Rules does not say that a direct recruitment shall be made only in consultation between the High and the Union Public Service Commission. It does not contemplate that the appointment should be made by promotion. The Rules do not contemplate any such consultation with UPSC. [397C D] 2(a). In the instant case, the seniority lists prepared by this Court are not based either on rules or Regulations framed under the Article 309. [398D E] (b) Rule 7 is read with rule 8(2) and in the manner contended by the respondents it may be appropriate to note on the question whether the petitioners were appointed regularly that all the promotees were appointed to temporary posts of Additional Distt & Sessions Judges on the recommendation of the Full court of the said High Court and appointments were made on merit cum seniority basis so much so that persons found not fit for promotion are ignored as in the case of Shri C.D. Singh. [399E] (c) Rule 8(1) provides for recruitment to the service, read with Rule 16(2), which provides that temporary posts shall be filled in consultation and with High Court from amongst persons belonging to the same Service. Rule 16 deals with the appointment by promotion on the basis of seniority cum merit. The first proviso to rule 7(b) provides that if a direct recruits is appointed on the recommendations of the Supreme Court, from amongst those members of service who are recruited in consultation or with High Courts from amongst them, the quota contained in the proviso to Rule 7 must inevitably break down when such appointments are made. [396E G] (d) The seniority lists of promotees and promotees prepared under Rule 16 are not binding on the Union Government. [394B C] (e) Rule 6(a), which requires that temporary appointments shall be by promotion in consultation, does not require that the direct recruits should have been appointed regularly. It is only when a direct recruited is appointed to substantive posts of the service that the quota prescribed for both the categories by Rule 16 and Rule 17 is read together that the promotees are appointed on probation.

The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee to income tax as "the income of the family of which he was a member". The Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment on the ground that the income belonged to the Hindu Undivided Family of which the assessee was a partner. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the business was carried on by an association of persons and the income from the business had been brought to tax on that footing. The High Court in reference set aside this order. In appeals to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Income tax officer was not competent to assess the members individually as a " association of individuals" and that the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner was wrong in holding that the assessee could not be assessed personally in respect of the income. HELD: The appeal must be allowed. (i) The Income tax Act, 1922, is a piece of social legislation enacted for the benefit of the people of the country. It is a welfare State which has to act with care and caution. It does not provide for any machinery for enforcing it. It merely provides for certain matters which are incidental or ancillary to its objects. It also provides for the making of rules relating to income. The Income Tax Act, 1961, is an Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to the levy of income tax on income. [392 E] (ii) The power of the Appellate Tribunal to make a reference under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax is not confined only to the assessment of income but also to the income of a Hindu undivided family. It has no power to make an order of reference under that section. [391 G H] Commissioner of Income tax, U.P. vs Parshad, ; , followed. (iii) The Appellate Tribunal was wrong when it set aside an order made in a reference and directed that the case be remanded to the Income Tax Officer for making a fresh assessment after setting aside the direction of the Assistant Commissioner.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share in the property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the valuation made by the appellant was correct and that the proper court fee should be paid on the memorandum of appeal. On appeal to this Court, Held, that the memorandum was not strictly applicable to the case as it did not attract the provisions of article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act. The suit was therefore rightly valued for purposes of court fees under section 7(iv)(b) of the Madras Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1947, and the proper Court fee paid on such memorandum of appeals should be taken to be the valuation even for the purposes of jurisdiction. Held further, that in respect of suits falling under section 8(iv), a departure has been made and liberty has been given to the plaintiff to amend his plaint and set out the amount at which he seeks to claim his value for the purpose of court fee and it provides for the determination of the value for purposes Of court fees. The valuation thus made by him in respect Of the relief of partition is ordinarily accepted by the Court in computing the court fees payable in respect thereof. It really means that in suits falling tinder section 7 (iv)(a) or under section7(v) of Act, the plaintiff should first value his claim for partition and it provided for the valuation also for the payment of court Fees not only on the plaint but also on the amended plaint. The Court fee payable on such a memorandum ofappeal is to be taken as the valuation for the trial of the relief sought by him for the pur pose of court Fee and it is on this valuation alone that the appellant can be legitimately called upon to pay court fees both on the original side of the High Madras High Court prior to 1953 there was no need to make any jurisdictional valuation.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought to challenge the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1989, by which it had decided that "Refuge areas" shall be provided on the external walls as a better and more reliable fire safety measure than those envisaged by the bye laws 16.4.1. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the decision was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (a) Bye law 16.8.1 is in addition to the requirements of bye laws 17.1 and 16.3.1; (b) Bye laws 164.8 are not inflexible and that in appropriate cases where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety measures than those contemplated by the Bye laws, 16.5.1, the NDMC would not be precluded from accepting them; (c) Byelaw 16.7.1 was an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the respondent NDMC to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire safety in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure; (d) Bye rules 16.2 are not mandatory, and that the clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 17.3 is an additional requirement and not as a limitation upon the power to the NDMC to meet itself that such a measure would better promote fire safety; (e) Bye bye laws 15.4 is in derogation of the bye law 16 4.1 which provides for the pedestrian walk way and Podium, and (f) Bye regulations 17.2 is an extra internal wall for purposes of the said bye law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The clearance from Chief Fire officer envisaged by bye law 171 is an addition to requirements of Bye laws 171. [608D] 2.1 The clearance of the plans submitted by the appellant on the condi tion that they file a written undertaking before the NDMC that the construction would be at the risk of the Respond ent 1 and 2, it would not progress beyond a height of 15 metres and in the event of an ultimate rejection of the plan, they would have no claim against the NDMC for any loss occasioned to respondent 1 and2. [613E] 2(a) The clearance is not a condition precedent to the exercise of the power by the NDMC under bye law No. 16.1 of the Bye law. [706F] (b). The clearance has been given in accordancewith Bye laws No.16.4, and the lack of a provision for the retrieval of the building and rescue operations are rendered possible. [625G H] 2.(a) In the context of specific objectives of bye law 15.1 it is an ad hoc condition and cannot be equated with a limitation imposed on the right of the re spondent NDMC to carry out its statutory obligations under Bye laws. The only way in which, perhaps, the zonal requirements in this behalf and the difficulties inherent in insisting upon construction of such pedestrian way in an isolated case could be reconciled is to direct the NDMC, in the eventuality of its proving the plans otherwise, to keep the requirement of the pedestri walk way. [650B C] (c). The only course in which the zonal development requirements in the instant case were satisfied was to direct that the constructions would be made at the expense of the respond ents 1 and 3.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for partition of his joint family property. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, Held, that the cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit was barred under Order II, rule 2(3), C.P.C., and the appellant was bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree upon it. The cause of actions in both the suits being identical and separate, the cause in both suits being different from the cause Of action in one suit, the same having been separately and distinct, the subsequent suit being barred under order II, r. 2(1), CP. C., was not barred by res judicata or by Order II of rule 2, C. P.C. Held, further, that there was no bar to the application of Order II Rule 2, Civil Procedure Code, as it stood prior to its amendment in 1945, and the cause which had been sought in the earlier suit was different from that of the previous suit. The suit having been filed after the coming into force of the new Act, the appellant could not be said to have abandoned his claim to account for the subsequent period. The fact that the parties did not care to ask that accounts of the motor business or indeed of all other businesses were to be taken up after the 1st April, 1946, and he was anxious to run the liquor business exclusively and not jointly or in partnership with his brothers after the 31st March, 1946.

The appellant was employed by the respondent company as a servant of the Salt Works. The Company carried on the business of manufacturing salt and supplying it to its customers. It entered into an agreement with the Company for the supply of salt to its consumers. Under the terms of the agreement, the Company had to supply salt to the consumers at their own cost. The appellant was also required to pay a certain sum as compensation for the use of salt. The company paid the amount to the respondent and the respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 92 Of the Indian Factories Act, 1948, on the ground that the salt works were not "manufacturing process" within the meaning of the expression in cl. (k) of section 2 of the Act read with r. 6 of the Rules framed thereunder. The trial court acquitted the respondent but convicted him under section 96 Of the Act and sentenced him to pay certain sums of money as compensation. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, Held, that the process of converting water into salt was carried on in the open air and not in building. The word " factory" is used in a general sense in contradistinction to "manufacturer". It is well settled that the word "premises" in section 2(m) means "premises", and it includes premises which are used for the purpose of business or trade, but does not include premises which have been used for any other purpose. The words "premises " and " things used in the Act do not mean "premises". The word 'premises " is generally used in contradistinction with "premises ". It is a well settled rule of construction that where the words "and " things" are used in an Act, it must be construed according to their ordinary meaning. In re: Chinniah, Manager, Sanguap Works (2) Ltd., , referred to.

The respondent was appointed as Tailoring Instructor in the Department of Technical Education in 1935. He joined the post on November 28, 1949. In 1951 he was absorbed in that department with effect from November 28. 1949. The respondent continued to make representations to the State Government for his absorption in that Department. On January 19, 1964, the State Govern ment referred him to the Public Service Commission and by a communication dated February 2, 1960, made these recommendations in favour of the respondent. In September 1965, the respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnics and all of them except the respondent were absorbed in the department of Technical education with effectfrom November 28 1949. On December 12, 1949, he was again absorbed in another Department of technical Education with effect From November 28 1950. The State Government referred him for further action under Rule 8(1) of the Mysore Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1957. The Public Service Commis sioner by his order dated February 19,1964 ordered that the promotions of the respondents therein be given effect from the initial date of joining duty on deputation. On March 31, 1965, he filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said orders. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed that the absorption of the respond ent in the departments of Technical Educational Education should be given effective from November 1, 1949 irrespective of the dates on which they were put in charge of sub divisions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in service of the Department; and (ii) the order of the Government dated February19, 1964 directing absorption of his in the Departments of Technical Educa tion was not justified. HELD: The High court was fully justified in granting the relief. [62 G] (i)(a) The respondent 's case that he was entitled to be placed in the various departments of technical education from a particular date or to be given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in the service of Department of the Technical Education, was not supported by any principle of policy in the case of the Respondent. [63 B] (b) The order of absorption in the Depart ment of Technical Engineering with effect on November 1. 1949, could not be said to have been made in contravention of the principles of policy. [64 C D] (c) The High ' Court was fully competent in granting relief to the respondent because the order dated January 19. 1964 directed that promotions of all the respondents should be granted effective from October 1, 1959 irrespective of whether they were actually working as Tailors or not. [66 E F] (d) The State Govern ments had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department for Technical Education from another department and he stayed on that other department for a reasonable long time, his absorption should be made relate back to the date on which he was initially sent". There was no justification whatever to depart from this principle of Policy in the present case.

The petitioner, a foreign parent, was married to the respondent on May 15, 1982. The petitioner filed an application for being appointed guardian of a child in the court of the Children Welfare Court under section 14(1) of the . The petitioner contended that the respondent had no locus standi to file the petition and that the petition should be dismissed. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent was not entitled to file an application under section 15(2) of 'the Act for appointment as guardian of the child in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [842C] 2.1 The petitioner has a right to move the Court for relief by way of appropriate writ or direction for appointment of a foreigner as guardian unless it is satisfied that the application of the foreigner for adopting a child has been sponsored by such social or child welfare agency. [884F G] 2:2. In the instant case, the petitioner had no right to file any application under Section 15(1). The respondent had not filed any application before the Court seeking appointment as the guardian of her child in terms of section 14 (1) and (2). The petitioner was not a foreigner within the meaning of section 2(d) of . [844E F] 3:3. In view of the fact that the petitioner has been residing in India for more than two years, it would be appropriate to appoint an advocate as guardian for the child. [864G H] 4:4. The Court is not concerned with the question whether the petitioner is a foreigner or not. It is only concerned with whether the person who is alleged to have taken a child under its care would have the child report, but it will be in the interest of the minor child to be taken in adoption by the foreigner according to the law of his country within a period not exceeding two years and as soon as the adoption is effected, it will send two certified copies of the adoption order to the social or family welfare agency in India through which the application for guardianship is processed so that one copy can be filed in court and the other can remain with the social/or family welfare agencies if it desires such child to he given in inter country adoption. [863G H, 844A] 5:5. The Indian Council of Social Welfare of the Indian Council should, with the assistance of the Government of India, send two copies of each of the application to the recognised social or economic agency in a foreign country for intercountry adoptions, and if the Indian family wants to see the child study report in respect of any particular child, child study reports must also be made available to the Indian Family welfare agency if it desire such child. The recognised social welfare agency should, on receiving an application from a foreigner for adoption through a licensed or recognised social child or welfare agency, send one copy of the same to the appropriate department of the government of each foreign country where the Indian children are ordinarily taken in adopt. [862B C] 6:6. The guidelines laid down by this Court in the case of "State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar and Ors., ; , are not applicable to the present case. In that case, it is not necessary that there should be only one social or welfare agent in India who has taken a son in adoption. If the parents are known, every effort must be made by the recognised Social or economic welfare agency to find placement for the children by adoption in an Indian family. [861D] 7:7. The State of West Benares vs Anwar Begum and Ors. ; , referred to.

The appellant, Indian Cable Company Ltd. was incorporated in the year 1964 and the workmen of the Indian Cable company Ltd., were paid bonus at 20% of the gross profits. The workmen of that company had to be paid bonus for the accounting year 1965 66. The management of the company claimed before the Tribunal that the allocable surplus should have been added back as allocable by the Company, but not the bonus payable to the employees. The Tribunal held that such a payment was not an item which could be deducted from gross profits under the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account had to he added back to arrive at the actual gross profits and deducting therefrom the prior charges under section 6 of the Act, the bonus paid for the year 1965 67 should have be added back. The company appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was not justified in allowing deduction of certain items from the gross profit for purposes of computing available surplus. [651 B] (ii) The claim made by the Unions that after distribution of bonus at20% for the years 1964 65, there must have been a surplus and it should have to be set on the next year, namely, 1965 66 was not correct. It is clear from the evidence that bonuses had been added in the profits and loss accounts as well as the available surplus and the rate at which bonus was granted could subject to scrutiny. [661 C D] (iii) The award of the Tribunal cannot be maintained even on the basis that the principle adopted by the Tribunal in respect of direct tax is found to be erroneous by this Court.

The appellant was appointed as a Commercial Tax officer in 1957. He was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on July 7, 1975 and later as Deputy Commis sioner of Commercial Tax in 1972. The enquiry revealed that the charges should be dropped. In 1969 he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in which certain adverse remarks were obtained. The Full Board of Revenue then reported that the charge should be drop. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Government retiring him from service on the ground that the enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored once he is promoted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The previous history in all these read together, read in all them read, in all its entirety, clearly and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But when there was nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, one might hark back to similar or similar entries in the past, read together in all the past read, read along with the 1969 entry. [80G H] 2. The earlier history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, should be totally ignored once the appellant is promoted and he is reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. [81A B] 3. The Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of appellant including the fact that the 1969 Entry noted that an enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against the appellant. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion a few months earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive ofeptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is impossible to sustain the order. [82C D] 4. The fact that a Government Servant should be wholly ignored once in service, once he was promoted does not mean that he has lost his utility as a Govt. servant. If the Government had come for the government servant to leave his utility and even remotely that he had outlived his utility, it would indeed odd to retire a Government serv ice. [83E F] 5. The order of November 29, 1974 of the A Government, and the effect of the entry was blotted out by the promotion of the appel lant as Deputy Inspector of Commercial taxes, and posted as member of the Madras Sales Tax Tribunal in 1969. There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of the Appellant in 1969 which was not at all favourable to him after his promo tion. The effect of this entry was that the appellant was promoted to a Selection post. [84F G] 6. The Tribunal has rightly held that the Government was not entitled to make any order of retirement.

The appellants, who were the owners of a stage carriage in Andhra Pradesh, challenged the validity of the scheme framed by the Corporation under Ch. IV A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, on the ground that it was inconsistent with section 68 C of the Act and that the scheme was not binding on them as the scheme had been framed by a competent authority. The High Court held that the schemes were valid and that there was no proof that the Transport Minister who heard the objections raised by the appellants to the schemes was influenced by the Chief Minister or acted at his behest, and therefore, the schemes which were published by the corporation could not be assailed as not in conformity with the requirements of section 68C. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the scheme in question did not originate from the Corporation, the State Transport Undertaking, but that it had been done under the direction of the Chief Secretary or by utilising the machinery of the Corporation as alleged by the appellant; and (ii) the schemes framed were fully approved and were fully in conformity. HELD: (i). The scheme was framed by an authority not competent to issue a permit by reason of section 63 C of Act. [368 D] (ii). The provisions of Ch. V A of Motor Vehicles Rules, 1939 are similar to those of Chs. IV B of the , and the rules made thereunder are to have effect notwithstanding anything in Ch. VI A of that Chapter or any other law for the time being in force. [369 C] (iii) The scheme framed under Chs IV A is not inconsistent with the provisions of section 69 C of . It is only when the scheme is approved by the State Government and implemented by it, that an authority may be deprived of the power to issue such a permit. But where as in Andhra pradesh there is no Regional Transport Authority at all, it cannot accede to the submission that such authority is deprived of its power to grant permits under Ch, IV A.

The appellant was a public limited company registered under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The question for decision in this appeal was whether under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940, furnishing of the declaration forms duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it, the appellant was not able to furnish the duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. Held, that the proviso to section 5 (2)(b) of tho Bengal Finance Act, 1939, is self evident and must be read along with the proviso. The object of section 5 is to prevent fraud and facilitate administrative efficiency and facilitating administrative efficiency. It is not necessary that the declaration form should contain a prescribed declaration in the manner prescribed by the section. That section provides for exemption from tax on certain sales to dealers if the sales are made to registered dealer for the purposes mentioned therein. The proviso to the said sub clause does not impose a condition on a dealer claiming exemption. Section 5(1)(a) of Act, however, imposes a condition upon a dealer for claiming exemption thereunder. It does not contemplate that the prescribed declaration forms must be furnished well and good; but if not, other evidence can be produced. The conditions imposed by section 5 are self evident. Therefore, presumably to achieve the twofold object, namely prevention of fraud and facilitating ' administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration in prescribed form in the prescribed manner under the section; but, if not furnished, other material evidence can he produced.

The petitioners were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. They challenged their conviction before the High Court on the ground that they had been falsely implicated in the case by the police officers who had investigated the case, and that the police had not taken any steps to arrest them. The High Court dismissed their writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the proviso to section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was mandatory and that no objection was raised to such lawyer on his behalf and if any application for bail was made, the Magistrates should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad guidelines set out by this Court in its judgment dated 12th February, 1979; (2) the State Government should provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application to the Magistrate in that behalf and (3) the Magistrate had not given any opportunity to the petitioners to make their representation. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to sub section (2), of section 167 of the Criminal Procedure Code is mandatory and it is the constitutional obligation of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trial to the accused. [528 B] 2. The State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trials and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. Supp. 1.2 The State Government is under an constitutional mandate, to ensure expeditious trial to all prisoners who are languishing in jail for long periods of time and it was not possible for us to examine the individual cases of these courts as on 31st December, 1978 and where such cases have been pending investigation by the Police in each sub division of the state as on 1st December 1978 and if no application for grant of bail is made,the Magistrates should disposed of the said cases as expeditiously as possible. [525 C D] 3. The petitioners are under a legal obligation to ensure that speedy trial is not unduly delayed. They are entitled to be released on bail in accordance therewith.

The appellant was the landlord and the respondent a protected tenant. The respondent filed an application under section 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar rejected the application on the ground that the notice had been given before the Amending Act came into force. The appellant 's appeal was dismissed by the Revenue Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 34(1) gave a right to the landlord to terminate the tenancy by one year 's notice which was given in December 1951 before the amending Act came in force, and therefore the notice having been given after the Amending act came into operation, the further limitation put on the right of the landlord by subs. (2 A) to terminate a tenancy by two years ' notice which is given in this case in December, 1951 before that Act came to be passed was not applicable to notices given before that date. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the amendment did not affect notices already given before it came into effect and the right to obtain possession had accrued to the respondent after the coming into force of the Amending Acts. The notice under section 34 (1) is merely a declaration to the tenant of the premises to terminate tenancy and this restriction would come into play on the day on which the tenancy actually terminates in consequence of the notice given to terminate it, and no further proceedings may be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof It is only when the period of notice has expired and the tenancy has terminated that the landlord acquires a vested right to obtained possession of land. The date on which a tenancy stands terminated by the notice will have to be taken into consideration in determining the right Of the landlord arising out of the termination of the tenancy, but it is always open to the court not to carry out his intention.

The petitioners were the sons of Khadim Ali who had never been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October 1, 1950. They filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order made by the Custodian on January 10, 1952, declaring two houses to be evacuee property. The petitioners contended that they were evacuees and their properties being the two houses in dispute, to be evacueees and the houses vested in the Custodian under section 8 of the Act and they took various steps to protect their rights but were unsuccessful. Held, that the orders made by Custodian on February 10, 1951, were without jurisdiction so far as the female petitioners were concerned and their interest could not in any way affect them. The acts of the Custodian in so faras he deprived the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. The order of January 10 was without jurisdiction as to the right of the evacueees to take possession of the houses. Held further, that there was no judicial determination by the custodian General of any fact affecting the rights of an evacuee which the petitioners could not have vested in him. The orders made under section 7 were therefore without jurisdiction and were rightly quashed. The Custodian General had no jurisdiction to make the order. The powers conferred on the Custodian by section 8 were not a judicial one and must be exercised in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held also, further,that the orders passed by the authorities under section 6 of the , were quasi judicial decisions and could not be challenged as being purely administrative or judicial.

The assessee company entered into a joint venture for distributing the net profits, after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses to the extent of 50% of the loss incurred by it from its remuneration. The assessee Company 's case was that the two amounts mentioned above were in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents after being satisfied about their respective shares and that therefore the amount paid to them could not be claimed by the assessee company as a deduction under section 191(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the agreement amounted to a joint contract resulting in division of net profits and therefore the amounts paid to agents were deemed expenses incurred by the Company in order to earn profits and would, therefore, fall within the ambit of section 10(2) (xv). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that there being an express provisions in the contract by which agents agreed not to share loss or profits but to prevent the assessee from distributing part of its clear profit if it is found that 'clear profits are in excess of the reasonable return as contemplated under the Act. HELD: The High court had exceeded its jurisdiction in travelling beyond the agreed statement of the case framed by the Tribunal and had relied on certain materials which were not at all found by the tribunal in its order nor those materials were at all considered by the High Court. [189 E] In the present case, there being no express provision either in the agreements or in the terms set out in the statement of case that there was positive proof of the fact that the transaction amounted to joint venture with a view to division of profits and, therefore the contract of agency is really a sort of a partner ship and has been given the cloak and colour of an agency to conceal the real intent and commercial purpose. The commercial venture is not one which is carried on by the company in its ordinary course of business. It is only when the company makes profit or gains that it can be said that there is a very thin line of distinction between a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits divisible.

The assessee, a company, was carrying on business in the manufacture of textiles. The Income Tax Officer treated the accumulated profits as income from business and computed the taxable income under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the claim of the assessee that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not be construed as including current profits for the purpose of section 2A(6 A)(e). The Tribunal held that the accumulated profit would not include current profits, but it rejected the contention that the two sums of Rs. 18950 constituted accumulated profits for purposes of section2(6AA)(e), and therefore the second question referred to the High Court was: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of this case, the Appellate Tribunal was legally correct in holding that the amounts earned by the company during the year in which loans were advanced to the assessee, that is to say the current profits could be regarded as included within the accumulated income of the company". The High Court answered the first question in favour of the Revenue. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words 'accumulation profits" occurring in section2 (6 A) (a) could only mean profits which had accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the business; (ii) the expression "accompulated profits", in that clause must mean profits actually earned by a company during its accounting year, while revenue profits would mean profits of a business; and (iii) the word 'accompanied profits" could not have been used as including the current profit. HELD: The High court was right in holding on the second point that the expression 'accumsulated profits ' in section 3(6B)(e)(i) could be understood to mean profits earned by an assessee during its business, while the revenue profits and gain were being taxed, while tax profits would be income of a particular year. [951 B C] Commissioner of Income Tax, Madras II vs M. Badiani, , followed.

The plaintiff was the absolute owner of certain lands in the State of West Bengal. The defendants claimed to be tenants under a Lakheraj grant and were granted permanent settlement of the zamindari of Burdwan. In 1931, the Maharaja of Burdwan granted those lands by way of rent free from all encumbrances. The plaintiff claimed that the lands were not Mal lands within the Zamindari of Burdwan but had been granted as Lakhearaj grant in 1936. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the District judge held that the defendants were entitled to fair rent and that the claim was barred by limitation. The High Court on a reference made at the instance of the plaintiff held that as there had been no determination of tenancy, no decree could be passed but that the plaintiff was entitled to assess fair and equitable rent on the holdings in their possession. On further appeal, Held, that the grant to the predecessors of the defendants was not shown to relate to the suit lands. The question whether a presumption should be made in favour of the correctness of the entry, because it was made in the ordinary course of business, and that it was sufficient to sustain a presumption of lost grant could be made by prescription. Held further, that on the facts found, no presumption of a lost grant can be made. The suit properties formed part of the Mal or assessed lands of the estate. The grant to those predecessors of defendants must have been made by the Maharaja in favour Of the predecessors in title of the plaintiffs and that they were not tenants within the Mal lands. Held, further, on the evidence, that there was no proof that the defendant claimed to hold under a jeraj grant in 1937 that the possession was referable to a grant by the owner entitled to the land. The mere fact that the predecessors had been in posses sion of the lands for a long time without payment of rent did not make the subject of an issue and there was nothing on record to show that the plaintiffs were tenants within Mal lands or assessed to revenue.

The appellant plaintiff entered into a contract with the respondent for sale of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas bearing Survey No. 25 situated in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon, Maharashtra State for a consideration of Rs. 42,000/ out of which Rs. 5,000 were paid as earnest money and a further amount of Rs 5,500/ was paid as an earnest money. The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of the contract on 15th December 1965 for sale and possession of land. The respondent denied that he had any right to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Tenancy Act. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was an agriculturist and, therefore, ineligible to purchase it under section 85A of the Transfer of Property Act. On appeal the High Court held that the jurisdiction of Civil Court to decide the issue arose out of a suit filed for specific relief of specific performance and not in respect of a claim for specific property. In this appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant plaintiff that the civil court had no jurisdiction to decide an issue arising in a suit relating to contract for sale or purchase of agricultural land governed by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939; that the Civil Court had no Jurisdiction to decide such issues and that the High Courts were not justified in holding that it was an incidental issue in a proceeding under the Tenancy Acts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The civil court would be competent to entertain the suit. If there is an issue which has to be settled, decided or dealt with by the competent authority under the Bombay Act, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arises in the context of the provisions contained in section 85 and the Civil Courts will have to refer the issue under section 86A for reference of the competent authorities under the tenancy Act. [592D E] 2.1 The civil Court would be incompetent to decide or deal with the same. If a civil court has jurisdiction to entertain an issue, which is required to be decided or disposed of by the authority under this Act, it will have no jurisdiction in the Civil court to decide it and deal with it. [593E] 2:2 The civil courts would be empowered to settle, decide or dealt all issues arising under the Rent Act. If the civil Court has jurisdiction, it is incumbent upon the Civil Judge to refer such issue to the competent Authority under the Ceiling Act. But if there is a dispute and consequent contest an issue in which is require ing to be determined, decided and dealt with under the provisions Tenancy Act is not excluded, the civil courts will have jurisdiction to deal with such issues. [594B] 3:3 The Civil Court would have jurisdiction, to decide and deal all the issues arising in the suit properly constituted civil court having jurisdiction to try it.

The assessee company was incorporated in the Indian Textile Machinery Corporation (I.T.C.) and it had its own business of manufacturing and selling textile products. The assessee company carried on the business of manufacture and sale of textiles. It also used to manufacture and sell textile products, which were being manufactured by the reconstruction of the assessee 's business already in existence. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the two industrial undertakings, namely, the Steel Foundry and the Jute Mill Division, were formed by the amalgamation of the former concern with the Cement Foundry Division, and that the latter concern was an industrial undertaking to which section 15C of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 applied. The Appellate Tribunal held that these two undertakings were not entitled to exemption under section 15 C(2) (i) of the Income tax Act, 1961. On reference, the High Court answered both the questions in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were right in holding that the Steel Plant set up by the assessee company is an industrial Undertaking to which Section 15C(2)(i) applies to any industrial undertaking which (i ) is not formed by splitting up, or the reconstruction, of business already existing and hence the assessee was not entitled (ii) to exemption u/s 15C. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The two undertakings are independent and distinct from each other producing arti cles which may be of aid to the principal business but yet the undertakings are distinct and not reconstruction out of the existing business of the asses see. [776B] 2. The fact that the articles produced by the two undertakings arc used by the Boiler Division of the assesses will not weigh holding that these are new and separate undertakings. Use of the articles by theassessee is not decisive to deny the benefit of section 15c. [771C D] 3. The question whether the two units are distinct or not has to be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The appellants filed a suit in the Subordinate Judge, Madurai under the proviso to section 44 B(2)(d)(ii) asking for a decree declaring that the inam grants consisted of melwaram only. The District judge held that the inams were personal inams burdened with services and the order of resumption was illegal and a nullity. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The appellants claimed to be permanent alienees of the inam lands adversely to the inamdars or the Government under whom the inamdar held the inam land. They contended that the Inam grants consisted only of melaram and the inams in the present case were resumable under section 44B(2) (a)(i). The appellants relied on the decision in Roman Catholic Mission vs State of Madras, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, to contend that the alienation was within the purview of section 44 C.P.C., and that the appellants were not entitled to resume the inam. (ii)The High Court was right in holding that the grant was not within the scope of section 4B(1)(a)(ii). The question whether an alienee from the inam granted a permanent lease and the Inam lands were resusable under s 44 B, was not raised before the revenue authorities or in the plaint or before the District Judge or in appeal either before the Revenue authorities or the District judge. (iii)The appellants ' claim to be resumables under section 4 B(1) (b)(i) is not barred by limitation. The appellants had claimed to have been permanent alienee of the lands under a grant from the Inamdars on the footing that the Inams were resinable under Section 44 B. Held, further, that the High Court erred in holding, that there was no limitation barring imposition of assessment on the inam after resuming the melwarar rights in the inam villages. The inams were granted to office holders as remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within the provisions of section 43B(3)(i), and therefore, they could not resume the Inam land under section 42 B(4)(ii); but there can be no doubt that section 44 A (2) is applicable if the holder of the inams has made an exchange, gift or sale of the Inam. The inam lands were granted by the Government to office holder as remuneration and were in fact resumble under section 43 B(3). The grant was for services rendered by the inam holders to be performed by them. The Inam grants were not adverse to the Government and thereby defeat the latter 's right to resume inam lands against the Government.

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The Municipality levied a house tax on the basis of gross annual letting value at the rate of 7% of its gross annual rent for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The appellant Corporation challenged the levy on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the gross annual let value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs or on any account whatsoever. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Corporation was entitled to levy the house tax at 7% and that the rate was not bound to deduct 10% allowance provided by sec. 2(c) and therefore the rate could only apply if the tax was assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions of section 73 of the Act. HELD: The saving and the deeming provisions in section 2(C) can only apply when the tax is assessed in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the old Act and has to be adjusted in the light of the provisions contained therein. [131 D] The saving provision in section 1(c), therefore, cannot be said to have been made under the 1958 Act. [132 E F] The Corporation was not entitled to demand the tax assessed on its gross letting value as also for the amount of tax leviable on the buildings or lands or both in any official year in which such list is in force. [133 G] The Municipal tax is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the strength of which the list is prepared for each such official year. If it were otherwise, the annual letting values or the amount assessed thereon for each official year would be impaired by section 73. Therefore to the extent that it was inconsistent with sec. 73 it is neither saved nor deemed to have be made under tho 1954 Act. The saving provisions in s.2(c). are not inconsistent with section 73 and therefore to the effect that it is inconsistent with the provision of section 74 it is not inconsistent With section 73 it cannot be held that the tax imposed on the ' gross annual rental letting value was saved by secs. 2 (c) & (d).

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. The Deputy Commissioner, however, relying upon the Memorandum of Association, which allowed the assessee Company to manufacture and sell chemicals, and on the Directors report, held that the assessee company was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 1,15,259. An appeal was then filed before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal at Trivandrum, and the Tribunal held that by the sale no business was done, and that the amount obtained only by way of realisation sale and was not, therefore, liable to tax. The High Court in reference held against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the transaction of sale of raw materials along with the business, including machinery, plant and premises was a revenue sale, and (ii) the sale was not a profit within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Indian Income tax Act. HELD: The High court was right in holding that the transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business but was for the pur pose of carrying out the business and, therefore. not liable to be taxed. [966 B] Commissioner of Income tax, West Coast Chemicals and Industries Ltd., Calcutta vs The State of West Bengal, ; , followed. (2) The High 'Court was right when it held that a sale of chemicals and raw materials for match factory was nothing more than a winding up sale, not with a view to trading in chemicals and the raw materials and the price with them.
